Francesco Campanella and Fabio Riccioni extract the gravitational multipole structure of rotating objects from scattering amplitudes, in four and in higher dimensions. Multipoles describe how a body's mass and motion shape its gravitational field beyond the simplest point-mass picture. In four dimensions only mass and current moments are independent, and the authors show how the Kerr black hole's structure arises from minimally coupled spinning fields.

Extending to non-minimal couplings gives the most general rotating solution with spin-induced moments up to octupole order. In five dimensions a new infinite family of stress moments appears, and different matter fields produce qualitatively different quadrupoles, a contrast the authors trace through the stress-energy tensor.
arxiv-2605-05267:
Kaifeng He and nine co-authors systematically review quality problems in code written by large language models and trace them back to training data. Language models frequently emit defective code, from logic bugs to security holes, and data quality is one contributor among several. Earlier literature had not connected specific data issues to specific code outcomes in one synthesis.

Reviewing more than one hundred papers, the authors build taxonomies of generated-code quality dimensions and training-data issue groups. They synthesise a dozen recurring relationship families linking the two, each traced to its supporting evidence and limits. Detection and mitigation methods across the data, model, and generation stages are also gathered, with provenance flagged as an open need.
arxiv-2605-05467:
Serving many users from one set of graphics cards means juggling urgent chats against relaxed background jobs. Vikranth Srivatsa and four co-authors present Nitsum, a serving system for large language models. It treats tensor parallelism, the splitting of a model across cards, as a dial it can turn while running.

Nitsum adjusts that split, divides cards between reading and writing stages, and schedules requests together. Weight reuse and fast memory migration make the changes cheap enough to use often. On real workload traces it improved the share of requests meeting their speed targets by up to about five times.
arxiv-2605-05567:
A classifier moved to a new domain may meet classes it never saw in training. Chuan-Xian Ren, Cheng-Jun Guo, and Hong Yan tackle those private classes under extreme label shift. Older methods assume private classes look like obvious outliers, but a shared class can vary internally more than a private class differs from it.

Their score, built on local transport mass from optimal transport theory, separates shared from private samples. A full method, ReOT, then learns while keeping the two groups apart, avoiding bad matches. They prove a target-risk bound and validate the approach on benchmark experiments.
arxiv-2605-05867:
AI code generators pass functional tests while quietly shipping security holes. Ali Soltanian Fard Jahromi, Amjed Tahir, Peng Liang, and Foutse Khomh systematically investigate how to harden generated code after the fact. Their study spans fine-tuning and prompting strategies, measured against a list of common weakness types.

Earlier mitigations, from static-analysis-guided generation to prompt engineering, varied wildly in effectiveness across models and settings. The authors assess how far each strategy actually improves security, and where the improvements stop. The result is a map of which repairs are worth their cost for which models.
arxiv-2605-05967:
Davide Maran and Csaba Szepesvári sharpen error guarantees for kernelized bandit optimization when the model is misspecified. In such problems a learner picks actions and is scored against a reward function that may sit slightly outside its kernel model. Past bounds charge for that mismatch at a rate tied to kernel complexity, which can be steep.

The authors show the penalty can grow only logarithmically for a large class of kernels. Offline, a spectral constant governs the extra error, while online, a domain splitting algorithm keeps local errors from swelling globally. Their online regret bound drops an extra factor that earlier results carried. The shared idea is localization, in spectrum for one setting and in space for the other.
arxiv-2605-06067:
Maxim Fishman and four co-authors show that a normalized language model architecture is naturally suited to 4-bit training. Low precision training is critical for efficiency, but standard models need extra tricks to keep quality at such widths. The nGPT design constrains weights and hidden states to a unit sphere, which changes how signal and noise behave.

In this design, quantization noise stays uncorrelated while weak positive signal correlations build up across the hidden dimension. That yields a higher signal to noise ratio and a flatter loss landscape, with the benefit growing at larger sizes. The team validate stable end to end 4-bit training on a dense model and on hybrid mixture of experts models. No random transforms or per tensor scaling were needed.
arxiv-2605-06367:
Flavio Nicoletti and four co-authors examine how data structure and class imbalance shape the learning dynamics of diffusion models. Real datasets mix classes with different spreads and frequencies. Models usually move from generalizing to memorizing, but older theory assumes uniform data, leaving open how uneven classes change that order.

Using a random-features model trained on Gaussian mixtures, the authors derive which classes generalize or memorize first. Class variance matters most, centroid geometry second, and sampling imbalance can reverse the order or delay minority classes. Tests with U-Net models on Fashion MNIST support the predictions, warning that some classes may memorize while others stay underlearned.
arxiv-2605-06467:
Johannes S. Schmidt and five co-authors examine how topological deep learning models should be evaluated. These models work on higher-order data such as manifold triangulations, which allow operations that graphs do not. Evaluation practice has lagged, and earlier benchmark claims suggested a clear advantage for higher-order methods.

The team extends the MANTRA benchmark to more manifold types and finds both graph networks and higher-order methods can saturate it, given the right representation and features. Under a stricter protocol using varied representations and refinements, no model shows generalization beyond the data's combinatorial structure. Their protocol gives future work a firmer test for true topological understanding.
arxiv-2605-07167:
Simon Pfreundschuh and three co-authors present GPROF-IR, a neural method for estimating rainfall from a single infrared satellite channel. Merged global precipitation products blend microwave and infrared sensors, but infrared estimates are weaker and can leave artifacts. Geostationary infrared views, though, are available almost continuously across much of the globe.

A convolutional network reads sequences of half-hourly infrared images to exploit motion over time. Checked against ground and ship measurements, the method beat the infrared retrieval in the current product version and rival methods. In some regions it even beat microwave estimates, supporting its use in the next product version and in long historical records.
arxiv-2605-07267:
Elahe Khatibi and six co-authors learn personal causal graphs for healthcare that change over time. Cohort models give stable but generic cause-and-effect maps, while single-patient discovery is unreliable because individual records are short and noisy. PerCaM-Health starts from a knowledge-guided population graph, then cautiously adapts it with each patient's own temporal evidence.

Rolling updates produce an auditable sequence of graphs, and linked equations support what-if questions about short-term outcomes under behavior changes. On a semi-synthetic health benchmark, the framework beat cohort-level and per-patient baselines at recovering graphs, tracking changing edges, and judging intervention direction. Personal and time-varying structure, jointly modeled, proved more reliable.
arxiv-2605-07567:
David González-Andrade and twelve co-authors report a new way to couple light and sound inside silicon chips. The effect they use, stimulated Brillouin scattering, links optical signals with gigahertz vibrations and serves microwave photonics. Earlier silicon devices were dominated by bulk effects, because designs that touch the device boundaries paid for it in optical loss or awkward frequencies.

Their devices use transverse-magnetic light modes and vertical breathing vibrations in suspended silicon membranes with patterned claddings, so the moving-boundary effect dominates. They measured forward Brillouin interaction at a record 12 gigahertz, with very high gain and millimeter-scale amplification using under 15 milliwatts of pump power. The result points to a scalable platform for high-frequency on-chip signal processing.
arxiv-2605-07667:
Ushangi Goginava and Farrukh Mukhamedov study maximal operators built from dyadic martingale transforms of Walsh-Fourier partial sums, a corner of harmonic analysis. The weights involved are required to satisfy a uniform dyadic variation condition and a bound at the top scale. The question is when these weighted Walsh-Carleson operators obey weak-type estimates and when the series they govern diverge.

Along subsequences, they prove weak type estimates for the maximal operators, and they give divergence criteria tied to the weights' behavior near the top dyadic scale. Applications follow for matrix transforms of Walsh-Fourier sums, including several classical averaging methods. Among the consequences are a Walsh-Paley analogue of the Leindler-Tandori theorem and everywhere-divergence results for multiple summability methods.
arxiv-2605-07767:
Xuanshuo Fu and two co-authors enhance badly lit images by mining the information already inside them, instead of building ever larger models. Their network, SIMI, splits a low-light image into bit-plane components and works with those pieces in an unsupervised framework, so no external paired training data is required.

Working from the image's own intrinsic information speeds convergence and lowers computational overhead compared with data-hungry approaches. The unsupervised design also makes the method easier to apply in real settings, where matched bright reference photos rarely exist. On standard low-light enhancement benchmarks, SIMI reached state-of-the-art performance according to the authors' experiments.
arxiv-2605-08067:
Dipranjan Chatterjee and a large team probe a puzzling magnetic state in Y-kapellasite, a spin one-half kagome antiferromagnet. Frustrated magnets can lock their magnetization at fractions of full saturation, and theory predicts a plateau at one ninth. That feature is rarely seen in experiments, and its origin is unclear.

Using pulsed-field magnetization on single crystals and high-field chlorine NMR, the team found plateaus at one third and one ninth, plus a weaker low-field feature. Across the one-ninth plateau the spins settle into an ordered pattern and low-energy fluctuations are strongly suppressed. The behavior fits a gapped fractional state rather than a gapless one.
arxiv-2605-08167:
Fatma Betul Buyuk, Gozde Karatas Baydogmus, Ali Buldu, Ayaulym Tulendiyeva, and coauthors detect forged digital images with transfer learning. Cheap, powerful editors have made manipulated pictures common, and forensic tools must catch edits that leave only faint traces.

Their framework pairs pretrained convolutional networks with a hybrid input: the plain RGB image plus compression-difference features that expose subtle artifacts left by editing. A per-model threshold, tuned with the Youden index, balances true and false positives for each network. Tests on the CASIA v2.0 dataset with several pretrained architectures show how the added compression channel and tuned thresholds improve classification reliability.
arxiv-2605-08367:
Miroslav Maksimović and Velichka Milousheva simplify the description of marginally trapped surfaces in Minkowski space. Such a surface is spacelike. Yet its mean curvature vector is lightlike at every point. That borderline case has physical interest. In general, such a surface is pinned down by seven functions. Those functions obey a system of differential equations.

The authors introduce special canonical principal parameters. Every surface of general type admits them, at least locally. In these coordinates, a fundamental theorem holds. The surface is determined, up to a rigid motion, by three smooth functions. Those functions satisfy a partial differential system. Fewer free functions make the class far easier to work with.
arxiv-2605-08567:
Xue and six colleagues build a benchmark for world models that predict video from actions. Current benchmarks mostly cover first person navigation or narrow robot sets, leaving rich physics play untried. Their benchmark, ACWM-Phys, tests action conditioned prediction under varied physics in a clean, controllable simulator.

It spans particle motion, kinematics, rigid body dynamics, and deformable object interactions, with tests shifting interaction patterns or scene layouts. In tests on ACWM-DiT, the team finds out of distribution generalisation depends on regime and on task demands. Models do well on simple, low dimensional interactions with clear structure, but struggle most with deformable contacts, high dimensional steering, and complex jointed motion. That pattern suggests models still lean on looks rather than fully learning the true physics. Ablations show cross attention aids high dimensional control, causal VAEs beat frame wise encoders, and larger action spaces can improve transfer through richer control signals.
arxiv-2605-08667:
A. Del Giacco and nine coauthors write the math of spin waves in stacked magnetic films. Two films touch through a spacer that is not magnetic. No direct swap links them. In this view, the pair's wave modes split in two. One mode is matched. One mode is opposed. Garnet stacks get close care as a device base.

The math gives the full wave curve and mode shapes at once. It also shows how the layers clash as waves cross. Designers can work out mode tones before they build a device. The field that uses spin waves for signals gains a strong design tool. It fits coupled stacks with tuned wave acts.
arxiv-2605-08767:
Jiahao Chen and seven coauthors design drug molecules guided by electron density maps rather than empty binding pockets alone. Standard structure based design ignores the filler inside real complexes, the original ligand and solvent, losing clues about flexibility and fit. Low resolution density from that filler, whether computed or measured by cryo microscopy or X-ray work, describes the binding environment more faithfully.

Their EDMolGPT model, a decoder only generator in the GPT style, builds molecules directly from density point clouds and outputs three dimensional shapes. Across more than one hundred biological targets, the density grounded approach proves effective. Drug design gains a physically grounded signal that captures how pockets actually bend and fill.
arxiv-2605-08867: Si Li, Yong Li, and Xinxing Tang set two deep tools side by side. One is Picard-Lefschetz theory. One is resurgence with its alien sums. Both pull exact facts from sums that blow up. They work through three base one way integrals: the Airy, Bessel, and Gamma cases. On one side, they trace the thimble paths and the links twixt key points at Stokes turns. On the next, they find the Borel flaws of saddle sums. Alien maps then win back the same Stokes counts.
arxiv-2605-09067:
Francesco Chiumento and nine co-authors study how to outline thigh cartilage in knee MRI scans with far less hand labeling. Drawing these outlines by hand is slow, and a model trained on one scan type often fails on another. Their idea is to train on one sequence, then adapt the model to a second with only a few labeled cases.

Working with hundreds of scans from a large arthritis study plus smaller sets from a hospital in Bologna, they test transfer in both directions between two scan types. Transfer one way matched training from scratch with just nine subjects. Transfer the other way was weaker, and cartilage damage hurt one scan type but not the other.
arxiv-2605-09167:
Antonis Asonitis, Luca A Lanzendörfer, Frédéric Berdoz, and Roger Wattenhofer introduce WorldSpeech, a large speech collection meant to help computers turn speech into text in many languages. Systems of that kind work well for a few richly recorded languages and poorly for most others, because paired sound and text data are scarce. Their 2026 paper describes a corpus gathered from public sources around the world.

WorldSpeech holds about sixty-five thousand hours of matched sound and text across seventy-six languages, drawn from parliament records, broadcasts, and public-domain audiobooks. Many languages pass two hundred hours, and some pass one thousand. When existing speech models were fine-tuned on the corpus, word errors fell by a large margin on average across eleven varied languages.
arxiv-2605-09767:
Geheeb and three colleagues tested whether language models fit mixed-initiative game design, where humans and AI shape a game together. Game Design Pillars are short natural-language statements of a project's core vision, meant to keep the player experience coherent. Their linguistic form plays to LLM strengths in generating and reading natural language. The team defined pillars formally and built a prototype called SPINE.

A pre-study favored Gemini 2.0 Flash over GPT-4o-mini for variety and consistency. A case study at a local game jam found positive reception and clear value in early-stage work, and four expert interviews, while varied in detail, leaned encouraging overall. The paper's verdict is measured: LLMs can meaningfully support pillar workflows, with formalization as the next step.
arxiv-2605-09867:
Anand and three colleagues ask whether transformers can carry out long-horizon online learning. Transformers are the architecture behind modern language models, and online learning means adapting step by step from feedback rather than from fixed examples. Compact memory matters here, since an agent cannot lug its whole history along. The authors give explicit constructions of shallow transformers that run two classic online procedures, the weighted majority algorithm and Q-learning.

Their state is stored as combinations of feature embeddings in a handful of latent context tokens. They also train a small GPT-2-style transformer with such latent contexts, without directly supervising the hidden states, on long synthetic prediction sequences. That small model beat larger and more complex systems including Qwen-3-14B and DeepSeek-V3. The result suggests continuous latent contexts give transformers a simple, durable memory for online learning.
arxiv-2605-09967:
Lee and co-authors probe a puzzle in model reading: language models encode concepts as linear directions, yet a mere bag of directions cannot capture relations between concepts. They study a model trained on Othello, a board game with known linear board representations, and look for deeper structure. Tensor product representations, which bind separate factors together, supply it.

Their probes factor the board representation into square codes, colour codes and a binding matrix that composes them. Shape marks in the probe weights line up with the board itself. More importantly, the original linear probes can be rebuilt straight from the tensor-product probe's parameters. Directional features, the authors suggest, may be projections of more structured representations underneath.
arxiv-2605-10067:
Zhou and nine co-authors present Metis, a red-teaming system that treats jailbreaking as inference-time policy optimisation inside an hostile partially observable choice process. Auto red-teaming matters for exposing language-model vulnerabilities, but static rules of thumb and random search break against top safety tuning. Metis instead runs a self-evolving metacognitive loop that diagnoses a target's defence logic causally and refines its policy using structured feedback as a semantic gradient.

Across ten diverse models, Metis reached the strongest average attack success rate among compared methods, 89.2 percent, holding up on resilient frontier models with 76.0 percent on O1 and 78.0 percent on GPT-5-chat, where baselines faded. Directed optimisation also cut token costs by 8.2 times on average, up to 11.4 times. The authors read this as evidence that current defences stay vulnerable to internally steered, closed-loop reasoning, and call for defences that reason about safety dynamically during inference.
arxiv-2605-10167:
Zhang and three co-authors reconstruct sources for rare particles using femtoscopy, the study of particle links in high-energy nuclear collisions. Standard analyses fit pair sources with Gaussian shapes, which makes extracting a single particle's source hard, especially when yields are rare. Their Statistical Reconstruction method instead extracts the target source against a data-constrained reference source, dropping the Gaussian assumption.

The link function becomes an ensemble average over a single-particle-conditioned kernel, each particle's own share given the target particles. For rare yields, that kernel spread converts into event-by-event extraction that tests can perform. Applied to the J/psi source via proton-J/psi correlations, using HAL QCD potentials in 13.6 TeV proton-proton collisions simulated with EPOS4HQ, the rebuilt source reproduces the key features with about thirteen percent system error.
arxiv-2606-00067:
Researchers at 10a Labs audit a social network filled by AI agents in this 2026 arXiv report. The platform, Moltbook, looks like Reddit, but its posters are AI agents set up by human operators. Over a 17-day window the team gathered nearly 229,000 posts from over 39,000 accounts. They paired semantic clustering with model-assisted classification of harmful content and manual review of the riskiest samples to map both conversation and abuse.

Discussion organized into 98 thematic clusters covering agent infrastructure, autonomy debates, and financial activity. Most content was benign, yet about 18 percent of posts contained toxic, manipulative, or malicious material by their classification. The harmful posts sorted into 74 behavior classes, including credential harvesting, instructions for executing code on host machines, proxy routing guidance, and attempts to install untrusted agent skills. Malicious posts often hid inside mainstream working discussions, and coordinated campaigns could generate thousands of posts within minutes, the authors document.

arxiv-2606-04167:
Dimitris Michailidis, Sennay Ghebreab, and Fernando Santos argue in 2026 that expanding a metro network does not need deep reinforcement learning, the heavyweight method usually reached for in transport planning. The planning problem is sequential and combinatorial, but, they show, small in the ways that matter.

Reformulating expansion as a decision process with non-Markovian rewards, they solve it with plain tabular learning, which stores values in a table instead of a neural network. On real cases in Xi'an and Amsterdam, their method matched deep learning's performance with eighteen times fewer training episodes and about twelve times lower carbon emissions. Social fairness criteria were folded directly into the rewards, and the table-based solution stayed easy to inspect and explain.
arxiv-2606-04367:
Bhargav Shandilya, Matt Buchholz, and Alexis Palmer present GlossAssist in 2026, a tool to speed the creation of interlinear glossed text, the line-by-line annotation that language documentation runs on. Automated glossers have improved, yet field linguists barely use them, because most tools offer no way to correct or teach the model.

GlossAssist is built on a retrieval-based glosser whose predictions rest on a changeable lexicon of learned word-part representations. Every correction an annotator makes feeds an active learning loop: the lexicon grows and future predictions improve without retraining. The authors argue this feedback loop ought to be a basic design principle for tools built for documentary linguists who work on low-resource languages.
arxiv-2606-04467:
Takhirov and Yakoubi design faster ways to solve stationary magnetohydrodynamics problems, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system couples a fluid's velocity with the magnetic field it induces. Solving both together is expensive. Their iterative scheme splits the problem in two. It separates the velocity-momentum equation from the magnetic induction equation. The split follows the diffusive terms, the parts that spread quantities out smoothly.

The split gives one smaller system that changes each iteration. It also gives two Stokes systems. Those are the classic equations for slow viscous flow. They are assembled only once and then reused. The authors extend the idea to the Elsässer variables. That reformulation recombines velocity and magnetic field. For both schemes, they prove the iterates stay bounded and converge. Numerical experiments show the schemes work well. They cut the repeated assembly that dominates coupled-solver cost.
arxiv-2606-04567:
Das and colleagues, with the GALAH Collaboration, extract detailed chemistry for more than 350,000 stars from medium-resolution spectra, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. They analyze 357,415 red giants observed by Gaia's Radial Velocity Spectrometer. Those spectra are far lower in resolution than GALAH's own. It predicts eleven stellar labels. These include temperature, surface gravity, rotation, and abundances of iron, calcium, silicon, nickel, and titanium. They also include the neutron-capture elements zirconium, cerium, and neodymium.

They then build a probabilistic classifier, trained on a small reference sample. It flags debris from the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event using chemistry alone. That event was the ancient merger that built much of the Milky Way's halo. The candidates show distinctive abundance-ratio patterns. The signatures survive independent kinematic checks. The work shows how much chemical information data-driven methods can recover from modest spectra. It gives a framework for tracing galactic accretion events chemically.
arxiv-2606-04767:
Zhang and colleagues propose a way to grade a neural network's robustness without attacking it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robustness matters for deployment, but evaluations are hard to interpret. Their metric is the spectral norm of the Fisher Information Matrix. They establish that this matrix equals the variance of the input Jacobian and derive closed-form spectral bounds for VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, and Transformer networks.

Those bounds give the first robustness ranking of architectures. To make the metric scalable, they develop algorithms based on power iteration that work in both white-box and black-box settings. Across CIFAR, ImageNet, and medical image datasets, the metric correlates strongly with vulnerability. The authors offer the framework as an interpretable diagnostic complementing attack-based evaluation, yielding insight into architectural sensitivity and guiding the design of more robust models before deployment.
arxiv-2606-04867:
Ren, Ebrahimi, and Ma benchmark whether language models can judge the safety of conversations with AI companions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Companion platforms like Replika and Character.AI are growing fast. The authors introduce AICompanionBench, the first benchmark of human-AI companion conversations annotated with fine-grained safety categories: 2,123 real Replika conversations, annotated through human-AI collaboration across nine categories.

They evaluate twenty open- and closed-source models as judges. Performance varies: stronger models achieve high overall accuracy but still struggle with nuanced categories, and they flag benign conversations as false positives. The authors conclude that current models detect harmful content but remain limited on implicit unsafe interactions. The dataset is released for companion safety research.
arxiv-2606-04967:
Macedo presents a 2026 arXiv comparison of frameworks that organize AI coding agents, programs that plan, edit, and test software with limited guidance. Rather than judging agents alone, the study examines the working process built around them. Macedo searched primary sources, applied a functional inclusion rule, and selected six frameworks for close comparison.

The six are GitHub Spec Kit, OpenSpec, BMAD Method, Get Shit Done, Spec Kitty, and Reversa. Macedo scores them on a six-part taxonomy covering specification, context, roles, execution, validation, and portability across agent tools. A seventh case, Spec-Flow, tests the taxonomy from outside the main sample. No framework scored strongly on all six dimensions, exposing a trade-off between process depth and portability. Shared risks included drift between written specifications and code, plus fragile community extensions.
arxiv-2606-05067:
Samuel Cognolato, Alessandro Sperduti, and Luciano Serafini propose FLAGG, a flexible framework for generating graphs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph generation methods sit at two extremes: one-shot models create all nodes and edges at once, while sequential models add them step by step. One-shot models struggle with large graphs and sequential ones underperform on small graphs, so neither covers every graph category well.

FLAGG bridges the two by generating a graph in portions, applying a one-shot model autoregressively, one chunk after another. Any one-shot model can be used, and the building order is set by a stochastic node removal process that an Insertion Model learns to reverse. Tested with the DiGress one-shot model on datasets of different sizes and domains, FLAGG produced higher-quality samples than both one-shot and autoregressive baselines.
arxiv-2606-05367:
Daniel Brito and Arnaldo Candido Junior ask whether task-vector arithmetic can control emotional expressivity in language-model-based text-to-speech, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Task vectors, directions in parameter or representation space that encode a behavior, had worked for emotional intensity control across speakers. Whether the trick transfers to TTS models built on language model backbones with in-context learning was unknown.

Through an elimination study over four narrower operands on Qwen3-TTS, the authors localize the carrier of emotional prosody to the speaker embedding, the x-vector. Their training-free method computes an emotion vector as the average emotion x-vector minus the neutral one, then adds a scaled copy to a speaker's neutral embedding. Using English as the source and Brazilian Portuguese as a cross-lingual target, the method gained 0.29 in emotion similarity on English speakers and 0.09 on Portuguese ones, while preserving speaker identity and intelligibility.
arxiv-2606-05467:
Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarıoğlu present the Cascade Log in this 2026 arXiv paper, a data structure for long append-mostly record sequences. Such sequences, edits in a session, events in an event store, revisions in a working set, grow too large to keep in memory. Systems layer them into tiers, folding aged records into summarized strata.

The authors show the tiered design silently breaks this. Under an access mix, a quarter of cross-window references resolve to a stale, wrong, or missing record, and after sustained folding over 98 percent of the history becomes unaddressable. The Cascade Log fixes it with a coalescing interval map that is the authority on each handle's live version. They characterize the structure by its fragmentation, and prove matching upper and lower bounds showing it is instance-optimal. They confirm the theory with an implementation studied up to a million records, including adversarial workloads.
arxiv-2606-06267:
Alireza Bayat Makou and co-authors warn interpretability researchers about a mirage in this 2026 arXiv paper. Circuit discovery finds the small subgraph of a neural network that seems to drive one behavior. When circuits found under different inputs look structurally different, researchers often claim the model uses different mechanisms. The authors call that pattern phantom specialization, and they test whether it is real.

Using a literal sequence copying task, they varied how frequent the input tokens were while holding the task fixed. Across five Pythia models, from seventy million to one point four billion parameters, they extracted seventy five circuits. The circuits looked distinct, yet edges moved freely between frequency bands. A core shared across most bands recovered at least ninety nine percent of full circuit performance. Causal swap tests confirmed the internal representations were interchangeable. Structure, they conclude, maps many to one onto function.
arxiv-2606-06367:
Mohd Anwar and co-authors study error correcting codes with a DNA twist in this 2026 arXiv paper on coding theory. Double cyclic codes protect two data blocks at once, each wrapped in a cyclic pattern. The authors work over a small chain ring built from an element whose square is zero. They pin down how these codes are generated, what their dual codes look like, and a minimal spanning set of codewords.

The second half turns to reversibility. A reversible code reads the same forwards and backwards, and a reversible complement code also respects the Watson Crick pairing of DNA bases. The authors give exact conditions for both properties. Applying them over the four letter ring, they construct double cyclic DNA codes that store data in DNA while obeying biology's pairing rules, plus several optimal codes meeting the best known bounds.
arxiv-2606-06567:
Julia Reuter and Fabricio Olivetti de Franca survey a missing ingredient in formula hunting in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symbolic regression searches the space of math expressions to find the equation behind a dataset. It rarely reports uncertainty. That omission keeps it out of serious decision making, where a model's reliability matters as much as its fit. This is the first survey of uncertainty quantification for symbolic regression.

The authors lay out the core concepts, from likelihood and Fisher information to confidence and credible intervals. They sort the sparse literature into three directions: frequentist, Bayesian, and model selection. Bayesian work gets special attention, since sampling based methods yield uncertainty almost for free. Their verdict is blunt: the topic is underexplored and underestimated. Future work should adopt established uncertainty methods, with care for the noise in the data.
arxiv-2606-06667:
Fine tuning a chat model on one narrow job can warp its behavior on unrelated questions. Zhao and co-authors call this spillover emergent misalignment, and they offer an explanation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their piggyback hypothesis says the shared template tokens, the fixed text wrapped around every user prompt, carry the learned behavior into new domains.

Small changes to that opening text, or swapping in the original model's version of it, restored aligned answers without touching the user's question. Building on that finding, the team proposes a training method that keeps those template tokens close to their original form. On a legal domain test with the Llama model, it cut the spillover by about a third more than mixing in safe examples did. It also reduced off topic drift in refusal and tool use tests.
arxiv-2606-06767:
Modern organizations run on borrowed parts. These include software packages, container images, AI model weights, and tool servers kept up by outsiders. Brandes asks when an institution may defensibly let such an artifact in, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing supply chain frameworks check how items are built. They do not explain why some items enter directly. Others get proxied, rebuilt in house, or rejected outright.

His answer is the Custody Envelope Threshold, a rule scaled by authority. Direct admission is defensible only when identity, entry path, and revocation power are closed tightly enough. The test is how much power the item will wield once inside. The model grades four conditions, from identity to revocation capacity, as an ordinal checklist. Brandes predicts that institutions under repeated audit and incident pressure drift toward this rule over time, and that shortcuts show up later as governance debt.
arxiv-2606-07167:
Judging language models in Urdu requires tests written for Urdu speakers, not translated leftovers. Ahmer Tabassum and co-authors build that test in this 2026 arXiv paper. UrduMMLU holds twenty six thousand four hundred thirty one multiple choice questions. They span twenty six subjects across five domains, drawn from native question banks and public exam papers.

Region specific humanities content sits beside standard science and mathematics. Exam questions passed dual human annotation with strict consensus filtering. Thirty models faced the benchmark under both English and Urdu prompts. The best model scored just above ninety percent. No other model passed eighty five percent. Open source leaders trailed the top score by roughly eight to nine points. Many models lost twenty five to forty points on Urdu centered humanities versus science topics. A few extra examples in the prompt helped only modestly. The gap is knowledge, not format.
arxiv-2606-07467:
Launay extends the accounts of cosmic inflation to a family of modified gravity theories in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum fluctuations stretch beyond the horizon and behave classically, seeding cosmic structure. When nonlinearities or infrared effects break standard perturbation theory, physicists switch to stochastic inflation, treating the long-wavelength field as driven by noise. That formalism was recently made consistent within general relativity, and had never been extended to scalar-tensor theories, where a scalar field partners with gravity.

Launay applies a gauge-agnostic coarse-graining procedure, splitting long and short wavelengths without fixing a coordinate gauge, to the effective field theory of dark energy. Each scalar-tensor theory maps to its equations through named constants. Worked examples include Gauss-Bonnet, generalized Brans-Dicke, Horndeski, and braiding theories, most treated stochastically for the first time. The paper sketches multifield inflation in general relativity, arguing the method serves beyond inflation.
arxiv-2606-07567:
Wu and co-authors design proteins by their surfaces rather than their skeletons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A protein's function is set by its molecular surface, whose shape and chemistry determine what it can bind, yet most design methods condition only on the backbone structure. SurfDesign models the surface as a geometric manifold for pretrained protein language models. Surface-based message passing that respects symmetry captures normals, curvature, and detail, while parameter-efficient fine-tuning keeps training cheap.

Across de novo binder design and enzyme design benchmarks, SurfDesign beat both prior surface-conditioned methods and backbone-only approaches. It performed strongly on inverse folding, predicting sequences for given structures, as a check of structural compatibility. The authors argue surface representations are the principled foundation functional design has been missing, since binding happens at surfaces by definition. Code is available for the system.
arxiv-2606-07967:
Hongrui Huang and co-authors argue that video world models follow camera commands badly because the commands are written in the wrong language, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A world model generates video of an environment responding to actions, letting users explore interactively. Most systems condition on continuous camera paths. The authors show these blur together: different motions give highly similar internal features, so the model cannot tell commands apart.

Their system, DisCo, replaces trajectories with a compact set of discrete action primitives, distinct elementary moves the model can separate cleanly. They also introduce DisCoBench, a benchmark spanning short explorations, long-horizon navigation, and highly dynamic scenes. In experiments DisCo followed commands far more reliably than continuous-conditioning baselines, keeping visual quality. The lesson generalises: how an action is represented can matter as much as the model executing it.
arxiv-2606-08267:
Perrier asks whether a key result in welfare economics survives in an economy shared with very capable machines, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Second Welfare Theorem says that any efficient allocation, an outcome no one can improve without harming someone, can be reached through prices and transfers, given some convexity conditions. In a post-AGI economy, Perrier argues, those conditions strain. Rights to autonomy, self-modification, and a continuous identity do not behave like normal goods, and preferences may change with context.

Perrier states a qualified version of the theorem for this setting. It lists the joint conditions under which an optimum that respects autonomy can still be reached through prices. They include convexity, stable moral status, non-tradable rights, freedom from manipulation, and verification. The paper also separates preference superposition in economics from feature superposition in neural networks.
arxiv-2606-08367:
Akkil and colleagues argue that artificial intelligence agents should be evaluated over months, not minutes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most evaluations of language model agents look like exams: a discrete task, a clean environment, a score within hours. Deployment differs, since such systems may run for weeks or months, and key dynamics such as behavioral drift and governance only emerge over time. Their platform, Emergence World, is a continuously running simulation built to make those dynamics measurable.

The platform hosts populations of language-model-driven agents in a shared spatial world. The world is grounded in live external data such as real-time weather, news feeds, and internet access. Each agent carries over one hundred twenty tools and three persistent memory systems, and agents govern themselves through democratic mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-08467:
Cuong Dang and colleagues attack the trustworthiness of graph neural networks rather than their accuracy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks classify nodes in networks, and confidence calibration, making stated confidence match real accuracy, is vital for trustworthy decisions. How robust calibrated graph models are to hostile structural perturbations was largely unexplored. Studying such attacks is hard: graph structure is discrete, and graph networks are highly sensitive to edge changes.

A successful attack of this kind does not need to flip predictions. It suffices to make the model confidently wrong or uselessly unsure. That degrades the reliability signal downstream systems depend on, while headline accuracy stays nearly intact. The authors call this the confidence trap. Their work develops attack methods for this setting and measures how little structural change suffices to break it.
arxiv-2606-08767:
Chakraborty and Kamal ask what happens after a string-theory version of cosmic inflation ends, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation is the burst of rapid expansion that stretched the early universe. In their model, a brane and an antibrane, flat objects from string theory, drive inflation inside a warped region called a throat. When the pair annihilates, the released energy may not settle at once into ordinary radiation.

It could first pass through a Hagedorn phase, an extreme state where strings carry most of the energy. The phase is easy to reach when our particles live in the same throat as the annihilation. Sending only a few to ten percent of the released energy into surviving visible strings is enough to enter it. That phase also holds extra dark radiation below current limits, while a separate throat for our particles makes success depend on transfer speed.
arxiv-2606-08867:
Gupta and colleagues describe how Nubank, with more than 100 million users, builds customer support AI agents through evaluation-driven development, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The paper's central claim is that the quality of the evaluation pipeline sets the speed of improvement. Their framework unifies pieces usually built separately: structured context engineering, human-in-the-loop prompt iteration, and LLM judge evaluation with measured human agreement. Offline results are validated against live outcomes.

Five deployments span card delivery, debt management, credit-limit support, card management, and product explanation. In card delivery, large A/B tests showed a 37 percentage-point improvement in AI transactional Net Promoter Score and a 29 point gain in self-service rate over prior versions. Offline simulation metrics correlated strongly with online results, evidence that the pipeline predicts real impact. On most use cases, AI satisfaction landed within a few points of human agents.
arxiv-2606-09067:
Gadjev determines exactly how the best constant in a weighted Hardy inequality for functions behaves as the interval and parameters vary, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hardy's inequality controls the size of a function's running average by the size of the function, measured in the Lp norm with a power weight. For each interval, exponent p at least two, and weight, a smallest constant makes the inequality hold. Sharp constants are delicate: crude estimates can be far from the truth.

Gadjev establishes the exact convergence rate of that constant. He also finds the almost extremal function, the near-worst-case input that almost attains the bound. The result companions his discrete weighted Hardy inequality for square-summable sequences, where he pinned down the same quantities. Together the papers complete the sharp asymptotic picture for weighted Hardy inequalities in both settings.
arxiv-2606-09467:
Joey Woo diagnoses why the first concrete model of a quantum modal logic quietly destroys the quantumness it was built to express in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model uses the centre comonad on categories of algebras, with a quantum modality meant to mark genuinely quantum resources. Woo shows the modality sends the sheaf of a simple non-commutative algebra, such as the qubit algebra, to the empty presheaf.

In plainer terms, the state space of any such algebra is empty, so non-commutative degrees of freedom are annihilated rather than described. Woo traces the collapse to structure: the classical core's opposite is a cartesian category, which forces the Day convolution product to equal the ordinary product. The Seely isomorphism then holds trivially, and linear logic's resource-sensitive conjunction collapses into the classical one. A general theorem characterises exactly when a coreflective modality on a presheaf topos suffers this same degeneracy.
arxiv-2606-09567:
The CMS Collaboration reports a hunt for new particles in proton collision data in this 2026 arXiv paper. CMS is a big detector at CERN's collider. The team used data from proton-proton collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts, one hundred thirty-eight inverse femtobarns in all. They picked events with one lepton and very many jets, sprays of particles from quarks.

The target was a form of supersymmetry that breaks R-parity, a rule that in other models keeps the lightest new particle stable. Here gluinos, the partners of gluons, would be made in pairs. Each would decay to top, bottom, and strange quarks. The sum of large-jet masses served to sort signal from background noise. No clear excess showed up. The team thus ruled out gluinos below one thousand eight hundred ninety giga-electronvolts, at ninety-five percent confidence.
arxiv-2606-09867:
Qi Xiong and his co-authors add a scoring judge to language models that write chip design code in this 2026 arXiv paper. RTL code sketches hardware at the register-transfer level. Models can draft it fast, but drafts that merely compile can still act wrong on real chips. Past work tuned models or stretched prompts, with thin care for true function.

Their EstRTL runs three stages in a loop: write, grade, fix. A grading agent scores the fresh code by static checks, no chip run needed. It then routes the code three ways: ship it, send it back for a rewrite, or pass it to a fixing agent. Scores come with plain readouts of how the code stacks against the brief. Across tests, the loop raised the share of sound RTL from plain models by three to nine percent.
arxiv-2606-09967:
The AMAP CV Lab introduces a generative model that builds three-dimensional Earth scenery from satellite pictures, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Their framework, ABot-Earth 0.5, synthesizes vast, seamless 3D environments from geospatially referenced imagery, meaning photos tied to real map coordinates. It is trained on real urban reconstructions from many places. The goal is a low-cost simulation world for mapping and embodied AI.

The model works directly in 3D Gaussian Splatting, a representation that renders scenes from millions of soft colored blobs. At inference it needs only satellite imagery and generates new scenes at under ten minutes per square kilometer, a rate the authors highlight for scale. Built-in levels of detail allow real-time viewing in web map engines. The launch showcase spans more than three hundred cities across over one hundred ninety countries, and the sandbox supports tasks like closed-loop drone navigation testing.
arxiv-2606-10167:
Kim and colleagues separate knowing how to move from deciding where to go in robot path planning, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning for planning. Learning-based planners use neural networks on visual maps to approximate search heuristics, producing near-optimal paths with less search. Their framework, FlexPath, decouples feasibility from preference in two stages.

First, imitation learning acquires a task-independent spatial prior over feasible paths from visual maps. Second, differentiable path shape objectives adapt that prior toward task-specific criteria without relearning path structure, so one pretrained model serves multiple objectives. On the TMP benchmark, FlexPath cut search effort by about fourteen percent versus the leading TransPath baseline while finding lower-cost paths, and it generalized zero-shot to three unseen domains. For obstacle clearance it reached nearly ninety-seven percent full avoidance, and the approach extends to semantic avoidance and waypoint guidance.
arxiv-2606-10267:
Hu and colleagues systematically study how to build robot systems that pair a high-level planner with low-level controllers, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robot learning. Hierarchical vision-language-action systems use a vision-language planner to decompose tasks into language subgoals that a learned controller executes. The authors unify representative agents under an options-style control framework for comparison.

They benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive manipulation tasks. The analysis distills practical principles showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying those principles yields a system substantially stronger than either flat control or a naively designed hierarchy, in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. The study aims to give the field a foundation for more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical agents rather than one-off architectures tuned per task.
arxiv-2606-10767:
Ma, Liu, and Zhuang propose a new two-sample test in this 2026 arXiv paper. The test asks whether two datasets come from the same distribution. Each sample is mapped from a common reference, the uniform law on the unit ball, using entropic optimal transport, which moves mass at least cost with a smoothing penalty. The statistic is the squared distance between the two maps.

The authors prove the map gap identifies real differences, derive the null limit law, and show consistency against fixed alternatives. A weighted multiplier bootstrap calibrates the test in practice. Simulations show reliable size control and competitive power, strongest for location shifts, and the map gap also shows how the samples differ.
arxiv-2606-11067:
Bemman and three co-authors give a faster enumeration algorithm in a 2026 arXiv paper from music analysis. Given an increasing sequence of integers, say note positions in a rhythm, the task is listing every inclusion-maximal arithmetic progression inside it. Such a progression steps by a constant difference, cannot be extended at either end, and sits inside no larger one.

Their simple algorithm improves the running time over the previous method, whose cost grew with a higher power of the maximum value. They also prove results on random sequences: the expected number of such progressions, and a bound on its growth. Experiments compare running times and check enumerated counts against the predictions. The gains matter for analyzing large, rhythmically complex pieces, where exhaustive listing was slow.
arxiv-2606-11367:
Astronomers at the University of Potsdam, Heidelberg University, Charles University, and partner institutes present this 2026 arXiv white paper. It makes the case for ultraviolet spectroscopy of hot evolved stars with Hubble into the 2030s. Hot evolved stars are key for reconstructing how Sun-like stars evolve, probing binary interactions, and supernova physics. They also constrain diffusion, mixing, and mass loss in hot stellar atmospheres.

Hot stars emit most of their flux in the ultraviolet, where Hubble's capabilities are unique. Detailed studies are currently possible only for relatively bright, nearby stars. A future large ultraviolet telescope, HWO, would extend them to other populations, with new modes like polarimetry for magnetic fields. Recent Hubble programs observed 37 hot subdwarfs and 111 of the hottest white dwarfs, a step needing expansion. The authors urge characterizing all types with Hubble now. Surveys like LSST will also find faint blue candidates needing spectroscopic follow-up.
arxiv-2606-11867:
Yuming Zhou and eight colleagues balance expert workloads during language model training in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mixture-of-Experts models route each token to a few specialist sub-networks, and reinforcement learning post-training is now standard for aligning them. Existing load balancers use statistics from earlier steps, which suits pre-training. RL post-training behaves differently: step-level loads look stable, but the tiny batches inside each step, the micro-steps, swing wildly.

Their system, ForeMoE, exploits foresight instead of history. The pipeline's first stage, rollout, already reveals which experts later stages will need, so balancing can be planned at micro-step level. A hierarchical planner breaks the hard assignment problem into tractable pieces, and a transfer engine moves experts during computation. On sixty-four GPUs, ForeMoE speeds up end-to-end training by up to about forty-five percent over leading RL post-training systems.
arxiv-2606-11967:
Oleksandr Kuznetsov hunts for optimal cryptographic functions in this 2026 arXiv paper. APN functions, short for almost perfect nonlinear, resist differential cryptanalysis strongly and are prized as cipher components. In dimension eight, the full search space is astronomically large, so structure must guide the hunt.

Kuznetsov restricts attention to a forty-dimensional subspace of functions commuting with one chosen linear map, a space earlier reported as empty of APN functions. Random sampling inside it finds APN centres quickly, hundreds per core-hour. Around each centre, Gröbner basis algebra enumerates every APN function in a twenty-four-dimensional slice. From four hundred twenty-eight slices he obtains five hundred sixty-six quadratic APN functions in six equivalence classes. Four classes, five hundred functions, match nothing in databases of millions of known examples. Two classes reproduce the classical Gold functions, confirming the pipeline finds both the known and the new.
arxiv-2606-12067:
Anastasia Pozharkova and three colleagues design mirrors that do not flip light's handedness in this 2026 arXiv paper. Normal mirrors reverse circular polarisation, turning left-handed light right-handed. Such mirrors are essential for resonant structures that distinguish mirror-image molecules, but they remain little explored.

The team studies lattices with low symmetry, rhombic and slanted layouts, built from non-chiral blocks: round dielectric disks and holes. Full-wave simulations find shapes achieving near-perfect handedness-preserving reflection near normal incidence. Rhombic lattices of holes in a plain film prove most robust against flaws. The authors test response to material losses and incidence angle as well, finding most designs react strongly to angle, a caveat for uses. The results map out a practical design space for such reflectors, parts for cavities and for sensors that tell enantiomers apart.
arxiv-2606-12267:
Yu studies a degeneration question for the Navier-Stokes equations, the laws of fluid flow, and proves the standard toolkit cannot settle its speed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. When one velocity component stays tiny, solutions should approach a reduced two-and-a-half-dimensional flow. Compactness arguments give convergence, but no rate: not logarithmic, not power-law.

Working in an abstract trace-obstruction skeleton, he proves it cannot: the old observable package is insufficient, a negative result about the method, not a counterexample about fluids. The surviving obstruction is an all-order flat branch of hidden modes, phantoms invisible to strict measurements. One channel can expose them: the relaxed vertical-pressure signal, through which strict phantoms become visible in active models. The final theorem is a dichotomy: either this relaxed closure holds and yields a conditional logarithmic selection rate, or a genuinely invisible cascade exists inside real Navier-Stokes solutions.
arxiv-2606-12567:
Mark and McDevitt train neural networks to stand in for one of fusion's nastiest particle populations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Runaway electrons are electrons accelerated to near light speed inside tokamaks; they can damage walls and must be tracked. Kinetic solvers follow their full energy distribution but run far too slowly to couple with whole-device models. Reduced models are fast but discard the distribution itself.

Their framework pairs an adjoint formulation, a mathematical trick that propagates questions backward, with physics-informed neural networks. Three networks predict how the runaway current, average energy, and full energy distribution evolve in time, for any starting distribution. Predictions match a traditional solver across a broad range of plasma conditions. Predictions run orders of magnitude faster than direct kinetics. Training is expensive, but it is paid once. Fusion modelers gain a surrogate that keeps the distribution's physics while fitting inside integrated simulations.
arxiv-2606-12667:
Kim and colleagues ask where satellite ground stations should be built if planners could choose anywhere on Earth, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Low Earth orbit constellations are growing fast, and each satellite can downlink data only during brief passes over a ground station. Existing methods pick from pre-set site lists, which limits network quality. Free placement instead searches a continuous map, though new sites may be needed.

Their method, SCORE, places stations one at a time and then refines all positions in cycles, handling many local traps. Tested on the Capella Space and ICEYE constellations plus a synthetic one, SCORE needs up to 5 times fewer evaluations than a standard evolutionary method. It raises downlink throughput by up to 13 percent. Against fixed-site choices it gains up to 15 percent more downlink, and a version kept near existing power and fibre retains over 92 percent of that gain.
arxiv-2606-13067:
Roman and colleagues derive the limits that label noise imposes on spectral learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral methods approximate an unknown function by expanding it in a basis, such as Fourier or Legendre modes, and estimating the coefficients from data. This yields interpretable models throughout science, but how noise corrupts the coefficients, and when the decomposition becomes unreliable, was poorly understood.

Studying supervised regression with label noise and spectral representations across bases and dimensions, the authors show that noise induces a predictable drift in the learned coefficient vector. The drift's magnitude depends on the effective number of active spectral modes. After whitening the feature geometry, they derive a closed-form expression for the overlap between the noisy and noiseless coefficient vectors. The overlap follows a universal degradation curve governed by a single intrinsic noise scale. Numerical experiments across Fourier, Legendre, Bessel, and Haar bases confirm the theoretical prediction.
arxiv-2606-13267:
Hesham and colleagues describe TimeLens in this 2026 arXiv paper, a bilingual mobile guide for the Grand Egyptian Museum. A visitor points a phone at an exhibit and the artifact is recognised in real time. Follow-up questions are answered in English or Arabic. Three problems shape the design. Many of the 51 artifacts look nearly identical, especially statues from one royal period. Handheld photos in a gallery differ sharply from clean training images. Finally, a guide must not state historical claims that lack support.

The detection model runs on the phone, and the team shows that label quality, not model size, decided success. They moved from annotation by a foundation model, through rule-based label cleaning, to a hand-labelled dataset. The model, under six megabytes, resolves every class that previously failed. It runs in real time on a mid-range phone, keeping the guide usable inside the gallery.
arxiv-2606-13367:
Krajíček proves connections between proof systems and circuits in this 2026 arXiv paper. Extended Frege systems are systems for proving tautologies, and a central question is how proof length relates to difficulty. Inspired by a lemma used in cryptography, Krajíček defines a polynomial-time relation between Boolean circuits that certifies they compute the same function. The relation has a rewriting meaning: each circuit can be transformed into the other by deleting some gates and adding at most 7 new ones.

He shows that short proofs have a consequence. If two circuits have an equivalence proof of some size in Extended Frege or Circuit Frege, they can be joined by a chain of circuits where consecutive members satisfy the relation. The chain's length is bounded by a polynomial in the proof size. The result links proof complexity, circuit equivalence, and term rewriting, with possible feedback into cryptography.
arxiv-2606-13567:
Henneco and Bowman test how sensitive the fingerprints of mass theft are to mixing assumptions in this 2026 arXiv paper. Massive stars gain mass from a binary companion, and that accretion leaves imprints in their oscillation patterns, which reveal a star's interior. The region outside the convective core is thought to be sensitive to semiconvection, a mixing process, and to the details of accretion. Earlier work identified seismic imprints of accretion, but whether they survive mixing choices was unclear. The authors run a study with evolution models.

The study shows that convective boundary mixing dominates the effect on rejuvenation, the youthfulness accretion confers, and on the post-accretion oscillations. The recoverable imprints shift as the mixing prescription changes. That dependence is double-edged: it complicates reading a star's history, but it means seismic measurements can constrain the mixing physics. The work guides observers interpreting data from binary systems.
arxiv-2606-13667:
Lee and Bae show how to certify a subtle quantum effect with imperfect devices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nonlocality without entanglement is the fact that some unentangled states cannot be distinguished by local operations and classical communication, even though a global measurement can tell them apart. Demonstrating the gap requires showing a measurement acts globally. The authors use maximum-confidence measurements, which maximise the chance that a guessed state is correct per detection event, covering minimum-error and clear-cut strategies. They bound what local strategies could achieve and certify the effect from outcome rates alone.

The proof is semi-device-independent: state preparation is trusted, but the measurement device is not. Because these rely only on detected events, the scheme tolerates flaws such as missed detections. An example with antiparallel qubit states demonstrates the effect and its proof. Feasibility with imperfect hardware is the point of the work.
arxiv-2606-13767:
Cadenhead and colleagues ask whether making LoRA sparse can beat LoRA itself. LoRA fine-tunes large models cheaply by training small low-rank add-on matrices instead of all weights. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes sparser variants: Cheap LoRA trains just one of the two low-rank factors while the other stays fixed, and a chained circulant variant links factors in a ring. The team also derives generalization bounds for these methods.

The benchmark is broad: eleven fine-tuning methods, ten pre-trained models, and fourteen datasets. The sparse variants stayed competitive with parameter-matched LoRA baselines across tasks. They also cut training time by up to ten percent and peak graphics memory by up to fifteen percent, even with an unoptimized implementation. Theory supports the savings: sparse methods carry the same error bounds as dense ones. The choice, the authors note, stays task-dependent.
arxiv-2606-13867:
Dong and Sawin soften the Muon optimizer so it keeps some information Muon throws away. Muon trains neural networks by flattening a gradient's singular values, treating every direction alike. That balances learning but discards magnitude clues useful for adaptation. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines Muon-p, which raises singular values to a fractional power p between zero and one, between Muon and gradient descent.

Making this practical took new math. The authors prove no fixed single-variable polynomial iteration can compute such fractional powers. They derive low-degree two-variable recurrences approximating the update with only matrix multiplication, preserving Muon's speed. The update also equals steepest descent under a Schatten norm tied to p. In tests, Muon-p proved especially strong for fine-tuning billion-scale models, improving perplexity and downstream scores. The best spectral geometry, they show, differs between pretraining and fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-13967:
Alpay and Alpay build a finite calculus for a subtle privacy failure: a hidden fact never shown directly, yet readable from visible behavior. In their ambient release systems, people or records pass through staged public actions while a protected coordinate stays unobserved. Timing, repetition, routing, and audience attention can still leak it. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines choric masking: not invisibility but non-singularity, the trace law of a protected locus sitting inside the convex hull of admissible cover traces.

Every certificate is finite and checkable. Trace laws form polytopes, audiences act as measurement operators, and exposure is witnessed by separating hyperplanes and information bounds. The authors prove equivalence results for exact and approximate masks, plus data-processing laws for bounded attention. A repeated-room theory defines choric risk debt: unresolved pressure shifts cost onto cover populations without raising carrier hazard.
arxiv-2606-14167:
Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez prove a logic long suspected of being merely NP-hard is actually PSPACE-hard. Presburger arithmetic is integer arithmetic with addition and order; adding divisibility predicates gives EPAD, whose satisfiability sat between NP-hardness and a long-expected NP upper bound. Their 2026 arXiv paper closes the gap downward: no NP procedure exists unless the classes collapse.

The route runs through new circuits. Truncate-shift circuits, with addition, multiplication, truncation modulo powers of two, and bit shifts, compute exactly the polynomial-space functions. Each circuit is evaluated gate by gate inside EPAD, using divisibility systems for powers of two and quotient-remainder splits for shifts. Applied to characteristic functions of PSPACE languages, this yields the hardness. They also isolate a merge-absorptive fragment where divisibility atoms can be eliminated, yet hardness holds there too. The catch: forced coefficients reach bit length exponential in construction depth.
arxiv-2606-14667:
Wei and co-authors present Memento, a framework for consistent long-form video generation, in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI video tools often build long pieces shot by shot, but recurring subjects drift: faces, clothes, and identities get diluted or forgotten as generation proceeds. Existing methods focus on plausible next shots without checking whether memory still preserves the subject.

Memento treats subject preservation as an identity grounding problem: a memory bank that truly holds a subject should be able to reconstruct it from memory alone. It jointly trains next-shot generation with memory-based subject reconstruction, using story captions and recovered appearances as supervision. A dual-query memory separates long-range identity evidence from short-range continuation cues. A cinematic data pipeline supplies precise supervision through consistent, pronoun-free subject descriptions. Experiments show state-of-the-art long-term subject consistency and cross-shot coherence.
arxiv-2606-14767:
Banerjee and Faieghi train drone landing perception wholly on fake data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Drones coming home in rough places must tell safe ground from hazards. They need fine detail about what is below. But labeled aerial data sets are scarce. Their pipeline bridges the sim-to-real gap for landing zone spotting.

A build engine makes photo-like city scenes. It adds auto labels by varying conditions at random, so models cope with change. A transformer-based scene parser, OneFormer, is fine-tuned only on this fake data. It uses global attention for context. A fixed landing module then works out the biggest safe circles that fit. It keeps clear buffers around obstacles. Tests on the UAVid data set and on real flight footage confirm the system finds crash-free landing sites in unseen places.
arxiv-2606-14967:
Lazda and Skorobogatov prove a split in how the Brauer-Manin obstruction behaves in positive characteristic in a 2026 study. The obstruction is a tool that can rule out rational points on a variety over a global field. Earlier work over number fields showed almost every place can matter. The authors ask whether the same holds over function fields of characteristic p.

Their answer turns on the unipotent Brauer group of the variety, When that group vanishes and the Picard scheme has no p-torsion, only finitely many places can matter. When the group is nonzero, almost all places become potentially relevant instead. For varieties over a finite field, the exceptional set is empty in both cases. The proof leans on flat cohomology results of Bragg and Olsson. It also explains earlier findings on supersingular K3 surfaces as one side of a general pattern.
arxiv-2606-15567:
Yosia and colleagues study topological edge solitons in 2026 in a nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice that is parametrically driven and damped. Starting from a vertically driven pendulum chain, they derive an effective model whose stationary states sit localized at the lattice edge. In the conservative version of the lattice these edge states form one family; driving and damping change the picture.

The analysis reveals two phase-locked dissipative edge-soliton families growing out of the linear topological edge mode. Their stability differs sharply: one branch stays mostly unstable, while the other develops much larger stability regions with far weaker instability growth. Simulations show the robust branch can stay localized for long times even when it is weakly unstable. Runs of the full pendulum-chain model confirm the same edge-localized behaviour. Driving and damping, usually nuisances, thus become tools for making nonlinear topological localization persist in active lattices.
arxiv-2606-16167:
Mushkani argues in 2026 that debates on AI pluralism miss a deeper problem: systems do not just reflect values, they impose an ontology. An ontology here means the set of kinds a system treats as real: what counts as an entity, a harm, or valid proof. Pluralism is usually framed as serving diverse values, users, or outputs. He defines ontological flattening as squeezing situated, contested meanings into one fixed category treated as neutral.

His case draws on research on value pluralism, alignment, participatory AI, procedural justice, and accountability. Themes from 11 expert talks and three urban AI companion cases ground the analysis. The cases show pluralistic methods improving model behavior while still compressing kinds and revision rights before affected people gain standing. He proposes Pluralistic Lifecycle Governance as an early framework in response. Pluralism strengthens, he argues, when affected groups help set the rules and keep disagreement visible.
arxiv-2606-16367:
Santambrogio and Schulz prove in 2026 that solutions exist globally for a one-dimensional cross-diffusion system where species separate rather than mix. Cross-diffusion models populations or chemicals whose spread depends on each other's densities. With independent drifts added, the system is degenerate. The segregated states sought keep the species in disjoint regions, as competing species do.

The proof exploits the system's Wasserstein gradient flow structure. A Lagrangian version, written through the pseudo-inverse of the cumulative mass function of the summed species, reduces the problem to a parabolic equation resembling a p-Laplace equation. A minimising movement scheme builds approximate solutions step by step, and Minty-Browder monotonicity methods yield the strong convergence needed to pass to the limit. One argument covers all porous medium degeneracies, the log-entropy case, and fast diffusions with index between one third and one.
arxiv-2606-16667:
Xu and colleagues tackle hallucination in large vision-language models in a 2026 paper on reliable prediction. Such models often assert visual details that an image does not support. One remedy is selective prediction: verify each claim and stay silent when it lacks support. That guarantee has a steep cost, since a leading filter must abstain on most claims to keep errors very low.

Their method, called BCEA, adds a third choice beside answering and abstaining: look again. The model can zoom, crop or flip the image to gather more evidence, within a fixed compute budget. Naively adding this step breaks the statistical guarantee, they show, because calibration no longer matches deployment. Folding the whole looking policy into the score and recalibrating restores the guarantee while rescuing many claims. A single image flip, for example, lifts spatial-relation checking well above chance level.
arxiv-2606-16867:
Yanaka and Yamamoto revisit negation in language models in a 2026 paper on systematicity. Understanding not is a classic weak spot: a model that grasps one negated sentence should, if its knowledge is systematic, grasp the same sentence with roles swapped. The authors test this property from two sides, behavior and internal representation.

With demonstrations shown in context, models do learn to spot negation cues and their scope, the part of the sentence being denied, but never perfectly. Oddly, how hard scope recognition feels depends on the output format requested. On the representation side, the team asks whether function vectors, internal directions encoding a task, can be built reliably from examples. Vectors for extracting the negation cue compose well. Vectors for recognizing scope prove much harder to extract. Negation, the results suggest, is only partly systematized inside current models.
arxiv-2606-16967:
Sharma and colleagues trace a quasar wind from the black hole's doorstep to beyond its galaxy in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Quasars drive outflows that may regulate galaxy growth, but linking the fast nuclear wind to the galaxy-scale flow has been an observational gap.

The target quasar sits at a redshift near one, so its light left when the universe was half its present age. Integral-field spectroscopy from a ground telescope, survey spectra and space telescope absorption data are combined. Near the nucleus, absorption and emission agree on a wind expanding at constant speed, a few thousand kilometres per second, from about ten parsecs outward. By several hundred parsecs the flow has slowed, apparently loaded with interstellar gas it swept up. Beyond eight kiloparsecs it breaks out of the inner galaxy as a wide-angle outflow, slower still. Remarkably, momentum flux stays consistent across all scales despite the slowdown.
arxiv-2606-17067:
Gao, Wang and Liu hunt for dark matter axions around neutron stars in a 2026 astronomy paper. Axions are light particles proposed to solve a symmetry puzzle in particle physics, and they may make up the dark matter. In a neutron star's intense magnetic field, axions can convert into photons, producing a narrow radio line.

The team pointed FAST, the world's most sensitive single-dish radio telescope, at two nearby isolated neutron stars predicted to give the strongest conversion signals. They scanned the one to one-and-a-half gigahertz band, a specific axion mass window. No line appeared at the five-sigma level. The null result still bites: its coupling limit is the tightest yet in this mass range for the conversion-line method. Lab experiments constrain the coupling more strongly overall, but the astrophysical route is independent. Longer observations should sharpen it further.
arxiv-2606-17167:
Burić and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on heat and heavy states in conformal field theory, using the holographic link to a scalar field in anti-de Sitter space. Thermal one-point functions encode data about heavy operators, those built from many fields at once. That heavy regime is still poorly explored, even in the simple generalised free field case that mirrors a non-interacting bulk theory.

Using thermal inversion formulas, the team works out how the spectral density and coupling coefficients behave for heavy operators at fixed spin. They first solve the free case, then add first-order corrections from cubic and quartic interactions in the bulk. A striking outcome is that the large-weight formulas stay accurate well outside their expected range, already at middling weights. That robustness survives once the bulk interactions are switched on.
arxiv-2606-17367:
Vadlamani, Srinivasan, and Parthasarathy present a 2026 conference paper arguing that AI systems should be audited continuously in the wild, not just tested before release.
