Deployed systems are shaped by shifting environments, drifting data, and feedback from users and infrastructure. Sandbox benchmarks capture only a slice of that behaviour, so consequential failures can emerge long after the pre-deployment checks that were meant to catch problems of exactly this kind.

The authors frame auditing as a statistical monitoring problem over constraint violations under uncertainty. Properties such as fairness and safety become risk-controlled constraints that must be checked again and again as the system evolves. That framing highlights three needs: monitoring methods that respect uncertainty, socio-technical ways to state audit criteria, and infrastructure for ongoing oversight. The paper is a call to build principled auditing frameworks across the whole system lifecycle.
arxiv-2606-17467:
Pai presents a 2026 arXiv paper on defending enterprise language model agents against prompt injection hidden inside retrieved documents. Defences tuned on synthetic benchmarks fail on real files, Pai shows, because real documents are longer, denser, and laced with legitimate authority language. The test bed uses real filings, rules, abstracts, papers, and postmortems across finance, law, medicine, science, and DevOps work. That gives the evaluation a realism short synthetic attacks cannot match in length or camouflage.

The proposed pipeline, PARSE, sorts each sentence by injection likelihood, extracts structured facts before any rewriting, then checks that the facts survived. A directiveness gate sends most documents down a light path, concentrating effort on risky ones. Attack success fell well below the baseline rate while utility stayed near the undefended level. Paraphrasing, the best synthetic defence, showed no real gain here.
arxiv-2606-17567:
Su and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on boosting, the ensemble method that trains learners one after another on the errors of those before them. That habit breeds redundancy, since each new learner revisits error parts its predecessors already covered. Their framework, SCBoost, replaces residual fitting with residual orthogonalisation, forcing every learner to chase only the error component that points somewhere genuinely new relative to the ensemble built so far.

A spectral projection step purifies each training target against the span of past predictions during training. A second step sets ensemble weights on validation data with an explicit penalty on correlated members. Theory gives an exact split of residual energy under the projection, plus conditions where the signal-to-noise ratio improves. Across ten benchmark data sets, the method performed strongly out of the box on accuracy and F1 score.
arxiv-2606-17667:
Sun and colleagues present a KDD 2025 conference paper on learnable graph patches, a fix for the feature mismatch that blocks a single pre-trained graph model from serving many domains. Graphs from finance, biology, and social networks carry features of different kinds and sizes, so models trained on one rarely transfer to another without text to bridge them. The authors propose cutting every graph into learnable units, patches, treated as the smallest pieces of meaning any graph data can be built from across domains.

Their PatchNet framework unfolds node features into patches, encodes each unit, then learns how units combine into a whole graph. Because nothing in the design assumes a domain, pre-training can mix graphs from many fields. Experiments show transfer to varied downstream tasks, with gains growing as more pre-training data is added. The analysis also links PatchNet to existing graph models in the literature.
arxiv-2606-17767:
Kovacevic and colleagues present a 2026 workshop paper on talking to your health data instead of charting it, through an embodied conversational agent. Wearable dashboards hand users graphs and averages, then leave all sense-making to them, and engagement fades within months. The authors built a system where a virtual character discusses the user's own wearable data in dialogue. It voices trends as spoken statistics while deliberately withholding clinical advice. The study thus isolates what the conversational form itself adds to reflection on personal metrics.

Inside, one agent computes descriptive statistics and trends while a second presents them through the character. Five participants role-played health personas from a public data set, comparing dashboard browsing with the embodied conversations. The study tracks perceived understanding, the concreteness of actions people formed, and the shift from passive viewing to active sense-making. Early results suggest embodiment changes how people interrogate their numbers.
arxiv-2606-17867:
Scardace and Ravì map how different kinds of Alzheimer's disease markers relate to each other, in a 2026 quantitative study. Modern research combines molecular, structural, clinical, and genetic measures, yet how those layers overlap or add new information stays unclear. The team integrated tau PET scans, structural MRI, two cognitive scores, and APOE gene data from the ADNI cohort.

Across nearly eight hundred subjects, they measured shared information and explained variance between the data types to gauge redundancy. They linked tau patterns to shrinkage across brain regions, split the tau and cognition link into parts with and without shrinkage, and found one main degeneration path that tracks cognitive decline. The results argue for picking measures that add distinct biological signal rather than piling up inputs, which could cut patient burden and scan costs.
arxiv-2606-17967:
Cox and colleagues untangle what a speech model knows about words from what it knows about voices, in a 2026 paper from the University of Sheffield. Speech foundation models learn rich general representations from unlabeled audio, but the facts inside are smeared together, while tasks like speaker verification and keyword spotting each need only part of that mix. The team refines the model after pretraining to split the space apart.

Using an interventional dataset and a multi-part contrastive loss, they learn a transformation that sends content and speaker information into separate subspaces. The split representations improved speaker verification on unseen domains and gave clear evidence that the two kinds of information really do separate. Keyword spotting held its ground, and the training stayed small, with only a few dozen speakers involved.
arxiv-2606-18067:
Beals and colleagues coax stable light pulses out of some of the smallest optical resonators yet, in a 2026 photonics paper from Columbia University. Kerr soliton combs, trains of light pulses that yield many evenly spaced colors, power precision measurement, communications, and LIDAR when built on chips. Tiny microresonators, though, suffer thermal instabilities that make soliton formation erratic, especially at the low comb spacings applications want.

Working with tight-spiral resonators, the team demonstrates deterministic, highly stable soliton generation with comb spacings as low as the mid-teens of gigahertz. A thorough, experimentally checked thermal model explains how absorption and self-heating drive several distinct instabilities, from a transient one while entering the soliton state to shifts between states. With active thermal control guided by that model, the compact devices hold their solitons reliably.
arxiv-2606-18267:
Gholami Shiri and colleagues question a quiet assumption in algorithm benchmarking: that graphs which look alike also run alike, in a 2026 paper. Rather than grading shortest-path solvers on pooled averages, they map each graph into a low-cost structural feature space and cluster the graphs into landscape regions of similar structure. Three suites are studied, weighted random graphs, random geometric graphs mimicking wireless networks, and real road networks.

Four solvers, from plain Dijkstra to bidirectional and heuristic-guided variants, are timed across the map. Generator settings carve out stable structural regions, yet runtime often shifts significantly between graphs inside the same region, so structural similarity does not guarantee performance similarity. A merged analysis across suites shows each solver family owns different territory. The landscape view gives benchmarkers a finer instrument than leaderboard averages.
arxiv-2606-18367:
Wang and colleagues ask whether standard benchmarks for time series foundation models hide failures that only appear in certain operating regimes, in a 2026 machine learning paper. They test three such models on two widely used traffic speed datasets from Los Angeles and the San Francisco Bay Area, where traffic flips abruptly between free flow and congestion.

Judged by overall averages, the models look sound, but splitting results by regime tells another story. During transitions, forecast error rose to about eleven miles per hour against roughly three overall, and coverage of ninety percent prediction intervals fell as low as fifty-five percent in the hardest stretches. A simple historical baseline covered transitions better, though with worse overall accuracy. Their proposed mixture augmentation blends model forecasts with historical distributions, nearly matching that baseline's transition coverage while keeping the foundation models' accuracy, and they urge regime-aware scoring for future benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-18667:
Marin-Llobet and colleagues introduce a system that translates the firing of individual neurons in mouse visual cortex into plain-language descriptions of what the animal is seeing, in a 2026 neuroscience paper. Knowing what single neurons in higher visual areas encode is a long-standing problem. Their responses resist simple parameterization, and the deep-network embeddings used instead are black boxes that still leave researchers to guess the semantics.

Their framework Neurrator trains an encoder mapping spike trains from arbitrary subsets of simultaneously recorded neurons into the patch-embedding space of a frozen CLIP model. From there a multimodal language model narrates the scene, with no language-side training. Applied to Neuropixels recordings during natural movie viewing, one model narrates from thousands of neurons, a single region, a local population, or molecularly defined cell types. This lets the team measure how decoding fidelity scales with population size and region.
arxiv-2606-18767:
Hakimi and the team at LMU Munich attack language-model memorization by editing what neurons write, not whether they fire, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Models memorize and reproduce training sequences, creating privacy, copyright, and security risks. But existing mitigations zero out neuron activations. An activation only gates engagement, though. The neuron's output vector is what actually writes the memorized content into the residual stream.

Output vector editing locates the few MLP neurons behind a memorized continuation. It minimally rewrites their output vectors, to inject a distractor that redirects their contribution, while activations stay untouched. Mining over six thousand memorized sequences from the OLMo-7B model, the method suppressed up to eighty-eight percent of them. That is a wide margin over zero ablation on the neurons. Four edit modes in ensemble covered all but a percent of sequences. A residual share proved unreachable by MLP-only editing.
arxiv-2606-19167:
Chen and colleagues study teaching software engineering with large language models and the Model Context Protocol in 2026. Industry practice now embeds these tools in daily coding work, which pressures universities to update how software engineering is taught. The study tests a collaborative teaching model that brings language model and protocol-driven tools into lectures, code help, and engineering simulations that mimic real workflows.

Embedding the tools in daily teaching aims to close the gap between classroom instruction and industry practice. The authors report gains in student programming skill, practical problem solving, and fluency with intelligent engineering tools. Industry internship partnerships let students apply the same tools in real settings, strengthening the link from study to work. The work offers a practical path for reforming software engineering education in the AI era. It treats new tools as core workshop equipment for students, not as shortcuts to ban or ignore.
arxiv-2606-19367:
Ding studies how the Weibull weight-scale parameter evolves during AdamW training in 2026, building on a two-parameter Weibull framework for diagnosing transformer weight distributions. During training the scale grows, overshoots, and then relaxes. The paper asks which forces in the optimizer update drive that pattern.

A leading-order decomposition splits the squared weight norm into three forces. An alignment force measures correlation between weights and the adaptive update direction. An injection force comes from adaptive step size, and a decay force from decoupled weight decay. On self-trained small models with true optimizer moments, alignment dominates the rise phase, supplying most of the force budget across seeds. Near saturation, alignment and decay balance, which explains the shift from growth to relaxation. A spline method recovers the alignment force from sparse checkpoints at high accuracy, about twice a naive baseline, extending the analysis to real models.
arxiv-2606-20167:
Jonathan Hecht, Lukas Arzoumanidis, Ziyue Li, and Youness Dehbi extend contrastive learning for location encoders beyond two kinds of data at once. Their 2026 paper tackles a bottleneck in spatial prediction: labeled ground truth is scarce, so models pretrain by aligning coordinates with other data from the same place. Earlier methods tied coordinates to one extra modality, such as satellite images. Their two architectures, MELT and SALT, exploit several unpaired data types together.

Both systems matched the strongest two-modality baseline, SatCLIP, across four downstream tasks. Yet adding more modalities did not reliably help, suggesting the location encoder itself is now the limiting factor. The contrastive objective seems to peak early, whatever the diversity of pretraining data. MELT trained more stably than SALT and looks like the firmer base for scaling. The negative result redirects the field: better location encoders, not more data types, are the next lever.
arxiv-2606-20567:
Alexandra Antoniouk and Anatoly Kochubei prove that the heat kernel of the non-Archimedean heat equation is monotone in the operator's order. Their 2026 paper works over a non-Archimedean local field, such as the p-adic numbers, where distance is ultrametric. The kernel belongs to the Vladimirov-Taibleson operator, the standard fractional derivative in this setting.

Raise the order alpha, and the kernel shifts in one consistent direction. That one-way behavior gives comparison principles for solutions of the p-adic heat equation. Such orderings are basic tools for bounding solutions without solving the equation outright. The field gains a clean, usable fact about its most studied operator. The result is small, clean, and easy to use in practice.
arxiv-2606-20667:
Iacovos Ioannou and colleagues propose a quantum-assisted framework in 2026 for running hybrid renewable microgrids under hard deadlines. A microgrid mixes changing solar or wind power, steady dispatchable units, storage, and users who can be curtailed. Each control slot requires solving dispatch and coalition problems fast enough to act. Their framework uses belief-desire-intention agents, software agents that track beliefs and commit to intentions, extended for this setting.

Each dispatch problem is written as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, a standard form for quantum and classical solvers. A coordinator agent chooses among quantum, quantum-inspired, and classical solvers based on learned beliefs about their speed, committing to the solver expected to meet the deadline. A storage agent prices stored energy at a discounted future peak value. Solver choice matters because the best answer arriving too late has no value.
arxiv-2606-20867:
Duc Nguyen and many colleagues introduce FOCA in 2026, a framework that helps vision-language-action robot models learn from very few demonstrations. Such models are pretrained on large multimodal data. Under few-shot imitation, their performance drops sharply as demonstrations shrink. A stress test of current models confirms that weakness. FOCA responds by conditioning on the future, not only the past.

FOCA predicts task-grounded future interaction embeddings directly. It also aligns implicitly to future goal observations. Long-horizon reasoning then happens in latent space, without pixel-level prediction. Action-free training with synthetic videos from world models is supported. Results are strong: high success with twenty demonstrations on LIBERO, gains on RoboCasa, and up to twenty-six percent absolute gains on real robots. Data-efficient adaptation matters because teaching a robot by example is costly in human time.
arxiv-2606-21167:
Shengyi Wang gives an experience report in a solo 2026 paper on AI-assisted completion of formal proofs for CertiGC, a verified generational garbage collector. The proof development lives in the Rocq prover, formerly Coq. It extends the collector from an immutable setting to a mutable one. Remembered-set forwarding is added to the collection path. The top correctness theorem, a graph isomorphism result, must be re-established.

The central issue was not low-level proof scripting. Mutable updates break an old global assumption about backward edges. The proof is reorganized around a new invariant: every backward edge is recorded in the right remembered-set part. The work completes a long-running verification in a mature codebase, with the Rocq kernel as final arbiter. Reports of this kind show where AI proof help actually pays off in large verified systems.
arxiv-2606-21567:
Johanna Hennebichler and seven colleagues measure the moving Fermi polaron in 2026. A polaron is a quasiparticle formed when one impurity atom swims through a sea of fermions and drags a cloud of them along. Most earlier work studied the polaron at rest. Using a new Raman acceleration scheme plus precise radio-frequency spectroscopy on an atomic quantum gas, the team maps the polaron's energy across a wide range of momenta. Both attractive and repulsive interactions are covered.

At low momentum the polaron behaves like a dressed particle of constant effective mass, matching Fermi liquid expectations. At high momentum it turns back toward a bare, weakly interacting particle. In between, the attractive polaron abruptly broadens and leaves the constant-mass curve. That happens exactly where theory says it enters a molecule-hole continuum and stops being the ground state: a motion-induced polaron-molecule transition, caught in the act.
arxiv-2606-21767:
Gebru and colleagues address a stubborn bottleneck in chip design in their 2026 study of analog circuit layout. Advanced FinFET processes, a transistor technology with very tight design rules, make hand-drawn analog layouts slow and hard to repeat. Their paper asks whether layouts built from fixed-height rows can stay electrically sound while becoming far more automatic.

The proposed flow first shapes a row-height fabric from circuit needs and layout limits, then maps analog building blocks into rows of fixed height. Across several test circuits, the synthesized layouts matched less constrained custom designs on postlayout performance. The gap between schematic predictions and finished-layout results shrank by up to 68.5 percent in the best case. Most testcases also used less area, with the largest saving reaching 24.1 percent of the original footprint.
arxiv-2606-22067:
Mei and colleagues lay out, in 2026, a design study for spin qubits hosted in detector-grade germanium, the material developed for radiation detectors. The qubits would be hole spins bound to indium acceptor atoms added to the crystal. The paper is a theory-guided design, not an experiment, mapping the route from purity to a five-qubit architecture.

The proposed material pairs a residual impurity background near ten billion per cubic centimetre with a target indium density giving acceptor spacings of about 170 nanometres. A one-micrometre channel would then hold roughly five acceptors, forming a register selected after fabrication rather than placed by design. The authors analyze strain and disorder limits, coupling channels, fabrication, and scaling. Their central conclusion is that the material can in principle suppress bulk disorder enough for acceptor-hole qubits, while keeping all-electrical control; placement spread and charge noise remain the principal challenges.
arxiv-2606-22167:
Knyazhitskiy and Di Francesco explore, in 2026, early exiting for graph neural networks used in link prediction. Link prediction guesses which new edges a network will form, and deep graph networks spend the same computation on every node. Early exiting lets easy predictions stop at shallow layers instead of running the full depth.

Their approach uses no auxiliary losses to force early exits. Exiting instead emerges as an implicit property of the architecture itself. On the HeaRT benchmark, the method moves the speed-quality Pareto frontier for both GCN and SAS-GNN backbones. Inference becomes faster on many link prediction problems while losing little prediction quality. In some setups the early-exit models even win on quality. The result matters most for large-scale domains, where inference latency limits deployment.
arxiv-2606-22367:
Zhao and colleagues demonstrate, in 2026, single-photon time-stretch ghost spectroscopy, a way to record fast spectra far beyond detector bandwidth limits. Time-stretch spectroscopy maps wavelength to time, but detector bandwidth and timing jitter cap its sharpness, especially when photons are scarce. Their method adds programmable encoding patterns to the stretched pulses and rebuilds spectra by correlation, using a low-bandwidth detector.

The system reconstructs near-infrared spectra with 450 channels across the 1530 to 1590 nanometre band, without direct high-speed waveform capture. Compressive sensing allows recovery at sub-Nyquist sampling rates, enabling operation at 210 kilohertz. In the single-photon regime, the correlation step suppresses detector timing jitter. High-fidelity spectra are obtained at light fluxes down to 0.01 photons per pulse. The approach suits ultrafast, photon-efficient spectral work on transient events.
arxiv-2606-22567:
Na Sang, Ding Ma, Rui Sang, and Yuxuan Liu improve few-shot adaptation of the vision-language model CLIP in this 2026 paper. Prompt learning tunes small text prompts for new tasks from a handful of examples. Training on class names alone can overfit the base classes and weaken transfer to unseen ones.

Their method, Concept-Constrained Prompt Learning, anchors learnable prompts to frozen concept prototypes, richer descriptions from a concept bank. Shared context tokens are learned, and a cosine consistency objective pulls the class prompt embeddings toward the prototypes. Random concept dropout stops the model leaning too hard on any fixed concept list. At inference, prompt scores can be blended slightly with prototype scores. Against CoOp, it improved the base-to-new balance on DTD and EuroSAT and stayed near neutral on OxfordPets. Ablations show the text-space regularization helps consistently.
arxiv-2606-22667:
M. M. McKinnon reanalyses the polarization of two pulsars in this 2026 astronomy paper. Pulsars are rotating neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth, and each pulse's polarization probes the emission region. Recent models predict the angles trace arcs of small or great circles on the Poincaré sphere, the globe of all polarization states.

Two effects can draw those circles: a switch in dominance between two orthogonal modes, or a rotation of the vector as the modes' phase difference changes. In part of the profile of PSR B1133+16, the angles follow a great circle. Across PSR B2016+28 they follow an arc like a great-circle portion altered by the star's rotation. Three models give similar readings of both pulsars and point to mode transitions as the cause. Such transitions, the study shows, are not confined to the sphere's equatorial plane, and partial arcs may be more common than recognized.
arxiv-2606-22967:
Ivan Kryven and Elena Magnanini study clumping particles that also carry a location in a 2026 mathematics paper. The starting point is the Smoluchowski coagulation equation, which tracks how particles merge into bigger ones. Here each particle has both a whole-number mass and a place in space. When two particles merge, the child keeps the summed mass and one of the parent locations. The merger rate mixes mass and space through a product kernel.

Kryven and Magnanini give a recursive formula for the solution. They show that some local mass averages stay fixed until gelation, the moment a giant particle forms. Other averages follow a closed set of differential equations. For spatial kernels of Mercer type, that system turns into a replicator equation after rescaling time. Known monotone quantities of replicator dynamics then yield bounds on when gelation happens.
arxiv-2606-23467:
Quentin Reynard-Feytis and colleagues observe a prethermal solid echo in a nuclear spin network in a 2026 quantum physics paper. The system is a network of carbon-13 nuclear spins in diamond, hyperpolarized for strong signal. Pulsed spin-locking drives the network into a Floquet prethermal state, a long-lived regime with an approximately conserved magnetization. Inside that regime, the team watches the rotating-frame signal decay over a delay, then applies a single pulse. The magnetization revives at twice the delay time, a rotating-frame solid echo.

Reynard-Feytis and colleagues find the revival peaks at a specific pulse angle. Its envelope decays as a stretched exponential over about thirteen milliseconds. Analysis and toy simulations attribute the echo to Floquet micromotion shuttling coherences between operator subspaces. The pulse therefore inverts only part of the dephasing.
arxiv-2606-23567:
Xu and colleagues learn the best order in which a diffusion language model should reveal its own words, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Masked diffusion models generate text by unmasking hidden tokens step by step, in any order. That order shapes which decisions come early and which stay open. Most systems pick it with simple confidence rules that favor easy tokens and can steer the answer badly.

The team derives a bound on decoding mismatch. It turns order choice into a policy learning problem with a reward per step. Their method, Self-Aware Scheduling, trains a light policy while the main model stays frozen. On Sudoku puzzles, accuracy jumps from about eighty-two percent under the best heuristic schedule to about ninety-two percent, and higher after a second tuning stage. Gains also appear on grade-school mathematics and code tasks with a large diffusion model.
arxiv-2606-23667:
Wang and Liu test whether language models answer questions from a given table or from memory, in a 2026 paper on database question answering. Models now answer natural language questions over structured tables. When a table holds familiar real world facts, a correct answer might come from reading the table or from recalling pretraining knowledge. For database work the table must be the source of truth, since values may be private or hypothetical.

Their benchmark, ContraTable, pairs two databases with the same schemas and links. One holds real facts about countries, clubs, and players. The other changes selected attributes while keeping the structure identical. Two hundred fourteen matched questions span simple lookups, multi table joins, and reasoning over time. Strong models handle direct lookups well, but reliability falls as joins and comparisons grow. The accuracy gap shows models leaning on what they already know whenever table evidence clashes with familiar facts.
arxiv-2606-24367:
Barumerli and colleagues put a Bayesian model of how humans locate sound through formal statistical checks, then extend it to the full sphere. The model explains how listeners infer a sound's horizontal and vertical direction. They compare noisy perceived features against templates built from their own head-related transfer functions, the personal acoustic prints of head and ears. Auditory models are usually judged by performance metrics. This 2026 study instead writes an explicit likelihood for directional responses.

A complete Bayesian workflow follows. Parameter recovery on simulated responses confirms the free parameters can be pinned down. Recovery degrades for spectral and prior parameters at extreme values, though. Fits to data from thirty-three people, across three experiments, converge on clear estimates. The validated framework is then applied to an open question in the model's form. Analysis extends from a narrow region to bearings covering the whole sphere around the listener.
arxiv-2606-24567:
De Paepe, Bousse, and Visvikis accelerate a stochastic reconstruction method for CT scans taken from very few angles. Sparse view tomography cuts radiation dose and scan time. So few projections make the rebuild severely ill posed, though, and analytical methods streak. Plug and play methods marry data fidelity with learned image priors. Stochastic variants re-noise the iterate to match the denoiser's expected input, gaining robustness at the price of many rounds.

A multilevel version performs the coarse to fine work inside multiscale spaces, from wavelet decomposition. The key point is structural. In those spaces, the prior coherence correction that would otherwise demand repeated costly denoiser calls vanishes in expectation. The multilevel speedup thus avoids guessing fine level prior gradients altogether. The result targets the bottleneck of stochastic plug and play, its convergence speed, while keeping it robust. De Paepe's 2026 method targets clinical workflows, where dose is precious.
arxiv-2606-24867:
Jooyoung Cha, Yuya Sasaki, and Nelson Matthew P. Tan bound the standard errors of estimates built by combining data from several samples. Researchers often merge moments from different, possibly interdependent sources, like surveys and administrative records. The uncertainty of the combined estimates depends on correlations across samples, which may be unknown. Their methods construct lower bounds on the standard errors anyway.

Sharp explicit bounds come from geometric inequalities when nothing is known about cross sample correlation. For settings with partial information, the authors develop sharp bounds that stay computable. Those bounds are obtained by solving a simple semidefinite program. Three empirical cases show the method at work. Two are macroeconomic: menu cost models and heterogeneous agent New Keynesian models. The third is a two sample instrumental variable study in microeconomics. The bounds tell researchers the best precision their combined data could possibly support.
arxiv-2606-25167:
Inside a fusion reactor's liquid metal blanket, a plasma disruption can make the applied magnetic field collapse at around a hundred tesla per second. Oleg Zikanov, Haroon Ahmad, and Sergey Smolentsev model what that does to the metal flowing in a blanket duct, solving the flow with a one dimensional approximation.

The decaying field induces eddy currents in the metal. Those currents meet a steady cross field and produce a Lorentz force driving the flow. Standing Alfvén waves turn out to govern the response, showing up as large oscillations of velocity, induced field, and current that decay only gradually. The first few milliseconds are severe: speeds reach several metres per second and forces pass a billion newtons per cubic metre. Power law formulas capture how the response scales. Adding compressibility and pressure waves changes little.
arxiv-2606-25367:
Galaxies hosting an active nucleus, a feeding black hole, often stop forming stars, but crowded group surroundings also strip gas. Shuanghao Shu and colleagues separate those two suspects in 2026 using hydrogen gas surveys covering huge galaxy samples, matched with optical spectroscopy. They compare gas content and star formation for nucleus hosting galaxies against ordinary ones, splitting by position inside galaxy groups from centre to edge.

Nucleus hosts carried roughly ten times less cold gas and formed stars far more slowly than comparable normal galaxies, wherever they sat in the group. Satellite galaxies with active nuclei stayed gas poor even at the group's outer rim, before strong environmental forces could act. A seeming gas rise near group centres proved to be a telescope beam artifact. Internal feedback from the black hole looks like the first quenching step.
arxiv-2606-25567:
Augmented Lagrangian methods are workhorses for constrained optimisation, but the safeguarded variant's convergence theory had a gap where its multipliers might run away. Christian Kanzow and Jannis Krüger close much of that gap in 2026 for composite problems, where the objective splits into a smooth part and a nonsmooth part like a sparsity penalty. Under a new constraint qualification named after Polyak and Łojasiewicz, they prove global convergence to a stationary point of the right generalised kind.

Boundedness of the multipliers does the heavy lifting, and it rests on the nonsmooth part being locally Lipschitz. A counterexample shows that assumption cannot simply be dropped. Numerical trials on sparse portfolio problems confirm the split: with a Lipschitz sparsity term the method behaves far better, while the non Lipschitz term repeatedly produced seemingly unbounded multipliers in practice.
arxiv-2606-25667:
Spicules are thin jets that shoot from the Sun's surface layer and may feed the corona above. Each telescope, though, sees them at a different temperature. Ravi Chaurasiya, Tiago Pereira, and A Raja Bayanna combined three observatories in 2026 to follow the same jets across layers. A Swedish ground telescope watched in hydrogen light. A spectrograph sampled the transition region, and a space observatory covered coronal channels. Diagrams, spectra, and wavelet analysis track how the jets move, flow, and sway.

The chromospheric jets lined up with coronal brightenings that evolved in step with them. Flow speeds from the two spectral lines pointed in opposite directions. That mismatch signals plasma at several temperatures sharing one structure. Swaying motions clustered near three minute periods. Faster wiggles carried a mean energy flux the authors judge large enough to matter for coronal heating.
arxiv-2606-25867:
Stakeholders rarely state what software they actually need. They describe their work, and the needs hide inside the description. Mithila Sivakumar, Martin Lochner, Shiva Nejati, and Mehrdad Sabetzadeh built LENS in 2026 to surface those latent requirements from interview transcripts. Alongside extracting requirements that are stated outright, the system reasons over what people said together with facts about their organisation's tools and infrastructure. Inferred opportunities become user stories, each linked back to transcript excerpts so a human can audit the leap.

The preliminary industry test used twelve interviews from cybersecurity operations. Explicit requirements came out with an average F1 score near eighty four percent. The inferred ones faced the sharper test: domain experts judged them. Three quarters of the latent requirements were rated as offering useful automation or time saving potential. The results suggest interviews hold a second, unspoken requirements list.
arxiv-2606-26167:
Peng Chen and Jun Jing find a simple rule for near-perfect quantum measurement. A probe coupled to one helper qubit can, in principle, reach Heisenberg scaling, the best precision quantum physics allows. The question is when the coupling is shaped right. Their criterion is spare: restrict the probe-qubit coupling to one direction, or to two, and that suffices. The effective generator then reaches the Heisenberg limit.

Quantum Fisher information does the scoring under the rule. It becomes the mean square of the effective generator in the starting state. Two probes confirm the criterion. For a bosonic probe, precision about displacement grows with mean excitation number. Heating the probe can thus help, a counterintuitive bonus. For a spin ensemble, precision grows with the square of the spin count. Even warm, unremarkable states far from prized resource states show Heisenberg scaling.
arxiv-2606-26467:
Max Zhu, Martino Mansoldo, Ching-Hao Wang, and Stefan Groha introduce TabPFN-CFM, a causal foundation model. A foundation model is one large pre-trained system reused for many tasks. Causal models go beyond correlation. They predict what happens when someone intervenes in a system. From observational data alone, it predicts causal structure and outcomes alike.

The model answers questions at all three levels of Pearl's causal hierarchy. Those levels cover seeing, doing, and imagining what would have happened. It can also use a known causal graph when one is available. A causal graph maps which variables drive which others. Training used synthetic data sets, yet the model generalised to real ones. It beat baselines at both structure prediction and outcome prediction. A refined training procedure also cut training cost almost fourfold, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-26767:
Alfonso Zamora surveys e-polynomials of character varieties, geometric spaces that encode representations of groups. A character variety collects all ways a group can act through a matrix group, up to symmetry. Its e-polynomial is a compact fingerprint of its shape, built from Hodge theory. Computing these fingerprints mixes arithmetic, counting points over finite fields, with geometry.

Zamora explains mixed Hodge structures and the counting and stratification tools used in the field. Stratification slices the space by parabolic type, a measure of flag-like structure. A complete worked example computes the e-polynomial for the three-by-three matrix case with a free group. The stratification is then extended to any reductive group. Explicit formulas follow, and certain mirror symmetry conjectures for these spaces are reduced to checkable forms.
arxiv-2606-27567:
Pant, Lohani, and Kumar prove that prompt injection in shared-embedding language models is not a bug to patch but a structural limit. Prompted systems are formalised as models whose outputs include control actions: refusals, tool authorisations, policy routing, memory writes. A security property, Semantic-Faithful Control, demands that such behaviour depend only on the meaning of untrusted input, never on quirks of its encoding. The analysis asks whether any mechanism inside the shared representational pipeline can guarantee that property in this security paper from 2026.

Provenance recovery, telling trusted instruction from untrusted content inside shared representations, has a Bayes-optimal error fixed by the distance between the two distributions, nonzero whenever they overlap. Attention routes untrusted content through the same pathway that decides control outputs. A finite-coverage argument then shows no internal mechanism can guarantee perfect control faithfulness. The analogy is code-data confusion in classical computers.
arxiv-2606-27767:
Optimising over probability measures is now routine in machine learning. The Wasserstein space gives such problems a geometry. It measures how far apart two distributions are. Many objectives are non-convex along its geodesics, though. So standard methods resist analysis here. Clément Bonet, Pierre-Cyril Aubin-Frankowski, and Youssef Mroueh study a structured subclass in 2026. Their objectives split as a difference of two convex parts.

The team lifts the classical convex-concave procedure into this space. Under smoothness assumptions, they prove near-stationarity along the iterates. Two widely used functionals get explicit decompositions. They are Maximum Mean Discrepancy and Energy Distance. Both compare distributions in learning tasks. Local convergence of the scheme is also established. Tests compare against Wasserstein gradient descent. Well-chosen decompositions converge faster and more stably. The choice of decomposition matters greatly, the authors note. Designing decompositions automatically is left as future work.
arxiv-2606-27867:
Model checking usually verifies a distributed algorithm for one fixed number of processes. Parameterized checking asks for correctness at every number. Nathalie Bertrand, Pranav Ghorpade, and Sasha Rubin study a harder setting in 2026. Their algorithms are asynchronous and round-based. Each process has infinitely many states, since it can run for infinitely many rounds. The general verification problem turns out undecidable, already for simple specifications.

A reduction rescues practical verification. The problem reduces to LTL model checking over finite-counter systems. The reduction is proved sound and complete. Existing symbolic model checkers can then be used off the shelf. The authors apply the nuXmv checker to several algorithms. Safety and liveness properties of asynchronous consensus and leader-election algorithms are verified. The work opens a route from an undecidable problem to push-button checking.
arxiv-2606-28167:
L. Giusti, M. Saccardi, and D. Toniolo lay out a theoretical framework for recovering spectral densities from lattice simulations of quantum field theory. A spectral density links what experiments measure to a theory's inner dynamics, and it is hidden inside correlation functions that decay over imaginary, or Euclidean, time.

Giusti and colleagues give analytic formulas, built from integral transforms, that undo the Laplace transform and extract the density from continuous or sampled correlator data, including smeared versions used to tame noise. They show the lattice answer approaches the continuum one as the grid spacing shrinks. Because real lattices end after finite time, they add incomplete transforms and prove rigorous bounds on the unknown tail's influence, which also tell simulators how large a lattice a target precision needs.
arxiv-2606-28967:
Zou extends a recent exact approach to Maxwell's equations, the laws of electric and magnetic fields, from empty space to media carrying electric currents. A solution method based on Fourier expansions of the starting field had worked neatly when currents are zero. It had been used to study conservation laws and to build waves with chosen features. With currents present, the structure of solutions turns out to be far more tangled.

No clean closed form exists in general, but an algorithm can still build the solution. Two special cases do admit analytic solutions. The first assumes Ohm's law, where current density is proportional to the field-driven flow. The second adds skew-symmetric parts under a generalised Ohm's law, the Hall effect, where a magnetic field bends the current sideways. Zou also handles an added independent local field, and builds parallel electric and magnetic waves as an example.
arxiv-2606-29467:
Yi releases two benchmarks for medical retrieval-augmented generation, systems that fetch guideline text before answering health questions. The focus is maternal, neonatal, and reproductive health, an area that general medical question benchmarks barely cover. The questions reflect what a nurse-midwife actually asks in practice. No public benchmark previously graded how relevant each small text chunk is for such questions.

The first benchmark, mamabench, holds nearly twenty-six thousand questions filtered from seven expert-authored sources. Formats include multiple choice, short answer, and rubric-graded tracks. The second, mamaretrieval, pairs over three thousand clinical queries with graded relevance labels. Labels run from zero to six across a corpus of more than sixty thousand guideline chunks. A decomposed rubric separates chunks that truly answer a query from chunks that are merely on topic. Yi also measures and discloses the limits of the labels themselves.
arxiv-2606-29567:
Jathanna presents SurrogateShield, a privacy tool for people who query large language models through third-party services. Assistants normally send user text verbatim to outside servers, where personal data can persist beyond the user's control. The usual fix, placeholder redaction, blanks out personally identifiable information, or PII, but leaves the query mangled and the answers weaker.

SurrogateShield instead swaps each detected PII item for a locally generated, type-consistent surrogate value before sending, then restores the originals in the reply. No real PII crosses the network. Detection runs through a three-stage cascade covering twenty-two PII types, grounded in the k-anonymity framework. Mappings sit in an encrypted per-conversation store that never leaves the device. On a corpus of over a thousand queries, detection reaches a very high F1 score. Surrogate substitution beats placeholder redaction clearly on semantic utility. A prompted adversary model recovered no original values.
arxiv-2606-29867:
Mohan, Kriegl, and Schön present RoAd-RL, a library and benchmark for robust adversarial reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning trains agents by trial and error from rewards, but small adversarial perturbations, inputs crafted to mislead, can badly degrade a trained agent.

Research in this area suffers from scattered code and inconsistent testing, so RoAd-RL unifies policies, attacks, defences, and robustness metrics in one reproducible package built on Stable-Baselines3 and Gymnasium. The authors test three algorithms on LunarLander and a highway driving task across 192 attack-defence combinations. Robustness varies widely by setting, some popular defences do more harm than the attacks, and temporal smoothing, averaging behaviour over time, protects agents consistently well.
arxiv-2606-29967:
Konstantinos Metaxas and Themistoklis Sapsis study how a large population learns under risk. The players share resources in a congestion game. One action carries the danger of a rare extreme event. Players update choices with a risk sensitive multiplicative weights rule. A belief variable tracks how risky they judge that action to be.

Metaxas and Sapsis map this coupled system across two control parameters. They chart where behavior settles, cycles, or turns chaotic. Several stable states can coexist in some regions of the map. Closed invariant curves and chaotic attractors also appear in others. Attractors are long run patterns that motion follows over time. Time averages of paths still converge to the steady equilibrium. The risk belief creates phase locking regions called Arnold tongues. Special resonance points organize the whole bifurcation picture. Chaos appears and vanishes through cascades and crises along the way.
arxiv-2606-30067:
Byeong Yoon reframes continual learning as housekeeping for a model's spare parts. Neural networks usually forget old tasks when learning new ones. Yoon's method, Neural Subspace Reallocation, treats LoRA modules as stored memories. LoRA modules are small add-on weight sets for a frozen backbone. Instead of discarding them per task, the system files them away.

A recurring cycle compresses, stores, recalls, and reallocates these modules. Compression uses singular value decomposition to shrink each module. A TaskKnowledgeBank holds the compressed results for later reuse. Similar past modules warm-start new or returning tasks. Distillation during training protects the older tasks from damage. On Split-CIFAR-100, the bank cuts cyclic recovery time tenfold. On a five dataset benchmark, forgetting drops close to zero. A controlled study shows simple similarity retrieval does the real work. It matches or beats a trained reinforcement learning controller.
arxiv-2606-30267:
J. Dreckhoff, U. Schwarz, and L. Lettermann simulate how clathrin coats on cell membranes choose among three fates. Clathrin assemblies can persist as flat plaques on the membrane. They can abort after bending partway inward. Or they can close into coated vesicles that pinch off. What decides among these outcomes has stayed unresolved.

Their kinetic Monte Carlo framework couples individual clathrin agents to a membrane. The membrane is an adaptive continuum in the hybrid model. Coat stiffness and preferred curvature emerge during growth, not as inputs. Connected lattices stiffen because bending them demands stretching or compression. Newly added triskelia hardcode a history-dependent preferred curvature into the coat. An analytical theory of non-Euclidean elasticity predicts the growth laws. Simulations validate those laws against the theory. Two sequential energy gates produce flat, stalled, and closed coats.
arxiv-2606-30367:
Lingfeng Zhang and nine colleagues teach a navigation agent to predict how the world changes, not just which action to take. Vision-and-language navigation sends an agent through real spaces by spoken instruction. The agent sees only its own first-person view. Most models learn navigation as direct action generation. World states and their future evolution go unmodeled. FutureNav unifies both kinds of learning.

Text, visual, and spatial features are jointly encoded for the model. Four objectives train it at the same time. An action policy predicts the next navigation step. Inverse and forward dynamics objectives model state transitions. A future generation objective predicts upcoming spatial states. Inference speed is not sacrificed for this richer training. With only a four-billion-parameter backbone, results lead the field. FutureNav tops several navigation benchmarks against prior methods.
arxiv-2606-30867:
Juan Manuel Alcalá and seven colleagues set out the science case for SHARP, a near-infrared instrument planned for the European Extremely Large Telescope, aimed at young stars in harsh environments. Young stellar objects in low-metallicity regions and massive clusters, in the outer Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds, are too distant and faint for current instruments to study well. SHARP's extreme adaptive optics promise resolution about three times sharper than the James Webb Space Telescope, plus sensitive multiplexing.

Using the instrument's exposure time calculator, the team show the needed signal-to-noise is reachable for both continuum and emission lines, even for embedded objects beyond 5 kiloparsecs. SHARP should reach stars near 24th magnitude, study accretion, jets and disk dispersal, and probe objects down to about 0.2 solar masses in the Clouds.
arxiv-2606-30967:
Dan Nguyen, Karen Cao and four colleagues ask how far computed crystal proposals stray from how real materials were found. Computer methods now propose millions of inorganic structures. Yet no one had a calibrated sense of how experimental chemistry explores. The team placed 167,500 entries from a major crystal database in a similarity space. They split the space into groups and replayed discovery over time. Real discovery hugged what already existed: 82.9% of new formulas landed in existing groups.

The share of new groups fell from 40.2% in the 1930s to 2.6% in the 2010s. The groups also picked out nine golden ages, from cuprates to battery cathodes. The team projected computed sets onto the frozen past maps. Every computed set departed from the real basins, not just the AI-generated ones. They propose a score, built from closeness plus precedent, to triage proposals.
arxiv-2606-31167:
Sun and four colleagues present MIRTH, a framework that upgrades vision-language-action models for robot control. These models turn web-scale knowledge into physical actions. Single-frame designs have three flaws. They forget how a scene evolved, they jump from instructions straight to motor commands with no plan, and they decode actions one scalar at a time, which is slow.

MIRTH adds three pieces. Dual-scale temporal memory hubs compress long-term scene change and short-term motion into compact embeddings. Latent reasoning tokens, trained with a mutual-information objective, carve out a plan space between context and action. A parallel decoder predicts whole action vectors at once, raising control throughput. Tests ran on the LIBERO simulation benchmark and a real-world LeRobot platform. MIRTH reached state-of-the-art results on both, and it showed emergent error recovery, such as remembering an object hidden from view.
arxiv-2606-31367:
Papadopoulos and four colleagues tackle multimodal fact-checking on real social media posts. False claims often ride on images, yet most training data are synthetic and most benchmarks too tidy to match wild posts. Models also tend to check each mode alone or fuse everything blindly, missing how a post relates to outside evidence.

Their X-POSE benchmark gathers real community-noted posts from X and pairs them with full news articles found through vision-language search. Their TRENT model runs three cross-attention streams in parallel and fuses them by explicitly modelling entailment and contradiction, a method they call evidence triangulation. TRENT beats specialised models and commercial vision language systems across the tests. Data, code, and prompts are released for reuse.
arxiv-2606-31567:
Longpre and colleagues survey how flaws in deployed AI systems get reported, and build a better way to file them. Reporters often do not know what to send or where, and the groups that receive reports rarely share them onward. Good-faith reporters end up filling many forms while recipients get reports that are hard to triage.

The team survey twelve reporting systems from AI developers, security groups, and flaw aggregators, and find five recurring design problems, from discoverability to coordination. With feedback from 49 experts at 32 organisations, they build Flare-AI, an open-source system that works with existing ones. It gathers triage-ready detail through conditional logic and early classification, then can send one standard, machine-readable report to many developers at once.
arxiv-2606-31667:
Cruickshank and five colleagues show how to calm a driven quantum system that keeps heating itself. Periodic driving, called Floquet engineering, tailors artificial Hamiltonians in cold-atom simulators, but it also triggers parametric instabilities that excite sound-like phonon modes and rapidly destroy the condensate. Single-tone driving offers no separate knob to fix this.

Using a Bose-Einstein condensate of cesium atoms in an optical lattice, the team tests two multi-tone schemes: pulsed driving built from odd harmonics, and two-tone driving with tunable amplitude and relative phase. Both control the effective tunneling amplitude and Peierls phase independently while strongly reducing phonon excitation and condensate decay. Bogoliubov-de Gennes modeling and simulations confirm that the unstable modes are suppressed under the optimized driving conditions.
arxiv-2606-31767:
Etemadi and Su build tooling for a neglected benchmark area: patches that make Java programs run faster. Existing collections of execution-time improvement patches cover Python, C++ or .NET, and they are fixed sets that cannot grow. Java adds its own difficulty, since just-in-time compilation and garbage collection make timing noisy.

Their tool, JETO-Mine, crawls GitHub with user-set filters, wraps candidate patches in Docker images, and applies statistical tests for real speed gains. Running it produced JETO-Bench: 660 candidate patches and 91 hand-verified executable ones from 174 repositories. A leading coding agent, OpenHands, fixed only 14.3 percent of the verified cases in their trial, matching results seen in other languages.

arxiv-2608-00167: Rhombohedral Graphene: A Tale of Many Crystals, arXiv 2608-00167. The graphene tale. Readers can access the paper here. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
arxiv-2608-00367: Sylvester's Theorem and Reduced Linear Systems, arXiv 2608-00367. The Sylvester theorem. It stands as a research record. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
assemblies-al-hariri-chenery-1867:
Thomas Chenery gave English readers al-Hariri's Assemblies for the first time in 1867, and this is Volume I. The Maqamat, or Assemblies, follow the rogue Abu Zayd from town to town, living by his tongue. A narrator meets him in disguise after disguise, each time dazzled by a flood of rhymed prose.

Classical Arabic literature prizes few books higher for sheer verbal art. Sermons, scams, and courtroom turns of wit show off every trick of the language. Chenery's volume opened that virtuoso performance to the West, where Abu Zayd still tricks and charms his way through fifty assemblies.
athenaeus-mechanicus-wescher-1867:
Athenaeus Mechanicus wrote for generals who had to break city walls. On Machines, in the Greek and French edition of Carl Wescher from 1867, gives his manual whole. Wescher's volume gathers the Greek writers on siege craft, with Athenaeus at its heart.

The text tells how to build and use rams, towers, catapults, and screens against a walled town. It weighs old engines, faults the weak ones, and backs the strong with reasons. The voice is that of a working engineer, not a poet of war. Readers see Greek war craft through the eyes of the men who built it.
bagehot-english-constitution-1867:
Walter Bagehot published The English Constitution in 1867, first as essays in a review he edited. Bagehot, a banker and journalist, wrote while the Victorian constitution was working at its height. He asked a simple question: how does Britain's system actually run, behind its ceremonies?

Bagehot split the constitution into dignified parts, which win loyalty, and efficient parts, which do the work. The Crown and the Lords were largely dignified; the Cabinet, drawn from the Commons, was the efficient secret. That contrast made the book a classic of English political thought. Politicians still quote it, and students still start with Bagehot when they want the unwritten constitution explained.
beccaria-crimes-punishments-1767:
Cesare Beccaria's Essay on Crimes and Punishments appeared in English in 1767, three years after the Italian original. Beccaria, a young Milanese writer, attacked the harsh criminal law of his day. Secret charges, torture, and cruel executions were normal practice across Europe when he wrote.

Beccaria argued that punishment should prevent crime, not avenge it, and should fit the harm done. He opposed the death penalty and torture and demanded public trials and clear laws. Rulers and reformers across Europe read him, and legal codes began to change. This first English edition carried the founding text of modern criminology and penal reform to Britain and America.
brentano-psychologie-aristoteles-1867:
In 1867 Franz Brentano, then a young scholar, wrote his doctoral work on the psychology of Aristotle. Its heart is one hard question: what is the active intellect, the nous poietikos, that Aristotle says makes all things thinkable? The text here is the German original. No English version in the public domain exists.

Brentano reads the few dark lines of Aristotle on the soul with the care of a man who would wrestle them for life. Martin Heidegger later said this book set him on the road that led to Being and Time. It also marks the start of Brentano's own school of thought on the mind. The little thesis is a seed with two great trees in it.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Samuel Birch shaped the last tome of Bunsen's great work, Vol. 5 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in 1867. Bunsen had died ere the set was done. Birch, a chief of the script's study in London, built this tome of script lore and dig finds to back the claims made in the four that came first.

Sign lists, word lists, and plates of finds crowd the pages. It is a tool, not a tale. Digs and sages mined it for years for facts kept in one place. The set stands whole with it.
canadian-constitution-act-1867:
The British Parliament passed the act that created Canada in 1867, then called the British North America Act. Delegates from the Atlantic and central colonies had agreed on confederation at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec. Westminster gave their plan the force of law, joining the provinces into the Dominion of Canada on July 1.

The act divides power between a federal parliament at Ottawa and the provinces, each with its own legislature. It borrows Britain's unwritten habits, a crown, a cabinet, and responsible government, and plants them in a written frame. Four provinces founded the Dominion; the rest joined over the next century. Confederation's charter turned scattered colonies into a self-ruling nation in a single statute. Renamed the Constitution Act in 1982, when Canada gained full control of it, the text still anchors the Canadian state.
cia-0000007567:
Spring 1966 brought volume 10, number 2 of Studies in Intelligence, the CIA's in-house journal. One heading appears in transliterated Russian, Otvetstvennost za izmenu, a phrase tied to responsibility for treason or betrayal. That signals an issue engaging closely with Soviet material.

Handling Soviet texts forced analysts to weigh translation, law, and motive with care. The journal let officers share such case knowledge across the agency. For modern readers, the issue shows how deeply the Cold War contest ran through language itself. Its declassified pages preserve internal teaching from a year when the Vietnam commitment was growing fast.
cia-0000008367:
Reports reached the CIA in 1964 that the Pathet Lao may have executed a downed American pilot in Laos. The heading itself marks the claim as possible, not proven, and part of the title is deleted. Laos was then sliding into the secret war that paralleled Vietnam.

Accounts of this kind were logged even when proof was thin, because a man's fate was at stake. Analysts had to separate fear, rumor, and fact under wartime pressure. The file's caution is instructive: it records an allegation without overstating it. Declassification lets readers see both the report and its limits on the page.
cia-0000010667:
On January 2, 1959, the CIA issued a short estimate on the outlook for Sudan, then one of Africa's newest states. Sudan had won its freedom from British and Egyptian rule only three years before. A military government had just taken power in Khartoum, and its hold on the country was still untested.

The paper looks at how firmly the soldiers rule and at the old split between the Arab north and the south. It also weighs the politics of the Nile, the river Sudan shares with Egypt. The estimate captures a young state whose early troubles pointed toward decades of conflict.
cia-0000012267:
Translation was the quiet labor that made foreign secrets usable, and a CIA document from June 1960 preserves one piece of it. The file holds a letter translated from Russian, marked to be passed to the appropriate authorities. It belongs to the traffic around the Penkovsky operation, then in its early months of contact and testing.

The document records the letter's chain of custody as it moved from translator to reader. Each link in that chain mattered, since the colonel's words guided real decisions. For readers, the sheet honors the invisible work that turned a spy's Russian into Washington's knowledge.
cia-0000013867: Three American pilots were captured in Quang Binh Province, and a CIA note dated July 2, 1967, reports all three. The same note names Hon Co Island as a possible American target or post. Quang Binh's coast was flown over day after day. Losing three crews there shows the cost of that steady air campaign.
cia-0000014767: A speech by Vidali on January 27 anchors a CIA file on Trieste's pro-Cominform party, dated February 5, 1953. Vittorio Vidali was a famed Communist organizer with a long, hard past. His words in Trieste carried weight on both sides of the Cold War line. The file keeps one speech from a winter of sharp disputes.
cia-0000015267: Unidentified airborne objects were sighted near Leningrad, in a CIA file dated September 5, 1958. The place tag at the end is cut out as deleted. Leningrad was the Soviet Union's second city and a naval hub. A sighting near it drew the same care as one near a missile range. The Leningrad sighting file is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015367: Who in intelligence should handle non-conventional types of air vehicles fills a CIA file dated May 1, 1954. The title's stiff phrase was the office term for strange craft. Settling whose desk such reports landed on was real bureau work. The file shows the saucer question turned into charts of duty by 1954.
cia-0000015467: Saucers sighted over Spain and French Africa make up a CIA record dated in 1952. Two shores of the western Mediterranean appear in one short title. The pairing hints at reports gathered along sea and air routes between Europe and Africa. Like its sister entries, this one shows the 1952 wave being logged region by region rather than as a single world story.
cia-0000022367: A report on the conclusion of the Powers trial, with the American reaction to the sentence, fills a CIA record dated in 1960. The sentence was ten years, handed down in Moscow that August. American reaction mixed relief that Powers lived with anger at the trial itself. Holding both halves in one report served readers who needed the whole picture fast.
cia-0000022667: A returnee, name deleted, commented on the January 8, 1973, helicopter crash in Quang Tri country, a CIA record dated in 1975 reports. The province name is clipped in the title. A returnee was a freed prisoner, whose words carried first hand weight. His comments, kept two years on, helped test what truly happened to the men of that flight.
cia-0000022967: Police were now convinced that Baez had been murdered, an untitled CIA record dated in 1950 reports. The title gives no first name and no place, so none is added here. A police judgment of murder turned a missing man case into a crime file. Early Cold War reporting from the field often arrived this bare, a single hard line.
cia-0000036567:
Three American prisoners of war were captured in Cambodia, and a CIA record dated June 3, 1970 holds the report. The title ties the capture to July 1970 and to the wider POW and MIA problem. Cambodia had become part of the war, and Americans taken there were hard to trace.

The record preserves the capture as officials logged it, with the three men at its center. Reports from Cambodia mattered because the country sat outside the main prisoner lists. The war there was fought in the shadows, which made firm news even harder to get. Each new account gave searchers one more lead to check against the names of the missing.
cia-0000037167:
An American jet allegedly crashed on an island named in the title, and its two pilots were buried there, a CIA record dated September 1, 1972 reports. The report came while the air war over North Vietnam was still going on. Burial reports mattered because they marked ground that might one day give back names.

Inside, the claim joins a crash, a burial place, and a two-man crew in one short account. Wartime reports like this were filed at once, even when they could not be checked. Keeping them meant that later searchers, working in peacetime, would know exactly which island reports to test first when access finally came.
cia-0000042667:
ORE 55-49, titled Theory and Practice of Communist Subversion, is a CIA study dated January 2, 1950. ORE papers came from the Office of Reports and Estimates. The study was written as the Cold War was taking its lasting shape. Its authors wrote for an agency that was itself only a few years old at the time.

Inside, analysts set out how communist subversion was thought to work. Theory and practice are paired in the title on purpose. The file shows the early Cold War mind at work in Washington. It helps readers see the framework officials then used. Through it, they read strikes, parties, and revolts across much of the watching world.
cia-0000049067:
A briefing paper on right-wing terrorism in El Salvador, written in 1983, lays out the problem for officials who had to act on it. By then, death squads linked to the far right and to men inside the security forces had killed thousands of civilians. The paper belongs to the files later gathered for the Truth Commission.

Briefing papers boil a subject down to what a busy reader must know: who the groups are, whom they kill, and who protects them. This one's subject was the central obstacle to American policy, since aid to El Salvador kept colliding with the squads' murders. It shows analysts framing the terror as a system, not a string of mad acts.
cia-0000049167: The FMLN's own evaluation of its November 11 offensive, with revised military plans, fills a CIA item from 1990. The November offensive had carried the war into the capital's rich districts and changed the war's terms. A movement grading its own biggest battle, on paper, gave watchers a rare inside measure of the movement's strength and mood.
cia-0000049267: An update on the Jesuit killings is preserved in a CIA item from 1990, kept under the Truth Commission's eye. The updates formed a chronicle in pieces: arrests, statements, and silences, filed as they came. Read with its numbered companions, this one keeps the world's longest look at the case from blinking.
cia-0000075267: Rightwing Terrorism is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000075267, dated March 5, 1981, marked for the Truth Commission. The item takes rightwing terrorism as its whole subject in two words. It survives as a brief declassified record whose blunt title matches its topic, filed among the agency's Salvadoran-era materials on political violence.
cia-0000096667: Probable Political Developments in the West German Situation During 1952, with an extra digit in the catalog year, is declassified CIA document 0000096667, dated January 2, 1952. The heading promises a forecast for West Germany that year. Readers get a short declassified estimate item, its doubled final digit a small cataloging flaw worth noticing.
cia-0000097467: A cable to Leopoldville about a traveler called Iden going to Brazzaville with assignment instructions is declassified CIA document 0000097467, dated August 1, 1960. The heading is cut short at the instructions wording. The brief file is a travel-and-assignment cable record from the Congo summer, the person's name rendered only as Iden.
cia-0000100167: Soviet Union consequences of the alleged 1979 Sverdlovsk anthrax outbreak explored, in cut-short heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000100167, dated January 3, 1991. The word alleged does careful work in the title. Readers find a short consequences record in the anthrax cluster, framed around an outbreak the heading still calls alleged. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.
cia-0000102967:
USSR: Alleged Use of Forced Labor on Pipeline is declassified CIA document 0000102967, dated July 6, 1982 in the catalog. The sample text carries an August 21, 1982 date. It reports the Soviets denying West European accusations that political prisoners were building the Siberian gas pipeline to Western Europe.

The charge first came from a human rights group based in West Germany, and two governments sent their Moscow embassies to check it. A Soviet paper called it a dirty lie meant to disrupt deals with Western countries. Parolees, not political prisoners, did some pipeline work, the text says, such as building compressor stations.
cia-0000106267: Consideration of a False Coup by General Phoumi, Prime Minister Souvanna Phou is the heading, cut off mid-name, on declassified CIA document 0000106267, dated September 5, 1964. The title weighs a staged coup idea tied to General Phoumi in Laos. The prime minister's name breaks off before its final letters. The brief record is a coup talk item from Vientiane reporting.
cia-0000109067: Intentions of Student at Central University of Venezuela to Launch Anti-united is the heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000109067, dated September 6, 1967. The title tracks one student's intentions at one named university in Venezuela. What the student meant to launch breaks off at Anti-united in the heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000119767: With information as of 5 p.m. Eastern time on October 31, 1956, this CIA report covers Hungary eight days into the revolution. Fighting had paused while the Soviet answer took shape. The paper captures that uneasy calm from the crisis watch in Washington. Halloween fell inside the revolution's strangest pause, when Soviet troops had left the capital and no one knew if they would return in greater strength.
cia-0000124267: A September 1957 CIA item reports that Soviet artificial satellites would work on radio frequencies of twenty and forty megacycles. Tracking stations needed those numbers to listen for the new satellite's signal. The item preserves a small technical fact that let the world tune in. Knowing the frequencies let stations from Alaska to Australia join the tracking effort, turning a Soviet secret into a sound heard around the world nightly.
cia-0000126867: A March 1964 CIA document reports the Zanzibar situation as being under the control of President Karume. The revolution's leader was tightening his hold on the islands that spring. The paper records the state of affairs as it was reported to the agency at the time. Reported calm after a revolution was always provisional, and Karume's control of the islands would be tested by plots and purges in the years just ahead.
cia-0000126967: A July 1968 CIA report gives the postelection outlook in Panama. The May vote had been bitterly disputed, and the National Guard waited in the wings of the country's politics. The paper forecasts what the contested result would bring in the months ahead. The disputed May election led within months to the National Guard taking power outright. That makes this July forecast a snapshot of a democracy in its last season.
cia-0000132567: A Uruguayan political leader praising Castro fills a CIA item dated October 3, 1960. Castro still had open admirers across the Latin American left at that point. Not every politician in the region was running away from Havana in 1960. The short item notes the praise and its source, adding a small counterweight to the file's many reports of governments cooling on Cuba.
cia-0000132667: Peru breaking its formal ties with Cuba fills a CIA paper dated November 6, 1960. A paper the August before had foreseen just such a step from Lima. Now the break had come in fact. One more capital shut its embassy in Havana that fall. The short paper records the break and the steps Peru took to carry it out.
cia-0000132767:
A companion to another June 4, 1960 paper, this CIA briefing returns to Cuba as seizures of American property accelerated. Two papers on one day suggest editors wanted the story told from more than one angle. The summer of 1960 was becoming a season of takeovers.

Read beside its companion, the briefing shows the agency's alarm compounding week by week: each new seizure answered by harsher measures in Washington. Together the pair mark the point where the dispute stopped being about single firms. The declassified text comes from the CIA Reading Room, via the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134267: The Castro government seeking a wide spread for its message fills item 11 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated February 2, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the word propa, short for propaganda. Havana's message machine was shifting into high gear that winter. The short item reports the push and the channels chosen for it.
cia-0000135867: Dated 1 November 1952 and now declassified, a CIA meeting record records a conference between two people, both names deleted, with an attachment kept in the file. All of it feeds into PBSUCCESS, the agency operation against the Arbenz government in the months before the June 1954 coup. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136067: Dated 1 March 1954, one CIA cable in the open files deals with following up opportunities in Medellin, a Colombian angle far from the Guatemalan target. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136267: The declassified CIA cable dated 1 May 1954 takes up a command message for CADICK reporting a general ultimatum to the enemy, the warning final. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136867: Names and addresses are requested in this February 1954 cable about a CIA-supported hemisphere anti-communist congress scheduled for Mexico City. The congress will appeal to all anti-communist groups but should naturally attract delegates politically influential in their own countries. Stations are asked for outstanding leaders who could be invited as speakers with round-trip paid, groups to receive invitations offering financial aid for a delegate's transport, and other groups to invite. No witting station agent should attend.
cia-0000136967: Sabotage efforts are reported in this cable dated 27 June 1954. Its older May cataloging is wrong. A situation report still rings true, it says. Despite overt reports, this is a rebellion, not a planned invasion. Liberation forces have done no bombing, the cable claims. But their sabotage groups have acted. Acts include oil storage fires. A bridge was blown forty miles outside Guatemala City. It stood on the road to Zacapa. Another office's telegram agrees in substance.
cia-0000137467: Timed at 1600 hours on December 10, 1961, document 0000137467 is a CIA situation report. It is the kind of short bulletin officers used to fix the state of a fast-moving matter at a set hour. The catalog leaves its year blank, but the date sits inside the title itself. No place or crisis is named in the record, so tying it to one event would be a guess. It is a snapshot from the Cold War's busiest years, kept in the Reading Room files.
cia-0000138967: European unity needs an integrated plan, this January 1950 letter argues. It concerns Economic Cooperation Administration support. Real assistance must run in all countries at once. The European field organization must fully back it. A survey of unity groups and persons is under way first. The writer shares one judgment. The European Movement is by far the most effective organ for political unity. He is skeptical of the European Parliamentary Union. The Kalergi group is practically non-existent, he believes. Strasbourg reports reached Washington through Ambassador Bruce.
