cia-0000139167: Office diary excerpts from the photo interpretation center fill this June 1978 file. They are resolutely mundane. One entry notes the value of working jointly with other offices. A speed letter went to the center's executive officer. Contact paper was provided for the 1968-1971 period. Some charts have no use for the center. An outstanding performance evaluation is noted. An employee applied for personnel office jobs. She cannot be promoted for lack of headroom. It is the intelligence bureaucracy's daily paper trail.
cia-03020467: December 21, 1955: the bulletin briefed leaders days before Christmas. The intelligence summary covered global developments as usual. The Cold War didn't take holidays. It retains its place in time. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-06627467: TWO CUBAN EMBASSY MEMBERS DISAPPEAR IN BUENOS AIRES - 1976/08/11, a CIA document. The vanished diplomats. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06810067: AGENCY SECURITY CLASSIFICATION COSTS ESTIMATES, a CIA document. The cost estimates. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
clement-alexandria-writings-vol-2-1867:
Clement of Alexandria was a Greek church scribe of the late 100s. William Wilson gave his Writings English dress in 1867. Book Two of the set holds the Stromata from Book Two to Book Eight. The Stromata are a vast mix of notes on faith, Greeks, and the right life.

Clement holds that Greek thought was a school that led men to Christ. He quotes poets, sages, and heretics in a great flood of lore. Faith, he says, must grow to true sight by keen study. The Stromata are a chief text for the first age of Christian thought.
crantz-history-greenland-1767:
David Crantz, a Moravian missionary historian, published The History of Greenland in English in 1767. The work runs to two volumes. Crantz drew on the records of the Moravian mission, whose brethren had lived among Greenland's Inuit people for decades.

Whales, icebergs, and northern lights fill his natural history. He describes Inuit hunting, dress, and belief in close detail for European readers. Mission history runs through the whole, earnest and detailed. Sea monster lore lingers at the edges of his sober pages. The book gives the Arctic world as missionary eyes saw it in full, ice, people, and marvels together.
dante-inferno-longfellow-1867:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow rendered Dante's Hell into English verse in 1867. His work was the first complete American translation of the Divine Comedy. Dante the poet walks as a character through his own grim invention.

Guided by the Roman poet Virgil, Dante descends through nine circles of the damned. The lustful whirl in storm winds, and the gluttonous lie in foul slush. Traitors lie frozen in ice at the bottom, near Satan himself. Longfellow's grave and stately verse carried the medieval masterwork to English readers. It let a new nation read the poem that has shaped ideas of sin and justice for six hundred years.
dante-paradiso-longfellow-1867:
Longfellow's Paradise closes his 1867 English Divine Comedy on a note of light. Dante now climbs with a new guide, Beatrice, in place of Virgil. The scene shifts from ice and fire to the turning spheres of Heaven.

Nine spheres rise past saints, mystics, and warriors of the faith. Each ring shines brighter as Dante nears the source of all light. The poem ends in a blinding vision of God that words can barely hold. Scholars call this part the hardest of the Comedy to translate well. In Longfellow's hands it turns into luminous English verse, theology made into pure radiance.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-49-january-:
Ice opens Volume 49 of Pepys's Diary, January 1667. It is a bitter, cold, frosty day, the frost grown old, and the Thames is covered with ice. Pepys lies long, then works all morning. On the Exchange he walks with James Houblon, the great merchant, speaking of their ill condition. Both doubt England can set out a fleet this year, and know the ill effect that must follow. The frozen river and the empty treasury belong together, and Pepys puts the talk beside the weather.

Winter business grinds on credit and promises. The office begs money; the yards beg men; the Dutch, everyone understands, will not wait forever. At home there are good fires and his wife's company. Readers get the dread before the Medway in this volume: a frozen, moneyless January in which the kingdom's defenders already know the summer's secret, and write it in shorthand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-50-february:
A misty river opens Volume 50 of Pepys's Diary, February 1667. Pepys goes down by water in thick rain, walks to Deptford from Rotherhithe, and keeps an appointment at the Bagwells' house. The wife is within, expecting him; the husband conveniently comes in and talks business while nothing is noticed. Pepys writes the visit in a salad of French and Spanish, the closest his shorthand comes to a blush. The Bagwell affair runs through these months like a smuggled cargo, half hidden in foreign words.

Above the mist, the kingdom's affairs are darker. The navy lies unpaid and unrigged after the Fire. Peace talks with the Dutch are beginning because England cannot afford a fleet. Readers get Pepys divided in this volume: the official watching his service go bankrupt, the man stealing afternoons in Deptford, both recorded in the same faithful, incriminating hand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-51-march-16:
Cold opens Volume 51 of Pepys's Diary, March 1667, cold after a spell of summer weather. Pepys is sent for to Sir George Carteret. The subject is the navy, its wants, and how to spend the little money in hand, some thirty thousand pounds against ten times the need. England's fleet is rationed in a deputy's office three months before the Dutch sail into the Medway.

The month is one long exercise in shortage: tickets unpaid, yards idle, and credit begged from goldsmiths. Pepys counts, warns, and goes home to his music because there is nothing else to be done. Readers get the arithmetic of disaster here. The Diary rarely shows its author helpless. March 1667 is the exception: a great administrator staring at a sum that will not stretch.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-52-april-16:
A garden walk opens Volume 52 of Pepys's Diary, April 1667. Pepys has the good fortune to walk with Sir William Coventry in the Whitehall garden. They read their melancholy letter to the Duke of York together. Coventry approves it, then says the quiet part flatly: peace is forced on them, for the fleet cannot be got to sea. The navy's second man is confessing bankruptcy among the flowerbeds. Pepys records the sentence the way he records prices, exactly, because he knows what it will cost.

April's entries live inside that admission. Ships stay laid up, seamen go unpaid, and the Dutch negotiate from strength. Pepys rides to Deptford and audits what is left. Readers get the prelude to disaster in this volume. Two months before the Dutch burn the fleet at Chatham, the Diary shows men who knew it could happen, and could not pay to stop it.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-53-may-1667:
An outing opens Volume 53 of Pepys's Diary, May 1667. His wife drives to the Park in a hired coach, incognito, with Will Hewer and his mother. Pepys lets them go and turns to money. At the Excise Office he meets the Cofferer and Sir Stephen Fox about the navy's cash. They agree on terms, then talk of the Lord Treasurer, Southampton, who is a little better of his illness. The old treasurer is dying, and with him the last hope of paying for the war.

May's entries count the cost daily: ships in ordinary, men unpaid, peace the only policy left. Pepys rides his rounds and takes his pleasures defiantly. Readers get the war's bankruptcy managed in real time here. A clerk with a perfect memory watches the state's credit fail in committee rooms, while his own fortune, built on fees and care, quietly passes another thousand.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-54-june-166:
A building plot opens Volume 54 of Pepys's Diary, June 1667. He hires Mr. Commander to find ground behind the office for a stable and coach-house. Hackney fares have grown so great that keeping a coach is now both honor and economy. The diarist who walked to work in 1660 will drive in 1667. Then, in the month's second week, the Dutch sail up the Medway. They break the chain at Chatham, burn the fleet at its moorings, and tow away the Royal Charles. Pepys's entries shake with the news.

He sends his wife and father out of London with his money. He expects the Dutch in the streets. Nothing in the Diary matches these days for fear. Readers get the kingdom's worst naval humiliation from the desk of the man who had warned, in April, that the fleet could not sail. June 1667 is his vindication and his nightmare in one.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-55-july-166:
A farmyard noise opens Volume 55 of Pepys's Diary, July 1667. A damned noise between a sow-gelder, a cow, and a dog wakes the house at nine. Nobody can afterward explain it. Pepys dresses, coaches sleepily to Gravesend, and inspects the new batteries rising there. After the Medway humiliation, England is fortifying the Thames at last. The guns he examines are the price of June's lesson, paid in earthworks and iron. He notes a plain fellow crying out his wares, and drowses home.

July ends the war. The peace signed at Breda gives England New York and a breathing space. Pepys audits the remains: prizes, arrears, and a fleet to rebuild from shame. Readers get recovery's first month here. The Diary's tone steadies as the batteries rise, its author already converting catastrophe into estimates, which was always his way of surviving it.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-56-august-1:
A bad dinner opens Volume 56 of Pepys's Diary, August 1667. At Sir William Penn's table he eats a damned venison pasty that stank like the devil. He learns it only when dinner is done. The pasty stands for the season: peace has just been signed at Breda, ending the Dutch war, and even relief tastes spoiled after the Medway. Pepys dines, jokes with the women, and goes home to an office full of unpaid bills and a service counting its burned ships.

August entries settle into the peace's arithmetic. Prizes are argued over, accounts disputed, and Pepys's coach-house rises behind the office. His wife, his music, and his growing library fill the evenings again. Readers get convalescence in this volume: a man and a navy recovering together from humiliation, one pasty at a time, while the Diary resumes the ordinary music of dinners, debts, and desire.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-57-septembe:
A glass of strong water opens Volume 57 of Pepys's Diary, September 1667. By water from the Tower at dawn, he calls at the Old Swan for the drink. He sends word for little Michell and his wife to dine with them today. He ferries a gentleman and lady to Charing Cross. Then to Mrs. Martin's, where two pair of cuffs wait for him. Peace is a month old. London is about errands again, and Pepys is visibly enjoying the ordinary.

September's business is inquiry business: the Medway reports are being written, and every officer sharpens his narrative. Pepys keeps his papers ready and his temper cool. Readers get the Diary's peacetime texture restored here. Strong water at dawn and dinner guests by boat: it reads like 1663 again, except everyone has survived plague, fire, and defeat since.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-58-october-:
A new servant opens Volume 58 of Pepys's Diary, October 1667. Pepys is pleased mightily with the girl they have got to wait on his wife. The girl is Deb Willet, destined to detonate the Pepys marriage within a year. This month she is only a pleasure: the household runs smoother with her in it. At noon Pepys dines with Sir George Carteret and the officers at Carteret's Broad Street house, over the great man's accounts, which Parliament is sniffing like hounds.

Autumn business runs on scrutiny. The Medway inquiry makes every navy man a witness or a suspect. Pepys attends, calculates, and keeps his own papers in perfect order against any summons. Readers get the calm before two storms here. The official reckoning gathers over the service. And a teenage maid is learning the house where she will soon cause its greatest scandal.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-59-november:
A dawn dram opens Volume 59 of Pepys's Diary, November 1667. He calls at Michell's on the waterside, drinks from the bottle, and does not see Betty. Then Whitehall, and Sir William Coventry's lodging, where the two men sit a good while alone. Coventry gives him the full of the matter: Albemarle's and Prince Rupert's narratives of the Medway summer, laid before the House yesterday. In them the generals fall foul of Coventry and of Sir George Carteret. The blame for June is being assigned, and Pepys's closest allies stand in its path.

November runs on defense: papers gathered, memories tested, friendships priced. The office works under a cloud of inquiry while London rebuilds around it. Readers get the Medway's political autumn here. The diarist listens, calculates, and writes the generals' attack into the record with the care of a man who knows his own name may be next.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-60-december:
Church opens Volume 60 of Pepys's Diary, December 1667, and Mr. Mills preaches a dull sermon. In the Pepys pew sits a great lady, afterward understood to be Lady Carlisle, a very fine woman in person. The diarist appraises her through the service, as he appraises everything. Then home, where young Will Hewer dines and the afternoon is spent reading. Christmas is coming to a house with a fine table and a master whose name is made. The war is over; the inquiries are the season's sport.

December's entries mix theatre, music, and Parliament's long reckoning. Pepys is rich enough to be generous, and known enough to be watched. His wife shines in new clothes. Readers get a Restoration Christmas here: sermons, plays, and paperwork. The city is two years out of plague and one out of ashes, celebrating like a convalescent who intends to live.
doe-osti-3375120-final-technical-report-: DE-SC0025667 got final-reported, and this DOE technical covers the report. The pages detail the final findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was final technical. The closeout was researcher. The DE-SC0025667 were technical. The researchers were closeout.
dumas-whites-and-blues-1867:
Alexandre Dumas published The Whites and the Blues in 1867, his late Napoleonic epic in French. The tale pits royalists, the Whites, against republicans, the Blues, from Valmy to the Consulate. It was his last great historical panorama, written in his sixties with undimmed narrative drive and zest.

Young Charles, a Strasbourg boy, follows the republican armies as drummer, spy, and growing witness. Royalist agents, émigré plots, and the Terror's shadow cross his path from Alsace to Paris in war. Bonaparte rises through the tale from gaunt artilleryman to First Consul of the French Republic in power. Dumas crowds the canvas with battles, marches, and cameo greats of the revolutionary age in France. The book shows his lifelong gift, making vast history feel like a friend's tale.
europmc-pmc10044767:
Maldonado and co-authors review the hallmarks of aging and the role of oxidative stress in a 2023 paper. Aging brings a slow decline in body function and a higher risk of diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and dementia. Scientists describe that decline through a set of shared hallmarks, or marks, seen across species.

The review focuses on oxidative stress, the damage done when oxygen-based waste overwhelms cell defenses. It links that stress to each hallmark of aging. The paper helps readers see aging as a set of processes that science can study and perhaps slow.
europmc-pmc10160267:
Kocak and co-authors present CLEAR, a step-by-step reporting checklist for radiomics research, in a 2023 paper. Radiomics extracts large sets of numbers from medical scans and uses them to guide care decisions. The field holds real promise, yet most studies stay in academia because methods and reporting vary too much to trust.

The checklist walks authors and reviewers through each stage of a radiomics study. Two major European societies endorse the text. Clearer reporting should help separate strong studies from weak ones and move the best methods toward patient care.
europmc-pmc10232367:
Lorach and a large team report that a brain-spine interface let a man with spinal cord injury walk naturally again, in a 2023 study. A spinal injury cuts the line between the brain and the cord regions that drive walking, which causes paralysis. The team built a digital bridge to restore that lost link.

Sensors on the brain read the man's intent to move, and a stimulator on the cord turned those signals into leg movements. He could walk with crutches and handle varied ground. The work marks a step toward restoring movement after paralysis.
europmc-pmc10287567:
Sikkema and a huge consortium present an integrated cell atlas of the human lung in health and disease, in a 2023 study. Single-cell methods can profile each cell in a tissue, but single studies cover few donors and often disagree on cell type names. Merging many datasets can fix both problems at once.

The team combined lung datasets into one atlas spanning millions of cells. They aligned cell types across studies and mapped rare and diseased states. The atlas gives researchers a shared reference for lung biology, asthma, fibrosis, and infection research.
europmc-pmc10372067:
Garrido-Trigo and colleagues mapped immune cells in the inflamed gut at fine scale. Two long-term gut diseases drive that swelling: ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. Patients differ widely in signs and in response to drugs, for reasons still unclear. The team read gene activity in single cells from human gut tissue.

The biggest gaps between patients sat in one cell branch, the myeloid cells. That branch holds macrophages and neutrophils, two types of white blood cell. A spatial scan then placed each subtype in the tissue. Place alone split macrophages into still more kinds. Garrido-Trigo also found a strong signal web between macrophages and inflamed support cells. The work points drug research toward those two cell groups.
europmc-pmc10384267:
Obidiro, Battogtokh, and Akala reviewed care options in 2023 for a hard form of breast cancer. The form is called triple negative, since its cells lack three known drug targets. Those targets are two hormone sensors and the HER2 protein. Survival rates for this form lag behind other breast cancers.

Chemo drugs stay the most used treatment, often before or after surgery. Obidiro also covers immune therapy, targeted drugs, and beam therapy. Two flaws limit chemo: cancer cells learn to resist it, and it harms healthy cells too. The review points to tiny drug carriers, called nanoparticles, as a way past both flaws. Trials of such carriers form part of the future outlook.
europmc-pmc10546867:
The GBD 2021 Rheumatoid Arthritis Collaborators tracked the burden of rheumatoid arthritis from 1990 to 2020. The disease is a chronic immune fault that attacks the joints. It brings pain, disability, and early death. The study spans 204 nations and areas, with forecasts to 2050.

In 2020, an estimated 17.6 million people lived with the disease. Rates per head had risen 14.1% since 1990. Women carried the disease at 2.45 times the rate of men. Deaths fell over the span, to 38,300 in 2020. Years lived with disability made up 76.4% of the total health loss. The team forecasts 31.7 million cases by 2050. Smoking was the one risk factor counted.
europmc-pmc10570367:
Verkhratsky and co-authors cast astrocytes as a new frontier for brain therapy in 2023. Astrocytes, also called astroglia, are support cells that keep the brain and spinal cord stable. They guard nerve tissue and join in its defence. In each brain disease, their acts can help or harm the outcome.

The review sorts their disease states into four kinds. Verkhratsky names swollen reactive states, worn states with lost function, cell death, and rogue forms that drive disease. States shift with the illness, its stage, age, and sex. The team walks through trauma, stroke, infection, epilepsy, and decline diseases. Each state may yield its own drug strategy, they argue.
europmc-pmc11019967:
Collins and a large team present updated reporting rules for medical prediction models in this 2024 statement. Prediction models estimate a patient's risk or diagnosis and guide care choices. The older TRIPOD rules from 2015 set the minimum for reporting such studies. Since then, AI methods have spread through model building, so an update was needed.

The new TRIPOD+AI checklist holds 27 items and replaces the 2015 list, which the authors say should no longer be used. It applies whether a model was built with classic regression or with machine learning. A shorter companion checklist covers study summaries. Each item comes with fuller explanation than before. The team states the goal plainly: complete and open reporting so readers can appraise a model and judge whether to use it.
europmc-pmc1141267:
Förstemann and colleagues identify a partner protein required to mature small gene-silencing RNAs in fruit flies in this 2005 study. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs, 21 to 23 letters long, that control target genes. They are cut to size in two steps by enzymes called Drosha and Dicer. The team tested a double-stranded RNA-binding protein called Loquacious, a relative of a human protein.

Loquacious proved necessary for Dicer-1 to process precursor microRNAs normally, they found. Silencing of a reporter gene and of an endogenous gene locus both failed without it. In mutant ovaries, germ-line stem cells were not maintained properly. The protein binds Dicer-1 directly, forming a working pair. The authors note every known Dicer-family enzyme in the fly is paired with such a binding partner. The finding completes the maturation pathway picture.
europmc-pmc11829167:
Major Depressive Disorder Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium led a huge 2025 study of depression genes. The team combined data from 29 countries. Their sample held about 689,000 people with major depression. A control group held more than 4.3 million people without it.

Across the genome, the team found 697 links at 635 places. Nearly 300 of those places were new. Many links point to brain cells and to drug targets now in use. Scores built from the data predicted depression risk across ancestries. The findings open new paths for treatment research. Fine mapping also pinned down 308 genes with high confidence for follow-up work.
europmc-pmc11836267:
Liu and co-authors reviewed energy use in the body in 2025. Cells burn fuel through paths that free stored energy. Key paths break down sugar, fats, and amino acids. Others build energy carriers inside cell power stations called mitochondria.

When balance fails, disease often follows. The review links faulty energy use to cancer, brain disease, and immune disorders. Three master switches get close attention for their control roles. Liu also surveys new tools, from glowing probes to tiny materials. Those tools may turn energy science into new treatments. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1253667:
Hauser and co-authors tracked urine phthalate levels in men over three months in 2004. Eleven men gave up to nine urine samples each. Eight breakdown products were measured with precise lab methods. The goal was judging whether one sample can represent average exposure.

Five products appeared often across samples. Monoethyl phthalate showed in every single sample. Four others appeared in over 90 percent of samples. Levels swung a lot within the same man over time. Hauser quantifies how much a single sample can misclassify exposure. That matters for any study tying phthalates to health.
europmc-pmc1282567:
Sommer made the case for immune gene diversity in wildlife studies in 2005. Conservation genetics usually tracks neutral DNA markers. Those markers miss adaptive change, the kind that affects survival. The major histocompatibility complex, or MHC, is her prime example.

MHC variants shape immune recognition and disease susceptibility. They also affect odors, mate choice, kin recognition, and pregnancy. Pathogen pressure likely maintains MHC variety over time. Two mechanisms dominate: advantage of mixed copies and rarity advantage. Sommer argues coding genes like MHC must enter conservation planning. It appeared in Frontiers in Zoology in 2005.
europmc-pmc1332667:
Wasserman and colleagues tested manganese in drinking water and child intellect in 2006. Inhaled manganese is a known adult nerve toxin. Drinking water effects were nearly unstudied. The study covered 142 ten-year-olds in Araihazar, Bangladesh.

Their tube wells averaged 793 micrograms of manganese per liter. Arsenic in the same water averaged only 3 micrograms per liter. Children took adapted Wechsler intelligence tests at a field clinic. Scores were adjusted for social and social factors. Wasserman isolates manganese effects in a setting famous for arsenic. Blood tests checked lead and manganese in each child.
europmc-pmc1560167:
Health budgets force hard choices among treatments. Baltussen and Niessen argued in 2006 that those choices weigh many criteria at once: total health gain, fairness for the worst off, and urgent need. Policymakers often decide by gut feel or politics, dropping key facts.

Single-criterion tools each cover one slice, like cost-effectiveness or disease burden. The pair propose multi-criteria decision analysis, a method long used in other fields. It lays all criteria out in the open and weighs them together. Baltussen calls it a route to rational, transparent priority setting in health care.
europmc-pmc1847467:
Klamt, Saez-Rodriguez and Gilles introduced CellNetAnalyzer in 2007, a software toolbox for probing the wiring of cell networks without needing rate numbers. Many systems biology methods study network shape alone, called structural analysis. Tools existed for metabolic flow networks, but not in one package for signal flow as well.

The MATLAB toolbox handles metabolic, signaling, and regulatory networks in an interactive, visual way. It characterizes working states, finds dependencies between parts, and predicts the effect of blocking a node. Two new methods get detailed treatment. One computes the shortest positive and negative paths and circuits in interaction graphs. The other finds minimal intervention sets, the smallest changes that force a logic network into a wanted state. It extends an earlier tool named FluxAnalyzer.
europmc-pmc1874167:
Jobling and colleagues linked in 2006 hormone pollution in British rivers to disrupted sexual development in wild fish. Steroid estrogens from human waste pass through sewage treatment into rivers. Male roach, a common river fish, had shown feminized traits in polluted stretches, prompting a national risk check.

The team modeled exposure at 45 sites on 39 rivers across the United Kingdom. Their model combined predicted levels of three estrogens in each sewage outflow with the dilution in the receiving water. Sites were classed as high, medium, or low risk from those estimates. Measured sexual disruption in roach at each site tracked the predicted exposure closely. The match supports using such models to find where discharge cleanup is most needed.
europmc-pmc1880867:
Kowluru and Chan reviewed in 2007 the role of oxidative stress in diabetic retinopathy, the eye disease that tops the causes of acquired blindness across the developed world. Oxidative stress means reactive oxygen molecules outpace the cell's defenses. Diabetes raises that stress throughout the body.

High blood sugar boosts superoxide, a reactive oxygen form, and that rise may link sugar to the other metabolic faults that damage the retina's small vessels. Many diabetes-driven abnormalities in the eye appear swayed by the elevated stress. Animal studies show antioxidants can slow the disease's development. The few human trials so far gave mixed, ambiguous results. The authors call for controlled clinical trials before antioxidants can be recommended for diabetic eye disease.
europmc-pmc1924867:
Bland, Hugenholtz and co-authors released CRT in 2007, a tool that finds CRISPR arrays in DNA automatically. These arrays are direct repeats split by unique spacers, a layout that defeats general repeat finders. They draw interest because they likely defend bacteria and archaea against viruses and other invading elements.

CRT scans large DNA strings, from single genomes to mixed environmental samples, for the repeat-spacer pattern. Head-to-head tests compared it with two rivals, Patscan and Pilercr. CRT proved very reliable overall and beat Patscan clearly on precision, recall, and an overall quality score. Against Pilercr it improved recall and quality. On speed, CRT ran far faster than Patscan, while matching Pilercr on small jobs and beating it on repeat-rich genomes.
europmc-pmc2100367:
Mathers, Ezzati and Lopez explained the Global Burden of Disease framework in 2007, with a focus on neglected tropical diseases. Health priority debates need reliable, comparable data on what kills and disables people. Traditional sources are often incomplete and hard to compare. The framework uses the disability-adjusted life year, or DALY, which combines early death and years lived with disability into one measure.

They trace the study from its first version for 1990 through World Health Organization revisions for 2000 to 2004. A new Gates-funded round was starting in 2007. In 2002, ten neglected diseases together caused about 177,000 deaths, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa. They also accounted for roughly 20 million DALYs, which is 1.3 percent of the global total, and a risk assessment covered 26 global risk factors.
europmc-pmc2125167: A medical paper with a note on the pathogenicity of Trypanosoma lewisi. The parasite's harm. This article preserves that parasitology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125767: A medical paper with studies on blood proteins, the albumin-globulin ratio in experiments. The blood's balance. This article preserves that biochemistry. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128367: Treponemes that shun oxygen found a home on blood agar in this cultivation study. The researchers grew the anaerobic spirals on plate surfaces. The finicky germs, coaxed into growth. The article preserves that bacteriological method.
europmc-pmc2128567: A medical paper on some cultural characters of Bacillus abortus. The cattle germ's habits. This article preserves that bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
europmc-pmc2362067:
Melzer and a large team ran a genome-wide hunt for gene variants that set blood protein levels in 2008. Protein levels matter in many diseases, yet genetics work had focused on gene messages, not the proteins themselves. A spot where DNA variation tracks a protein level is called a protein quantitative trait locus.

They tested about 496,000 DNA variants against 42 proteins in blood from 1,200 fasting adults in an Italian study. Eight strong local effects turned up, each variant sitting in or near the gene for its own protein. The strongest involved the interleukin-6 receptor gene, with a significance level far beyond chance, written as a p value of 1.8 times ten to the minus 57. One distant effect linked the ABO blood group gene to an inflammation protein, but it vanished with a different test method.
europmc-pmc2386967:
Barger and colleagues tested whether a red wine compound mimics calorie cutting in mice in 2008. The compound, resveratrol, had extended life in worms and flies at high doses. Calorie restriction, eating much less, is the classic way to slow ageing in lab animals, but few people can sustain it.

Mice entered the trial at 14 months and stayed on their assigned diets until 30 months: a normal diet, a low resveratrol dose, or a restricted diet. Gene activity patterns overlapped strikingly between the two treated groups in heart, muscle, and brain. Both blocked gene patterns tied to heart and muscle ageing and prevented age-related heart decline. Resveratrol also matched restriction's boost to sugar uptake in muscle. The dose, 4.9 milligrams per kilogram daily, is one humans could realistically reach, the authors noted.
europmc-pmc2538567:
Wilson and colleagues traced the sources of campylobacter food poisoning in this 2008 study. The bacterium Campylobacter jejuni is the leading bacterial cause of gut infection in rich countries, and it lives in farm animals, wild animals, and water. Which reservoir feeds most human cases was disputed, so the team genotyped bacteria from 1,231 patients in Lancashire, England.

Using a method called multilocus sequence typing, they compared patient strains with strains from each candidate source and assigned cases by probability. Animals farmed for meat and poultry accounted for 97 percent of sporadic disease, with chicken and cattle the main sources. Wild animals and the environment explained just 3 percent. The authors argue the food chain is the route to block, through farm hygiene and safer food handling.
europmc-pmc2586367:
Beller and colleagues screened fruit fly genes in 2008 for controllers of lipid droplets, the fat storage particles inside cells, and found a vesicle transport complex in charge. Droplets store triglycerides and sterol esters for energy, and their surfaces are coated by PAT proteins that gate access to fat-burning enzymes. The team silenced genes one by one and used automated image analysis to spot droplets gone wrong.

Silencing the COPI complex, a coat machinery that ferries cargo between cell compartments, changed which PAT proteins sat on droplets. It also promoted docking of the lipase ATGL, the enzyme that starts fat breakdown, so COPI normally limits lipid storage. Two drugs that block COPI copied the effect, and the pathway proved conserved in mouse cells. The authors show vesicle traffic and fat storage are directly linked.
europmc-pmc2627667:
Cosivi and colleagues reviewed in 1998 zoonotic tuberculosis, human disease caused by the cattle bacterium Mycobacterium bovis, in developing countries. The World Health Organization projected 88 million tuberculosis cases and 30 million deaths for the 1990s, mostly in poorer nations. How much of that burden came from the animal species was unknown, because surveillance and control there were weak or absent.

In industrialised countries, cattle control programmes and milk pasteurisation had slashed M. bovis disease in animals and people alike. In developing countries the bacterium remained widespread in livestock, pasteurisation was rare, and risk factors for animal-to-human spread were present throughout the tropics. The authors warn that the HIV epidemic, concentrated in the same regions, could turn zoonotic tuberculosis into a serious threat, and they recommend actions to measure and control it.
europmc-pmc2631467:
de Wit, van Straten, van Herten, Penninx, and Cuijpers tested in 2009 whether the link between body weight and depression is U-shaped rather than straight. Studies had conflicted, some tying obesity to more depression, some to less, and most had only looked for a straight-line trend. The team analysed 43,534 Dutch adults aged 18 to 90 from a national survey of living conditions and health.

Both underweight and obesity were tied to depression. Together they formed a very clear U-shaped curve across weight categories. The link was significant at the 0.001 level or better. A straight-line test on continuous body mass index showed no association at all, which explains the earlier confusion. The curve differed slightly in shape between men and women, a trend the authors flag. Their conclusion is that both ends of the weight range carry raised depression risk.
europmc-pmc2683567:
Korkaya and colleagues examined in 2009 a signaling chain that keeps breast stem cells, and possibly breast cancer stem cells, renewing themselves. The chain runs through PTEN, a brake protein often lost in tumors, then Akt, then beta-catenin, a growth messenger. Stem-like cells are thought to seed tumors and survive treatment, causing relapse.

The paper gathers evidence that this chain acts as the stem cells' throttle. When PTEN is lost, the PI3-K/Akt pathway runs hot, a pattern tied to poor outcomes and drug resistance in breast cancer patients. In mouse prostate, PTEN loss swells the stem cell pool and starts tumors much like the human disease. The same wiring helps keep normal breast stem cells in reserve. Blocking the chain, the authors argue, could strike the tumor's root cells, the ones standard therapy misses, and make treatment last.
europmc-pmc2695767:
Kauder and colleagues showed in 2009 that chemical tags on DNA help keep HIV silent inside resting immune cells, the hiding place that defeats cure attempts. Even on strong drug therapy, the virus sleeps in resting CD4 T cells and rebounds when treatment stops. Screening a gene library, the team found a tag reader, MBD2, that enforces the silence.

Two tag-dense islands flank the virus's start switch, and in sleeping cells they carry methyl tags. MBD2 and a partner silencer, HDAC2, sit on one island. A drug that strips methyl tags drove both off and, combined with virus-awakening signals, reactivated the sleeper powerfully. The authors propose adding such tag strippers to therapy: wake the virus under drug cover, and the awakened cells can be cleared, a possible route to true eradication.
europmc-pmc2696767:
Nilsson and colleagues reported in 2009 that urine carries tiny tumor parcels whose RNA could betray prostate cancer without a biopsy. Tumors shed exosomes, small bubbles packed with molecular cargo, and the prostate drains toward the urinary tract. The team asked whether two known prostate cancer RNA markers could be found in exosomes filtered from patients' urine.

Both markers were there. One, PCA-3, is already used clinically as a urine test. The second is a fused gene, TMPRSS2:ERG, formed when two genes break and rejoin wrongly, a signature found in many prostate tumors. Detecting cancer RNA in a cup of urine, rather than in tissue snipped from the gland, promises diagnosis and monitoring with far less pain and risk. The authors present it as proof of concept: exosome cargo mirrors the tumor that shed it.
europmc-pmc2700967:
Chandrasekaran and colleagues measured in 2009 the natural statistics of spoken faces: how lip movements and voice sounds line up in ordinary speech. The brain merges sight and sound when we listen, but no one had precisely charted what the raw signals offer before the brain does its work. The team recorded speakers and tracked mouth shape against the audio, frame by frame.

Four regularities stood out. The area of the mouth opening tracked the loudness envelope of the voice closely. Its strongest partner was the resonance pattern of the vocal tract, the part of sound that distinguishes vowels. Both mouth area and voice pulsed in the same slow rhythm, two to seven cycles per second, the beat of syllables. And mouth movements consistently led the voice by 100 to 300 milliseconds. Speech, the authors argue, arrives pre-synchronized: the signal itself does much of the binding work.
europmc-pmc2714467:
Ye and Doak introduced MinPath in 2009, a stricter way to rebuild biological pathways, the chains of chemical steps a cell uses, from gene data. Common tools call a pathway present if even one step is found in a genome or a mixed sample of microbes. The authors show that loose rule inflates the count and overstates what a sample can do.

MinPath instead seeks the smallest set of pathways that still explains the protein families found, a principle called parsimony. On known genomes it cut many pathways that the loose method called and removed plainly false ones. On mixed microbe samples it also gave far lower, more faithful counts.
europmc-pmc2784367:
Rello and co-authors, with the H1N1 SEMICYUC Working Group, described in 2009 the first thirty-two adults admitted to intensive care in Spain with severe respiratory failure from influenza A (H1N1)v. The new pandemic virus could progress fast in the lower airways. They reviewed charts of confirmed cases whose illness began between late June and the end of July 2009.

The median age was thirty-six. About a third were obese, two were pregnant, and half had prior medical problems. Nearly all had primary viral pneumonia. Three quarters developed multiorgan failure, and three quarters needed mechanical ventilation. Six died within twenty-eight days, with two more deaths later. Antiviral treatment started two to eight days after onset. The authors warn clinicians to watch for lung complications, especially in pregnant and young obese patients.
europmc-pmc2796667:
Rehm and co-authors reviewed the full body of evidence in 2009 on drinking and tuberculosis. That lung disease caused about two and a half percent of all deaths worldwide in 2004. People had long noticed the two together, but the strength and direction of the link stayed in dispute.

Pooling the studies gave heavy drinkers roughly triple the tuberculosis risk of others, and the team estimated about one tenth of cases worldwide trace to alcohol. Alcohol weakens immune defenses, and heavy use also brings missed doses, poor drug handling, and social hardship that raise relapse and drug resistance. The authors treat heavy drinking as a true risk factor, not just a fellow traveler.
europmc-pmc2879567:
Lim and colleagues mapped in 2010 the gene activity of the cell types that build mouse and human breast tissue. They sorted four groups from mouse mammary glands: stem-enriched cells, early luminal cells that line the ducts, mature luminal cells, and surrounding support cells. Each group's active genes were read and turned into a signature.

The four signatures were sharply distinct, confirming the sort had captured real cell identities. Matched against the human counterparts, many genes and pathways proved shared across species, which validates mouse work for human questions. The team then used the signatures to interrogate mouse tumor models and ask which normal cell each tumor resembles. Shared circuits point to the likely cell of origin for several breast cancer forms.
europmc-pmc2966567:
Lateef surveyed simulation-based learning in medicine in a 2010 article, describing how guided practice in lifelike settings builds skill without putting patients at risk. The approach, borrowed from aviation and the military, swaps real encounters for interactive replicas.

Simulated training lets whole care teams rehearse procedures and teamwork until they master them, and it doubles as a measuring tool for team skills. It can also soften ethical tensions that arise when learners practise on real people. More medical schools and hospitals were adopting it, drawn by repeatable scenarios and room to fail safely.
europmc-pmc2967467:
Sanz-Arigita and colleagues applied graph analysis to resting brain scans of people with mild Alzheimer's disease in a 2010 study. Earlier work disagreed on whether the disease disrupts local connections or long-range ones.

Eighteen patients and twenty-one matched healthy volunteers rested during scans while regional activity coupling was computed. Patient networks kept normal local clustering, yet their characteristic path length drifted toward the values of random networks, a loss of orderly small-world layout. Regional changes mixed frontal increases with parietal and rear decreases. Overall synchrony, though, matched that of the control group closely.
europmc-pmc2987867:
Beran and Violato wrote a primer on structural equation modelling for medical researchers in a 2010 article. The technique tests relationships among measured and hidden variables at once, something like regression but with measurement error handled directly.

They lay out ordered steps for applying the method to a research problem, from theory through model checking. Three worked examples from health research show the range, from simple links to layered measurement models. With careful planning, they argue, the method can sharpen analysis and open fresh angles for medical and health science questions.
europmc-pmc3022767:
Roos wrote this 2010 clinical review of Huntington disease, a rare inherited disorder that damages the brain over time. It causes unwanted jerky movements called chorea, along with behavior changes, psychiatric problems, and dementia. Symptoms most often begin between thirty and fifty years of age, though a youth form starts earlier with school and behavior troubles.

One faulty gene copy is enough to cause the illness, and the fault is a repeated stretch of DNA that grows too long. Longer repeats tend to bring earlier illness. Diagnosis rests on symptoms, family history, and a DNA test. No cure exists, so care focuses on easing movements and mood problems with drugs and support. Most patients slowly need full time care, and chest infections are the most common cause of death.
europmc-pmc3038267:
Cognigni, Bailey, and Miguel-Aliaga showed in 2011 that gut nerves and body wide signals in the fruit fly jointly control feeding, water balance, and gut function. The gut is now seen as a regulator of appetite and metabolism, but mammal gut nerves are too tangled to untangle easily. The team built a simple measure based on defecation behavior to probe the fly system.

They found brain insulin producing cells that adjust appetite through a brain to gut circuit. A hormone system much like vasopressin proved essential for holding body fluids steady. Gut nerves also carried the changes in gut function that follow mating signals in females. The parallels with mammal gut and hormone control are striking. The fly now offers a fast, gene friendly model for studying whole body balance.
europmc-pmc3042667:
Zaragoza and many coauthors surveyed in 2011 the animal models used to study heart and blood vessel diseases, the leading cause of death in rich countries. No single animal copies a human condition exactly, since genes and environment both shape these diseases. Models range from mice and rats to large animals, each recreating part of a condition such as artery clogging or heart failure.

The review sorts models of artery disease into those where vessels narrow shut and those where weakened walls balloon out. It also covers heart failure models and the cost, facilities, and expert staff each option demands. Choosing the model that best fits the exact disease question matters more than choosing the most advanced one. With the right match, animal work can point to better diagnosis and treatment for people.
europmc-pmc3166167:
Ellen Yeh and Joseph DeRisi pinned down the one essential job of a malaria parasite's odd inner compartment in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. The compartment descends from an ancient alga and has no counterpart in human cells, making it an attractive drug target. Parasites whose compartment is disabled by antibiotics die a generation later, but what they actually miss was unclear.

Supplying a single chemical, a building block for a family of greasy cell molecules, rescued the disabled parasites completely. Nothing else the compartment makes proved essential during the blood stage of infection. The result simplifies the target enormously. Drugs blocking that one production line should kill the parasite, and the rescue trick gives researchers a clean way to study the compartment's other roles.
europmc-pmc3218867:
Craig Mermel and colleagues presented GISTIC2.0, a refined method for locating cancer-driving gene changes, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Tumors often gain or lose small stretches of DNA, and the challenge is pinpointing which genes inside those focal changes actually drive growth. Earlier tools struggled to separate those focal events from broad chromosome-arm changes.

The new version treats arm-level and focal alterations separately, which improves estimates of the background rate for each type. It also adds a probabilistic way to draw the boundaries of selected regions with a user-chosen confidence level. Together these changes make the calls more sensitive and more trustworthy. The authors validated the method on both real tumor data and simulated datasets with known answers.
europmc-pmc3219967:
Christopher Miller and colleagues introduced EMIRGE, a tool for rebuilding full-length ribosomal genes from short sequencing reads, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Ribosomal small-subunit genes are the standard ID card for microbes in a community. Yet assembling them from short reads generally fails, leaving researchers unable to say exactly which organisms are present.

Their method works iteratively, using an expectation-maximization approach that assigns reads to candidate gene sequences and refines those sequences until they converge. It also estimates how abundant each organism is. Tested on natural and simulated communities, the method recovered community structure, including gene sequences never reported before. The software was released freely online for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc3261167:
Paola Sebastiani and colleagues searched the genomes of centenarians for signatures of exceptional longevity, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Living past a hundred reflects both lifestyle and inheritance, and the team compared more than eight hundred centenarians with genetically matched healthy controls in a genome-wide association study.

From the data they built a model of just under three hundred genetic markers. It separated cases from controls with high accuracy in the discovery set. In independent groups its accuracy was moderate, and it worked better the older the subjects were. One marker near the well-known APOE region stood out decisively, though removing it barely dented the model. Most centenarians fell into clusters with different genetic signatures of differing predictive strength, three of which tracked with different lifespans, suggesting extreme longevity splits into genetic subtypes.
europmc-pmc3287467:
Zhao and colleagues compared computer programs that rebuild gene messages from short sequencing reads, in a study published in 2011. Labs use this rebuilding step, called assembly, when an organism has no reference genome to match reads against. The team tested how choices such as piece length, read depth, and stranded reads changed the results.

Seven program setups were tried, covering four tools used with a single piece length and three that combine several lengths. Combining lengths worked well across weakly and strongly expressed genes alike. One program, Trinity, scored well in most conditions but ran slowest, while another used the most memory. The authors turn these trade-offs into practical guidance and show improved assembly for a tea plant.
europmc-pmc3291367:
Luby and colleagues investigated how Nipah virus reaches people in Bangladesh, in a paper published in 2006. The virus first appeared in Malaysia in 1999, where sick pigs passed it to farm workers with deadly results. Bangladesh saw repeated smaller outbreaks from 2001 onward, each in the colder months, and the routes of infection there were less clear.

Evidence in the paper points to fresh date palm sap as one route. Fruit bats, which carry the virus, lick the sap as it collects, and people drink it raw. The genetic variety of viruses found in patients also suggests repeated jumps from wildlife rather than one chain of spread, a pattern that shapes how outbreaks there can be prevented.
europmc-pmc3338667:
Moran, Hansen, Powell, and Sabree took a deep census of the gut bacteria of individual honey bees, reporting in 2012. Earlier surveys, pooling many bees and reading few sequences, had found eight characteristic bacterial types in worker bee guts. With deeper methods, the team read hundreds of thousands of sequences from forty single bees kept at sites in Arizona and Maryland.

Nearly every sequence belonged to the known bee types, confirming a distinctive, stable community. Four types appeared in every single bee, though in varying shares. Community profiles still differed between colonies and sites, partly because some Arizona colonies carried two gut bacteria never before reported from bees. Single bees also hosted many distinct strains of the same type, and some strains clustered by location. The authors say this deeper view sets a baseline for studying bee health and colony losses.
europmc-pmc3349467:
Sinka and fellow malariologists assembled a global map of the mosquito species that matter most for malaria transmission. Rather than treating the disease as one uniform problem, they charted which dominant vector species occur where, drawing on occurrence records and expert knowledge across the endemic world.

The resulting maps show that a small set of Anopheles species drives transmission in each region, and that these species differ in habitat, biting behaviour, and susceptibility to control measures. Because interventions such as insecticide-treated nets and indoor spraying work unevenly against different vectors, control programmes should be planned around the local dominant species. Generic assumptions, the authors argue, are not enough.
europmc-pmc3355067:
Agren and co-workers built computer models of metabolism tailored to individual human cell types, at genome scale. Generic metabolic maps ignore the fact that a liver cell and a neuron run different chemistry. The team therefore applied their INIT algorithm to reconstruct which reactions are active in each tissue.

Feeding protein abundance data from the Human Protein Atlas into the algorithm produced active networks for 69 healthy cell types and 16 cancer types. Comparing cancer networks against healthy ones exposed metabolic features shared by tumours, which the authors nominate as possible drug targets. The collection is presented as a first step toward a Human Metabolic Atlas.
europmc-pmc3398667:
Liu and colleagues compared the major next-generation DNA sequencing systems in 2012, drawing on heavy hands-on use. Their institute ran more sequencing capacity than anywhere else, with well over a hundred machines from several makers. The paper reviews each system's technology and sums up first-hand operating data.

Systems from Illumina, Life Sciences, and Roche each carry distinct strengths and quirks in speed, accuracy, and cost. The comparison walks through sample handling, the runs themselves, and the computing that follows. It closes by surveying what the technology is used for, from decoding genomes to tracking germs. For labs choosing a platform, the review offers rare experience-based guidance.
europmc-pmc3404667:
Lepeule, Laden, Dockery, and Schwartz extended a famous air pollution study in 2012, following the Harvard Six Cities cohort through 2009. The study links fine particle pollution to earlier death, but critics questioned model choices and low exposure levels. Eleven extra years of follow-up brought cleaner air and a longer record to test those doubts.

Each standard step up in fine particles came with a clear rise in overall death risk, and larger rises for heart-related and lung cancer deaths. The relationship stayed straight down to quite low particle levels, with no safe floor in sight. Results held across different statistical approaches. Cleaner air, the team concludes, should keep paying public health dividends.
europmc-pmc3417167:
Lahnakoski and colleagues mapped the brain's social perception network in 2012 using movies instead of still pictures. Most earlier work used static faces, leaving real-life social reading poorly charted. Nineteen volunteers watched well over a hundred short clips inside a scanner while raters scored each clip for social features such as faces, speech, emotion, and pain.

One groove along the side of the brain, the superior temporal sulcus, answered every social feature and no non-social one. Four wider networks split the work: one for bodies, motion, and pain; one for faces and speech; one for pain and feeling; and a broad front-to-side system. The study shows naturalistic scanning can chart the social brain efficiently.
europmc-pmc3439967:
Shao and colleagues presented MAnorm in 2012, a method for comparing genome-wide binding maps between cell types fairly. The technique behind the maps, ChIP-Seq, shows where gene-control proteins sit on DNA, but comparing two maps quantitatively had few good tools. Without them, claims about cell-specific binding rest on shaky ground.

Their model normalizes two datasets against each other and calls true differences in binding strength. Those calls lined up strongly with changes in the target genes' activity and with the binding of cell-type-specific regulators. The method handles epigenetic marks as well as transcription factors. Simple and sturdy, it gives researchers a common ruler for a measurement the field makes constantly.
europmc-pmc3469467:
Comeron, Ratnappan, and Bailin mapped recombination across the fruit fly genome at fine scale in a 2012 PLoS Genetics paper. Recombination shuffles genes when sex cells form, and its rate varies along chromosomes. Past maps were too coarse to test how that variation shapes evolution. The team tracked the products of thousands of female meioses using millions of genetic markers.

They charted more than one hundred thousand recombination events, some narrowed to very short DNA stretches. Crossing over rates spiked and crashed sharply along chromosomes, and the hot spots differed between flies. Gene conversion, the second outcome, spread more evenly and appeared even where crossing over was absent. Comeron's group says future models of selection must build in these layers of variation.
europmc-pmc3474767:
Schellong and co-authors pooled studies on birth weight and later overweight in a 2012 PLoS ONE meta-analysis. Doctors have long claimed that conditions before birth shape adult weight, with birth weight as the handy sign of those conditions. No global test of that claim existed. The team gathered studies from many countries covering people from early childhood to old age.

Their pool held 66 studies and well over six hundred thousand people. Risk rose in a straight line with birth weight: babies born light carried lower later risk, while babies born heavy carried clearly higher risk. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors. Schellong's group argues that preventing overfeeding before birth could be a true route to preventing overweight.
europmc-pmc3483167:
Krstic and colleagues tested whether body-wide infection can set mice on a path like Alzheimer's disease, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2012. Inflammation inside the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's, but no one had shown that infections elsewhere in the body can start the process. The team gave pregnant mice and adult mice a mimic of viral infection that stirs the immune system.

Mice exposed before birth developed brain changes with age: lasting inflammation, buildups of a protein tied to Alzheimer's, altered forms of a second protein, and failing memory. A second immune hit in adulthood made the pattern far worse. In mice already prone to Alzheimer's, deposits formed right at the inflammation-driven buildups. Krstic's group suggests repeated infections may be a real risk factor for the disease.

The Combined Intelligence Committee estimated the enemy situation in the Pacific and Far East on September 9, 1944. The study ranges over Japanese politics, economics, and military strength. Economically, Japanese shipping was barely adequate, sinkings exceeded launchings, and fuel oil stocks might last only about nine months. Militarily, her air force had declined and her navy suffered serious losses, though ground forces kept their strength. The committee expected fierce resistance along the inner line from Japan through Formosa and Luzon to Mindanao, and a strong defensive posture in Manchuria against the Soviet threat.
frus-1944-quebec-d267:
The United States Chiefs gave their formal answer on British Pacific participation in C.C.S. 452/27, dated September 13, 1944. They would welcome a British naval task force in the Pacific to take part in the main operations against Japan. Two qualifications followed, and they were the sentences London would spend the next day's meeting trying to remove.

The force's initial use, the Americans considered, should be on the western flank of the advance in the Southwest Pacific. They also assumed the force would be balanced and self-supporting. The paper repeated acceptance of the separate British Empire task force under MacArthur. Brooke told the Combined Chiefs the British were disturbed by the statement, which predated the plenary session's warmer assurances.
frus-1944-quebec-d67:
President Roosevelt wrote to the War Shipping Administrator, Emory Land, on September 12, 1944, at Quebec. The catalog heading misspells the title as “War Shinning Administrator.” The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Land's agency allocated the merchant fleet on which every Allied plan depended, and Quebec took up the shipping terms of continued aid to Britain. A presidential message to the shipping chief during the conference ties the summit's grand questions to hulls and cargoes. For readers, it shows the President reaching from the conference table to the administrator whose numbers bound them all.
frus-1945-50-intel-d167:
A letter from the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) reached the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) on 4 September 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 167 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d267:
On 26 April 1948, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the Members of the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 267 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d367:
On 14 February 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 367 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d67:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 7 January 1946, as the intelligence settlement reached its final fortnight. McCormack's research and intelligence office at State stood to gain or lose much by the outcome. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A special assistant writing to his secretary at such a moment usually pleads a last point or reports a last danger. McCormack had built the State office from the OSS's research branch in four months, and its fate hung on the directive being drafted. Readers should read his January papers as the work of a man near the finish line. His own place beyond it was growing less sure. The new system, when it came, owed his office much and kept it little.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d167:
“General Balkan Policy” is the heading of a briefing book paper written for the President's trip. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The paper argues that the three chief allies should weigh the problems of Southeastern Europe against the welfare and safety of Europe as a whole.

Old lines are fading, the paper notes, as beaten satellite states pass under Allied Control Commissions and near the rank of co-belligerents. The danger is that one ally plants its own sway in a single country, or that the allies parcel out fields of sway between them. Merely standing apart from such deals is no policy, the paper warns. Washington must press the others to hold back, so each people can freely choose its own form of rule.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d267:
The Joint Chiefs told the President what they needed from Russia on 23 January 1945. Their memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sets out the principles guiding them toward Soviet entry into the war against Japan. It also reports how the Moscow talks stand.

Russia's entry, at the earliest date her forces can attack, is necessary for the Pacific operations. America will give the fullest support that does not weaken her own main effort. Russia's tasks are named. She is to defeat the Japanese forces in Manchuria. She is to join in air operations against Japan from eastern Siberia, and to cut Japan's sea traffic with the mainland. The supply project is moving well. Of 750,000 tons of dry cargo for the Siberian stockpile, a quarter million should be in American ports by 1 March.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d367:
Five subjects crowd the foreign ministers' table in Edward Page's minutes of February 7, 1945. Stettinius opened by asking whether any Dumbarton Oaks points needed clearing up. Molotov replied that the world security body had not been sent to the ministers for debate. He had a few questions, but was not ready to press them.

The ministers then turned to dismemberment. They weighed the surrender formula, and a commission to study how Germany might be broken up. France's place in the control machinery followed, tied to a French zone. Reparations closed the list. Page records a working lunch where the conference's hardest files changed hands.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d467: Only the handling of a telegram survives here, in notes attached to a message from press secretary Stephen Early to Jonathan Daniels, dated February 11, 1945. A notation in the Hiss Collection copy records that Early took the original at 10:30 that morning and said he would send it. By 1:30 p.m. the Map Room reported it sent. A copy from the Roosevelt Papers adds one change: release was to come twenty-four hours after the communiqué appeared, not forty-eight. The fragment documents the conference's news management rather than its diplomacy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d67:
Writing from the cruiser Quincy at sea on 28 January 1945, President Roosevelt updated Churchill on the hard journey still ahead. The telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Roosevelt was already traveling toward the meeting code-named Argonaut.

The approaches to the conference, he says, look much harder than first reported. His advance party will recommend how he should travel after Malta. He also agrees that Stalin should be told the schedule as soon as it can be fixed. The editors' notes add that earlier messages dealt with the Malta to Yalta flight and with poor travel conditions from the Crimean airport.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d167:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk reported a plea for a quick Trieste settlement in a telegram from Caserta on June 23, 1945. The message is document 167 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. General Morgan, the Allied commander on the spot, had sent the embassy a memorandum about Venezia Giulia, the disputed region around Trieste.

Morgan argues that now a military agreement on occupation is in place, a final settlement should be arranged as soon as possible. If the region stays reserved for late settlement, he warns, the Allies face a long stretch of Yugoslav penetration and propaganda west of the Morgan Line, with rising incidents. A prompt settlement by joint Allied action would impress European opinion, he holds, and ease similar problems later. He recommends taking the question up at the Big Three meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d267:
The British Embassy proposed reviving the European transport conference in an aide-mémoire dated July 11, 1945. The note is document 267 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Lancaster House conference on European inland transport had stalled, largely because the Soviet delegation would not sit with an unrecognized Polish government.

Now that Britain, the United States, and France have recognized the Polish Government of National Unity, London argues, the way is open. As host, Britain would tell Moscow it is urgent that the conference resume and finish its work. London is ready to invite a Polish delegation at once. But it wants assurance first. It wants to know the Soviet delegation, still in London, will be ordered back to full participation. That would happen once the Poles can take their seats. A similar note went to the other governments concerned.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d367:
Agreed reparations principles are announced in Pauley's top secret cable from Moscow of July 6, 1945. Weeks earlier, at the first meeting of the Reparations Commission's steering group, he had proposed a set of principles drawn from his instructions. After long talks, he reports, every delegate had now agreed to recommend them to their governments.

The first principle holds that removals for reparations should chiefly end Germany's power to make war. They would take out the factory capacity that counts as war potential. The next holds that reparations should speed recovery and rebuilding in the lands Germany had laid waste. The cable, relayed to Secretary Byrnes at sea, marked a rare three-power agreement in Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d467:
Future allied policy toward Italy is transmitted in Ambassador Kirk's despatch from Rome of June 27, 1945. He sends a report prepared in the Allied Commission for the Supreme Allied Commander, Mediterranean Theatre. Kirk suggests it be read with his embassy's reports urging a simple interim arrangement in place of the present armistice regime, and a Tripartite Economic Advisory Council.

The enclosed report, signed by Ellery Stone, opens by calling Italy a country at the parting of the ways. Defeated in 1943, she had been fought over and occupied for two years, and had suffered civil war in the north. Neither domination by the western allies nor a harsh peace, it concludes, fits a policy of preserving Italy as a bastion of democracy in the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d567:
An extract from a Belgrade wire of June 22, 1945, forms document 567 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. U.S. charge Harold Shantz sent it to the Acting Secretary of State. It quotes words Marshal Tito spoke the day before to a group from Trieste.

Tito told the group, in town for an anti-Fascist women's congress, that he had done all in his power. Yugoslavia, he said, was forced to submit to a great sacrifice with a heavy heart. The problem of civil government, he added, was still open. He vowed to fight for the rights of the people of Trieste and the Slovene coast. He also said Slovene and Italian anti-Fascists had a moral right to resist a return of fascist courts by lawful means.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d667:
Secretary of State Byrnes told Ambassador Caffery in Paris that Russia should be invited into the Tangier talks at once. The urgent secret wire of July 5, 1945, is document 667 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It reverses the earlier plan to keep the talks to three powers.

Byrnes argues the present talks have a narrow task only. They are to prepare the speedy replacement of Spanish control by a temporary regime. A later conference of all interested powers would settle the zone's future. Small nations, he says, have no reason to seek seats now, though their joining would draw no strong U.S. objection. It must stay clear that no plan for a permanent government of Tangier is to be drawn at these talks. Russia, he adds, could hold a position much like the one the U.S. sought for itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d67:
Edward Page, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote up a June 15, 1945 meeting with Soviet official Andrei Vyshinsky. His memorandum of conversation is document 67 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman came to raise the groundwork for the Berlin meeting of the Big Three.

Harriman told Vyshinsky that General Deane had orders from Eisenhower to get permission for an advance group to reach Berlin on June 17 and start the arrangements. He left a copy of Deane's letter on the subject and said he was ready to discuss the matter at any time. The short memo records the first formal American approach to Moscow about the conference's practical setup.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1067:
George Kennan cabled Washington from Moscow on July 24, 1945, about a Soviet letter on Greece. Vice Commissar Dekanozov had written to the British chargé, answering a British protest over Soviet press and radio attacks on the Greek government. Moscow sees no grounds for the charge, he wrote, since the journal in question is not an official Soviet organ.

Dekanozov then turns the complaint around. He cites a July 8 meeting in Athens where speakers attacked the USSR and crowds shouted slogans about marching on Sofia, Belgrade, and Moscow. Such speeches, he claims, grow more frequent and more extreme. Moscow calls the situation improper in a country hosting its British ally's troops.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1167:
The Soviet team set down this memorandum on 30 July 1945, in the summit's final stretch. Late Soviet papers tended to fix Moscow's terms as the bargaining closed. Once written and passed to the other teams, a memorandum became part of the formal record.

A paper of this kind could restate a demand, offer a draft, or mark a line that would not move. Readers can set it beside the final protocol to see which Soviet words survived. It is Moscow's stand, stated in Moscow's phrasing, days before the leaders went home. The American files kept it whole.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1267:
On 17 July 1945, the summit's opening day, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. A staff paper from day one set the armed forces' view before the team as the talks began. The chiefs' office worked in step with the conference from its first hours.

Opening-day papers framed the questions as the soldiers saw them. Later notes would react to the bargaining; this one preceded it. That gives it a clean value: the military view before the trades began. It is the first of the long chiefs-of-staff run in this part of the volume, and it sets the tone for the rest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1367:
Edwin Wilson, the American ambassador in Turkey, cabled the acting secretary of state on 19 July 1945. Turkey had stayed out of the war until its final months, then joined the winning side. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Ankara's post mattered because Turkey guards the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, a passage Russia had coveted for ages. Soviet pressure on Turkey was rising in 1945, and Wilson reported from the front of that squeeze. His cable shows how a regional strain reached Washington during Potsdam, where the straits question sat on the leaders' own table as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-67:
Cavendish Cannon, an embassy secretary in Portugal, reported a subcommittee's evening session to James Dunn on July 22, 1945. The memo is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subcommittee was working on the Yalta declaration paper's second and third sections.

Ambassador Gromyko and Mr. Golunko sat for the Soviet side. They said they were not prepared to discuss point 3 that evening. A Soviet paper on changes in the control commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary would circulate the next morning. It had to be taken into account on the subject, but it was not yet ready. The group therefore agreed to work on point 2 only, the press question. No report would go to the foreign ministers until point 3 had been considered. On the press point, the Soviets tabled a draft on easing entry for press and radio.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d767:
Document 767 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 24, 1945. It comes from the day the conference reached its midpoint. Staff used such papers to frame choices for the sessions ahead. The paper remained in the delegation files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

Midpoint drafts show a negotiation taking stock. Early claims have met resistance; new shapes are being tested. Readers can trace a topic's movement by its papers. The document adds one clear step in that chain. It also shows the quiet industry of the American staff, whose writing filled the hours between the leaders' meetings.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d867:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, sent this report to the Secretary of State on July 21, 1945. It passes on findings from the Intelligence Section of SHAEF's Psychological Warfare Division. The findings rest on a wide field survey of German opinion. The subject is how ordinary Germans viewed Nazis and Nazism right after the war ended.

The survey found that many Germans saw a Nazi as an outsider sent in by the Party. Blame thus shifted away from the person's own town. It also records the label Muss Nazis for people who joined from fear of losing jobs. On war guilt, answers ranged from true believers to people who blamed Himmler and the SS.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d967:
Britain's delegation drafted this reparations text at Potsdam on July 31, 1945. A note on the paper says the drafting committee was still at work on it at 11 p.m. Soviet claims would be met from the Soviet zone, and the USSR would settle Poland's claims from its own share.

Western claims would be met from the western zones and from German external assets, two points the Soviet delegate reserved. The USSR would also receive 15 percent of surplus western equipment in trade for eastern goods, plus 10 percent free. Removals must finish within two years. The amount to remove must be fixed within six months at the latest.
