frus-1950v07-d67: A 1950 FRUS editorial note on the U.S. request for UN Security Council action on Korea. The diplomacy moved fast. This note provides that context. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
frus-1969-76v32-d267: Another 1969-1976 FRUS editorial note from the SALT I volume on Kissinger's diplomacy. The negotiator. This note provides that background. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
gao-gaoreports-b-297367: Hera Constructive and Synthesis took their December 2005 contract fight to GAO as a joint venture, and this ruling is the verdict. The venture said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Joint ventures get the same full hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298767: Omega Systems took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-307767: The Interior Department's oil-for-cash program got a fiscal ruling in this November 2006 GAO call, which tests the royalty-in-kind preferences. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the crude-for-government deals were legally sound. The barrels had to follow the law.
gao-gaoreports-b-309267: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Relief of Accountable Officer at Veterans Affairs Medical Center. Decided January 15, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-310667: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Silynx Communications, Inc. Decided January 23, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-267: The border cops' trade software was coming along in 2005, and GAO's report says the new system worked, though the bosses needed to mind it. The review checks the code. The border's software deserved the polish. The polish had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-667: Working families' child care subsidies needed more data in 2005, and GAO's report says additional information was required. The findings demand the details. The report warns that the kids deserved counted care. The information had to come. The kids deserved counted care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-767: War on terrorism funding needed fuller accounting in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon should consider all requested funds. The findings demand the honesty. The report warns that the war dollars deserved complete counting. The funds had to be considered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-867: Amtrak's food service needed better controls in 2005, and GAO's report says improved management of the dining cars was required. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the rail meals deserved honest books. The controls had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-967: Sealed radioactive sources needed better DOE tracking in 2005, and GAO's report says the department needed better information for the recovery effort. The findings demand the data. The report warns that the hot sources should not go missing. The information had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-167: Trade negotiators needed better people management in 2006, and GAO's report says the USTR would benefit from strategic human capital principles. The findings prescribe the approach. The report warns that the deal-makers needed good management. The principles had to be used.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-267: HHS's cyber program needed full implementation in 2006, and GAO's report says the department had to complete its information security program. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the health agency's vault needed locking. The program had to be implemented.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-367: The Future Combat System needed a better business case in 2006, and GAO's report says an improved case was required for success. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the Army's techno-dream needed grounding. The case had to be improved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-567: Reallocating federal aid by headcount got simulated in 2006, and GAO's report models using statistical population estimates. The findings run the numbers. The report shows the funding map could shift with better counting. The simulations had to be studied. The funding map could shift.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-67: OMB's PART reviews sharpened agency attention in 2005, and GAO's report says the reviews increased focus on evidence of results. The findings give the credit. The report warns that the program grades needed honest backing. The attention had to be sustained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-967: The Biscuit Fire's aftermath got a GAO accounting in 2006, and the report analyzes the recovery project, salvage sales, and activities. The findings do the math. The report warns that the burned forest's ledger deserved scrutiny. The salvage had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-167: One-stop job centers were earning their keep in 2007, and GAO's report says employers found them useful for hiring low-skilled workers, though the performance data lagged. The findings balance praise and prodding. The report shows the job hubs worked, even if the scorecards did not. The centers deserved credit and counting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-67: Katrina's health billions got a GAO accounting in 2007, and the report tracks the allocation and use of the two billion for Medicaid and care. The findings follow the money. The report asks whether the sick of the storm got the help Congress sent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-167: Here GAO turns its audit lens on the SEC, the Wall Street watchdog, checking the agency's own books for 2007 and 2006. Outside auditors probed its accounts, money controls, and reports to see if the numbers held up. The report gives a formal grade on the agency's finances — a neat twist, since the SEC spends its days grading everyone else's books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-367: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at vehicle Donations: Selected Charities Reported Mixed Experiences after Changes in Vehicle Donation Rules. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-567: GAO published its findings on internal Revenue Service: Fiscal Year 2009 Budget Request and Interim Performance Results of IRS's 2008 Tax Filing Season in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-67: GAO's 2007 report finds the immigration cops needed clearer playbooks for deciding who gets sent home. With packed lockups and endless cases, officers had to pick — but the picking rules were thin. The report calls for crisp guidance so the life-changing call of removal lands the same way twice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-967: GAO published its findings on visa Waiver Program: Actions Are Needed to Improve Management of the Expansion Process, and to Assess and Mitigate Program Risks in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
hard-cash-pg3067:
Charles Reade called this novel a matter-of-fact romance, a fiction built on truths, and his preface of December 1868 defends the method at length. He lists his sources like a barrister: reports, blue-books, journals, letters, and living witnesses cross-examined. The prologue settles into the villa of the Dodd family outside the seaport of Barkington.

Mrs. Dodd, a well-born lady married to a merchant captain, is raising her son Edward and daughter Julia there. From that household the plot spreads to sea, to money, and to the book's famous battleground, the private lunatic asylum. Reade's madhouse chapters, drawn from evidence he offers to show any visitor, made the novel a campaign document against asylum abuses. Two chapters are both numbered XLI in the text, as the transcriber notes.
hughes-manual-of-pharmacodynamics-1867:
Richard Hughes sought to put homeopathic drug study on a firm footing in A Manual of Pharmacodynamics, first issued in 1867. Hughes, a leading British homeopath, asked a plain question: what does each drug actually do in the body? His answers bridge the remedy lists and daily practice.

Drug by drug, he sets out actions and effects in an order made for study at the desk. He weighs proving reports against wider medical knowledge of each substance. The manual shaped British homeopathy's more scientific wing, and its calm, testing tone still sets it apart from more dogmatic works of the school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublin-10167:
Lublin, a city of Russian Poland southeast of Warsaw, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal, Judah David Eisenstein, Joseph Jacobs, and Bernhard Friedberg. Jews lived there by the fourteenth century, confined to a suburb assigned in 1396. From the mid-1500s to the mid-1700s, Lublin was a center of Jewish life.

The article details special taxes, trade limits, and the licenses of 1596, when one hundred Jewish houses stood in the Podzance quarter. Lublin hosted meetings of the Council of Four Lands, the central body of Polish Jewry. It also records a riot in 1648 and the Cossack massacre of 1656, which killed most of the city’s ten thousand Jews. A protective charter of 1675 and later royal restrictions follow. Readers get a rich period history of a major Polish Jewish community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manne-mordecai-:
Mordecai Zebi Manne, a Russian Hebrew poet and painter, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Rodzkowitz, in the government of Wilna, in 1859, he had the usual Talmudic training. His father taught him Hebrew grammar. At thirteen he entered the yeshivah at Minsk. He died in his home town in 1886.

The article follows his turn from study to art. At Wilna he entered the school of painting and design while still at the yeshivah. In 1880 he enrolled at the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts in St. Petersburg. Two years later the grand duke Vladimir gave him a silver medal for extraordinary progress. His poems placed him among the foremost Hebrew poets of his day. One, Mas'at Nafshi, is still sung at Zionist gatherings. He also wrote a pioneering series of essays on painting and Jewish art. His collected writings filled two volumes, printed at Warsaw.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massarani-massa:
Massarani is the name of an Italian Jewish family traced from the fifteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The name comes from Massarano, a small town near Novara in Piedmont. Members of the family appear first as manuscript copyists. They then appear in Mantua, and later in Milan.

The most vivid figure in the entry is Bezaleel ben Samson Massarani. He worked to save Hebrew books when the Inquisition threatened them with destruction. He chaired the Mantua deputation that agreed at Padua to censor the Talmud in advance. He then went to Rome and won from Pope Sixtus V the right to print and own it in censored form. Around him the article gathers copyists, rabbis at Cento and Salonica, and a Milan lawyer of about 1850.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-b-david-10:
Meir ben David was a grammarian of the last third of the thirteenth century. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He survives only in the books of other men. His one known work, “Hassagat ha-Hassagah,” was a criticism of the grammatical treatise of Ibn Janah, “Kitab al-Mustalhak.” The work itself is lost; what remains is the passages Profiat Duran quoted in his own grammar, the “Ma'aseh Efod.”

Two more traces follow him. Joseph ibn Kaspi, who knew Meir personally, records in his supercommentary on Ibn Ezra an explanation heard from the lips of Meir himself. The editors judge him probably identical with a grammarian called simply R. David. Abraham Bedersi quotes a note of his on a verse of Job in his book of Hebrew synonyms. The entry is a small lesson in how medieval scholarship is recovered, quotation by quotation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-10667:
Mendes is one of the oldest Sephardic families. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 traces it across four continents. Cyrus Adler, H. Pereira Mendes, Joseph Jacobs, and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote the article. The family held on in Spain and its possessions long after the expulsion of 1492. Branches reached Aquitaine, Holland, Italy, and Turkey. The French branch was rooted at Bordeaux and Bayonne. It intermarried with the Pereiras, Da Costas, and Fonsecas. It produced municipal councilors and a president of the tribunal of commerce. Its earliest Bayonne tombstone dates to 1637.

The Holland branch produced writers. It produced the editors of the Sephardic ritual as well. Modern prayer-books still rest on that ritual. The American line runs through David Pereira Mendes. He fled Spain for Bayonne and reached Jamaica in 1786. The article follows his descendants onward. It ends with Abraham Pereira Mendes, the Kingston-born rabbi who died in New York in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyuhas-10767:
Meyuḥas was an Oriental Jewish family that produced a line of rabbis and writers for Jerusalem and Constantinople, traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by M. Seligsohn, M. Franco, and Joseph Jacobs, published in 1906. Four members get their own sketches, spanning the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Most of their books were printed at Salonica.

Abraham ben Samuel wrote homilies on the Pentateuch and responsa printed between 1784 and 1798. Raphael ben Samuel, chief rabbi of Jerusalem, published Talmudic and legal novellae at Salonica in the 1750s. His descendant Moses Mordecai Joseph, Jerusalem's chief rabbi from 1801, rallied the city's Jews to dig defenses as Bonaparte's army approached in 1799. Samuel Ḥayyim closes the line as chief rabbi of Constantinople in the 1830s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miphkad-r-v-ham:
Miphkad is a name in Nehemiah's wall-building list that may not be a gate of Jerusalem at all, as Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn explain in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nehemiah iii. 31 mentions it between the Horse Gate and the Sheep Gate, but the catalogue of gates in chapter twelve omits it. In Ezekiel the word marks the place by the Temple where the sin-offering was burned.

The name seems to mean an appointed place. Jerome translated it porta judicialis, the gate of judgment, which led Lightfoot to guess at the Prætorium's judgment hall or the Temple's east gate. Barclay identified it instead with the high gate of Benjamin at the Tyropæon bridge. A one-verse toponym that kept scholars guessing for centuries, in one compact note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monticelli-1096:
Monticelli, a small town in the province of Piacenza, got its Jewish community from a catastrophe elsewhere, as Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When the Jews were expelled from the duchy of Milan in 1597, the Soavi and Sforni families of Cremona settled here. They brought the German ritual from Lombardy and kept it ever after.

A society for nursing the sick and for study, founded in the sixteenth century, was still alive when the article was written. The numbers tell the later story: 143 Jewish inhabitants in 1865 had fallen to 32 by 1901. Flaminio Servi served as rabbi in 1863. A six-line entry, sourced to the Corriere Israelitico, for a community fading in place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-botarel-c:
Moses Botarel of Cisneros was a Spanish scholar of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries with a reputation for wonders. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied Cabala under Jacob Sefardi, and also medicine and philosophy. To him philosophy and Cabala taught the same truths in different words.

Botarel believed in amulets and claimed he could join the names of God for magic, so many took him for a sorcerer. He even let it be believed that Elijah had appointed him Messiah, and he wrote to the rabbis asking for their hard questions. Yet he also attended the Tortosa disputation of 1413 and 1414. His commentary on the Sefer Yezirah, made for a Christian scholar, was printed at Mantua in 1562.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-zeeb-wolf:
Moses Zeeb Wolf ben Eliezer was a Lithuanian rabbi born at Grodno at the start of the nineteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He first headed the yeshiva at Grodno. In 1813 he was called to the rabbinate of Tiktin, and in 1824 to Byelostok, where he died.

His Mar'ot ha-Zobe'ot treats the chapter of the Eben ha-Ezer on the agunah, the wife whose husband is missing. His Aguddat Ezob gathers homilies for holy days, with nine funeral orations added. His novellae on the Shulhan Aruk came out after his death, one part printed by his son at Warsaw. Three volumes of his responsa followed at Wilna in 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagari-moses-be:
Moses ben Judah Nagari was a philosophical writer who, by Steinschneider's reckoning, lived at Rome about 1300. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Even his name is in doubt: Steinschneider reads it Na'ar, from the Ne'arim family. Later bibliographers mangled it into Nagara, Najara, and Nigdi.

His one work is the Ma'amar ba-Ma'areket, an index to Maimonides' Guide with explanations of its philosophical terms. It was printed at Venice in 1574 together with Saul Cohen's questions to Isaac Abravanel. Because it looks like part of a larger work, it was wrongly called Kezat Bi'ure ha-Moreh. The entry spends much of its space untangling him from men of similar names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-mordecai:
Nathan Mordecai was a French doctor at Avignon. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the middle of the fifteenth century. Joseph Colon praised his medical skill in their letters. Colon gave him the honorific title of mori.

Between 1450 and 1456 Nathan ordered a full Talmud copy. The work copied was Meiri's Bet ha-Behirah, with his own marginal notes. Scholars identify him with several men of like names. One is the mathematician Mordecai Nadi. Another is an astronomer called the great luminary. Scribes copied Alfasi and Averroes for him in those years. The entry also warns against confusing him with Isaac Nathan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-angelo-:
Angelo Neumann was an Austrian director of opera. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Vienna on Aug. 18, 1838. He went on stage in 1859 as a barytone. He sang at Cologne, Cracow, Presburg, and Danzig.

From 1862 he sang at the Vienna court opera. In 1876 he became operatic director at Leipsic. There he staged Wagner's full Ring in 1878. No company had yet performed the cycle entire. The feat seemed impossible until he achieved it. In 1882 he formed a traveling Wagnerian company. Three years later Prague took him as theater director. Berlin also owes him its first Cavalleria Rusticana.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nizza-solomon-b:
Solomon Nizza was a rabbi of Venice. Isidore Singer and J. S. Raisin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Sage, Talmudist, and liturgical poet describe him alike. He succeeded his father Isaiah in the post.

His father wrote on ethics and on the Zohar. His grandfather had been rabbi of Padua earlier. Great Talmudists wrote to Nizza and printed his decisions. His formal approbations were sought after widely then. He taught Moses and Gershon Ḥefeẓ in Venice. A eulogy for Gershon came from his pen. His penitential poem holds eight rimed stanzas. The Roman rite sings it on New-Year's morning still.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orion-11767:
Orion is a group of stars seen in the night sky. The board and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word Kesil is held to name this group. Old Greek and Aramaic texts so render that word. They render it in Isaiah and in the book of Job.

In the Targum, the word is Nefila, which means giant. In the Peshitta, it is Gabbara, which means hero. Both names are held to point to Orion as well. The Talmud reads Kesil as Orion, the piece says. Jerome reads it that way in Amos and Job too. Some later sages read the word as the star Canopus. New scholars lean to the old view of the word. In Amos and Job, Orion stands by the Pleiades stars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palestine-holin:
The holiness of Palestine is its rank as a sacred land. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews hold the land dear as the land of their fathers. It was the cradle and the grave of the Patriarchs. It was the Promised Land of the old tales.

Many laws of Moses could be kept in that land alone. The holiness of those laws shone on the land itself. The Bible calls it a land God cared for at all times. God calls it my land, in the words of Joel. The phrase holy land stands just once in the Bible. The Mishnah calls Palestine the most holy of all lands. In law, that holiness may have ceased with the Temple's fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peach-prunus-pe: Peach trees came late to the Jewish sources of Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The fruit first shows up in the Mishnah. The plum, its kin, appears even later, in the Gemara. The entry gives just two source notes and stops there. It names no use, law, or story tied to the fruit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pethahiah-b-jac:
Pethahiah of Regensburg was a Jewish traveler of the twelfth century. He was born at Prague and traveled between 1175 and 1190. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His book is called the Sibbub, or Circuit.

He set out from Ratisbon toward the East. His road crossed Poland and southern Russia. It ran through Armenia, Persia, and Babylon to Palestine. Part of his notes were lost in Bohemia. Judah the Pious gathered what remained of them. The book was printed at Prague in 1595 and often after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinheiro-moses-: Moses Pinheiro was a leading follower of Shabbethai Zebi. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Leghorn in the seventeenth century. His learning won him great esteem there. He urged the Jews of Leghorn to believe in Shabbethai. Even after the apostasy came, he clung to the false Messiah. He taught Cardoso the Kabbalah and the Shabbethaian mysteries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontoise-12267:
Pontoise is a French town in the department of Seine-et-Oise. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish community lived there as early as the eleventh century. The entry follows that community through two hard centuries.

In 1179 the Jews of Pontoise were charged with killing a Christian boy. The boy, Richard, was honored as a martyr at Paris. A paper of 1294 names Jews of the town in a house sale. Their names were Sanson, Meuns, and Abraham. In 1296 Philip the Fair gave one Jew and his children to his brother. That same man later served as agent for the crown. He dealt with Jews of Amiens, Senlis, and Champagne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-elijah-b-m: Elijah b. Menahem Rapa was an Italian Talmudist of the sixteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He is also called Elijah Rapoport. He wrote Be'er Mayim Hayyim, printed at Corfu in 1599. That book treats Talmudic and other subjects. A second work, Erez Hefez, covers Bible and Talmud topics. No date is given for that second book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reischer-jacob-:
Jacob b. Joseph Reischer was an Austrian rabbi born at Prague. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was also called Jacob Back. He died at Metz in February 1733.

The article says his teacher Simon Spira gave him a wife. She was the daughter of Spira's son. Reischer served as judge at Prague, then rabbi at Rzeszow. That city's Jewish name, Reische, gave him his surname. Later posts took him to Anspach and Worms. From 1719 he served at Metz until his death. His many books comment on the Shulhan Aruk. They also include responsa, or legal answers, in three parts. The entry shows a working judge across central Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rings-12767:
Rings served Jews as ornaments and as signs of rank. Cyrus Adler and Albert Wolf wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Finger, ear, and nose rings appear in the Bible. Seal rings and dignity rings were known then too.

The article notes that neither Bible nor Talmud links rings to marriage. Betrothal once used money, a valuable object, or a document. The groom spoke a hallowing formula at that moment. About the seventh century the ring became frequent in betrothal. Roman influence in Palestine may explain that change. Betrothal and wedding were then split apart in time. Later both rites joined on the wedding day. The groom placed a ring on the bride's right middle finger. Jews did not exchange rings as Romans did. The entry traces one symbol's slow path to the wedding.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-herma:
Herman Rosenthal was an American author, editor, and librarian born in Courland, Russia, on October 6, 1843. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began as a printer and poet in Russia.

Rosenthal served in the Red Cross during the Russo-Turkish war and won its medal. He helped found Zarya, Kiev's first daily paper, in 1878. In 1881 he sailed to America to build farm colonies for Russian Jewish newcomers. Colonies rose in Louisiana and South Dakota under his hand. He also helped run the Woodbine colony in New Jersey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabbatical-year:
The Sabbatical year is every seventh year, when the land must lie fallow. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The jubilee is the fiftieth year, after seven such cycles.

Leviticus bids farmers sow and reap for six years only. In the seventh, none may harvest for private gain at all. Owner, servants, strangers, and animals alike share the soil's wild yield. A shofar blast on the Day of Atonement announces the jubilee year. Then hereditary land returns to its family, as the law commands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samfield-m-1306:
M. Samfield was an American rabbi born at Markstift, Bavaria, in 1846. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He earned a doctorate at Würzburg and ordination from Bamberger.

Samfield emigrated in 1867 and served Congregation B'nai Zion at Shreveport, Louisiana. In 1871 he was called to Memphis, Tennessee, and its Children of Israel congregation. He still held that pulpit when this entry was written. He helped found the United Charities of Memphis and its Hebrew association. He also founded and edited The Jewish Spectator, a weekly paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanballat-13167:
Joseph Jacobs and Ira Maurice Price wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sanballat. He was a chief foe of Nehemiah in the Bible. Nehemiah was rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem. Sanballat was called the Horonite. He worked with Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian. His home seems to have been at Samaria.

When Nehemiah announced his building plans, Sanballat mocked the feeble Jews. He gathered forces to fight Jerusalem. Five times he called Nehemiah to meet in the plain of Ono. Nehemiah refused and kept building. Sanballat then tried to trap him inside the Temple. That plot failed too. Nehemiah later found that a grandson of the high priest had married Sanballat's daughter. He drove the man out of Jerusalem. The article ends with Josephus, who tells a later, different story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiff-emil-132:
Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Emil Schiff. He was an Austrian journalist. Schiff was born in Raudnitz, in Bohemia, on May 30, 1849. He died in Berlin on January 23, 1899. He was a petty merchant's son. He studied law at Vienna University.

In 1871 Schiff became a political writer on Vienna's Deutsche Zeitung. He was among the first journalists to champion Schliemann's finds. In 1874 he moved to Berlin's Spener'schen Zeitung. For twenty-five years he reported Berlin for the Neue Freie Presse. He also studied higher mathematics at Berlin University. In 1894 he graduated in medicine, though he never practiced. Virchow read a memorial address for him. His learning, friends said, served truth in his reporting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbat-goy-134:
Shabbat goy names a non-Jew hired to do Sabbath tasks in a Jewish home. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the role. Such a helper put out candles on Friday night. On cold Sabbath mornings, the helper lit the oven or stove.

Often a poor woman did this work for a small payment. Strict law bars asking a non-Jew to break Sabbath rules for a Jew. Rabbis still allowed it in set cases, like heating homes in northern winters. Tales even replace the helper with a golem, a made being. The entry shows custom bending, carefully, around a strict day of rest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sheshbazzar-ass:
Sheshbazzar, called prince of Judah, led the first Jews back from exile to Jerusalem. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Cyrus granted the exiles leave to return in 539 or 538 B.C. A hard question followed about the royal succession.

Sheshbazzar may have been a son of the last king, Jehoiachin. That claim rests on matching him with Shenazar in Chronicles. At Jerusalem he fell into disputes with a conservative party. Scholars once identified him with Zerubbabel, but that view is now dropped. Few firm facts about him survive, the entry admits. He remains a shadowy first leader of the return from Babylon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silva-lucius-fl: Lucius Flavius Silva governed Judea in the year 73 and became consul in 81. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His hard task was taking the fortress of Masada. That desert stronghold was held by the Sicarii, Jewish daggermen. Silva accomplished that difficult capture, the brief entry records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sinaitic-comman:
Sinaitic commandments are laws said to have come from Moses on Mount Sinai. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Mishnah and the Talmud use that label for certain halakot. Yet many laws so labeled did not start with Moses. Some do not even rest on ancient tradition.

The Talmud itself shows the label was not always literal. Akiba once used it just to sharpen his pupils' minds. Other so-called Sinaitic rulings were debated and even set aside. Asher ben Jehiel said the phrase could mean a rule is clear. It was as clear as if Moses had received it on Sinai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-syracuse-14167:
Syracuse is a city in New York state on Lake Onondaga. Cyrus Adler and Godfrey Morse wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Jews first settled there in 1839. A warehouse hosted meetings for traders from nearby towns. In 1841 they formed a permanent religious society.

The Society of Concord first met in an upper room. In 1846 it bought a house on Madison Street. A new synagogue rose through Jacob Stone's efforts. Isaac M. Wise dedicated it in September 1850. Reforms under Dr. Deutsch split the congregation in 1864. The departing members formed Adath Jeshurun that year. More congregations followed in 1854, 1870, and beyond. The entry traces one upstate community's growth and splits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tausig-carl-142:
Carl Tausig was a Polish pianist born at Warsaw in 1841. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on November 4 of that year. His father Aloys, a Thalberg pupil, taught him first. He died at Leipsic on July 17, 1871.

At fourteen, Tausig went to Weimar to study under Liszt. He soon became Liszt's favorite pupil there. In 1858 Bülow conducted his orchestral debut at Berlin. Vienna rejected his classical programs in 1862, though. He settled in Berlin and opened an advanced piano school. Critics rank him with Liszt and Rubinstein. They call the three the century's greatest pianists. He championed Wagner's music of the future warmly. The entry mourns a master dead before thirty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-toy-crawford-ho:
Crawford Howell Toy was an American Christian scholar of the Orient and Hebrew. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Toy was born at Norfolk, Virginia, in 1836. He studied at the University of Virginia. He pursued Oriental studies at Berlin from 1866 to 1868.

Toy taught Hebrew at the Southern Baptist seminary in South Carolina. In 1880 he became Hancock professor at Harvard University. His books include The Religion of Israel, from 1882. Judaism and Christianity, from 1890, studies the two faiths with sympathy. He edited Ezekiel for the Polychrome Bible in 1899. A Proverbs commentary came the same year. He also edited this encyclopedia's Hellenistic department.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-typography-1236:
Hebrew typography, the art of printing in Hebrew, is sketched across five stages. Joseph Jacobs and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews called printing the art of writing with many pens. Early printers named their craft holy work. The stages run from 1475 to the modern period.

Incunabula came first, in southern Europe before 1500. Venice ruled Hebrew printing from 1542 to 1627. Amsterdam held the lead for the next century. Frankfort, Vienna, Wilna, and Warsaw rose after 1732. The first Hebrew printed book appeared at Reggio in 1475. Mantua, Ferrara, and Bologna soon set up presses. The Soncino family printed in many Italian towns. Spain and Portugal added presses before 1500.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-venice-14667:
Venice was an Italian city and once a great republic. Gotthard Deutsch and Eude Lolli wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews appear in Venetian records as early as 945. A Senate decree that year barred ship captains from carrying Jewish merchants. The rule was hardly ever enforced.

The first lasting settlement stood on a nearby island. That island, Spinalunga, was called Giudeca by 1252. Jews also came from Constantinople's fall in 1204. Others fled persecution in Germany in the twelve hundreds. The entry follows their trade, their limits, and their daily life. It shows a community that kept growing despite tight rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waller-stein-ab:
Abraham ben Asher Wallerstein was a German rabbi and scholar. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served at Schnaittach, in Bavaria. He worked in the eighteenth century. Three printed works carry his name.

His first book holds Hebrew sermons on the weekly Torah readings. It appeared at Fürth in 1757. His second book teaches ethics in eighteen chapters. It draws on Bible and rabbinic sources alike. His third work indexes the four great ritual codes. It arranges the codes in alphabetical order. All three books came out at Fürth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wertheimer-jose:
Joseph Wertheimer was an Austrian philanthropist and author. Isidore Singer and Siegmund Salfeld wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Vienna on March 15, 1800. He died there on his birthday in 1887. At fifteen he entered a banker's business. By 1821 he was his father's partner.

On travels, Wertheimer studied London's infant schools closely. He translated a book on early education into German. He urged Austria to found such schools too. In 1830 he opened Vienna's first kindergarten. A Catholic priest worked beside him on it. A central society for infant asylums followed. The empress herself patronized the cause.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wogue-jules-149:
Jules Wogue (born 1863) was a French writer and teacher, the son of Lazare Wogue. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Paris, he passed his exams at the Ecole Normale in 1885. He then taught at schools in Saint Quentin and Reims.

He later taught at two Paris schools and then at the Lycee Buffon. His books treat French plays and tales of past centuries. One book studies the poet Gresset. He also made school editions of two plays by Racine. Those editions carry long notes on the Bible tales in the plays. He wrote for big Paris papers and reviews as well. The entry shows a teacher who brought old French stage works to new readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yashar-sefer-ha:
Sefer ha-Yashar is a late book of tales on the Hebrew Bible. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is also known as Toledot Adam to its readers. It tells the past of the Jews from Adam to the Judges.

Three parts in four treat the time before Moses. One part in five treats the time of Moses. Just three pages treat all the time that came after. The maker forged whole tales to fill gaps in the text. One tale tells how Cain slew his brother Abel. One long kin list traces the sons of Noah's boys. In that list the dark root of Seir is made clear. The life of Abraham fills a large share of the book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zaphnath-paanea:
Zaphnath-Paaneah is the name Pharaoh gave to Joseph in Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Muller wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Book of Genesis at part forty-one. It seems to be an Egyptian name of that land.

Its root sense is in doubt to this day. The first sage notes give it a set sense in words. They read it as the man to whom dark things are shown. Josephus gives much the same sense in his book. The King James text gives that sense at its edge too. Yet no Egyptian root backs those old guesses, men say. Jerome claims a sense of savior of the world for it. That claim rests on a Greek text form, it seems. The entry shows a name that still keeps its core hid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zionides-or-son:
Songs of Zion, called Zionides in Hebrew Shire Ziyyon, are hymns of longing for Jerusalem restored. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such songs began soon after Babylon destroyed Solomon's Temple. Poets sang of Zion's past glory and prayed for the city, the Temple, and the nation to shine again.

The oldest Zionide named here is Psalm 137, a lament from the fifth century before Christ. Medieval poets made these songs a chief comfort of the people, and many entered the prayer book. Ibn Gabirol wrote Zionides in the eleventh century. Judah ha-Levi, the greatest of them, addressed Zion directly in his famous greeting to her captives.
lessing-minna-von-barnhelm-1767:
Minna von Barnhelm, Lessing's comedy of 1767, is Englished here in Ernest Bell's translation of 1878. Major von Tellheim, cashiered and wounded after the Seven Years' War, waits in a Berlin inn. He believes his honor ruined by a charge of bribery he did not commit.

Minna, his Saxon fiancee, arrives to find him proud, poor, and set on ending their match. Wits, servants, and a ring change hands until pride gives way. Lessing built the play on living speech rather than stage tricks. It became the first great German comedy and the model for the form. Its warmth toward both Saxons and Prussians was itself a plea for peace.
lettres-alchymiques-a-m-andre-i-e-andrea: Johann Friedrich Meyer's alchemical letters were printed at Paris in 1767. Claude Hérissant, printer and bookseller on Rue Neuve Notre-Dame, issued them. The title says they were addressed to a Monsieur André. The sample survives in rough, broken scan text. Author, title, place, and year still ground the work. It is a set of French letters on alchemy from the trade's late years.
liddon-divinity-of-our-lord-1867:
Henry Parry Liddon was an Oxford canon and the leading High Church preacher of his day. His Divinity of Our Lord, published in 1867, prints the Bampton Lectures he gave at Oxford on the full deity of Christ. The lectures became the High Church classic of Victorian Christology.

Liddon marshals scripture, the early fathers, and church councils to argue that Jesus is truly God, not a gifted teacher only. He answers the liberal lives of Jesus then coming from Germany and France. Anglo-Catholic readers treated the lectures as their arsenal, and the book's learning still commands respect.
macdonald-unspoken-sermons-1867:
MacDonald's Unspoken Sermons, First Series, published in 1867, were never preached aloud in this form. He wrote them as essays in sermon shape, setting out the theology behind his fantasies and novels. Readers who loved his stories found here the mind that made them.

The sermons preach the fatherhood of God, the slow cure of sin, and a hope that reaches beyond death for every soul. MacDonald refuses a God of mere punishment and insists that obedience grows from love, not fear. His universalist hope, voiced in pulpit form, shaped Lewis and a line of later writers.
mariette-apercu-histoire-egypte-1867:
Auguste Mariette gave a brief tale of old Egypt in his Apercu, a French sketch of 1867. Mariette was the man who found the Serapeum, the vast tomb of the bulls, in the sand. He went on to found the state guard for old sites in Egypt. No one knew its past at closer hand than he did then.

His sketch runs from the first kings to the Greeks in short, clear strokes. It was writ for a great show in Paris. In French, it is the chief dig man's own sum. Its brevity is its charm.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume eight of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter fifty five. Matters brighten a bit in Spain, but France stays in gloom. Failed peace and a drained realm throw the King into deep pain.

Paper bills of all kinds flood trade and lose their worth fast. Folk forced to take them lose half or more of their pay. Taxes double and triple at the will of local intendants. Desmarets turns at last to a royal tithe on all property in the realm. The tithe had been Vauban's plan, and Boisguilbert's as well. Both men were shamed for it when they first put it forth.
mercier-ordre-naturel-1767:
Le Mercier de la Rivière published The Natural and Essential Order of Political Societies in French in 1767. Mercier was a leading physiocrat, the school that held land to be the source of all wealth. His book is the physiocrats' political manifesto, the most systematic statement of their program.

He argues that society has a natural order written into the economy. The ruler's task is to find that order and enforce it, not invent laws of his own. Property, free trade in grain, and a single tax on land follow from the scheme. Adam Smith studied the physiocrats closely, and their system taught him much even where he dissented. The book's paradox, a despot bound hand and foot by natural law, sums up the school's strange blend of freedom and authority.
milton-paradise-lost-1667:
John Milton published Paradise Lost in 1667, the great English epic in blank verse. Blind and fallen from power, Milton set out to justify the ways of God. His subject is Satan, Adam, Eve, and the Fall of man in Eden.

Satan, cast from heaven, rallies his hosts in hell and plots revenge. He tempts Eve with the fruit, and Adam eats from shared love. War in heaven and scenes of creation fill the vast middle books. Adam and Eve leave Eden hand in hand, sad but not alone. The poem's music and scope shaped English verse for centuries.
nasa-tm-19660008599-aerodynamic-characte:
James C Patterson Jr at Langley tested a small model of the X-15A-2 research aircraft in the Langley eight-foot transonic tunnel. The model was built at a scale of about one part in fifteen. The X-15A-2 was a modified version of the famous rocket aircraft. Tests ran at speeds from well below sound to just above it, across a wide range of attack angles.

Patterson reports the model's aerodynamic characteristics from those runs. Transonic flight is where shock waves first form and control grows tricky. Even a rocket aircraft must pass through that range twice on every flight. Tunnel data on the modified shape helped judge its behavior before the full-size aircraft flew the profile.
openalex-w2032772167:
Ariel Herrera-Vasquez, Paula Salinas and Loreto Holuigue reviewed how two signals control plant defence genes. Their mini review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. One signal is salicylic acid, a plant hormone. The other is reactive oxygen species, a group of reactive molecules. Both surge when plants face stress or attack.

Salicylic acid switches on sets of defence genes. It does so at set times and places in the plant. Evidence shows this signal interacts with oxygen species. It also interacts with glutathione, a cell protector. These links change how gene switches are modified. Modifications turn defence genes up or down. The review maps what is known about that control system.
openalex-w2078352967:
Marcus Teixeira, Raquel Theodoro, Gustavo Nino-Vega and colleagues reviewed a group of disease-causing fungi. Their article appeared in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. The fungi belong to the Paracoccidioides complex. They cause a chronic lung disease in Latin America. New gene work had split the group into hidden species.

The authors traced where each species lives. Five related lineages are now recognised. Some spread widely across the region. One lineage became isolated and does not mix. A Venezuelan lineage split off through long-distance spread. The review covers sexual reproduction in these fungi. It also covers traits that affect disease strength. Knowing species borders helps diagnosis and tracking.
openalex-w2110871267:
Luis Carlos Mata-Gomez, Julio Montanez, Alejandro Mendez-Zavala and Cristobal Aguilar reviewed making carotenoids with yeasts. Their paper appeared in Microbial Cell Factories in 2014. Carotenoids are pigments used in food and cosmetics. They also serve as vitamin A precursors. Chemical and plant routes give low, costly yields.

Yeasts can produce carotenoids in fermenters instead. They grow fast on cheap farm waste materials. Those wastes supply carbon and nitrogen for growth. Using waste also cuts a pollution problem. Several yeast species produce high pigment levels. The review covers strains, feeds and process choices. Microbial production could lower costs substantially.
openalex-w2184405267:
Martyn Kirk, Sara Pires, Robert Black, and colleagues published this synthesis in PLoS Medicine in 2015. For the World Health Organization, they estimated the global and regional burden of twenty-two foodborne diseases for 2010. The germs covered were bacterial, protozoal, and viral, and no such worldwide estimates had existed before.

The team synthesized data on illnesses, after-effects, deaths, and years of healthy life lost. Sources ranged from systematic reviews to surveillance studies, spanning 1990 to 2012. Study counts per germ ranged from a handful to several hundred. Estimates were built by age and region, giving health planners their first shared yardstick for foodborne disease harm.
openalex-w2522746967:
Cosme Damião Cruz described an updated version of the Genes software in this 2016 paper in Acta Scientiarum Agronomy. Genes is a free program for analyzing data from plant and animal breeding research. It handles both visible traits and molecular data using statistical models. The new version links Genes with three other programs: R, Matlab, and Selegen.

That link lets breeders run extra analyses, including genomic selection and prediction of genetic values. It also adds neural networks and fuzzy logic tools. Genes helps researchers estimate the values they need to judge whether a breeding strategy will succeed. The program comes in Portuguese, English, and Spanish, with a user guide online. It also exchanges numbers and figures with Word, Excel, and Paint.
openalex-w2581251167:
The ATLAS Collaboration measured the mass of the W boson in this paper, out in the European Physical Journal C in 2018. It uses data from proton-proton collisions recorded during 2011 at the Large Hadron Collider. The beam energy was seven TeV. The W boson carries the weak force, and its mass is a key quantity in the Standard Model.

The team selected millions of W decays into electrons or muons plus unseen neutrinos. They fitted the shapes of lepton momentum and transverse mass curves against templates. Separate error counts were kept for statistics, the detector, and theory modeling. They also measured the mass gap between the positively and negatively charged W bosons. The final value is precise to within about nineteen mega-electronvolts. Such precision makes the result a demanding test of the Standard Model.
openalex-w2974335667:
Fuad Yassin, Saman Razavi, Mohamed Elshamy, and colleagues published this paper in Hydrology and Earth System Sciences in 2019. It tackles how computer models of rivers and land surfaces should handle dams and reservoirs. Reservoirs change both the size and the timing of streamflows downstream.

Many of the world's river basins are heavily regulated, yet models often leave reservoir operations out. That gap limits how well the models work and how far they can explore future climate or land use scenarios. The authors present a general reservoir operation model built on simple piecewise-linear rules. Their improved setup lets models mimic real water releases more faithfully, giving a truer picture of downstream flow.
openalex-w3114612967:
Ricardo Masini, Marcelo Medeiros, and Eduardo Mendes surveyed machine learning for time series forecasting in the Journal of Economic Surveys in 2021. Time series, from prices to weather, are data ordered by time, and forecasting them is a classic hard problem. The survey covers the newest supervised learning methods.

On the linear side, the authors stress penalized regressions and ensembles of models. On the nonlinear side, they cover neural networks, both shallow and deep, plus tree methods such as random forests and boosted trees. Hybrid models that blend the two families also feature. They review tests for judging which forecast is truly better. Applications in economics and finance close the survey, with an example using high-frequency trading data.
openalex-w3139157067:
Hernando Estupiñán, Anna Berglöf, Rula Zain, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology in 2021. It compares inhibitors of BTK, a kinase enzyme that B cells need to develop and survive. Blocking it treats blood cancers, but the drugs differ in their side effects.

At least twenty-two BTK inhibitors had reached the clinic when the authors wrote. The first, ibrutinib, binds the enzyme permanently; newer drugs such as acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib aim for a cleaner grip. Trials now extend beyond cancer into multiple sclerosis, arthritis, and lupus. The review links each drug's binding style to the harms reported. That mapping helps doctors pick an inhibitor whose risks fit the patient in front of them.
openalex-w4378905467:
Johan Rockström, Joyeeta Gupta, Dahe Qin, and colleagues set out safe and just boundaries for the Earth system, in Nature in 2023. Human economies now reshape the planet through heavy resource use and consumption. The harm falls unevenly: some groups and countries gain, while others bear the damage. Any honest limit-setting must therefore weigh safety for the planet together with justice for people.

The paper assesses boundaries that keep the Earth stable while protecting human wellbeing and fairness. It builds on the well-known planetary boundaries idea and asks what justice adds. Crossing safe limits risks tipping the climate and ecosystems into new, harsher states. The authors argue that shared, science-based limits can guide fair policy in a crowded, unequal world.
openalex-w4384663467:
Tatsuya Amano, Valeria Ramírez-Castañeda, Violeta Berdejo-Espinola, and colleagues count the costs of working in science without native English, in PLOS Biology in 2023. English is science's shared language, which helps ideas travel. Most of the world's people, though, are not native speakers. For them, reading, writing, and presenting in English adds a heavy, often invisible burden on top of the research itself.

The paper argues that this language barrier holds back talented researchers and narrows science. Diverse teams solve problems better, yet the barrier keeps many out or slows their careers. Costs show up as extra time, money, stress, and lost confidence across a career. Naming the burden plainly is a first step toward reforms that share it more fairly.
openalex-w4386100167:
Camille Delavaux, Thomas Crowther, Constantin Zohner, and colleagues test whether rich native tree communities resist invasion. Their study appeared in Nature in 2023. Planted and spreading non-native trees can transform forests and harm local species. Earlier research on invasion resistance mostly covered small regions, with mixed answers. The team used global tree databases to ask the question at world scale, weighing native diversity alongside human pressures.

As their title states, native diversity buffers against the severity of non-native tree invasions. Where native communities were richer in relatedness and function, invasions stayed milder. Human activity still shaped where invaders arrived and spread. The result revives the old idea of biotic resistance, now with global evidence, and it argues for protecting native variety as a defence.
openalex-w7171801567:
Toshihito Osada, of the University of Tokyo, released a 2026 study proposing a new mechanism behind the nonlinear anomalous Hall effect. In which a sideways current grows with the square of the applied field in certain crystals with no magnet present. His setting is a tilted, two-dimensional Dirac fermion system, where electrons behave like near-massless particles and a small energy gap exists.

Alongside the standard explanation based on Berry curvature, Osada adds an interband mechanism: electrons tunneling across the small gap shift sideways as they cross. In lightly doped systems this contribution can be major. The mechanism may explain the effect seen in an organic Dirac content with an extremely small gap, where nonlinear sideways and forward transport appeared together.
openalex-w7204536367:
Luara Dantas de Souza dos Santos and Patrícia Maria Dusek published a Portuguese-language historical study in Brazil in 2026 on ENEM, Brazil's national high school exam, across its first twenty editions. ENEM began as a way to evaluate high school schooling and was gradually improved into the main gateway to Brazilian higher education. The documentary research connects the exam to two larger themes: local growth and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal 4, quality schooling, in the 2030 Agenda.

Across the years, the authors conclude, the main goal of those who take ENEM remains entering higher education, public or private, through the unified selection system, the university-for-all program, or student financing. The exam's history shows an assessment tool reshaping a whole country's school expectations.
openalex-w7204899567:
Analluyza Nunes Coelho Inocêncio and Ana Beatriz Dantas das Mercês published a Portuguese-language integrative review in Brazil in 2026 on digoxin, a plant-derived heart drug, in the pharmacological treatment of cardiac arrhythmias. The six-stage review searched a health library's databases for 2010 to 2025 work, relating the drug's routes of administration, therapeutic and side effects, and quality-of-life impacts.

Digoxin stands out for controlling ventricular response, especially in atrial fibrillation, the authors find. It absorbs best by mouth, though the intravenous route is preferred for rapid effect. It works by increasing vagal tone and slowing conduction through the heart's atrioventricular node. Its narrow therapeutic window demands rigorous vigilance against toxicity, and nursing care is crucial for spotting clinical signs early and educating patients for safe treatment.
openalex-w7212184967:
Charel de Matos Neves leads a team that built a board game to teach safe handover of care in surgery. A handover is the point where one team passes a patient to the next. Weak handovers are a known source of harm. The team first asked nursing techs where the weak spots sat. Two themes rose to the top: how staff talk, and how care is passed on.

From those flaws, the team built a game trail through the steps of safe surgery. It formed part of a kit on the trials of safe care. The games were made in mid 2020. Games built from real flaws, the authors conclude, teach with force. Staff play out the right moves and fix the wrong ones. A strong safety ethos, they argue, can grow from play as much as from rules.
openalex-w7212359767:
Andressa Assis Teixeira leads a team on a cell group that may hold a key to sepsis care. Sepsis is the body's wild swing at a germ: first a storm of attack, then a deep hush of the guard. The cells at the core are myeloid-derived suppressor cells. They curb harm to flesh, yet they can lock the guard in that hush. The team read past trials to weigh drugs that aim at these cells.

Fast growth of the cells early in sepsis, the work shows, tracks with poor ends and more deaths. A web of gene switches and small RNA bits runs their growth. To tame the cells, then, could free the guard to fight the germ once more. The risk is the flip side: loose too much, and the first storm may rage. The review maps that tight line for those who build new care.
openalex-w7213984967:
Maria Eduarda Santana Santos leads a review on errors before analysis in blood collection. Most laboratory errors happen in that early phase, covering patient identification, collection, transport, and storage. Their 2026 review covers 2020 to 2025 work in four sources, in three languages.

Main error types include haemolysed samples, insufficient volume, wrong tubes, and patient identification failures. Causes span human, technical, and organizational factors together. Standard protocols, quality indicators, automation, and ongoing schooling cut such failures, the results indicate. A safety culture grows from those steps. Investment in training and quality management, the authors conclude, protects both result reliability and patient safety.
openalex-w7214113867:
Cláudio Luiz Ferreira Júnior leads a team tracing Brazilian pharmacy schooling from the apothecary shop to person-centred care. Their 2026 narrative review joins document analysis of school and professional landmarks. Pharmacy training has changed repeatedly since its imperial-era institutionalization, they show.

Four movements structure the history. Training first centred on preparing and knowing medicines. Minimum curricula and specializations followed in the twentieth century. A generalist model arrived in 2002, and health care gained force in the 2017 course plan guidelines. Clinical pharmacy, communication, patient safety, and follow-up entered training. Unevenness between institutions persists, they conclude, yet the object of training has widened to people's needs.
openalex-w7214684567:
Elysson Leonty dos Passos and Jennifer Cristina Kovalski surveyed education professionals in São Mateus do Sul, Brazil, for a 2026 study of PROERD, a police-taught school program against drugs and violence. The program had been interrupted the previous year, then resumed and expanded in 2026. The researchers asked the professionals who accompanied its activities how they judged its impact on school life.

Perceptions were broadly positive. Respondents credited the program with civic formation, prevention of drug use and violence, more positive behavior, fewer conflicts, and stronger ties among school, family, and the military police. Support for continuing the program was strong, sharpened by the memory of its interruption. The authors conclude that the return and expansion of PROERD were seen as relevant to the school environment. They fed social prevention, a culture of peace, and closer integration between education and public security.
openalex-w7214978667:
Luiza Atamantchuk de Ávila led a 2026 case report on removing a large dentigerous cyst from a twelve-year-old boy's upper jaw in Cascavel, Brazil. Dentigerous cysts grow around the crown of an unerupted tooth. This patient arrived with swelling at the front of the left upper jaw, linked to an impacted canine tooth, after a routine dental visit spotted the problem.

Surgeons removed the whole cyst together with the impacted tooth, and laboratory examination confirmed the diagnosis. Such cysts are benign and often silent, the authors note, yet they can distort the face, displace teeth, and erode roots. Computed tomography proved essential for judging the cyst's extent and its relation to nearby structures, and for choosing among removal, partial opening, or decompression. Early diagnosis and proper treatment, they conclude, prevent complications and recurrence.
openalex-w7220697167:
Liliane Benevenuto de Souza led a 2026 integrative review on the abandonment of older people and nursing's role before its psychosocial consequences. Abandonment grows more visible as populations age and family and social bonds weaken. The qualitative review gathered health literature to analyze what abandonment does to older people, identify its associated factors, and discuss how nurses should act with this public.

Abandonment relates to family, social, economic, and cultural factors and is frequently associated with neglect. Its main repercussions are social isolation, emotional suffering, loss of autonomy, and reduced quality of life. Nursing plays a fundamental role, the authors conclude, in identifying these situations early, welcoming the older person, and promoting integral care. The review speaks to front-line teams who often meet the abandoned elder first, in clinics and home visits, before any other service does.
othello-pg2267: The handkerchief damns her in this edition: Iago plants Desdemona's strawberry-spotted token on Cassio, and Othello's jealousy hardens to murder. "O, beware, my lord, of jealousy." The most painful tragedy, intimate as a wound.
outer-space-treaty-1967:
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 laid down the basic rules for activity beyond Earth. The United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain led the signing as the space race reached its peak. Nations feared that the Cold War rivalry might spread to the Moon, so they wrote a charter before anyone got there.

The treaty bars any nation from claiming the Moon or other bodies in space as its own territory. It also bans weapons of mass destruction in orbit and says exploration must serve the benefit of all countries. Astronauts are treated as envoys of mankind who must be helped in distress. Every spacefaring nation still works under these principles today.
ovid-metamorphoses-golding-1567:
Ovid's Metamorphoses came to England in Arthur Golding's version of 1567, in fourteen-syllable verse. Golding's was the first English Ovid, and the Ovid that Shakespeare read and used most. Many call it the most influential Elizabethan translation in the whole rich age of them.

Ovid links some two hundred and fifty tales of change into one flowing poem. Gods chase nymphs who turn to trees, rivers, birds, and stars to escape their lust. Daphne, Narcissus, Pyramus, and Orpheus pass in a stream of love, grief, and wonder. Golding's pace is brisk and his English earthy, close to speech and song of England. The poem fed English poets a store of myths they mined for centuries.
plos-pbio-0000067:
Zachary Lippman, Bruce May, Cristy Yordan, and their team published this paper in PLOS Biology in 2003. It studies transposons, the DNA stretches that can move around a genome. Cells keep them quiet with chemical marks called methylation and with small RNAs that guide the silencing.

The puzzle is how a cell passes that quiet state to the next generation. The authors show that the routes for keeping marks and for handing them down are not the same. Small interfering RNA and changes to histones, the spools DNA wraps around, play separate parts. The work sharpens the picture of how genomes stay stable while their jumping genes stay under control.
plos-pbio-0020167:
June Yao, Tu Cam Le, Claudine H. Kos, and their team explained a genetic kidney disease in PLOS Biology in 2004. The disease, FSGS, scars the kidney's filters and can end in kidney failure. Some families pass it down through a faulty gene for α-actinin-4, a protein that helps hold cell shape.

The study shows the faulty protein clumps together and breaks down too fast, wrecking the cells that form the filter. That gives a clear chain from gene to disease. Clear chains are what treatment design needs. If clumping is the problem, drugs that keep the protein stable or clear the clumps become plausible goals for this inherited form of kidney failure.
plos-pbio-0020367:
Hannah E. Volkman, Hilary Clay, Dana Beery, and their team studied tuberculosis in zebrafish in PLOS Biology in 2004. In TB, immune cells wall off the bacteria in ball-like clusters called granulomas. The team found a bacterial factor that helps those clusters form and grow.

That flips a common view. Granulomas were long cast as the host's defense alone, yet here the germ itself promotes them. The clusters may shelter bacteria as much as they trap them. If so, blocking the bacterial factor could help the host clear infection. Zebrafish larvae, clear enough to watch live, make the process visible in a way mammal studies cannot match.
plos-pone-0000067:
Rajesh Khanna, Qi Li, and Elise F. Stanley analyzed a nerve ending protein complex in PLOS ONE in 2006. At the synapse, where one nerve cell passes signals to the next, proteins must be pulled back inside after use. Synaptotagmin 1 anchors a complex that runs that retrieval, called endocytosis.

Their fractional recovery analysis measures how much of the complex can be drawn back into action after stress. Precise numbers for recovery help model how synapses keep up during heavy use without running dry. Fast, faithful recycling is what lets nerve signals stay reliable at high rates. The study gives synaptic physiology a careful measure of a key machine.
plos-pone-0000167:
Long-Jun Wu, Shanelle W. Ko, Hiroki Toyoda, and colleagues published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies mice with the GluR5 gene knocked out, removing one type of receptor for the brain signal glutamate. The authors focus on the amygdala, the brain region tied to fear and anxiety.

The knockout mice showed more anxiety-like behavior and stronger synaptic responses in the amygdala. Linking one receptor to both changes ties a molecule to a mood-related trait. The work helps map how glutamate signaling shapes anxiety, a connection of interest for treating anxiety disorders.
plos-pone-0000267:
Jaspreet Singh Jaggi, Erik Henke, Surya V. Seshan, and colleagues published this cancer therapy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Alpha particles are heavy, short-range radiation that can kill cells precisely. The authors use alpha-particle treatment aimed at a tumor's blood vessels, selectively depleting the vasculature. The treatment also brings about vascular normalization, a brief window where remaining vessels work better.

Starving a tumor by cutting its blood supply is an established strategy; doing it with targeted radiation is sharper. The normalization window can let other drugs reach the tumor more effectively. The study explores that combination logic in a cancer model.
plos-pone-0000367:
Nitika Pant Pai and colleagues evaluated a rapid HIV test in rural India, publishing their work in PLOS ONE in 2007. Instead of drawing blood, the test uses fluid from the mouth, which is easier and less painful to collect. The team checked three things: how accurate the test is, whether it can work in rural clinics, and whether clients prefer it.

Fast, simple testing matters where lab access is limited and many infections go undiagnosed. A mouth-fluid test that people accept could bring screening to places that blood-based programs reach poorly. The study weighs test performance against real-world use, a balance that decides whether a good test actually helps in the field.
plos-pone-0000467:
Matthew D. Smith and colleagues folded an artificial protein and studied what made the fold stable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is non-biological, designed rather than evolved. The team drew structural insights into its evolution. They focused on surface residues, the amino acids on the protein's outside. Those residues proved important in optimizing its fold.

Designers often focus on a protein's core, but the surface also decides whether a chain settles into one shape. Lessons from a designed protein's trial-and-error improvement read like a compressed evolution experiment. They feed back into protein engineering, where stable, well-folded designs are the starting point for new enzymes and materials.
plos-pone-0000567:
Maren N. Vitousek and colleagues measured the price female choice exacts in a lekking lizard, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. In a lek, males gather to display and females visit to choose mates, gaining no resources, only genes. The team documented high costs of female choice in this system.

Choice can cost time, energy, and exposure to predators while a female compares males. If costs are high, females should be choosy only when the payoff is large, which shapes how the mating system evolves. Measuring the cost side of choice, not just its benefits, gives a fuller account of sexual selection in the wild.
plos-pone-0000667:
David Emerson, Jeremy A. Rentz, Timothy G. Lilburn and co-authors described a new lineage of iron-eating bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacteria that oxidize iron are tied to hydrothermal vents, where iron-rich fluids rise around underwater mountains called seamounts. For decades the evidence for these microbes came almost entirely from the mineral remains they leave behind.

Living members of this new proteobacterial lineage help build marine microbial mats, layered communities on surfaces. Naming the organisms behind the rusty mats turns geology into biology: their genes and growth can now be studied directly. Iron cycling shapes ocean chemistry, so the microbes doing it matter well beyond the vents.
plos-pone-0000767:
Hoorig Nassanian, Ana M. Sanchez, Alice Lo and colleagues streamlined a standard gene-silencing tool, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. RNA interference, mediated by small interfering RNA, silences genes after they are transcribed. Once inside target cells, siRNAs join the RNA-induced silencing complex, whose antisense strand guides it to matching RNA for destruction. Labs build DNA cassettes to produce siRNAs inside cells.

Their cassette uses a minimal H1 promoter, inverted for easier handling. The design eases exchange of both the promoter and the siRNA sequence. Tool papers rarely make headlines, but faster cassette building speeds every experiment that knocks a gene down to see what happens.
plos-pone-0000867:
Fabio Moroni, Lino Nobili, Giuseppe Curcio and colleagues recorded sleep activity inside the human hippocampus, in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. The hippocampus is a deep brain area tied to forming new memories of facts and events. Sleep is widely thought to help lock those memories in place.

Using stereo-EEG, fine electrodes placed inside the brain, the team watched how this area behaves across sleep. They set its activity beside activity in the outer cortex. Work of this kind is rare because it needs direct recordings from inside the human brain. It sharpens our picture of how sleep and memory fit together.
plos-pone-0000967:
Richard Edwards, Norman Davey and Denis Shields built a probabilistic tool for finding short working motifs in proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Short linear motifs are tiny stretches, three to ten building blocks, that do key jobs in cells. As few as two positions in a motif may matter, which makes them very hard to spot.

Their program, SLiMFinder, looks for motifs that appear more often than chance allows and that evolved independently in separate proteins. Convergent evolution, the same trick found twice, is strong evidence a motif is real. Better motif hunting expands the map of how proteins talk to each other.
plos-pone-0001067:
Jinshun Zhao, Vasu Punj, Hittu Matta and colleagues studied a viral protein that blocks its own virus's active phase, in PLOS ONE in 2007. KSHV is the herpesvirus behind Kaposi's sarcoma. Growing evidence ties disordered expression of its lytic genes, the genes of active copying, to tumor formation.

A viral protein called K13 blocks that lytic replication, the team report, and also deregulates viral and human interleukin-6, immune signals tied to growth. Their model suggests lytic slips help select clones that become tumors. A virus holding its own accelerator and brake helps explain the slow, patchy way this cancer develops.
plos-pone-0001167:
Wound healing requires cells to know when to multiply, move, and settle into new tissue. Srinivasulu Chigurupati and colleagues examined the Notch signaling pathway in that process, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Notch is a communication system between cells that is deeply involved in fate decisions during development.

The team used both animal and cell culture models, looking at the healing of full-thickness skin wounds. Their findings place Notch among the signals that coordinate repair. Knowing which pathways drive healing could eventually point to ways of helping wounds that heal slowly, a common problem in diabetes and old age.
plos-pone-0001267:
When oxygen returns to tissue that has been starved of it, the returning oxygen itself causes damage, a well-known problem in mammals. John Lighton and Pablo Schilman set out to study that reperfusion damage in an insect, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A small, genetically well characterized animal model with reproducible, quantifiable damage was lacking.

The authors present the insect as such a model for oxygen reperfusion injury. In plain terms, they show the damage can be produced and measured in a convenient laboratory animal. That opens the genetics of reperfusion injury, relevant to heart attack and stroke care, to fast experimental study.
plos-pone-0001367:
Martha Hamblin, Marilyn Warburton, and Edward Buckler wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study that compares two kinds of DNA markers in maize, or corn. One kind is short repeated DNA stretches. The other kind is single letter changes in the DNA code. Breeders use both kinds to judge how alike two corn plants are.

The authors weigh how well each marker type shows the spread and the family links in maize. They note that the two types change at unlike rates, so they can give unlike views of the same plants. Their results help breeders and gene banks pick the right test for the task at hand.
plos-pone-0001467:
Maja Trenner and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how the brain handles cues across the senses. Past work compared brain replies to targets that cues had flagged as right or wrong. Less was known about brain work in the gap between cue and target. The team recorded brain rhythms in that gap.

They found that wave patterns in the wait help set up the gain from a good cue. In short, the brain does key work before the target shows. That work spans senses, since the cue and target can be in unlike modes. The study helps explain how alertness is held over a brief wait.
plos-pone-0001567:
Daniel Macqueen and Ian Johnston wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE update on a muscle gene called MyoD in fish. MyoD is a master switch for making muscle in backboned animals. Some fish hold two or more copies of it, a legacy of past genome doublings. Other fish hold just one. The pair reviewed the full record across fish lines.

They set out a shared naming plan to keep the copies from being mixed up. Mixed names had bred false claims on which copy does what. A clean roster helps labs compare muscle growth across species. It also frames how gene copies split jobs after a doubling.
plos-pone-0001667:
Takeshi Hase, Yoshihito Niimura, and Tsuguchika Kaminuma compared the wiring of protein networks across evolution in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Proteins in a cell form a web of interactions. Such networks are scale-free, meaning a few hub proteins hold many links while most hold few. The authors focused on heterodimerization links, pairs where two different proteins bind.

They asked whether these links survive at the same rate across the yeast protein interaction network's history. Their answer, signaled in the title, is no: survival is non-uniform, with some link types lasting far longer than others. The full text gives the network data and the survival rates by link type. Uneven survival shows where natural selection guards the web most tightly.
plos-pone-0001767:
Ricardo Águas, Lisa J. White, Robert W. Snow, and their co-authors modeled malaria elimination in sub-Saharan Africa in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plasmodium falciparum infections build clinical immunity gradually through repeated exposure. How that protection works at the gene level was not yet known. Its effects on spread patterns are strong and must enter any elimination plan.

The authors weigh the odds of wiping malaria out, given this built-up immunity. The full text gives the model, the transmission settings, and which areas look feasible. Immunity changes the math of elimination: as transmission falls, protection fades, which can set up rebounds. Plans that ignore this cycle risk declaring victory too early.
plos-pone-0001867:
Tiago Fleming Outeiro, Preeti Putcha, Julie E. Tetzlaff, and their co-authors watched a Parkinson's-linked protein clump inside living cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Misfolding, oligomerization, and fibrillization of alpha-synuclein are thought central to the onset and progression of Parkinson's disease and related disorders. Fibrillar alpha-synuclein is a major component of Lewy bodies, the clumps found in patient brains, but recent data implicated prefibrillar forms.

The team reports the formation of toxic oligomeric alpha-synuclein species in living cells: small assemblies, not the big fibrils, doing the damage. The full text gives the cell model and toxicity assays. If small oligomers are the toxic species, drug screens should target them rather than the visible end-stage clumps.
plos-pone-0001967:
