Publishing the plan first guards against cherry-picking later. Transplant teams get a promise of a careful, unbiased verdict on a cheap technique that might protect scarce donor kidneys.
pmc-13237267:
Morgan R Dillon and colleagues mined public records for 1,445 Major League Baseball pitchers from 2015 to 2025 in a 2026 study of shoulder and elbow injury burden. The pitchers, each with at least a thousand career pitches in the window, accumulated about 148,000 injured-list days. Models linked that lost time to performance numbers and pitch-tracking traits while accounting for workload and starting role.

Higher strikeout rate, faster four-seam fastballs, and higher fastball spin each came with greater combined shoulder and elbow burden. The joint-specific signals split: longer release extension tied to less shoulder trouble, while bigger pitch-to-pitch velocity swings tied to more elbow trouble. The findings give medical and coaching staff measurable traits to watch in prevention planning.
pmc-13237367:
Hoda S M Abdel-Ghany and colleagues tested essential oils from dill, lime, and wormwood against larvae of the mosquito Culex pipiens in 2026, seeking plant-based replacements for chemical insecticides. The team analyzed each oil's chemistry, tried blends, and made nanoemulsions, tiny oil droplets meant to improve delivery. Young larvae were exposed for up to 48 hours.

Dill oil killed larvae fastest and at the lowest dose, with its main components identified as apiol, carvone, and limonene. Surprisingly, the nanoemulsions did not beat the plain oils, and blends needed much higher doses than dill alone. Enzyme measurements in the larvae shifted in mixed directions depending on the formulation. The authors back dill-based products as biodegradable candidates, while asking for toxicity and environmental checks before wide use.
pmc-13238267:
Wang and colleagues replace animal serum in sheep embryo culture with a defined substitute. Labs growing sheep embryos in vitro rely on fetal bovine serum and ewe serum, which vary batch to batch, raise ethical concerns, and face supply limits. Those swings make experiments hard to repeat and hard to scale for breeding programmes.

The team tested a commercial serum replacer, called XRS, as a complete stand-in for both serums across maturation and fertilisation steps. They then judged embryo yield and quality against the old recipe. A chemically defined system that performs as well would clean up sheep embryo science and ease its move into routine farm breeding.
pmc-13238767:
Xu Zhang, Rongyang Wang, and Zhongyou Zhou redesigned a rotary drum screen for sorting fresh tea leaves in 2026, using particle simulations joined with statistical optimization. Conventional drums clog and tangle leaves, and their settings are usually guessed. The team compared the usual small-to-large hole sequence with a new alternating pattern that repeats small and medium holes before the large ones.

The alternating layout reduced entanglement and clogging in simulation and in bench tests. Experiments then tuned drum speed, tilt, and feed rate together, landing on thirteen revolutions per minute, a gentle tilt, and a modest batch size. Under those settings the machine sorted about 70 percent of leaves correctly on average. The authors offer the coupled method as a foundation for standardizing early tea processing.
pmc-13239367:
Shashi Gujar and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on an unexpected cancer finding linked to COVID-19 vaccination. A recent study by Grippin and others found that people receiving an mRNA COVID vaccine near the start of checkpoint inhibitor treatment lived notably longer.

Checkpoint inhibitors release brakes on immune cells, yet many tumours still resist them by keeping the surroundings hostile. The vaccine's early immune jolt appears to undo several of those defences and rally tumour-killing T cells. Gains were largest in lung cancer, melanoma, and even tumours classed as immunologically cold. Because such vaccines already exist, pairing them with cancer drugs could move to clinics quickly.
pmc-13239867:
Leonardo López and co-authors test whether weather shaped the Omicron wave of COVID-19 in a 2026 global analysis. Early pandemic debates asked whether temperature and humidity helped the virus spread, and the team checked whether the later variant showed the same climate signature once immunity was widespread.

Combining worldwide case and climate data from 2021 and 2022, they found incidence rose as temperature and absolute humidity fell, especially in mid-latitudes during cold months. Transmission seemed favoured within a moderate temperature band rather than at extremes. A model letting infection rates vary with temperature reproduced epidemic curves far better than fixed-rate versions, cutting errors by roughly half.
pmc-13240167:
Hu and colleagues build microscopic helices that form and move on command, copying a trick from climbing plants. A plant tendril coils when one side of it swells more than the other. The team recreated that uneven swelling in tiny hydrogel fibres, using electric fields to drive water in or out of one side and so bend the fibre into a helix.

Flipping the field's polarity and patterning the surface let them control where and when each helix formed, and reverse it. The moving helices could rotate and could catch and release a tiny sphere. Precise, reversible micro-coils like these point toward soft micro-robots and artificial muscles that work at scales fingers cannot reach.
pmc-13240767:
Pilar Cataldo-Miranda and colleagues publish a 2026 umbrella review of beta-blocker treatment after heart attack. Beta-blockers are a long-standing part of care after myocardial infarction. Doubt remains about their value when heart pumping strength is midrange or preserved in the modern treatment era.

The authors gathered recent systematic reviews and pooled data from unique primary studies. Trial evidence showed a clear drop in repeat heart attacks but no significant drop in overall or cardiovascular deaths. Observational studies tended to report larger benefits, which may reflect bias. Patients with preserved pumping strength gained no clear survival benefit in trials. The review supports tailoring long-term beta-blocker use rather than assuming equal benefit for everyone.
pmc-13240867:
Aynalem's team looked at how adults in Addis Ababa meet preconception care, years after Ethiopia issued its first national guideline in 2024. Such care still sits outside routine practice. The team spoke with eighteen adults, ten women and eight men, at two public hospitals. Talks explored social, cultural, and structural pressures around preparing for pregnancy.

Seven themes showed knowledge came late, often only after complications struck. Marital gatekeeping, faith beliefs, stigma, and poverty all narrowed access, and single women felt shut out. Men mostly paid the bills but wanted a larger role. People asked for simpler messaging, easier clinic entry, and visible state backing.
pmc-13241767:
Ma del Rosario García Calderón and a large team report a 2026 case of a benign blood vessel tumor inside the chest wall muscle of a 54-year-old woman. Routine breast imaging showed one breast larger than the other and raised suspicion of a breast lesion. Such muscle tumors are rare and often mimic breast disease.

Mammography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and computed tomography together located the mass in the pectoralis major muscle, separate from breast tissue. The combined imaging features fit an intramuscular hemangioma. The patient declined a biopsy, so no tissue confirmation was obtained. The authors stress that cross-sectional imaging can prevent a wrong breast-centered workup when a chest wall tumor hides behind breast asymmetry.
pmc-13241967:
Bing Jie Zheng and a large team report a 2026 imaging analysis from a breast cancer treatment trial. Women with triple-negative breast cancer received combined immune and chemotherapy before surgery. Their scans showed a curious pattern the authors name tumor flare-like response: new bright nodules appearing away from the main tumor, then fading.

The pattern appeared in most patients in the small trial group. Nodules were usually oval with smooth edges, often in both breasts, and first showed after two treatment cycles. The pattern alone did not predict complete tumor disappearance. Size did matter: patients whose largest nodule passed a set threshold cleared the tumor far more often. The authors suggest nodule size could help forecast treatment success.
pmc-13242367:
Lannon's team in Belfast asked fourteen nurses why weak students pass clinical placements anyway. The nurses assessed students on the wards. Long online interviews probed the 'failing to fail' pattern head-on. All were in postgraduate nursing courses while assessing students. Careful sorting split their accounts into four groups.

Failure carries a stigma that graders dread pinning on a student. Time pressure and thin workplace support squeeze honest skill grading. Close bonds, low grader confidence, and fear of blowback complete the barrier set. Kind workplace cultures, school teamwork, training, and clear guidance enabled firmer calls.
pmc-13242467:
Simone Giovacchini and co-authors tested whether water samples could guide conservation work across freshwater sites in central Italy. Their study appeared in Environmental Management in 2026. Using a DNA test on water from 53 sites, they searched for 11 endangered species, four invasive aliens, one harmful fungus, and one moved fish at the same time. European law already requires member states to track many of these species.

From the results they built three scores that rank sites for protection, for invasive-species removal, and for further survey work. The scores flagged 39 sites as protection candidates, 22 for eradication work, and 33 where DNA surveys would help most. The survey also recorded the target species in 53 map cells where they were not known before. The authors say one combined test can serve several legal duties at once.
pmc-13242767:
Jianning Lan and co-authors publish a 2026 retrospective study of scalp nerve blocks during deep brain stimulation surgery for Parkinson disease. Blocking scalp nerves may smooth the long procedure, which implants electrodes in a movement-control nucleus. Records came from one Chinese teaching hospital across several years.

Patients treated after the block was adopted had shorter electrode implantation times than the earlier local anesthesia group. Lung infections after surgery were less frequent in raw counts. Once other factors were weighed, the block itself no longer predicted infection, while longer time to breathing tube removal did. The authors note that era differences and selection bias limit the comparison. They frame the block as helpful for workflow, not proven protection.
pmc-13242967:
Hiroshi Kiyomatsu and co-authors used three-dimensional CT planning to ask which ball size suits reverse shoulder replacements in small shoulder sockets. Their study appeared in Bone and Joint Open in 2026. The patients were Asian women with small glenoid anatomy, a group where implant fit is tight. The team simulated three glenosphere sizes and three amounts of downward overhang in every patient, measuring how far the joint could move before bone met bone.

The smallest ball, thirty-two millimeters, gave the widest arcs in bending, lifting, and rotation, while the largest consistently restricted motion. Placing the ball with at least three millimeters of overhang also helped in every plane. The authors recommend downsizing with adequate overhang for small sockets. They caution that soft tissue and stability, absent from the simulation, must confirm the choice in the operating room.
pmc-13243067:
Chao Meng and co-authors present a 2026 review on how heart muscle heals badly after a heart attack, a process called ventricular remodelling that can lead to heart failure. Their focus is DNA from mitochondria, the cell's energy units, which can leak out and act as an alarm signal.

The authors propose a three-threshold model covering how this DNA escapes, how it travels between cells, and how strongly it switches on an immune alarm pathway. It can move as bare DNA, in tiny cell-made bubbles, or inside whole mitochondria. They suggest timed drug combinations aimed at each step, while noting parts of the model still need direct proof.
pmc-13245067:
Robert Connacher and colleagues asked whether a fruit fly developmental protein must actually grip RNA to do its job. Their study appeared in RNA Biology in 2026. The protein, Brat, guides neural stem cell development and is named for the brain tumors its loss causes. Lab work showed its NHL domain binds specific RNA sites, untested inside a living animal. The team used CRISPR to edit single amino acids at the binding surface, directly in the fly's own gene.

Three independent RNA-binding-defective versions resulted, and each behaved as a strong loss of function. Flies carrying only the edited gene died, mostly as late larvae or pupae, just like flies missing Brat entirely, and the edits failed to rescue known brat mutants. The verdict is clean: RNA binding is not an accessory to Brat's work but its essence. The alleles give biologists a precision tool for separating Brat's roles.
pmc-13245467:
Yiwen Lu and co-authors explain why a blood fat called lipoprotein(a) is so hard to measure fairly in a 2026 review. Levels of this particle are set mostly by genes and raise heart risk on their own. Yet its odd structure fools common lab tests.

Copies of one protein segment vary by person, which skews tests that count by weight. The review favors reporting in moles, the count of particles, and warns against fixed swaps between units. High levels can also inflate standard cholesterol scores and mislead risk calls. Automated tests suit screening, while lab-grade methods anchor accuracy. Fair measurement matters more as drugs aimed at this particle near the clinic.
pmc-13246467:
Hasan and co-authors designed an off-grid power system for a coastal island community in Bangladesh, in this 2026 Global Challenges study. Char Ishwar, in Noakhali district, has weak grid access and growing demand. Using planning software, the team modeled a hybrid microgrid combining solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and a hydrogen loop with an electrolyzer, storage tank, and fuel cell to cover calm, cloudy spells.

Of three designs tested for one hundred eighty households, the full hybrid won, delivering power at a modest cost per unit with near-zero net emissions. Wind speed and demand growth most affected the economics. The authors present the design as a practical template for reliable, low-carbon electrification of isolated coastal settlements.
pmc-13247167:
Gong, Fan, Fang, and co-authors built swimming microrobots from living algae in this 2026 Microsystems and Nanoengineering paper. Synthetic microrobots struggle to squeeze through the body's tight, complex spaces, a requirement for reaching tumors. The team instead harnessed Euglena gracilis, a soft, shape-shifting single-celled swimmer, fitting it with magnetic structures so external magnets could steer, propel, and deform it on command.

The biohybrids threaded through dense three-dimensional biological matrices and gathered around tumor spheroids, guided both magnetically and by their own drift toward tumors. The algae themselves add therapy: their chlorophyll supports light-driven tumor killing, and their natural products modulate immunity. The authors present the platform as precision medicine that needs no loaded drug cargo.
pmc-13248967:
Zhang reviewed ultrasound for diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis in this 2026 article. The disease inflames joints and destroys them slowly, and early treatment changes its course. Blood tests miss some patients, especially those whose marker tests come back negative, so imaging that can see inflammation directly has drawn growing interest.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound can reveal swollen joint lining, fluid, increased blood flow, and early bone erosion in real time. It excels at catching hidden inflammation before damage shows elsewhere. Results still depend on the operator's skill, the author notes, but shared scoring systems, standard scanning routines, and early artificial intelligence tools are tightening the method for everyday clinics.
pmc-13249167:
Katayama and colleagues compared two ways blood vessel cells grow old, in a 2026 PLOS One study. Cells can senesce by dividing until they wear out, or early under stress. Both states appear in aging vessels, which grow prone to clots, and the team asked whether the two aging routes affect clotting control differently.

Worn-out cells unexpectedly boosted the vessel lining's anti-clotting behavior in dish tests, while stress-aged cells did not. Mice engineered for stress-aged vessel cells formed worse vein clots, closely matching naturally old mice. Gene patterns agreed. The authors conclude stress-driven aging, not division-driven aging, is the main culprit behind age-related clotting trouble.
pmc-13249567:
Pickersgill and a large drilling expedition team dated the hot water system inside the Chicxulub crater, in a 2026 study. The crater, in present-day Mexico, was blasted out sixty-six million years ago by the asteroid linked to the dinosaur extinction. Heated water circulated through its fractured rock long afterward, the kind of setting where life may first have arisen.

Rock dating and computer simulation together show the hydrothermal activity lasted at least eight million years. That is roughly four times longer than earlier estimates from rock magnetism and mineral studies. The authors call Chicxulub the longest-lived impact-driven hydrothermal system yet documented on Earth, with implications for how life might start on other worlds.
pmc-13249867:
Sato and a Japanese team found a protein that helps the spinal cord rewire after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. Surviving corticospinal fibers, the brain's movement command lines, sprouted into the emptied side of the neck cord and reconnected with V2a interneurons, relay cells for premotor circuits. Silencing those new links chemically weakened the recovered movement, proving they carried real function.

A secreted protein, secretogranin II, rose after injury in helper astrocytes and in the relay neurons during rehabilitation. It pushed axons to grow through familiar growth signals, and removing it blunted rewiring. The authors nominate the protein as a therapeutic lever for stroke and other central nervous system injuries.
pmc-13250167:
Lorenté and co-authors film shock waves moving through a safe stand-in for an explosive. Their 2026 Scientific Reports experiments used compressed sucrose, ordinary sugar pressed into a solid, instead of real energetic material. A short green laser pulse struck the sample to launch each shock wave.

Because the granular material is opaque, the team used high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging to watch the shock form inside it. Follow-up tomography let them estimate the shock pressure and speed, which reached about four times the speed of sound in the material. Adding aluminum nanoparticles made the sample absorb more laser light and raised the pressure. The results point toward detonators triggered by light rather than by impact.
pmc-13250767:
Ruchama Charles and co-authors recount a cancer scare that ended well in this 2026 case report. A 68-year-old man treated two years earlier for colon cancer had rising blood marker levels, and scans found a growing mass inside a hip muscle.

The lump lit up on a PET scan, which raised fears the cancer had spread. Two needle samples gave no answer. Tissue study after closer work showed nodular fasciitis, a harmless, fast-growing knot of repair cells that often mimics cancer. A gene test confirmed it. Since removing such lumps cures them, the authors stress firm diagnosis to spare patients needless cancer treatment.
pmc-13250867:
Lee, Shin, and Song test ear-based nerve stimulation as a drug-free helper for eczema-like skin inflammation in mice. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study uses a chemical called DNCB to trigger atopic dermatitis on mouse skin. Gentle electrical pulses on the ear stimulate the vagus nerve, a pathway known to calm immune responses.

Stimulated mice showed healthier skin structure and lower inflammatory markers than untreated dermatitis mice. Blocking acetylcholine receptors partly erased the benefit, pointing to cholinergic signaling, including one nicotine-type receptor, as part of the mechanism. Treatments ran a few minutes every two or three days for one or two weeks. The authors call the approach a promising add-on and ask for deeper mechanism and translation studies.
pmc-13251167:
Karin Dalhammar, Maria Schelin, and Marie-Louise Möllerberg compare end-of-life care settings in Sweden in this 2026 study. About half of Swedes who die receive municipal care first, and people at home face more emergency hospital trips than those in care facilities.

The study covered 50,219 people in the national palliative care register during 2023 and 2024, all in their last week of life. Facility residents were more likely to get symptom checks than people in ordinary housing. Yet they were less likely to receive end-of-life information, support for relatives after death, or outside pain advice. The authors say each setting has distinct weak spots needing targeted fixes.
pmc-13251767:
Stephanie T.D. Pham and colleagues characterize human kallistatin, a blood protein that restrains an enzyme involved in blood vessel control, in a 2026 study. Kallistatin belongs to the serpin family, whose members can link into inactive chains called polymers. Its sugar decorations, tissue locations, and tendency to polymerize were poorly mapped before this work.

The team built custom antibodies and a sensitive test that measures kallistatin in plasma and in fluid from cultured tissue, including vessel tissue from patients with aortic aneurysm. Mass spectrometry confirmed a predicted sugar attachment site on the protein. Experiments showed kallistatin does polymerize, and that stripping its sugars sharply increased polymer formation, meaning the sugars act as stabilizers. Polymerized kallistatin lost its ability to block its target enzyme, while sugar-stripped protein still worked. The authors say the tools and maps they built open the way to studying this protein in disease.
pmc-13252767:
Isa Spiero and a large team compare Dutch language models for mining medical notes in this 2026 study. Health records hold rich symptom detail in free text, and automated extraction could save hours of hand labelling, but most tools are built and tested in English.

Two Dutch models were tried on primary care notes from patients with chest infections, against hand-labelled examples. Used as direct classifiers, both did well after enough training, the medical one slightly ahead. Prompt-style use failed badly, with very low scores. Uneven class sizes and missing symptoms dragged performance down, and at least 800 labelled examples were needed. The authors back direct classification for Dutch research use.
pmc-13252967:
Vishal Dalal and colleagues report a heart attack mid-treatment in this 2026 case report. An 80-year-old man arrived with gut bleeding and fainting while taking a blood thinner for a recent leg vein clot, so doctors gave a reversal drug to stop the bleeding.

The reversal drug, since withdrawn from the United States market, was known to raise clot risk days later. This patient, the authors say, is the first known to suffer a major heart attack while the drug was still running into his vein. pmc-13253267:

pmc-13253767:

Light therapy used a red LED device, and care was given before a muscle-damage exercise routine.

Blood, strength, flexibility, and jump results were checked up to 72 hours later. Only the combined group had a distinct pattern, with a key muscle enzyme near its start level within 48 hours and a sharp drop by 72 hours. Strength gains were not firm, so the authors treat them as an early trend.
pmc-13253867:

Melon peel worked best against germs, cutting three bacteria groups by 72, 68, and 51 percent versus plain beef on day six. It also wiped out Listeria by day six. Prickly pear peel gave the best taste scores, while the control beef spoiled. The authors call for cost studies next.
pmc-13255067:
Andreas W. Wolff and colleagues report a 2026 reanalysis of a trial testing fasudil in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that spreads weakness from region to region. At day 90, fasudil-treated patients showed fewer newly affected muscles than placebo patients, with stronger doses doing better. pmc-13255167:

pmc-13255767:

pmc-13256067:

Many tumors escape the usual death pathway, apoptosis, and thereby resist standard drugs. Ferroptosis kills differently, through iron-fueled damage to cell membranes' fatty layers.

The process also talks with the tumor's surroundings, sometimes helping and sometimes hindering immune attack. New drugs designed to force ferroptosis, especially alongside existing therapies, headline the treatment section. The authors map mechanisms and crosstalk so researchers can aim these drugs precisely at resistant cancers rather than broadly.
pmc-13256767:
Jiaqi Zhang and co-authors test in 2026 whether a defined starter culture can steady air-dried mutton as it ferments. Left alone, the mutton's wild microbes make quality vary from batch to batch. Sequencing found the started batches led by lactic acid bacteria, with fewer Pseudomonas, and their flavor profile grew more diverse, with eight key aroma compounds tracking bacterial levels. pmc-13256867:
Yunyun Han and co-authors test in a 2026 postharvest study whether ultraviolet-C light can slow the rapid quality loss of fresh shiitake mushrooms, whose loose, moist tissue spoils quickly after picking. Treated mushrooms lost about a third less weight, opened their caps far less, and stayed firmer with better color. Antioxidant enzyme activity rose while cell wall breakdown slowed. The dose gives growers a practical setting for extending shiitake shelf life.
pmc-13257067:

Some medicines lengthen the QT interval on an electrocardiogram, a danger signal in drug development. Earlier predictors name single chemical alerts but explain little about combined effects.

A chemical language model encodes each motif, and attention-based graph learning models how motifs interact. Training used regulatory label data and real-world adverse event reports, with steady performance across both. Attention maps showed risk arising from cooperating groups, notably compact positive centers joined to flexible, heteroatom-rich frames. Drug safety teams gain both a predictor and a chemical story they can inspect.
pmc-13258167:
Filip Pantelić and colleagues test a sound-based, touch-free method for probing heritage materials in a 2026 study. A modified acoustic resonance setup with two microphones measured stiffness and damping in dense natural stone and in porous unfired clay. Results were checked against impulse excitation and ultrasonic pulse methods.

Knowing where the method wobbles, namely in porous historic clay, is as valuable as the readings themselves.
pmc-13258567:
Xingzhong Zheng and coauthors propose a 2026 review framework for treating tofu wastewater with heated digestion plus a modified biochar. Tofu effluent carries heavy organic load and low acidity, which can overwhelm disposal systems. Hot anaerobic digestion can recover biogas, yet acid buildup and toxic gases often disrupt it.

The proposed additive pairs biochar with tiny calcium peroxide particles. Slow breakdown of the peroxide should buffer acidity and curb ammonia and sulfide problems. A structured failure analysis compared risks against standard digestion. Leftover solids could serve as nutrient rich soil material. Engineers weighing food waste treatment options get a combined risk and cost view of the concept.
pmc-13258767:
Shalini Purwar and co-authors profile mahua flowers, whose sweetness decides whether they fetch good prices for food and drink processing. Gas analysis found over three hundred volatile compounds separating the best and worst accessions. Mature BM-5 brimmed with aroma and fermentation-friendly molecules, marking it as the prime processing candidate.
pmc-13258867:
Zhinan Li and colleagues project cold region rice yields under climate change in a 2026 modeling study from northeast China. Yield rose notably when extra carbon dioxide fertilization was included. Water demand still grew, yet added carbon dioxide softened that growth. pmc-13259167:

Fracture imaging and simulation explained how grooves spread stress at the interface. Grid patterns handled multi direction loads better despite lower peak strength. pmc-13259767:

Severe dry mouth was the main side effect reported. Blood counts stayed stable through observation. Nuclear medicine teams gain a rare dual tumor success worth cautious replication.
pmc-13260067:
Alireza Shahbabaie and colleagues proposed in 2026 a scan-based method for choosing where to aim weak electrical brain stimulation. Such stimulation, called tDCS, can shift activity across whole networks, yet target choice often rests on habit. Their framework uses resting and task brain scans from 37 healthy adults drawn from two earlier studies.

The team traced networks seeded at two target sites, one tied to vision and memory and one tied to language. Both networks proved stable across repeat scans for most of their volume. Only part of each resting network lit up during the memory and learning tasks, and the share varied widely by target. The authors argue that pairing resting maps with task maps before a trial gives sharper, testable predictions about network effects.
pmc-13260567:
Ningning Shi and colleagues present a 2026 materials study of nickel-iron phosphide catalysts for water oxidation, the slow half of splitting water to make hydrogen fuel. pmc-13262067:

pmc-13262267:

pmc-13262367:

pmc-13262567:

pmc-13262667:

pmc-13263367:

pmc-13263567:

pmc-13263767:

pmc-13263867:

pmc-13264067:

pmc-13264167:

pmc-13264267:

pmc-13264767:

pmc-13264867:

pmc-13265167:

pmc-13266367:

pmc-13266567:

pmc-13266767:

pmc-13266867:

pmc-13266967:

pmc-13268167:

pmc-13268767:

pmc-13269167:

pmc-13269467:

pmc-13269567:

pmc-13269767:
Giulia Notini and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Trop2, a surface protein targeted by a class of cancer drugs that carry a poison payload into tumor cells. pmc-13269967:

Families were left to interpret symptoms, watch for decline, and handle new complications without structured guidance. The authors recommend a stronger clinical role for primary care after discharge. pmc-13270067:

pmc-13270467:

pmc-13270667:
Miriam Kesselmeier led a 2026 journal article on POLAR_MI, a German project that hunts for drug risks in patients taking many medicines at once. The work used routine hospital records held at German university hospitals, handled through each site's own data centre to protect privacy.

The team built a two-step method: each centre first gathered and summarised its own data locally, then a central team pooled the summaries. They describe the technical hurdles caused by differing local systems and how repeated rounds of fixes solved them. In the end the pipeline covered ten centres, nearly 800,000 hospital encounters, and about 500,000 patients.
pmc-13270767:
Gamal M. Abdalla led a 2026 prospective randomized trial on cutting early bleeding after sleeve gastrectomy, a weight-loss operation that removes part of the stomach. The trial tested rinsing the staple line with warm salt water before a standard stitching step, against the usual room-temperature rinse.

Between December 2024 and June 2025, 200 adults were split evenly between warm rinse, at body-like warmth, and the cooler rinse. The combined bleeding outcome occurred in 5 percent of the warm group versus 15 percent of controls. Warm rinsing also gave lower drain output and a smaller drop in haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying part of blood, after surgery.
pmc-13270867:
Mom Ean is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on discussion and interviews, on engaging young people in health and research in rural Cambodia. Since 2021, school students in Siem Pang have worked with a tropical medicine research unit through a youth advisory group called YAGHRE.

Thirty-five people took part, including 14 youth group members, teachers, health staff, other students, and family members. Members were seen as a bridge between researchers and the community. Taking part seemed to build their confidence, speaking skills, computer skills, and leadership, and the knowledge spread to families and peers. The authors present the group as a model for community-based research partnerships.
pmc-13272167:
Minghao Li and coauthors review in 2026 animal models of chronic rhinosinusitis across several species and how to choose among them. This long-lasting sinus inflammation burdens quality of life, and treatment progress lags behind the disease's immune complexity. Mice dominate the lab, yet their sinuses differ greatly from human ones.

Sheep drain their sinuses in ways closer to humans, while pigs mirror stubborn tissue remodeling in severe disease. The review judges each model against human disease types, from allergy-driven type 2 inflammation to other forms. A decision framework steers researchers toward the model that fits their question rather than the most convenient one.
pmc-13272267:
Rithvik Gundlapalli is lead author of a 2026 systematic review on radiomics for vestibular schwannoma. That is a tumour on the balance nerve. It is hard to reach, grows unpredictably, and threatens key nerve functions. Radiomics extracts large numbers of quantitative features from scans, beyond what the eye can see, and might predict outcomes and treatment response.

Searching three databases, the team found thirteen retrospective studies, eleven using machine learning on MRI features. Models from scans before treatment predicted moderately, while models after treatment reached moderate to strong accuracy. One deep learning model of facial nerve outcomes after surgery beat traditional models. Small samples, backward-looking designs, and manual tumour outlining limit the field, the authors note.
pmc-13272367:
Atefe Yadollahi Khales and coauthors test in 2026 a two-signal blood signature of long non-coding RNAs for Alzheimer's disease. Such RNAs are stable in blood and specific in pattern, making them attractive diagnostic candidates. One signal rises in patients while the other falls, and both track thinking severity.

A public dataset screen nominated the candidates, which were then measured in plasma from twenty-five patients and twenty-five healthy controls. Each RNA alone separated the groups with good accuracy, and their expression levels correlated with standard mental test scores. Network analysis suggested how the pair might regulate disease genes through shared microRNA partners.
pmc-13272467:
Iryna Vasyliv and coauthors test in 2026 whether a computer-aided tool speeds the staging of childhood Hodgkin lymphoma without losing accuracy, and how reader experience changes that benefit. Staging whole-body PET scans by eye is slow and varies between readers. Fifty-six children's scans were split into two matched groups for the comparison.

One group was staged traditionally and the other with a new web-based tool, by readers ranging from a resident to senior specialists. A joint expert reading set the reference standard, and agreement statistics measured accuracy in both arms. Timing results are reported by experience level, showing where the tool saves the most effort.
pmc-13272567:
Andreas Gold and Kayvan Bozorgmehr wrote a 2026 comment on how Germany now shares out European asylum and integration funds. The fund is a main European tool for reception and integration, worth 10.94 billion euros for 2021 to 2027. Germany runs its share through its federal office for migration and refugees.

They argue the revised German plan favors return advice and buildings, while people with pending claims get mainly short orientation courses. They also fault awarding funds first come, first served, noting that one call was oversubscribed by 30 percent in 27 hours. A minimum open period, a lottery among fit bids, or quality-based awards would be fairer, they say.
pmc-13273067: Correction notice from Samar El Achy and co-authors. It concerns a study of gold particles loaded with a small RNA against liver cancer cells. Figure 7 had an error when first published. The microscope images in panel A were a copy of those in panel C. The original figure and its legend are shown in the notice. The paper has now been corrected.
pmc-13273367:
Yi-Hsuan Li and a large team tested a plant extract against a honey bee parasite in a 2026 study. Nosema ceranae is a spore forming parasite that lives inside bees and causes the disease nosemosis. The extract came from Bidens pilosa, a plant used in traditional remedies.

Newly emerged worker bees were infected in lab cages and then given the extract, with fifty bees in each group. Treated bees survived better and carried fewer parasites than untreated infected bees. Gene reads from the parasite inside bee guts showed wide gene shutdown early in infection, including a key energy pathway. Knocking down that pathway in a separate test also lowered parasite load somewhat. The authors say the extract reshapes parasite activity in a stage dependent way.
pmc-13273467:
Ruoyan Cao leads a 2026 multi-omics study of the genetic mechanisms behind periodontitis, a chronic gum disease driven by immune dysregulation. The team joined genome-wide data from two large cohorts with single-cell and spatial gene maps of tissues. They also used an AI-driven drug screening framework and molecular docking to predict treatments.

Genetic signals for gum disease were enriched not only in jawbone and teeth, but also in brain and kidney cortex, which may explain links to body-wide illness. Monocytes and natural killer cells emerged as key immune subsets, and 23 genes linked causally to the disease. One gene, GNLY, was prioritized, and five candidate compounds bound it well in simulations.
pmc-13273567:
Charlotte Cresens and co-authors gave a protocol in 2026 for making polyacrylamide hydrogels of tuned stiffness for cell culture. Cells respond to how stiff their surroundings feel, so labs need gels that mimic tissues from soft brain to firm muscle. This gel system is cheap, and its stiffness is set by recipe.

The protocol makes large round gels that sit unattached, in custom shapes and sizes, and explains how to measure their stiffness by rheology. Mixing more or less of the two building chemicals sweeps stiffness across the range found in healthy and diseased tissue. The authors also cover using the gels for cell culture, collecting what cells secrete, and imaging proteins by fluorescence. Full detail points back to their earlier methods paper.
pmc-13274567:
Gyujoon Hwang and a large team present a 2026 study protocol for brain imaging research on grief in older adults. Most bereaved people move from sharp early grief to an integrated, livable grief, but some develop prolonged grief disorder. Why paths diverge is unclear, and faulty emotion control is a leading suspect.

The single-site study plans to follow 170 adults aged fifty to eighty-nine for one year, 115 recently bereaved and 55 matched non-bereaved volunteers. Brain scans at start and twelve months include rest imaging, a face-matching task for emotion, and a stop-signal task for self-control. So far 103 bereaved and forty comparison participants are enrolled and matched, with good-quality scan data collected.
pmc-13274867:
Debiao Luo and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on spotting abnormal network traffic, an early sign of cyberattack. Their pipeline first cleans the traffic signal by splitting it into simpler waves, a step called empirical mode decomposition. A hybrid neural network then reads the cleaned signal, pairing an attention-based transformer with a memory network that reads sequences both ways.

Tuning such a network by hand is fiddly, so a firefly algorithm, a search method mimicking flashing insects, tuned its settings automatically. On benchmark data sets, the authors report their combined model beat rival and baseline systems on every metric they tested. The gains in prediction error and in the F1 score for catching anomalies were statistically significant.
pmc-13274967:
Tianqing Fan and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study asking whether internet addiction predicts new self-injury in Chinese middle school students. Cross-sectional links were known, but direction over time was not. The team recruited 1,315 students with no history of nonsuicidal self-injury, and 704 completed the six-month follow-up.

Among those followed, 9.8 percent began self-injuring within six months. Risk rose in a straight line with the severity of internet addiction at baseline. After full adjustment, addicted students had about double the odds of starting self-injury. The link was significant in girls, with roughly triple the odds, and in a middle 'internet-dependent' state, but not in boys. The authors urge sex-aware prevention.
pmc-13275767:
Alessandro Antonelli and co-authors report a 2026 clinical trial on removing stuck lower wisdom teeth. Such surgery often leaves patients with swelling, pain, and trouble opening the mouth. The trial tested piezosurgery, which cuts bone with fine sound vibrations, against the usual spinning drill tools.

Forty-seven healthy adults had one side treated each way, giving ninety-four extractions in total. Three-dimensional face scans measured swelling two and seven days after surgery. The vibration method left less swelling and less jaw stiffness at day two. Pain was lower at every check, and the drill side bled more and needed more painkillers. The new method took longer in surgery, but patients reported less disruption to daily life and higher satisfaction.
pmc-13275967:
Grigorios Avdikos and Stephen Smith wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about heart attacks caused by a fully blocked artery. Some of these attacks never show the classic pattern on an electrocardiogram, the heart tracing called an ECG. The letter comments on a report of three such cases that got delayed artery-opening treatment.

The authors argue the first patient's tracing actually pointed to a different artery than the report claimed. They explain how a common tracing quirk can hide or mimic warning signs in the second case, which they say was very high risk. They close by noting that the usual split between two heart attack types misses many blockages. A newer approach, focused on blocked arteries themselves, could speed up life-saving treatment, they argue.
pmc-13276467:
Jojo Yan Yan Kwok and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol for a home exercise programme in Parkinson disease. Most people with Parkinson disease struggle with balance and walking, raising fall risk and lowering quality of life. The programme, called MY-PACE, blends mindfulness, yoga, and mindful walking.

The randomised trial enrolled 132 people with Parkinson disease and balance problems, split evenly between groups. One group follows a twelve-week programme delivered by video call at home. The other receives usual outpatient care first and gets the programme after the study ends. Balance is the main outcome, with walking, mood, thinking, and falls also tracked over six months.
pmc-13276567:
Ramamurthy Shanmugapriya and co-authors report a 2026 randomized study on a moringa leaf gel as an add-on to standard gum disease care. Deep cleaning below the gumline is the main non-surgical treatment for advanced periodontitis. Plant-based adjuncts could help, since moringa is rich in protective compounds.

Thirty patients with stage three disease, covering ninety sites, were split into three groups. One got cleaning alone, one got cleaning plus antibiotic fibers, and one got cleaning plus a moringa gel that sets with body heat. All groups improved clearly after two months. Both add-on groups reduced plaque, gum inflammation, and bleeding more than cleaning alone. The moringa group showed the biggest drop in a nitric oxide marker and a rise in a tissue repair protein. The authors rate the gel comparable to antibiotic fibers and want larger, longer trials.
pmc-13276767:
Lilla Markel and colleagues evaluate routine follow-up phone calls after gynaecologic cancer surgery, in a 2026 study. The programme ran at an urban safety-net hospital, where patients face complex medical and social needs. Nurses called every surgical patient two to three days after discharge with a structured question set.

Four months before and after the launch supplied 466 patients for comparison, about half called. Called patients attended follow-up visits more often and had more complications managed without hospital care. Emergency visits and readmissions were similar, though repeat readmissions fell among called patients. Two in five called patients raised concerns, most often pain, constipation, or vague symptoms needing advice.
pmc-13276867:
Takashi Watanabe writes a 2026 letter critiquing a recent paper on so-called neuromelanin-sensitive MRI. The scan is used to study the substantia nigra, a brain area that degenerates in Parkinson disease. Watanabe argues the technique is really T1-weighted imaging with magnetisation transfer effects, a distinction that changes its meaning.

White matter and grey matter differ in water content, which sets their basic signal behaviour. Off-resonance pulses saturate bound water in proportion to T1 shortening, the letter explains. Magnetisation transfer then cancels much of the T1 contrast, leaving mostly proton-density contrast. Bright signal also appears in areas regardless of neuromelanin content, so the scan is neither specific nor sensitive to that pigment alone.
pmc-13277767: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2025 article comparing the chemistry and biological activity of leaf extracts from spinach and a related plant, Basella rubra. The journal editor-in-chief and the publisher agreed to the retraction over serious concerns about the reliability of the stated authorship and individual contributions. Evidence suggested the article may not have been produced as described. All authors agreed when notified, except one who did not respond.
pmc-13279167:
Megan Sheehan and colleagues report a 2026 study of blood pressure in early pregnancy. High blood pressure disorders in pregnancy can harm mother and baby, yet early risk tools are weak. The team tests whether paths of blood pressure from conception to twenty weeks can flag later illness. Illness here means preeclampsia and pregnancy high blood pressure.

Health records covered close to twenty six thousand single births from 2012 to 2020. About twenty two percent later had a high blood pressure disorder. Risk rose step by step across six blood pressure path groups. Adding the paths to known risk facts sharpened forecasts. The result supports closer watch for those on high paths.
pmc-13279367:
Md Mamunur Rashid and colleagues report a 2026 study that tests blood markers for liver cancer. The cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, is the top liver cancer type and a top cause of cancer death. It is most often found late, when cure odds are low. Old blood markers miss too many early cases, so new ones are sought in people with liver cirrhosis, meaning scarred liver.

Blood came from fifty cancer cases, half at stage one, plus fifty cirrhosis patients and twenty five healthy peers. A lab method that weighs molecules with high precision measured thirteen body chemicals picked from past work. The write up centres on aims and methods at this stage. Sound early markers could shift care by flagging cancer while treatment can still cure.
pmc-13279567:
Mariana Bezerra Miranda and colleagues give a 2026 systematic review of LED light care for chronic leg wounds. Long lasting leg wounds heal slowly and return often, at high cost. LED photobiomodulation uses low light to nudge tissue repair, with no cuts and low cost. Proof from trials was mixed, so the team pooled randomized trials, the strongest trial type.

Six trials met the bar, with searches in four databases to May 2026. Light colours spanned red to near infrared, and doses spanned a wide range. Most trials hinted at gains: smaller wound area, better wound bed and more blood flow, most in diabetic foot ulcers. One trial at the highest dose showed no gain. Dose may have a sweet spot, so set dose rules are the next step.
pmc-13279767:
Yinshan Wu and colleagues published a 2026 prospective study of how infection in fluid collections around the pancreas changes over time in severe acute pancreatitis. Twenty patients undergoing their first drainage procedure for suspected infected pancreatic necrosis had fluid tested two ways: standard culture and metagenomic sequencing, which reads all DNA from microbes in a sample. The team compared detection rates before and after fourteen days from illness onset.

Sequencing found microbes in 45 percent of cases against 30 percent for culture. Early collections were usually sterile, with positive results near 14 percent in the first two weeks. Later drainage turned positive far more often. Sequencing also uncovered mixed infections, anaerobes, and fungi that culture missed. Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterococcus species were the most frequent finds. The authors say the timing pattern supports the view that early pancreatic necrosis is usually sterile. Sequencing earns its keep mainly in later disease.
pmc-13279967:
Ibrahim Kasujja and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of how food insecurity and children's mental health feed into each other in Masaka District, Uganda. In resource-limited schools, the authors used realist thematic analysis to explain the mechanisms behind the link. They traced how hunger at home shows up in classrooms, and how children's and caregivers' distress loops back into household food trouble.

Three pathways organize their findings. Social causation runs from hunger, food-related shame, and emotional distress toward inward difficulties such as anxiety and withdrawal, and outward behaviors such as aggression and truancy. Social drift runs the other way, as mental health problems erode caregiving capacity and school attendance. Feedback loops lock the two together, compounding disadvantage over time. The authors argue responses must work at school, household, and social protection levels. They propose longitudinal and intervention studies to test the pathways.
pmc-13280267:
Esther Serra-Baldrich and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review of chronic prurigo nodularis, a skin disease of intensely itchy nodules that can persist for years and damage quality of life. The condition mostly affects older women and travels with other skin, psychiatric, and metabolic diseases. Its engine is a self-feeding itch-scratch cycle. Type-2 immune signals, nerve peptides, and scarring pathways reinforce one another in what the authors call a neuro-immune-fibrotic axis.

The disease's definition and name remain contested, with European and American guidance documents diverging. Treatment is shifting from improvised off-label drugs toward targeted biologics. Dupilumab and nemolizumab are the only agents backed by phase III trial evidence. JAK inhibitors look promising but remain investigational and need careful safety framing. The authors catalogue what is settled about causes and epidemiology. They press for standardized guidelines and treat-to-target strategies tuned to patients.
pmc-13280767:
Yan-Ning Chen and colleagues published a 2026 cell study of plumbagin, a plant compound, as a partner drug that makes cisplatin hit leukemia cells harder while sparing healthy cells. They treated MOLT-4 leukemia cells and normal macrophages with the chemotherapy drug alone, plumbagin alone, or the pair at low doses for one day. The combination is aimed at acute lymphoblastic leukemia, the commonest childhood cancer, where gentler regimens would be valuable.

Cell survival fell to 45.5 percent under the combination, against roughly 76 to 81 percent for either drug alone, while normal macrophages stayed 93 percent viable. Two antioxidants reversed the effect, pointing to oxidative stress as the mechanism: the pair flooded leukemia cells with reactive oxygen species, drained their glutathione defenses, and collapsed mitochondrial voltage. Downstream, the death machinery switched on, with killer caspases activated and DNA damage markers climbing. The authors present the pairing as an oxidation-driven strategy worth developing.
pmc-13280867:
Xiaohui Zhang and colleagues linked sleep and movement to constipation in a 2026 survey study. Constipation means hard, dry stools that are tough to pass. The team used a United States health survey from 2007 to 2010. More than five thousand adults gave sleep and activity data. Stool form was used to mark who had constipation. The team then weighed sleep length and weekly activity, alone and paired.

People who slept seven to eight hours had lower odds of constipation. So did people who stayed active each week. The link was strongest in men aged sixty and older. Active people had lower risk at every sleep length, short, right, or long. The authors say good sleep and regular movement may each help the gut. They note a survey can show links, not proof of cause.
pmc-13280967:
Luo Chen and colleagues built a family tree for a plant tribe in a 2026 study. The tribe, Sonerileae, is the second largest in its plant family. A full tree has been missing, which blocks work on its past. Gene data for its plants sat in many forms from many labs. The team merged four kinds of gene data into one set. They covered forty-one of forty-seven genera, with samples from one hundred eighty-four plants.

A new shared reference of thousands of gene spots let the mixed data line up. The tree that came out was clear and near complete. It beat trees built from one data type alone. For a long-stuck Asian branch, it matched a tree that needed a full genome draft. The authors offer the merge method as a model for other plant groups.
pmc-13281767:
Theng Choon Ooi and colleagues set grip strength norms for older Malaysians in a 2026 study. Grip strength is a quick gauge of muscle health. Low grip flags sarcopenia, the muscle loss of aging. The team used data from a long study of community elders. More than two thousand adults aged sixty and older were measured. Grip curves by age and sex were built, raw and weighed against body weight.

Grip peaked in the early sixties for both sexes. Men topped out near thirty-one kilograms and women near twenty. A regional cutoff set flagged close to half of elders as low grip. A local cutoff, the bottom fifth, flagged only about one in five. Both flags still tracked with muscle loss outcomes. The authors say the regional line may overcall weakness in Malaysia. They ask for long-term data to settle which line predicts real decline.
pmc-13281867:
Shengbo Yang and colleagues studied a Chinese herbal brew for liver cancer in a 2026 paper. The brew blends thirteen herbs and is used beside standard care. Its workings are poorly mapped. The team first ran computer models of its parts. They found close to two hundred active compounds and over one hundred possible targets in the body. Twenty-five targets sat at the hub of the web. Then forty patients joined a four-week test, half on standard care and half with the brew added.

Blood markers of liver strain fell in both groups. One clotting time clearly favored the brew group, improving there while worsening in the other. Symptom scores in the Chinese medicine frame also improved with the brew and worsened without it. The authors say the brew seems to act on many targets at once. They call the clinical edge early and in need of firmer trials.
pmc-13282067:
Hélène Platteeuw and co-authors report a 2026 study on a way to protect donor livers before transplant. Some livers come from donors after circulatory death, when the heart has stopped. Flushing the belly organs with warm, oxygen-rich blood may limit damage. The team asked whether such livers caused more postreperfusion syndrome, a sharp blood pressure drop when blood flow returns, than livers from brain-dead donors.

One hundred six recipients were compared, forty-seven with treated livers and fifty-nine from brain-dead donors. The pressure-drop problem struck about a quarter of each group, with no real gap after adjustments. Early graft failure, kidney injury, rejection, and bile or vessel problems also looked similar. The authors say the approach appears safe in the short term and can widen the donor pool.
pmc-13282267:
Faizan Ahmed and co-authors present a 2026 study comparing two strategies for older adults newly diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. Rhythm control tries to restore normal rhythm early, while rate control only slows the heart. The team used a large global health records network and matched patients on many traits to make the groups comparable.

After matching, each group held more than two hundred thousand patients aged sixty-five and over. At one year, death rates were higher with rhythm control than with rate control. Rhythm control also brought more dangerous rhythm events, fainting, hospital stays, and rhythm-restoring procedures. Blood clot events and major bleeding, though, were less frequent. Results split sharply by method: drug-based rhythm control drove the harm, while procedure-based control linked to lower death and hospital use. Careful selection, the authors say, is essential.
pmc-13282467:
Yu-Mei Li and co-authors published a cross-sectional study in 2026 on gut microbes and stool chemicals in polycystic ovary syndrome, called PCOS here. The work centred on women of normal weight, a group studied less often than women with obesity. It asked how gut bacteria, stool metabolites, and clinical measures relate to each other in this condition.

The team re-analysed gene sequencing data, then added metagenomic and stool metabolite tests on a small local group. Overall diversity did not differ between patients and controls. The PCOS group held more Ruminococcus and less Prevotella, and some bacteria tracked with insulin resistance and lower HDL cholesterol. Changes in bile acid and fat pathways stood out, pointing to the gut as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13282867:
Sweden's dental register holds the data behind a 2026 implant survival comparison whose lead author is Fernando Jose Mota de Almeida. The damage type is external cervical root resorption, which can destroy a tooth near the gum. The question is whether implants last as well in such sites.

Swedish register data from 2009 to 2022 yielded 605 matched pairs. One group had prior root damage and the other did not. Ten-year survival was high in both groups, and the gap was not statistically clear. Few implants were removed in either group. The authors note that low failure counts limit firm claims.
pmc-13283167:
Exercise beliefs among chemotherapy outpatients are surveyed against daily activity in Ozge Gumus's 2026 cross-sectional work. Patients getting outpatient chemo often move less and face fatigue. The team asked how activity levels link to social life and quality of life.

Surveys covered 101 patients, most of them women with gut or breast cancer. About 45 percent were inactive, and the rest were only lightly active by standard scores. Most agreed that exercise lifts mood and cuts stress in daily life. Fatigue, bad weather, and low drive were the top barriers named. More active patients reported fewer barriers and better function and health scores.
pmc-13283467:
Didi Mwengela, Nimah Ather, and John Kunesh described in 2026 a severe gullet infection in a 64-year-old man with a healthy immune system. Herpes simplex infection of the oesophagus usually strikes people with weakened immunity, so it is easy to miss in others. He arrived with strong burning behind the breastbone and could not tolerate swallowing food or drink.

A camera exam showed severe inflammation of the gullet, and a tissue sample confirmed herpes infection. He also had a history of acid reflux, which may have left the lining open to attack. Treatment with intravenous acyclovir, then tablets, plus an acid-blocking drug brought rapid relief. The report urges doctors to weigh viral causes when gullet symptoms resist standard care.
pmc-13283967:
Claudia Emmanuela Sanchis-Sanchis led a Spanish team in 2026 linking diet, gut bacteria, and mood in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The disease steadily destroys motor function and often brings gut and emotional trouble too. Forty-eight patients with bulbar or spinal onset disease recorded their food intake, answered mood scales, and gave stool measures for bacterial counts.

Statistical modelling drew out one nutrition factor made of vitamins B1, B2, B9, and C plus fibre. That factor tied inversely to anxiety and depression scores. Its effect ran partly through Bacteroides abundance and stool consistency, and the model explained about nineteen percent of the spread in distress. The authors suggest vitamin- and fibre-rich diets as a support strategy worth testing in this disease.
pmc-13284567:
Yu Jin Kim commented in 2026 on whether the diabetes drug metformin protects against stomach cancer, and at which stage. Evidence has conflicted: a nationwide cohort tied long-term metformin use to lower gastric cancer risk in patients not on insulin, while a Swedish cohort found no link. Lab work shows metformin slows gastric cancer cell growth, triggers cell death through energy pathways, and may even check the stomach germ Helicobacter pylori.

The commentary discusses a study comparing metformin and insulin use across stages of gastric cancer development. Cancer was less common in metformin users not on insulin, and more common in insulin users whatever else they took. Precancerous dysplasia showed no treatment pattern. Kim cautions that insulin use may itself mark worse metabolic disease, and that any metformin effect may act late in cancer development, with thin mechanistic proof so far.
pmc-13284867:
Nhan Truong Vu and Hoang Tran Viet report a 2026 two-case series on keyhole surgery for esophageal duplication cysts in children. These rare birth cysts near the food pipe can press on airways, and removal is advised to prevent infection, bleeding, or rupture. Both boys had repeat wheeze or cough, and scans showed cysts beside the esophagus.

Surgery used three small ports with low-pressure gas, took about two hours, and caused minimal blood loss in these two cases. One child had a small tear in the food pipe lining, fixed during surgery, with feeding back by day five. The other ate by day one. Both left within a week and stayed free of return at one year.
pmc-13284967:
Yoshihito Mima, Masako Yamamoto, and Ken Iozumi report a 2026 single-center survey of nemolizumab treatment for prurigo nodularis in Japan. The chronic skin illness causes severe lasting itch, and patient satisfaction with older care was low. Twenty patients who stayed on monthly treatment for at least twelve weeks were assessed at a Tokyo hospital.

Itch scores fell sharply by week sixteen, and clinician ratings of lesions also improved in the group tracked here. Patients recalled far less daily time spent on skin creams and far less time preoccupied by the illness after treatment. The authors note standard scores may miss daily burden, so patient reports add a fuller view of benefit.
pmc-13285267:
Yuanmin Huang and co-authors compare two grades of sauce-flavor Daqu, the starter brick for Chinese baijiu, in a 2026 study. Aroma grade marks Daqu quality, so the team joined chemical measures, enzyme tests, microbe surveys, and flavor profiling for first-grade and second-grade samples. Links between traits and grade were then mapped.

First-grade Daqu held more acid and amino nitrogen, lower pH, and microbes tied to flavor building blocks in the data reported here. Second-grade samples had stronger starch-breaking enzymes and microbes linked to off-odors. Eleven scent compounds split the grades, with aldehydes tracking good aroma and one sulfur compound tracking faults. The authors offer the markers for quality checks in production.
pmc-13285367:
Md Osman Hossain Zabir and colleagues tracked flu-like and severe respiratory illness in young children in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, from 2021 to 2023. Their 2026 study fills a gap, because little local evidence described which viruses circulate in children under five there. Crowding and monsoon rains shape illness patterns in the district.

Hospital surveillance enrolled 968 children, most of them infants. Swab tests looked for flu viruses, the coronavirus behind COVID-19, and RSV. Only about one child in eight tested positive, and flu made up most positive results. Detections peaked during the monsoon months, with one flu type leading early and another later. Severe illness and breathing trouble were linked to testing positive.
pmc-13286867:
Mario Assenza and co-authors trace breast cancer's rare spread to the uterine cervix in a 2026 case report and literature review. A 59-year-old woman treated in 2015 for hormone-sensitive ductal breast cancer, with surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and endocrine therapy, later saw a tumor marker climb and settle near four times its ceiling. Bleeding prompted imaging that lit up a metabolically active lesion in her uterus.

Biopsies of womb and cervix returned a poorly differentiated carcinoma matching her breast primary's lineage rather than a new uterine cancer. Marker stains for mammary origin, including GATA3 and mammaglobin, anchor the diagnosis in their review. The tumor's receptor profile had flipped since 2015, a discordance the authors say makes re-biopsy essential. She began combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy in March 2024, tolerating it well as treatment continues.
pmc-13287467:
Kimberly Milleman and co-authors ran a blinded trial in 2026 of mouth rinses holding essential oils in 154 adults with diabetes, a group prone to gum disease. Volunteers used a rinse with alcohol, one without alcohol, or a plain control rinse, alongside twice-daily brushing for twelve weeks.

Both oil rinses cut plaque and gum inflammation scores far more than the control rinse at twelve weeks. Gum bleeding fell by roughly two thirds or more. Users also reported better mouth comfort, and soft tissue tolerance was good. Many participants had never been told diabetes raises gum risk. The authors urge joint work between diabetes and dental teams.
pmc-13287567:
P J Pappoe-Ashong and colleagues ran four blood surveys in Accra, Ghana, between August 2020 and January 2022 to track past coronavirus infection across pandemic waves. Samples totalling 1,096 were drawn from stored clinic material and weighted to match the city's age and sex mix.

Adjusted share with antibodies rose from 58.3% in the first wave to above 90% by the second, then stayed at or above 96%. Adults reached near-total exposure earlier than children. Antibody strength kept climbing through the third wave even after spread plateaued, pointing to repeated exposure. The authors describe intense, repeated transmission shaping immunity in the city within eighteen months.
pmc-13287667:
Pauline Potratz and colleagues sampled human lung tissue in 2026 from transplant and surgery patients, comparing upper airway regions with deep air-sac regions. Gene sequencing often reports rich microbe life even in deep lung, so the team added growing tests and imaging to check whether those microbes are alive.

Sequencing showed a shift along the airway: skin-like and mouth-like bacteria gave way to air-shunning kinds deeper down, with wide differences between patients. Growing and imaging found almost no living microbes in the deep regions. The authors conclude that deep lung DNA signals likely come from very few bacteria or from dead remains, not a thriving community.
pmc-13288867:
Elin Allansson Kjolhede and co-authors quantify flu danger for people with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 Swedish register study. Linking the national diabetes register to population, patient, and statistics records, they followed 371,811 patients and 1,728,856 matched controls across six influenza seasons from 2013 onward.

Hospital admission for flu touched 1.6 percent of patients with diabetes against 1.0 percent of controls in their data, and flu-related death was also more common in the diabetes group. Adjusted hazards stayed clearly elevated for both outcomes. Absolute danger concentrated in people with heart, kidney, or lung disease, while relative risk peaked in younger patients. Worse sugar control and weaker kidney function each tracked with more admissions.
pmc-13289067:
Anne Juul Grabmayr and colleagues study emergency calls from public housing in Denmark. Their 2026 study deals with cardiac arrests outside hospitals. It covers four housing areas in Copenhagen. Most residents there are from minority groups. Calls ran from 2017 to 2022.

The team heard 17 calls about 13 arrests. Good calls fit the script used by dispatchers. Those calls led to fast CPR guidance. Hard calls broke from the script. Crowded calls and language gaps caused delays. Raw emotion and low first aid skill also hurt. Many witnesses phoned kin before calling for help. Calm tone and plain words helped dispatchers cope.
pmc-13289367:
Anouk C Meijs led a 2026 first-in-human trial of SOL-116, an antibody aimed at bile salt-stimulated lipase for rheumatoid arthritis. That enzyme helps digest fat and may also drive joint inflammation, making it a fresh drug target. The randomized, blinded study tested single rising doses and repeat doses under the skin in healthy volunteers, plus one dose in patients.

A total of 48 healthy participants and 8 patients with arthritis took part in the trial. The drug was safe and well tolerated at doses tested, and blood levels rose in line with dose size. Free levels of the target enzyme in blood fell, proving the antibody hit its mark as intended. Immune reactions against the drug stayed uncommon, supporting larger patient trials.
pmc-13289467:
Lea Gölz, Julius Rosenhan, Kaloyan Kamenov, and Birgit Prodinger carried out a 2026 scoping review on training health workers in disability inclusion. People with disabilities face deep, avoidable gaps in care, and many clinicians feel unready to give fair, rights-based help. The review maps what current courses teach and which themes dominate across published and gray sources.

Literature from January 2011 to August 2024 was searched across medical databases, web sources, and organization sites. A total of 172 publications qualified, mostly from the Americas and Europe, run at local or national level. Charting covered course scope, disability views, involvement of disabled people, teaching style, and target professions. Nineteen themes emerged from the set.
pmc-13289867:
Sowmya Pujari headed a 2026 interview study on health and child nutrition views among Koraga tribal mothers in Southern Karnataka, India. Child malnutrition drives nearly a third of child deaths worldwide and stays high in India despite growth. Koraga families face added poverty, access, and cultural barriers, so maternal views are central to designing help that families will actually use.

Twenty mothers of children aged 5 to 10 were interviewed in depth from October 2023 to March 2024 in Tulu and Kannada. Five themes emerged: shifting health views, nutrition beliefs and habits, hygiene promotion, mixing traditional healing with modern care, and barriers with community fixes. Health workers and government food schemes featured as trusted supports.
pmc-13290567:
Driving cholesterol to very low levels did not raise bleeding in heart attack patients on two blood thinners, according to a 2026 prospective cohort study by Tianfu Fu and colleagues. The worry was that ultra-low LDL cholesterol might disturb clotting in patients taking PCSK9 inhibitors after stenting for acute coronary syndrome.

The single-center study followed 120 such patients for 12 months, splitting them by achieved LDL cholesterol at a cutoff of 0.78 mmol/L and tracking clotting tests and platelet function. Clinically relevant bleeding was similar in the low and non-low groups, though with only seven events the comparison was underpowered, and clotting measures stayed stable throughout. Major heart events also did not differ significantly. Fu and colleagues describe the safety signal as reassuring but exploratory.
pmc-13291167:
Railway switches wear out and fail in costly ways. Mohammad Adoul Amin and co-authors build a 2026 system to sort vibration events at these junctions. Their aim is honest accuracy, not inflated scores from leaky test design.

Shake data came from a full-size outdoor test track. All readings from one event stayed in one data split. That rule blocks a common source of false gains. A smart generator made extra samples for rare classes. Twenty-one sorting models from eight families were compared. Group models proved most stable across checks. Best held-out accuracy passed four fifths of cases. Careful data order mattered as much as model choice.
pmc-13291267:
Severe lung infection may split into three hidden types. Mark Jeffrey leads a 2026 study of patients in critical care. Pneumonia kills more people than any other infection. Its deep biology is still poorly mapped.

Wash fluid from lungs was tested many ways. Gene activity, immune signals, microbes, and clinical notes were joined. Three lung-only types, called Pneumotypes, emerged. All looked alike at the bedside at first. Their paths then split sharply. One type healed fastest with balanced defense. Another dragged on breathing machines with young immune cells. The types may guide targeted drugs in future care.
pmc-13292067:
Lei Luo and co-authors hunt a 2026 lead on sunitinib resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a kidney cancer where the drug often stops working. Mining a public dataset comparing resistant and parent cells pointed them to PARP9 as a hub gene. They confirmed the lead in two resistant cell lines and in patient-derived organoids.

Resistant cells and patient tissues both carried extra PARP9. Silencing it restored sunitinib sensitivity, while adding it to parent cells created resistance. PARP9 partnered with STAT1, boosting its phosphorylation and switching on the IRF1 program, including ISG15 and IFIT1. The PARP inhibitor olaparib weakened that signaling, and olaparib plus sunitinib outperformed either drug alone in organoids. The authors propose the PARP9-STAT1 route as a treatment angle.
pmc-13292467:
Zirui Fu and co-authors compare a 2026 cooking question with lab digestion: how do steaming, microwaving, and baking change tilapia protein quality and bioactivity? Cooked fish went through the static INFOGEST in vitro digestion protocol. The team measured hydrolysis, molecular weight spread, amino acid release and scores, then checked health-related activities in cells and computer simulations.

Heat generally improved digestibility by loosening protein structure and exposing enzyme cut sites. Baking scored highest on hydrolysis degree, essential amino acid index, and biological value. Steaming released amino acids fastest. Baking also boosted blood-sugar enzyme inhibition, with alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase inhibition at 51.48 and 51.74 percent in digested samples. Steaming led on antioxidant power, its ABTS scavenging reaching 69.00 percent against 57.96 percent for fresh fish.
pmc-13292567:
Lubna Fawaz's team runs a 2026 single-center trial comparing weekly phone-based telemonitoring against ordinary clinic education for children with type 1 diabetes. One hundred forty young patients were randomized evenly. The intervention group reviewed glucose records, diet, and insulin doses with educators by phone each week, while controls learned during routine outpatient visits, with checks at start and six months.

Blood sugar control diverged clearly. Mean HbA1c read 8.21 in the telemonitoring group against 9.25 under standard care, in the study's reported units. Dangerous ketoacidosis episodes hit 18 percent of controls but only 1.7 percent of the phone group. Overall complication rates also ran higher in controls, 37.7 against 15.5 percent across the groups. Quality-of-life scores improved significantly with telemonitoring, and the authors endorse the approach.
pmc-13292667:
Xingzhao Wen and co-authors chase a 2026 brain link in childhood arthritis: children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis show more mood and behavior symptoms, and nobody knows why. Blood from sixteen children with active disease, matched healthy controls, and twelve of the same patients in quiet phases went through Olink protein profiling. Mouse arthritis experiments then probed the brain directly.

Active patients carried distinctly altered neurobiological protein patterns that tracked with pain and life-impact scores, and the changes lingered even when joints quieted. Mice with long-running arthritis showed fired-up microglia and stunted new neuron growth in the hippocampus, with the cortex spared. Gene data blamed mitochondrial strain and oxidative stress. A blood protein, HMOX2, mirrored the hippocampal microglial activation closely. Interleukin-6 and interleukin-18 emerged as candidate messengers in patients.
pmc-13293367:
Sonalee Arun Joshi and colleagues present, in 2026, a new memory task that tests how people use scene context to tell new sights from seen ones. Faulty context use appears in many mental illnesses, yet older tasks test single cues, not full scenes.

A total of 44 healthy adults finished the Context Discrimination and Recognition Task, which uses complex scenes at graded levels of sameness. Scores for telling scenes apart and for spotting seen scenes rose together strongly. As scenes grew less alike, both skills improved, showing the task senses fine shifts. The team offers it as a sharper tool for clinic research.
pmc-13293567:
Runze Hu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, Chinese language models tuned for motivational interviewing, a counseling style that helps people change health habits. Skilled human counselors are scarce, and Chinese training material for this style is limited.

The team screened five public counseling datasets and rebuilt 2040 talks into the target style with a structured prompt, using 2000 for training and 40 for testing. Three open models were tuned and then scored by automatic measures and by trained raters using a standard fidelity manual. Tuned model talks were compared with 30 real sessions. The work tests whether tuning lifts counseling quality.
pmc-13293667:
Alba Mena-González, Raquel Leirós-Rodríguez, and Pablo Hernandez-Lucas pool, in a 2026 review, evidence on physical therapy for endometriosis symptoms. The condition grows womb-like tissue outside the womb, causing pelvic pain and lower quality of life in many women.

Study highlights state that therapy methods cut endometriosis pain and improved quality of life across the trials pooled. Massage, electrical therapy, exercise, and health teaching each helped ease pelvic symptoms in the included work.
