Better handling of differing treatment effects across patients is one promised gain. Equity also features, since simulated patients can expose gaps before real enrollment begins.
pmc-13415767:
Xin-Mei Hu and colleagues stabilize the hidden bottom interface of blue perovskite light emitting diodes, in 2026. Blue devices lag behind green and red ones, partly because solvents damage the layer beneath the light emitting crystal. Their fix lays a three-dimensional cross-linked network of pentaerythritol tetraacrylate over the hole transport layer.

The network shields the layer below from solvent attack and its carbonyl groups grip the perovskite, sealing defects. An electric dipole at the junction also eases hole entry. Devices reached external quantum efficiencies of about 28 percent at 488 nanometers, with strong results at two deeper blue wavelengths. Peak brightness topped twenty-six thousand candelas per square meter.
pmc-13415867:
Elizabeth E. Hoy leads a team describing NASA airborne laser surveys of Arctic and boreal land under the ABoVE campaign, in 2026. The Land, Vegetation, and Ice Sensor flew thirty-two missions in the summers of 2017 and 2019. Coverage topped 91,000 square kilometers across Alaska and northwestern Canada, spanning twelve ecoregions from boreal forest to tundra.

The sensor records full waveform laser returns, giving surface height and vegetation structure together. Coverage reaches far north of the limits of the GEDI space sensor. Overlap with the ICESat-2 satellite allows direct comparison between airborne and orbital measurements. Open tools for access and visualization accompany the data records described.
pmc-13416367: Adil Farooq Wali and co-authors issued this correction in 2026 for their 2025 Pharmaceuticals review on epigenetic changes in liver cancer. The notice is a correction only: five numbered references in the published article are replaced with the correct ones. Swapped entries cover cancer molecular markers, liver cancer causes and drugs, Lynch syndrome genetics, epigenetic remodeling in liver cancer, and RNA modification in cancer. Nothing in the article's own analysis changes. Readers citing the review should use the replacement reference list given here.
pmc-13416567:
Adrienne Bruder, Naomi Laventhal, Raja Rabah, and Jacqueline Meadow report a preterm infant whose liver failure traced to a rare gene disorder, in a 2026 case. The growth restricted girl, born at thirty-two weeks, developed feeding intolerance and blood clotting failure and was first treated for sepsis. Her course stretched through a long hospitalization with extensive testing.

She progressed to acute liver failure and end stage brain dysfunction from liver failure. Autopsy tissue showed neonatal hemochromatosis, an iron overload pattern, alongside infantile liver failure syndrome type one. Faults in the LARS1 gene, which charges a transfer RNA for leucine, caused that syndrome. Overlapping signs with sepsis delayed recognition.
pmc-13417267:
Kevin A Rodríguez-Fernández and colleagues track jump changes in teenage female volleyball players after nine weeks of complex training, in a 2026 single group study. Complex training pairs heavy lifts with jumps. Only eight athletes took part, so the team used Bayesian statistics, which suit small groups by giving probability based readings.

Three jump types rose by about 14 percent each, with parallel gains in peak power. Body mass and muscle share, checked by an electrical body scan, barely moved. Without a control group or muscle structure measures, the cause of the jump gains stays open. The study mainly shows a workable way to judge small squad training effects.
pmc-13417967:
Osman Onur Sarı, Hasan Sözel, and Yıldız Kılar Sözel examine smoking exposure and muscle loss in a 2026 cross sectional analysis. Sarcopenia, age related loss of muscle mass and strength, was judged from the psoas muscle area on abdominal scans. The group held 261 adults scanned between 2019 and 2022, sorted into active smokers, passive smokers, and non smokers.

Muscle index values did not differ significantly across the three groups. Sarcopenia rates also overlapped, though passive smokers sat a little higher without reaching significance. Blood measures were similar, apart from higher haemoglobin in active smokers. In this clinic group, smoking exposure alone did not track with lower measured muscle mass.
pmc-13418467:
Rudong Li, Zhipeng Zhao, and Xudong Wang review adaptor proteins called 14-3-3 and their partner proteins in digestive cancers, in a 2026 evidence graded review. These adaptors grab tagged partners and change their place, stability, and activity under stress. The review grades partner modules in stomach, bowel, pancreatic, liver, and bile duct cancers by strength of proof.

Named pairings explain drug tolerance in each cancer: one shields a death protein in stomach cancer, others sustain stress responses or gemcitabine resistance elsewhere. Liver and bile modules look context dependent so far. The useful unit is the specific stressed pairing, not total adaptor levels, the authors argue.
pmc-13419967:
Zhoushan Gu and colleagues review focused radiation as a treatment for rapid heart rhythm that resists drugs and standard ablation. Stubborn ventricular tachycardia brings high illness and death rates, and options run out for many patients. The method aims a tight radiation beam at the faulty heart tissue, guided by imaging and electrical maps of the heart.

Pooled data from 23 studies found episode cuts above 90 percent after treatment in this hard group, along with fewer shocks from implanted devices. The review covers patient choice, target drawing, motion control, and dose planning in practical detail. Short-term results encourage, yet dose and long-term safety remain open. The paper gives new centers a grounded path into a fast-growing therapy.
pmc-13421267:
Lea M. Bartsch, Eda Mizrak and Klaus Oberauer investigate, in a 2026 paper, how working memory and long-term memory cooperate during immediate recall. The two systems overlap in practice, and the authors probed their interaction using interference from earlier material and a distracting task during the waiting interval.

In one experiment, volunteers learned word-object pairs; a second used object-colour pairs with a colour reproduction test. Interference hurt performance mainly at larger set sizes, suggesting long-term memory carries more of the load there, while the distracting task hurt most at small set sizes, where working memory dominates. When interference blocked long-term memory, people leaned harder on working memory, which the distraction then disrupted. The authors favour a flexible partnership between the systems.
pmc-13421467:
Xiaoyi Wang, Raif Remigio Alves, Qiuyu Hu and Hanlin Chen examine, in a 2026 study, how the framing of AI-written product pitches changes consumer trust. Drawing on regulatory focus theory, they contrasted promotion framing, which stresses gains, with prevention framing, which stresses avoiding losses, across pleasure products and practical ones.

The team recorded brain waves with event-related potentials while participants judged the pitches. Promotion-framed messages earned higher trust ratings and faster decisions for both product types. Neural signals diverged by pairing: for pleasure products, promotion framing drew stronger attention-related responses and easier semantic processing. The authors caution that brain signals index attention and processing rather than trust itself, though the pattern in choices was clear.
pmc-13421567:
Muhammad Anwar Ul Hassan and five colleagues map, in a 2026 study, the tiny forces cells use to feel how stiff their surroundings are, and show that oxidative stress scrambles that sense. Cells on flexible micropillars bend them as they pull, letting the team read traction forces at submicron scale during spreading.

Mouse fibroblasts exposed to a sublethal dose of hydrogen peroxide failed to remodel their skeletons and adhesions normally on stiff surfaces, and their nanoscale force units lost coordination. Their mitochondrial networks fragmented, with matching shifts in dynamics genes. Cells genetically lacking a mitochondrial fusion protein copied the defect exactly. The authors name mitochondrial integrity as a key control on stiffness sensing under stress.
pmc-13423067:
Lucantonio and colleagues studied in 2026 how a signal protein, IL-27, shapes natural killer cells inside bowel cancers. Natural killer cells are innate immune cells that can kill tumours early, but inside colorectal cancer they often stay immature and weak. The team grew engineered mouse bowel tumours and profiled the immune cells within them using single-cell gene readings.

Tumours were dominated by immature natural killer cells with fewer activating receptors and weaker killing power. The tumour setting held these cells in the immature state instead of letting them mature. IL-27 made by the tumour itself kept the killer cells present, active, and producing interferon-gamma, a key attack signal. Blocking IL-27 reduced killer cell numbers, their activation, and the immature subset share. Human data showed the same IL-27 signal pattern in tumour killer cells.
pmc-13423867:
Marcelo D. T. Torres, Fangping Wan, and Cesar de la Fuente-Nunez use deep learning to mine prion proteins, famous for misfolding and disease, for hidden bacteria-killing peptides. Proteins prone to clumping are increasingly seen as part of host defence, and the team wondered whether their sequences conceal ready-made antimicrobial fragments.

Their screening program swept 19.3 million fragments cut from 2,897 prion-related proteins and flagged 1,179 candidates, dubbed prionins. The lab then made 75 of them: 59 killed bacterial pathogens, 53 damaged bacterial membranes, and 2 eased Acinetobacter baumannii infection in mice. The authors propose prion sequences as an untapped library for antibiotic discovery at a time of rising drug resistance.
pmc-13424167:
Bin-Bin Liu and seven colleagues argue that translating botanical floras should be run like a software release: versioned, audited, and checked for the small details machines will reuse. Floras pack dense taxonomic knowledge written for expert readers, and a fluent translation can still corrupt a measurement, a symbol, or a negation, quietly breaking later searches and links.

Using the rose family volume of Flora of China as the worked example, the team shows how large language models can translate at scale under tight controls. Their workflow adds quality checks, terminology control, and name normalisation, with integrity metrics steering each revision. The goal is text that stays searchable across languages and safe for databases.
pmc-13424467:
Dolev Perez and seven colleagues examine whether prostate size changes the results of aquablation, a robot-guided waterjet operation for enlarged prostates, in a prospective single-centre cohort treated between 2023 and 2025. They compared 324 men with glands under 80 cubic centimetres against 304 with larger glands, using standard symptom and sexual function questionnaires for two years.

Larger glands meant more preoperative catheter dependence, 34% against 18.2%, slightly longer operations, and a modestly longer hospital stay. Relief was large and durable in both groups: symptom scores fell from about 25 to near 6 by twenty-four months, with irritative symptoms improving as well. Size, the authors conclude, should not bar men from the procedure.
pmc-13425967:
Yuzhen Ding and colleagues mapped distance-dependent brain connectivity in untreated first-episode depression in a 2026 resting-state MRI study. Scans came from 191 patients experiencing a first episode without drug treatment and 130 healthy controls. The team quantified global, long-range, and short-range functional connectivity strength at each brain location, then probed specific circuits with distance-constrained seed analyses.

Spatial patterns of altered connectivity were also matched against atlas maps of neurotransmitter receptors and transporters. Linking wiring distance with chemical systems may explain why depression disrupts some networks more than others and suggest circuit targets for treatment.
pmc-13426367:
Jiaqi Chen and colleagues report a giant liver adenoma of unknown cause in a 24-year-old man in a 2026 case study. He had no definite risk factors, and symptoms plus imaging were nonspecific, so cancer was suspected before surgery. Frozen-section reading during the operation disagreed with later routine pathology, which first suggested focal nodular hyperplasia instead.

Expert consultation at a tertiary center finally confirmed hepatocellular adenoma, a benign tumor easily confused with its malignant cousin. The patient had his right liver lobe and gallbladder removed and stayed well through one year of follow-up, and the authors urge keeping adenoma in the differential for young patients.
pmc-13427367:
Tian and colleagues published a 2026 study on brighter, longer-lasting deep-red LED lights. Perovskite crystals can glow deep red, suiting screens and lighting uses. The glow layer forms on a base plate whose surface can spoil it. The team doped that base with magnesium to tame its harsh surface.

The doped base carried fewer surface flaws and less unwanted chemical bite. Glow layers grown on it formed slowly and evenly, with fewer defects. The finished lights hit a peak efficiency above 23 percent in their tests. They also ran for a 376-hour half-life under steady power stress. Careful base tuning, the authors show, lifts both brightness and lifespan. Gentler film growth also slowed the breakdown seen under heat stress.
pmc-13427467:
Ibrahim A. Bakari, Lulu Sakafu, and Mwajabu A. Saleh report a toddler whose dengue bleeding in the brain was first read as gastroenteritis in a 2026 case study. The 22-month-old boy arrived at a Tanzanian regional hospital with prolonged fever, coffee-ground vomiting, nonbloody diarrhea, and repeated convulsions, and was treated for gut infection with sepsis. Deterioration prompted transfer to the national hospital, where focal nerve deficits, enlarged liver with jaundice, and severe clotting failure emerged.

Brain MRI showed extensive bleeding into the ventricles with obstructive fluid build-up and multiple fresh infarcts from dengue-driven coagulopathy. The authors blame incomplete examinations, especially skipped nervous system checks, for dangerous diagnostic delay in febrile children.
pmc-13427667:
Felipe A. Cini and Luke Remage-Healey study, in a 2026 paper, how groups of brain cells act together when songbirds hear songs. Single neurons are usually studied one at a time, yet learning may depend on ensembles, sets of cells firing in precise patterns. The work focuses on a hearing region in the songbird forebrain that helps birds recognize songs they have heard before. Dense electrode arrays recorded many cells at once during song playback.

Several ensembles answered each song in parallel, mixing excitatory and inhibitory cells that sat near one another. With repeated plays over tens of minutes, the groups grew pickier about which song they answered. Their makeup also reshaped quickly. Findings like these shift attention from lone cells to flexible teams as the unit of auditory memory.
pmc-13427867:
Gilson and colleagues published a 2026 study of fish bones from old sites in Fuerteventura. The island's first people, the Majos, are often told as a farming story. Fish remains from three sites let the team test how much the sea fed them. Their work spans the full span of native life on the island.

The team identified bones from 27 fish species across the three dig sites. Parrotfish turned up most often, pointing to a focused way of catching them. Shellfish gathering added more food from the shore zone. Traces also hint at use of turtles and monk seals at times. The authors link fishing rounds to where settlements sat along the coast. The sea, they argue, anchored Majos life from first settlement to conquest.
pmc-13430167:
Alaa G. Al-Maaitah and co-authors present, in a 2026 case report, a late bleed at a tumor site as a possible herald of returning cancer. Their patient was a 27-year-old man with a large right frontal lobe tumor and pressure symptoms. Surgery removed the growth fully, and pathology named it rhabdoid meningioma, a rare grade III tumor with a fierce reputation. Radiation followed without major problems.

Six months later headaches returned, and scans showed a growing blood collection where the tumor had been, with no new tumor tissue visible. No injury or medical cause explained the bleeding. Two months after that, scans found spread to his lungs and bones, and he died soon after. The authors urge doctors to treat unexplained late bleeding at a meningioma site as a possible early sign of recurrence, prompting closer watch.
pmc-13430267:
Timothy Moreels and colleagues argue, in a 2026 Belgian study, that quality of life in older dialysis patients is being measured with the wrong ruler. Health-related questionnaires ask about symptoms and function, yet patients judge their lives more broadly. The team studied 111 in-center hemodialysis patients aged 65 and older at four Flemish hospitals. Each completed a full geriatric assessment, frailty and daily-living inventories, two standard health questionnaires, and one personal self-assessment that anchors life quality against their own best and worst times.

The standard utility score did not correlate at all with the personal assessment. Thinking ability, usual activities, hospital admissions, self-rated health, and social functioning together explained about 31 percent of the personal score's variation. Three patient clusters emerged, from resilient to psychologically frail. Care aimed only at lab values and symptoms, the authors say, misses what older patients call a good life.
pmc-13431467:
Chen and co-authors construct a wound dressing with a disguise in this 2026 study. The disguise is nanoparticles wrapped in the membranes of freeze-killed M2 macrophages. Macrophages are immune cells; the M2 type calms inflammation and promotes repair. The core particle is MXene, a two-dimensional material. It converts near-infrared light into heat. That gives the composite antibacterial photothermal power.

The coating kept the macrophages' structure and working proteins. It converted light to heat well. In lab tests it cut inflammatory cytokine release and neutralized harmful oxygen radicals. It killed both E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. It also spurred new blood vessel growth. In diabetic mice with skin wounds, the material plus near-infrared light sped closure. It increased collagen deposition and nudged wound macrophages toward the healing M2 state. No obvious toxicity appeared at the tested dose.
pmc-13431967:
Izadian and colleagues engineered an injectable artificial photoreceptor in 2026 that could restore light sensing in blind retinas without implanted electronics or gene therapy. The particles pair gold nanoparticles with a plastic coating on a mineral core, and they absorb green light most strongly, converting it into local electrical stimulation for surviving retinal cells.

In lab tests, light shone on human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells with the particles present raised their electrical firing. The cells also shifted energy production toward the mitochondrial route without signs of programmed death. Injected into the eyes of blind model mice, the particles restored light-driven retinal activity in tissue tests. The mice also showed a stronger pupil response to light and larger brainwave responses, confirming function in the living animal.
pmc-13432867:
Pang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how Orf virus causes its crusty skin sores and dodges the immune system. The poxvirus spreads from sheep and goats to people and can infect the same host again and again. The review gathers recent molecular and immunology work on the virus's life cycle, from entry and copying to lesion growth.

Orf virus carries a toolkit of proteins that blunt host defenses step by step. They damp the interferon alarm, jam the NF-κB command pathway for inflammation, and block infected cells from self-destructing on schedule. Together these tricks let the virus finish its cycle before immunity clears it, and they help explain repeat infections. The authors argue that decoding this evasion kit is the route to better vaccines and new antiviral drugs for livestock and exposed workers.
pmc-13433267:
Guoqin Wei and co-authors found a fat-like signal in 2026 that wakes eye guard cells and shields sight in mice whose light-sensing cells waste away. Waste of those cells drives blind turns in many eye diseases, where nerve, vessel, and glial ties fray at once. A wide chemical sweep flagged one fat amide as far off its sound level in sick eyes.

Doses packed in holed silicon grains lit guard cells, which then poured out vessel and nerve guard factors that slowed both vessel and nerve loss. The team pinned a grip protein that the signal needs to fire the guard cells. With that grip gone, the shield failed. The authors pitch the signal and its kin as drug leads for eye waste diseases.
pmc-13434567:
Ziheng Ni and coauthors build a light based beam steerer for wireless links in 2026. Silicon delay lines let every antenna part feed every beam, unlike older split designs. Stronger, wider beams with fast switching are the goal for next generation networks.

Beams pointed in 13 directions past plus or minus 50 degrees with no squint across the band. Switching took just 60 nanoseconds. Signal strength beat the split design by 2.9 decibels at the test frequency. A dense data signal crossed 20 meters outdoors with low error. The chip scale plan suits future 5G and 6G base units.
pmc-13435567:
Jantri N Pahut and coauthors interview seven Sama Dilaut graduates in the Philippines in 2026 about how belief in their school selves grew. The sea nomad group faces bias and deep poverty, and few reach university. Long talks in three languages trace each path from childhood to degree.

Graduates credit family, peers, and community backing for pushing through bias and money strain. Faith, clear goals, and grit kept that belief alive in hard terms. School links to home and scholarship rules helped from outside the home. The lens of nested social worlds frames the tale. Colleges serving isolated groups can copy the supports named here.
pmc-13436567:
Shareef and colleagues tested in 2026 whether astragalin, a plant compound, can slow colorectal cancer in lab dishes and in rats. Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, and plant compounds are a steady source of candidate preventive drugs. The team measured growth of two human colon cancer cell lines and early precancerous changes in rat colons.

Astragalin slowed both cell lines at modest doses. In rats given a cancer-causing chemical, two months of the compound cut early abnormal crypt clusters and improved colon tissue structure. It also lowered a key growth signal while raising a cell-death signal. It also boosted antioxidant defenses and calmed inflammation signals. The authors conclude the compound shows preventive promise, while noting animal findings are an early step.
pmc-13436667:
Clifford M Marks and coauthors audit spine transfers to a level one trauma center over five years in 2026. The set holds 1,918 transfers sent for spine review from 2017 to 2022. Transfers counted as needed only if surgery, key scans, intensive care, or specialty admission followed.

By that rule 617 transfers, or 32.2 percent, look potentially avoidable. Just 3.3 percent went to surgery within twelve hours of arrival. About eighteen percent went home straight from the emergency ward. Stays there ran just over fifteen hours for needed transfers. Better triage rules could spare many patients a long move.
pmc-13438567:
Wang and co-authors traced how kidney tubule cells in hormone-driven hypertension order neighboring macrophages to self-destruct by inflammatory pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death. In mice made hypertensive with a salt-and-hormone regimen mimicking aldosterone excess, urinary ATP and the ATP-release channel PANX1 both rose sharply in kidney tissue.

Blocking the hormone receptor with finerenone cut urinary ATP, PANX1 expression, tubule injury, and macrophage inflammation together in the treated animals. Interrupting the signal at any step, the release channel, ATP itself, or its P2X7 receptor on macrophages, likewise eased tubule damage and pyroptosis in the kidney cortex. Co-culture experiments confirmed tubule cells under hormone stimulation drove macrophage death and migration, reversible by silencing the channel in the tubule cells. Single-cell sequencing verified the pathway's activation in real kidney macrophages.
pmc-13440567:
An and colleagues built a tumour-based printing ink in 2026 for modelling glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer.  The team grew glioblastoma cells in gels tuned to tumour stiffness and squeezed them to mimic pressure inside the skull. This workout pushed cells to release their own matrix, which was collected as a bioink, a cell-friendly printing material.

The ink carried stronger tumour signals than plain gel controls, including higher levels of GDF15, MMP2, and MMP9, all linked to tumour spread. Printed models made from the ink grew faster and switched on more invasion-related genes. Adding vessel cells or fibroblasts, which are support cells, recreated stromal activation and matrix change seen in real tumours. The authors present the ink as a repeatable platform for glioblastoma-on-chip studies and drug tests.
pmc-13441167:
Silvia Piunno and co-authors follow patients with a puzzling form of lupus: blood tests show active disease, yet they feel clinically well for long periods. Their 2026 longitudinal study asks whether two blood markers, anti-dsDNA antibodies and complement C3, can predict future flares in this group.

Sixty patients from a London lupus cohort contributed 531 visits over an average follow-up of 3.3 years. Despite their quiet clinical picture, 63.3 percent experienced at least one flare. Visit-by-visit analysis showed that rising anti-dsDNA levels and falling C3 independently predicted a flare or sustained activity at the next visit, including moderate-to-severe flares. Patients who flared were also more often anti-Ro positive. The authors argue this state is rarely benign and needs close clinical and blood monitoring.
pmc-13443767:
Francis Smit and colleagues argue that specialist training is a national asset for South Africa in a 2026 essay. Training a specialist takes 12 to 15 years of public funds, deep in wards where trainees also carry real patient loads. Universities, provinces, hospitals, and councils share the build.

Since training lives inside care, ward quality and school quality rise or fall together. Staff gaps, broken gear, and weak rule hit both patients and pupils at once. The authors say pass marks on school checks now double as a gauge of system health. A specialist's worth spills past one career into leadership, research, and service reach. They urge leaders to fund and guard training as core national wealth, not a side cost.
pmc-13444267:
Gabriel França Toledo Pinto and colleagues measure food insecurity in children and teens with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 study. The clinic sat at a Rio de Janeiro child institute, and a Brazil food scale graded home food stress. The pool held 130 young patients, most of them girls, with mothers as main carers in most homes.

Food insecurity touched 67.4 percent of the group in the count. Mild stress led at 50.4 percent of cases, while severe stress sat at 5.4 percent of cases. Income, carer schooling, and benefit receipt each tied to food stress in the checks. Most children held healthy weight for age, and height ran on track. The authors call for joint health and social policy, since tight food budgets fight the strict meal plans diabetes demands.
pmc-13444367:
Ting Xie and colleagues link felt stress, symptoms, and hippocampus part sizes in first-episode schizophrenia in a 2026 study. The pool held 97 patients at first break and 47 healthy peers. Stress scales, symptom scales, and 3.0-T MRI scans fed subfield maps of the hippocampus.

Patients felt more stress than peers in the checks. Their fimbria zones ran smaller, while tail zones ran larger, after head size and trait fixes. In healthy peers, many zone sizes rose with felt stress in tidy lines. Those lines broke or vanished in patients. In patients, felt stress rose with positive symptoms and with worry-low mood marks. The authors read the break as a sign that stress wiring itself is off in the illness.
pmc-13446367:
Murat Ferhat Ferhatoğlu and colleagues compare two cold storage tricks for kidneys from living donors, in a 2026 prospective study at an Istanbul transplant clinic. A graft must stay cold and viable between removal and implant, and plain cold storage still rules in living donation for its ease and low cost. The rivals were a chilled sponge wrap and a bag of ice.

Graft results at six months matched between the two methods. The ice bag showed a modest edge in the first days after surgery, in early lab signs of graft work. The authors count both as sound picks, with the bag a touch kinder at the start. Their data fill a gap on early chemistry reads for living donor grafts.
pmc-13447067:
Zhenyu Lu and colleagues open a journal collection on sensing, learning, and control for robots that work with people, in a 2026 editorial. The field is shifting, they argue, from robots as tools to robots as partners that read people and settings, learn from feedback, and act with care. The collection prizes whole-loop builds over lone clever algorithms.

Four contributions show the range. One has robots ask people smart questions to learn reward from feedback. Others cover long action reading, farm perception, and self-running medical scanning. Shared ground runs through all four: better senses, learning that takes user taste on board, and control that holds safety while work gets done. The editors frame the set as a step toward robots fit for human spaces.
pmc-13447267:
Linlin Fang leads a team mapping new antibody targets on a cattle coronavirus protein in 2026 laboratory work. The virus causes calf diarrhoea, winter gut illness in adults and breathing disease, with heavy farm losses. Its nucleocapsid protein, the most stable viral protein, suits early diagnosis and vaccine design, provided exact binding spots are known.

Lab-made protein was used to immunise mice, yielding two specific antibodies through fused-cell methods. Both reacted only with the target virus in blot and cell tests and shared the same antibody class. Cutting the protein into pieces pinpointed two short stretches that each antibody grasps, both lying on the protein surface and stable across strains. Those mapped spots give concrete starting points for targeted diagnostic tests.
pmc-13447367:
Víctor Carballo-Uicab and colleagues build synthetic gene switches to detect Listeria bacteria in raw milk in 2026 proof-of-concept work. Listeria can cause severe foodborne illness, yet direct detection in complex foods without lab amplification had not been shown. Toehold switches are RNA devices that turn on a signal only when a matching RNA sequence appears.

Analysis of a variable gene region found a short trigger stretch unique to Listeria among related bacteria. Three switch designs were built, and the most stable was tested against synthetic triggers across a wide dose range. RNA extracted from pure cultures and from spiked raw milk both activated the switch, while clean milk gave a clearly different signal. Activation stayed modest, yet detection without amplification in a messy food matrix marks a step toward cheaper food safety tests.
pmc-13447667:
Su and colleagues tackled in 2026 a stubborn flaw in cryo-electron microscopy, where sample particles stick to the grid in one preferred pose, leaving missing views that blur the final structure. Fixes such as detergents or tilted imaging are slow and case-bound. Their approach varies the temperature at which samples are frozen, which shifts how particles settle, then merges data sets taken at different temperatures.

Su merged heat-loving ribosome data from several temperatures and rebalanced the particles using a draft three-dimensional model. The merged set gave smoother quality curves, higher roundness scores, and a narrower blind zone than single-temperature data. They proved the method on a protein complex known for severe posing problems, winning a high-quality reconstruction. The authors offer the recipe as a simple, widely usable cure for a bottleneck that limits high-resolution structure work.
pmc-13449367:
Liang and colleagues study anakinra, an immune calming drug, for the brain toxicity that can follow CAR T cell therapy. That treatment reprograms a patient's immune cells against blood cancer. The syndrome, shortened to ICANS, can be life threatening, and steroids fail many severe cases. Their 2026 study reviews 101 patients treated with anakinra at two centers and asks whether improvement in the first three days forecasts the course.

Early response was far from assured. Only about 43 percent reached neurologic improvement by seventy two hours. The median time to resolution ran eight days. Treatment related death at twenty eight days touched about one in eight. Yet the seventy two hour mark proved decisive. Patients who hit it cleared the syndrome faster, needed less steroid exposure, and died less often. The authors propose that checkpoint as the moment to judge whether anakinra suffices or escalation must begin.
pmc-13449967:
Fu and colleagues presented in 2026 a step-by-step protocol for mapping where long non-coding RNAs bind, with fine spatial detail. These RNAs guide gene control by gripping chromatin, the packaged DNA in the cell. The classic mapping method needs huge cell numbers, suffers noisy background, and shreds the RNA it hunts during preparation. Their variant, ChIRP-Tag, swaps the shredding step for an enzyme that tags DNA in place.

Fu lays out each stage. Cells are softened so probes can enter. Tagged probes latch onto the target RNA. Antibodies then fetch a cutting enzyme that builds the sequencing library at the binding sites. The swap cuts the needed cell input sharply, spares the target RNA, and speeds library preparation. Sensitivity and spatial detail stay high across cell types, the authors report. The protocol aims to serve studies of rare samples the older method could not handle.
pmc-13450567:
Alvaro Andres Saavedra and co-authors relate a 2026 case where lasting clots in the penis hid a rare cancer for two years. Their patient, a man aged 36, had clots on both sides of the erection chambers with steady pelvic pain. Scans at the time found no tumor, and his care stayed cautious and drug based.

Later a fast-growing mass appeared with spread to groin nodes, and surgery plus tissue tests named it synovial sarcoma, a cancer almost never seen in the penis. The disease came back soon after surgery, and he died eight months later. The team urges doctors to suspect hidden cancer when such clots persist with no clear cause.
pmc-13451867:
Kelsey McAlister and co-authors review in 2026 outcomes for adults who got online therapy for gambling disorder through one provider. Few people with the disorder seek care, and real-world proof for virtual care is thin. Records covered 1,305 adults treated between mid 2024 and spring 2026, with weekly scores of gambling symptom weight.

Patients arrived with mid-level symptoms, and over half carried another mental health condition, most often anxiety. The study tracks how scores moved over the first twelve weeks and which starting traits tied to faster gains. It also times when a gain large enough to matter in daily life first shows. The authors frame the cohort as a base for judging virtual gambling care at scale.
pmc-13452767:
Luka Flegar and five co-authors reflect on their nationwide study of surgery for urachal cancer, a rare cancer of a leftover bladder cord. Their 2026 piece sums up German hospital billing records from 2006 to 2022, covering 2,593 cases. Care for this cancer usually removes part or all of the bladder along with the cord and navel.

The share of cases treated by removing only part of the bladder rose over time and reached 74 percent in 2022. Stays after that smaller operation fell from 14 days in 2006 to just 9 days in 2022, and robot help shortened them further. The piece flags uneven care coverage across the country as a worry. Since the cancer is rare and harsh, the authors call for joint work across centers and countries to test whether the smaller operation stays as safe.
pmc-13453467:
Kaveh Ebrahimzadeh, Mohammad Mirahmadi Eraghi, and Farahnaz Bidari Zerehpoosh report a rare spine tumor that crushed a vertebra in a young man. The tumor, called pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma, grows from blood vessel tissue and sits between benign and cancerous. Their 2026 report covers a 24 year old with a burst fracture at the T12 vertebra, growing back pain, tingling legs, and weakness.

Surgeons removed the whole T12 vertebra from behind, freed the spinal cord, and rebuilt the front column with an expanding cage and screws. Lab checks on the removed tissue confirmed the rare tumor type. Two years on, the patient had no return of the tumor or new problems. The authors stress that this tumor can mimic other bone tumors on scans, so tissue proof and full removal matter.
pmc-13453567:
Xu Xiaomin and five co-authors report a prostate cancer first read as an abscess in a 36 year old man with a transplanted kidney. Transplant patients face a two to four fold higher cancer risk from drugs that mute the immune system. Their 2026 case report follows a man 16 years past his transplant who came in with pelvic pain, fever, and a rising PSA level.

A needle draw from the prostate pulled bloody fluid instead of pus, which pushed the team to biopsy at once. The tissue showed a poorly formed prostate cancer with changes in three DNA repair genes, among them BRCA2. Surgeons removed the prostate with a reshaped laparoscopic plan that kept clear of the graft kidney. One year on, his PSA was undetectable and the kidney worked steadily. The authors urge fast biopsy when a presumed abscess bleeds.
pmc-13453667:
Ryoma Oda, Takeshi Kinoshita, Nobuo Tomizawa, and Minoru Tabata report a case where a moving CT scan exposed silent poor blood flow to the brain. Their 2026 report follows a 72 year old woman with a chronic tear in her aorta, the body's main artery, forming a 53 millimetre bulge found by chance. The tear squeezed the true channel of two neck bound arteries, starving the right side of her brain.

The four dimensional scan, which shows flow over time, caught a delayed peak on the right side that plain scans would miss. Guided by that map, surgeons rebuilt the brachiocephalic and right carotid arteries, the vessels feeding that side. Scans after surgery showed the flow delay had eased. The authors present the moving scan as a planning tool for tears that quietly threaten the brain.
pmc-13454067:
Ghina Fakhri and nine co-authors chart childhood heart muscle disease at a single major center in a resource limited setting over twenty years. Their 2026 review covers 244 children diagnosed before age 18, with an average age of 5.9 years. Dilated cardiomyopathy, where the heart stretches weak, led at 62.7 percent, ahead of the thickened form at 30.3 percent.

Half the children had no symptoms and were found by chance. Suspected inflammation drove most of the stretched cases, while inherited causes led the thickened ones. Five year mortality reached 13.1 percent, concentrated in the stretched group. Two signs at diagnosis predicted death on their own: badly reduced pumping power and high pressure in the lung arteries. Subtype, age, and sex did not. The authors stress early pumping and lung pressure checks.
pmc-13455267:
Yin and co-authors profiled the immune checkpoint TIM-3 in tumors from 117 patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, an aggressive bile duct cancer usually found too late for surgery. They stained tumor tissue for TIM-3 and companion checkpoints, counted infiltrating immune cells, and linked the patterns to clinical outcomes for these patients.

High TIM-3 expression in tumor cells appeared in 61 patients, 52.1 percent of the cohort, and correlated significantly with poorer tumor differentiation in the pathology analysis. Those patients relapsed and died sooner, and high TIM-3 independently predicted shorter disease-free survival with a hazard ratio of 1.589 after multivariable adjustment. TIM-3 levels also tracked with the density of CD4 and CD8 tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in the tissue samples examined. The authors propose TIM-3 staining as a prognostic and inflammation biomarker and TIM-3 blockade as a therapeutic strategy worth testing in this cancer.
pmc-13455367:
Tambaro and colleagues pooled real-world results for 132 patients with advanced urothelial cancer treated with second-line pembrolizumab immunotherapy. The patients came from six centers of the Campania oncology network in Italy, treated between January 2021 and November 2023. Trial populations are fitter than everyday patients, so the network tested whether trial benefits survive routine practice.

The median age was 67 years and 73.5 percent were men, with most patients still reasonably fit at performance status zero or one. Median progression-free survival came to 3.75 months on the standard 200 milligram, three-weekly dosing schedule used. Median overall survival was 7.3 months across the full cohort, and the objective response rate was 13.5 percent, with disease control in 33.9 percent of patients treated. The authors present the figures as a realistic benchmark for counseling patients outside trials.
pmc-13457067:
Hee-Jung Hong and Ju-Dong Jang analyze, in a 2026 national study, how daily habits line up with how older Koreans rate their own mouth health. The data came from a community health survey of 210,212 adults aged sixty and over, gathered across 2022 and 2023. Self-rated mouth health is a practical stand-in for pain, chewing trouble, and unmet care in this age group.

Schooling showed the steepest gradient: college graduates had more than double the odds of rating their oral health well. Brushing after dinner or before bed lifted the odds by about half. Low stress and regular walking also helped. Smoking, low income, and above all unmet dental needs dragged ratings down; unmet need cut the odds to under a quarter. The authors argue that mouth health in old age mirrors social position as much as toothpaste.
pmc-13458967: Giuseppe d'Orsi and co-authors issued this 2026 correction concerning their article on tailored use of cenobamate for epilepsy that resists standard drugs. The notice is a correction only: it supplies an acknowledgements section that the published article had left out. The added text credits two researchers at Children's Mercy Research Institute in Kansas City for sequencing the CYP2A6 gene and testing it for copy number variation. Readers are told the original article has been updated with that section.
pmc-13459167:
Rafael Gutiérrez-López and co-authors asked whether mosquito species living in Spain could spread Oropouche virus, an emerging pathogen from South America and the Caribbean. Imported human cases have reached Europe, but biting midges, not mosquitoes, are the known carriers. In their 2026 study, the team fed three mosquito types on virus laden blood, including the tiger mosquito and the common house mosquito. They then checked over three weeks whether the virus infected them, spread through their bodies, and reached their saliva.

Results were reassuring for Spain. The tiger mosquito showed low infection rates with only rare spread. The other two species became infected and sometimes carried virus beyond the gut, but never transmitted it in these experiments. A second plain blood meal changed nothing, mosquito survival was unaffected, and no virus passed to offspring. The risk of the virus establishing in Spain through these mosquitoes looks low.
pmc-13459767:
Jiajia Mai and co-authors ran an early phase trial of HTD1801, a compound pairing the plant alkaloid berberine with a bile acid. It was tested in patients who have both type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. The drug is designed as a gut and liver modulator. In their 2026 phase Ib study, forty eight patients took the drug or placebo twice daily for twenty eight days across doses of 500, 750, and 1,000 milligrams. Twelve patients were already on stable metformin. The team tracked safety, drug levels, blood sugar, lipids, and liver enzymes.

The drug was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate side effects and no serious events reported. Metabolic gains grew with dose. In the metformin group, the top dose beat placebo clearly: fasting glucose fell by 1.271 units against a rise on placebo. Post meal glucose fell by 4.167 units in the reported comparisons. Cholesterol measures and liver enzymes also improved.
pmc-13459967:
Juan Zhang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether calycosin, an active compound from the herb Radix astragali, can protect the heart after a heart attack. Heart attacks are the commonest route into heart failure, and the compound had shown promise in earlier work. The team used heart cells starved of oxygen and glucose, plus rats whose coronary artery was tied off, measuring oxidative damage, iron levels, and cell-death markers.

Calycosin lowered harmful oxygen radicals and iron accumulation, restored cell energy, and revived protective proteins. Those benefits flowed through a defense pathway switched on by the protein NRF2, since silencing NRF2 undid much of the effect. In rats, treatment eased scarring, improved pumping, and limited mitochondrial damage, suggesting a candidate therapy worth further study.
pmc-13461367:
Sina Fathieh and a large team showed in 2026 that faint traces of a heart injury protein in the blood can reveal silent coronary artery disease on CT scans. Their study covered 1,613 adults who underwent coronary imaging, comparing high-sensitivity troponin I levels against calcium scores and plaque measurements. A level above a low threshold enriched strongly for actionable disease, defined by a calcium score of at least one hundred, especially among people lacking the usual risk factors.

Dividing troponin by heart muscle mass, with age and kidney function factored in, sharpened prediction further and explained why baseline levels vary. A two-stage pathway, blood test first and scans only for those flagged, raised diagnostic yield while cutting the number of scans needed. Prospective trials are the authors' stated next requirement.
pmc-13461567:
Katerina Kyriakouli and co-authors report a 2026 interview study with partners of people who received a kidney transplant. Care centers on the patient, yet partners carry much of the daily support work at home. The authors wanted to hear how partners live through illness, surgery, and the months after. Their study sits in one social and cultural setting.

Twelve partners took part in interviews, and the team grouped what they said into five themes. Partners often felt pushed into the background, even while taking on hard emotional roles. They spoke of moving from illness toward a new normal, of wanting clearer talk and more support from health staff, and of rethinking their life as a couple. Transplant also struck many as a lesson that changed how they saw life. The authors argue that care should treat the couple as a unit and give partners a voice of their own.
pmc-13462067:
Rodothea Amerikanou leads a 2026 UK study of trametinib, a drug, for adults with histiocytic neoplasms, rare disorders where immune cells called histiocytes grow in a tumor-like way. Many such diseases are driven by faults in a cell growth pathway. Patients whose disease resists standard chemotherapy often need pathway-blocking drugs. Trametinib blocks a pathway step called MEK. Cases came through a national expert panel.

Thirty-seven adults who started the drug before May 2024 were included, some alone and some paired with a second drug. At a median follow-up of about twenty-one months, roughly four in five patients showed a clinical response: their disease signs improved. Scans showed a response in two in three patients. The diseases covered included Erdheim-Chester disease, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, histiocytic sarcoma, and Rosai-Dorfman disease. The authors offer the results as wider evidence for trametinib across this disease family.
pmc-13462367:
Zhuona Zhang and colleagues adapt, in a 2026 study, an empathy fatigue scale for Chinese intensive care nurses. Intensive care nurses face patient suffering, death, and hard moral choices daily, which raises their risk of empathy fatigue: exhaustion from caring deeply too long. China lacked a tool for that specialty setting. The team translated the professionals' scale with two translation frameworks and checked it in 300 nurses at a hospital in Inner Mongolia.

All 21 items were kept, yet the version split into factors, emotional load and exhaustion state, covering most of the score variation. Scores were consistent, stable on retesting, and steady across split halves. A check against a compassion fatigue scale gave a moderate positive link, supporting the tool's target. Factor testing favored the two-part structure over the original form. The authors offer the scale as a screen to guide health support for intensive care nurses.
pmc-13462767:
Jingjing Yin and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, two keyhole approaches to breast cancer surgery: endoscopic surgery through small cuts and robot-assisted surgery with the Da Vinci system. Both aim to match open surgery's safety while leaving patients with better cosmetic results. The team searched four databases through spring 2026 for studies comparing the new approaches with standard ones.

Endoscopic surgery, first developed in East Asian centers, gave better cosmetic results in early-stage disease with acceptable short-term outcomes. Robotic nipple-sparing removal adds a 3D view, wristed tools, and tremor filtering. Pooled data show fewer deaths of skin flap and nipple tissue than open surgery, with similar short-term results, though operations run longer and cost more. A single-port robot reaches a true single cut hidden in the armpit. The authors judge both approaches reasonable minimally invasive options with growing support.
pmc-13463067:
Shaohui Zhong, Xiaofei Liu, and Caihua Chen present, in a 2026 engineering study, a detection model for electric bicycle safety and plate recognition called P-YOLOv10. Small objects and fine plate details are hard for standard detectors in street scenes. Three upgrades tune the base detector: an attention module spotlighting key local features, a new box-fitting loss sharpening placement for small targets, and a smoother activation function for steadier training.

The team trained the model on a set of 2,237 images from Guangzhou and Foshan, with labels marking the region a plate comes from. Detection precision reached about ninety-six and a half percent, one point above the base model. Riders' safety factors, such as helmet use, and plate attributes are read in one pass. The authors offer the system as a technical base for smart traffic enforcement aimed at e-bike fleets.
pmc-13463367:
Valera-Calero and colleagues present a 2026 didactic ultrasound manual for finding the lumbar plexus nerves in the lower limb. This nerve bundle, running from the lowest spine levels, supplies the lower abdominal wall, groin, and front and inner thigh. Its six main branches are targets for pain blocks and can be injured by surgery, so clinicians need reliable ways to see them.

For each nerve, the manual gives its usual course, clinical warnings, surface landmarks, probe positions, and the look of the nerve on screen. Illustrations show probe placement and schematic pathways through the tissues. Ultrasound guidance has replaced blind landmark techniques for many blocks because seeing the nerve cuts complications. A structured manual that pairs anatomy with scanning recipes helps trainees standardize a skill that is otherwise learned by apprenticeship and feel.
pmc-13463967:
Zhang and co-authors compared two operations for massive rotator cuff tears in 2026. These large shoulder tendon injuries often defeat simple repair. The retrospective study covered 53 patients treated between 2016 and 2023. Twenty-four received partial repair. Twenty-nine received a combined reconstruction. That operation bridges the gap with a graft of the patient's own thigh fascia. It also repositions the biceps tendon for support.

Both groups improved over at least two years of follow-up. The combined operation came out ahead on both standard shoulder scores. It reached about 89 against 84 on one scale and about 83 against 77 on another. Imaging told a stronger story. The combined group regained more of the normal space between arm bone and shoulder blade. Repeat tears appeared in only about 7 of every 100 combined patients, against 38 of every 100 after partial repair. Range of motion gains were similar in both groups.
pmc-13464067:
Jiongjiong Lu leads a team that finds a gut germ living inside liver tumors and boosting drug treatment. The germ, Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, turned up in mouse models that answered well to a paired therapy of apatinib plus an immune drug. Patients rich in the germ also fared better on pre-surgery treatment.

The germ leaks formic acid inside tumors, and that acid blocks a sensor protein from entering the cell nucleus. With the sensor held back, vessel growth signals and immune dampening both fell. Adding formic acid or a sensor blocker to the drug pair strengthened the effect in mice. Germ checks could one day help pick who gains most from the pairing.
pmc-13464267:
Garg wrote this 2026 editorial about a pacing wire that migrated inside a patient's heart over 24 years. Temporary epicardial pacing wires are placed after heart surgery. They are normally pulled out at the bedside. When removal fails, surgeons usually snip the wire flush with the skin. The case discussed here involved an 81-year-old man whose retained wire crossed the atrial septum and the mitral valve and lodged in his left ventricle, without causing symptoms.

Left-sided wire migration is rare, and a path through the atrial septum had never been reported before, the author notes. The treating team chose not to retrieve the wire, judging open surgery riskier than watchful care for an elderly patient with other heart disease. Garg endorses that caution, reviews the blood-thinning dilemma after bleeding forced a change, and urges clear documentation of any retained wire.
pmc-13464567:
Kim M. Summers and seven co-authors read gene and protein patterns in nerve tissue from horses with grass sickness. The disease, a mostly fatal nerve disorder of grazing horses, likely stems from a nerve poison made by a plant or microbe. The team examined neck nerve hubs from eight sick horses and six healthy ones.

Sick tissue showed a clear shared signature against the healthy group. Genes and proteins for nerve signaling, synapse work, and cell power units all ran low. Stress, cell death, and inflammation markers ran high in the same tissue. Gene and protein shifts pointed the same way, which strengthens the picture. The signature frames how a nerve poison may unravel horse nerves cell by cell.
pmc-13464767:
Anthony Hesser and five colleagues published this 2026 survey study on how a prognostic test is really used in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer. Guidelines worldwide recommend cell-of-origin classification, which sorts the cancer by the cell type it arose from, for every untreated patient. The authors interviewed and surveyed cancer doctors and pathologists in the United States about the common stain-based method, immunohistochemistry, and its pain points.

The study drew on 18 interviews plus surveys of 60 haematologist-oncologists and 60 pathologists. Respondents said 83 percent of untreated patients get tested, and 85 percent of cancer doctors use the result in treatment decisions. Doctors preferred the stain method over gene profiling for its access, speed and cost. Yet 10 to 15 percent of samples first return unclear results, and about 3 percent stay unclear after retesting. Respondents blamed non-standard pathology reports and asked for clearer guidelines and criteria.
pmc-13465067:
Young Jung Yang and three co-authors teach an AI model to invent post-contrast heart MRI maps from scans taken without any dye. Contrast dye carries cost and risk, yet its maps reveal heart muscle scarring and swelling shares. Their model builds the missing dye map from the native map alone.

Eight hundred thirteen matched image slices from patients with suspected heart muscle disease trained and tested the system. Virtual dye maps landed close to real ones in value spread, with a steady offset between them. Converting to tissue volume share largely erased that offset. Agreement on held-out scans was fair, with slice-to-slice wobble the main flaw. Dye-free mapping could cut cost and risk if accuracy firms up.
pmc-13465167:
Kaja Plucińska leads a team that builds a tagging method to read what single cell types in an organ secrete. Signals between cells run whole-body energy balance, yet who sends what stays hard to trace. Their tool parks a tagging enzyme in the protein factory of chosen cell types in mice, under genetic switch control.

Liver cells, fat cells, and B immune cells were each tagged in turn. The tags captured each type's factory proteome at rest and under fasting, inflammation, and fattening diets. Each tissue answered the challenges in its own pattern, redrawing its outward signal set. The shared atlas gives the field fresh leads for blood markers and drug targets across metabolic disease.
pmc-13465467:
Harisankar Kunnamkulathil Chandrababu leads a team that cooks six seaweeds into carbon dots and tests them as shrimp preservatives. Seaweeds carry rich chemistry, and boiling them down yields glowing specks under ten nanometers wide. Each seaweed gave dots with its own surface chemistry and talents.

One dot type blocked ultraviolet light best, while two others topped the antioxidant charts on rival tests. A red seaweed dot also fought two mold species, and all dots slowed bacteria, though weakly. Normal human cells tolerated the dots well at working doses. Dots from one brown seaweed, folded into shrimp at low levels, slowed fat spoilage across ten cold days better than vitamin C did.
pmc-13465767:
Takkar and colleagues studied in 2026 how fat tissue damaged by obesity and by radiation changes the prostate in ways that favor cancer. Using mice fed a high-fat diet, with or without targeted radiation to fat, plus lab cultures of fat cells, they tracked the prostate tissue around the gland.

Prostates of obese mice showed overgrowth, activated support tissue, oxidative damage, and cell aging. Radiation mostly kept those obesity effects in place rather than making them worse, except for more fibrosis features and more immune cell entry. Fluid from obese fat cells switched on prostate fibroblasts, and those fibroblasts pushed cancer cells to migrate and change character. Blocking one signal route between them sharply cut cancer cell migration, flagging it as a drug target.
pmc-13466367:
Gabriyanchik and co-authors pool comparative studies in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of a surgical technique meant to prevent pain after limb amputation. The technique is called a regenerative peripheral nerve interface. It wraps the cut end of a nerve in a small graft of the patient's own muscle. This happens at the time of amputation. It gives stray nerve fibers somewhere harmless to grow.

Five comparative studies covering 238 patients fed the analysis. Symptomatic neuromas, painful nerve tangles, formed in none of 97 interface patients against 20 of 99 patients managed conventionally, and phantom limb pain risk fell by roughly half in the interface group. Chronic opioid use at twelve months was also sharply lower. Results held across children, vascular patients, and cancer patients, though the authors grade the underlying evidence as low certainty and call for larger prospective trials.
pmc-13466667:
Andrei Gritsiuta, Parsa Radfar, Shawn Nishi, and Roman Petrov describe a lung apex tumor that hid behind an infection diagnosis, in a 2026 case report. A forty-eight-year-old woman who smoked first showed a hollowed right upper lobe lesion, and testing confirmed a nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. Antibiotics brought partial improvement on scans, which deepened the disguise.

Lingering symptoms and changing images pushed the team to look again with a robotic scope, which uncovered a superior sulcus tumor, an aggressive lung cancer at the chest's top edge. The cancer had grown into nearby vertebrae. The case warns that a proven infection does not rule out cancer in the same spot, a mix-up growing likelier as these infections spread.
pmc-13467167:
Yuanxiao Gao, Wenyu Zhang, and Guang Hu review proteins that pair with copies of themselves, and how those self-partnerships run and reshape cell networks, in a 2026 article. Self-pairing into twins and larger assemblies is everywhere in living cells and sets the precision of signaling systems. When the pairing goes wrong, sticky clumps, amyloid fibers, or runaway droplet formation can follow, feeding brain and body diseases.

Methods surveyed include proximity tagging in living cells and deep learning models, including protein language models, that predict pairing from sequence. Evolution enters too: networks keep self-pairing proteins under dose-balance pressure. The authors close with therapeutic ideas for fixing broken pairings rather than the proteins themselves.
pmc-13467467:
Anirudh Suresh and co-authors combine the research in 2026 on a fat-tissue hormone called CTRP1 and its link to type 2 diabetes. The hormone appears to help the body respond to insulin, so researchers have asked whether its blood levels differ in people with diabetes. The team searched six medical databases for studies that measured circulating CTRP1 in adults with diabetes and in controls.

Eight studies qualified, covering 525 adults with diabetes and 612 without. The authors pooled the results with standard meta-analysis methods and graded each study for bias and quality with established checklists. A clear pooled answer on whether CTRP1 runs higher or lower in diabetes would help decide if the hormone is worth pursuing as a marker or treatment lead. That answer is the very question the review was built to settle.
pmc-13467767:
Spaggiari and co-editors introduce a research collection on exercise for patients living with heart rhythm problems and implanted devices. Their 2026 editorial frames three questions the collection pursues. How should exercise be prescribed for people with arrhythmias and implanted devices? Which physiological mechanisms produce its effects? And how can it be delivered safely in ever more complex patients?

The editors trace a shift in the field from conservative advice toward personalised, therapeutic prescription. Included studies span individualised training programmes through mechanism and safety work. One ten-month plan served a patient with a painful conduction disorder. It cut resting heart rate by fifteen beats per minute. The roadmap they draw combines personalisation, mechanistic grounding, and technological monitoring. The editorial presents the collection as a step toward exercise prescriptions as precisely specified as drug doses for this population.
pmc-13467967:
Sandro La Vignera and Rosita A. Condorelli review in 2026 how three eating patterns affect testosterone in men with obesity. Obesity lowers testosterone through several routes, including extra conversion to estrogen, insulin resistance, and suppression of the hormone control axis. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the authors searched for human studies of the Mediterranean diet, ketogenic diets, and intermittent fasting in men with a body mass index of at least 30.

From 697 initial records, 52 studies survived screening into the final synthesis. The very-low-calorie ketogenic diet showed the most consistent testosterone recovery among the patterns compared. The review gives clinicians a side-by-side account of what diet alone can and cannot restore in obesity-related low testosterone, and where the support for each pattern remains uneven. That comparison matters because diet is usually the first, drug-free step offered to these patients.
pmc-13468067:
Zuoquan Zhu and colleagues solve in 2026 the heat-buckling problem for cylindrical shells reinforced with graphene origami, a folded graphene form that gives the material unusual stretch behavior. Thin shells in hot environments can suddenly crumple when thermal expansion builds stress. The authors model shells with four patterns of reinforcement through the wall thickness, using standard shell theory with large-deflection effects and heat-sensitive material data.

Their worked solution gives the key temperature rise at which buckling starts. It is found by repeated calculation for both heat-sensitive and fixed material models. Follow-up studies then vary filler content, fold degree, edge constraints, and shell size. The critical temperature depended strongly on how the graphene origami is distributed, and more filler improved heat resistance. Aircraft and energy engineers gain a formula-based way to predict failure in hot thin-walled structures before building hardware.
pmc-13468467:
Run-Ze Tan, Jin-Feng Chen, and Wan-Ning He improve train localization in 2026 for systems fusing ultra-wideband radio ranging with inertial sensors. Railway anchors sit far apart along the track with little sideways spread, so any ranging error from a blocked, non-line-of-sight signal gets geometrically amplified into a large position error. Their method grades the reliability of each radio path before trusting its measurement.

The trick starts by recognizing the train can only be on the track: each range becomes a candidate position along the known centerline. Reliability is then estimated in a sliding time window by comparing how successive measurements agree with the train motion increments from the inertial unit. Unreliable paths are downweighted or discarded for the fusion filter. Cheap anchor layouts are economically attractive for railways, and this reliability layer keeps them from paying for sparse anchors with wild position jumps.
pmc-13469967:
Rodríguez-Sánchez and co-authors investigate a little-studied gene in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Their 2026 paper focuses on ZMYM3, a gene on the X chromosome whose mutations appear in a small share of patients at diagnosis. The team analysed 487 cases from 16 Spanish centres and ran experiments in cell lines and patient cells to learn what these mutations do.

ZMYM3 variants often occurred alongside NOTCH1 mutations, and patients carrying them reached their first treatment sooner, a pattern that separated outcomes even in early-stage disease. In the experiments, the mutations lowered histone acetylation, the chemical tagging that loosens DNA packaging, and reduced how accessible the DNA was to the cell's machinery. Gene activity fell broadly as a result. The authors argue ZMYM3 status refines risk prediction and may expose treatment weaknesses.
pmc-13470567:
Natalia Mejia and colleagues argue in 2026 that plastic surgery patients labeled allergic to penicillin can usually receive the standard preventive drug cefazolin safely. Cefazolin is the workhorse for preventing surgical site infections. Yet patients carrying a penicillin allergy label often get other drugs instead. Those substitutes are tied to more infections, longer stays, and higher costs.

Fewer than one in ten reported penicillin allergies turns out to be real on formal testing. Even for truly allergic patients, cefazolin odd shape among its drug family makes cross reaction very unlikely. Plastic surgery also lacks clear guidance on choosing preventive drugs, which lets the mistaken idea persist. The authors call for teaching doctors when cefazolin is truly unsafe. They recommend it as the first choice whenever preventive drugs are called for in plastic surgery.
pmc-13471067:
Samantha M. Fortin and eight colleagues published this 2026 neuroscience study on a brainstem site that can suppress appetite without causing nausea. The locus coeruleus, a cluster of neurons known for arousal, carries calcitonin receptors, which respond to the satiety peptides amylin and CGRP. Existing obesity drugs trigger nausea, so a feeding circuit that skips it is valuable. The team tested the site in rats and mice with drugs, genetics and behaviour assays.

Activating these receptors in the locus coeruleus cut food intake and body weight in the animals. It did so without signs of nausea and without changing heart rate, temperature or stomach emptying. Gene labelling showed the receptors carry the partner protein needed to answer amylin and CGRP. Injecting either peptide into the region reduced eating without nausea. The authors say this circuit helps explain how amylin-based obesity medicines work, and may offer a cleaner drug target.
pmc-13471467:
Moshi and Millanzi surveyed rural Tanzanian men about going with their partners to pregnancy care, applying the theory of planned behavior, a framework linking attitudes and social pressure to intentions. Their 2026 community study asked 546 randomly picked male partners, whose mean age was 31 years and 71.8% of whom were married.

Most men had never gone along: 61.7% of partners had never gone along with a spouse to a maternal health visit. Negative attitudes, cold social norms, and low perceived control each appeared in roughly 57% to 59% of respondents across the sample. A positive attitude was the strongest predictor of planning to go along, with adjusted odds of 3.616 times those of men with negative attitudes.
pmc-13471567:
Amarasiri and co-authors ran Sri Lanka's first national-style survey of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, using the international BOLD protocol with lung-function testing before and after a bronchodilator. Their 2026 cross-sectional study sampled 1,985 adults across seven of the country's nine provinces, in three rural and four urban areas.

Overall COPD prevalence came to 7.3% of adults, rising to 10.5% among participants over 40 years old. Men were hit harder than women, at 10.4% prevalence versus 4.7% in the same survey, and stage 2 disease was the commonest grade at 45.8% of cases. Strikingly, 54.8% of those with COPD were non-smokers, pointing at firewood smoke and dusty work, and most cases had never been diagnosed before.
pmc-13472567:
Hengpu Zhou and seven colleagues published this 2026 study on extracting mulberry polysaccharides, plant sugars with liver-protective promise, and testing them against fatty liver disease in mice. A gentle enzyme-plus-ultrasound extraction should preserve the sugars' structure better than hot water. The team optimised the process with two approaches, response surface methodology and a neural network, then compared the preparations in a 30-day mouse trial with gut microbe sequencing.

The response surface method predicted extraction outcomes more accurately than the neural network, and its optimum, 107 minutes at 52 degrees with an enzyme dose, yielded 10.06 percent polysaccharide. The gentle product kept its molecular linkages intact and beat the hot-water product on every disease measure: less liver fat, less gut damage and inflammation. It restored short-chain fatty acid producing gut bacteria and suppressed inflammatory species. The authors back the extraction method and the product as a functional food candidate.
pmc-13472867:
Tripathi and colleagues report a 2026 multi-omics study of vitamin D3 supplementation in multiple sclerosis patients. Low vitamin D is a known risk factor for the disease, but how supplements reshape immunity in the body is unclear. The team profiled blood immune cells over time with gene activity and chromatin openness measures, in patients starting high-dose vitamin D, patients on regular doses, and healthy people on monthly doses.

 Responses depended on context: starting state and disease status shaped what changed. The team integrated receptor binding data to separate direct vitamin D targets from downstream echoes. Vitamin D appears to nudge specific circuits, so trials should stratify by immune state.
pmc-13473267:
Tang and colleagues used spatial transcriptomics in 2026 to map gene activity inside kidney tissue from children with ANCA-associated vasculitis, a rare disease where the immune system attacks small blood vessels. The rapid kidney damage it causes is well known, but the tissue-level picture in children was largely blank. Spatial methods show which genes switch on in each exact spot of a biopsy.

The team mapped biopsies across disease stages and found four zones with distinct gene programs: immune and scar-forming tissue, the kidney's filtering units, scar-driving cells, and blood vessels. Immune and scarring signals rose together and matched how severe the tissue damage looked. Two molecule pairings sat inside the scar-forming zone and were confirmed by staining. Adult data shared the core injury programs but added age-linked stress signals.
pmc-13473867:
Akay and colleagues test whether early scans can show how breast cancer answers drug treatment. All patients had triple-negative disease, a fast type that lacks three common drug targets. Each woman got drug therapy before surgery to shrink the tumor first.

Twenty-two patients had PET scans, which map sugar use in tissue, before and after one drug round. Both tracer types passed set checks for steady repeat readings. The sugar tracer won on image quality and wide supply for the next stage. Falls in tracer uptake after one round matched later scan response and less leftover cancer at surgery. Rises in immune cells inside tumors also matched stronger scan falls.
pmc-13473967:
Chong Li and fellow researchers build a targeted drug carrier in 2026 for colorectal cancer, a cancer of the large bowel. The carrier is a hollow ball made from a manganese mineral, coated with a natural sugar that homes to tumor cells. Inside ride two loads: a drug that chokes tumor blood supply, and a building block that forms a gas which fights drug resistance. The ball breaks down in the sour, harsh tumor setting.
