In mouse tumors, the combined action shrank growth by about three quarters. Spread of the cancer also fell in the tests. A single carrier that stacks three attacks could help where single drugs fail.
pmc-13474567:
Eric A Cardona and co-authors use a tiny worm in 2026 to trace how a gene risk for Alzheimer disease spreads harm. Worms carrying the APOE4 risk variant show nerve cell loss in a set pattern. Behavior tests showed faults beyond the first known cell group, hinting at wider circuit harm. Damage levels tracked with amounts of the worm version of tau, a protein tied to brain decline.

Deleting the tau gene eased faults across many behaviors at once. Tau in the most loaded touch cells also harmed distant cells that it never touched directly. The worm offers a fast living system for testing how tau spreads APOE4 harm. Such work may point to early intervention spots.
pmc-13474767:
Becerra-Lucio and co-authors traced the microbes of artisanal mezcal from agave field to final spirit, using shotgun gene surveys on four production batches. The goal was to learn where a wild fermentation's workforce actually comes from. Their 2026 study sampled plants, environment, equipment, and the fermenting must itself across the whole process.

Bacteria, not yeasts, ran the fermentation: Leuconostoc and Lentilactobacillus dominated the vats while the classic fermenter Saccharomyces made up only about 10% of the microbial share. The phylum Bacillota exceeded 60% of the community at every stage. Community structure barely shifted between batches, depths, or fermentation times. Agave weevils, an insect pest of the crop, carried the same dominant bacteria as the ferments, marking them as plausible natural reservoirs that seed each batch. Microbial functional shifts tracked the flavor notes expert tasters recorded.
pmc-13474967:
Yu Qin and co-authors apply gene sequencing in 2026 to fetuses with fluid buildup not caused by blood mismatch. This state, called nonimmune hydrops, has many possible causes and a high loss rate. Records covered 121 pregnancies at one referral center over three years. All got copy-number sequencing, and ninety-five also got full exome reading.

Just over half of cases gained a firm genetic answer. Copy-number reading alone solved about two fifths, covering whole chromosome errors and smaller structural faults. Exome reading added answers in about one seventh of those tested, led by growth-pathway and bone disorders. Early diagnosis age raised the solve rate, and results shaped pregnancy choices.
pmc-13476567:
Hopkins and Kates introduced a 2026 ethics statement from the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation, updating its 2022 position. Transplant medicine keeps growing more complex as international collaboration expands, and earlier hard mandates proved hard to apply fairly in practice. The new statement aims for clear principles with a workable governance framework.

Three principles anchor the update, as Hopkins explains: respect for persons, utility, and justice in organ transplantation. Respect means donation stays voluntary and free from coercion or exploitation, a stand against organ trafficking, transplant tourism, and organs taken from executed prisoners. Utility calls for responsible and transparent allocation of scarce organs. Justice requires fair access based on clinical need without discrimination, and the framework shows how centres can put each principle into practice.
pmc-13476767:
Thomas Berger and co-authors test helium beam therapy predictions in 2026 on radioresistant throat cancer cells. Helium beams promise sharp dose edges, yet cell data in full spread-out beams stay thin. Cells were placed at three depths in the beam and dosed from one to four gray. A simulation model predicted survival at each depth for comparison.

Measured survival at top dose sat near ten percent at all depths, with no clear depth trend. The model foresaw a fall with depth that the cells did not show. Gaps between forecast and measure ran from a fifth to over a third. Potency ratios still matched fairly between model and bench.
pmc-13479567:
Elizabete Brikune and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study of immune signal proteins in the placentas of pregnancies hit by acute fetal distress. A healthy pregnancy needs careful immune balance at the placenta, and sudden fetal distress breaks that balance. Tissue came from fifteen distressed pregnancies, five each at 28, 31, and 40 weeks, plus five full-term controls.

Seven interleukin proteins were stained and scored by eye on a set scale. Some of them drive inflammation, some brake it, and some calm it. Distressed tissue showed more of the inflammation-driving members, with patterns varying across the three time points. The small pilot design suits a first map of which signals move in this emergency. The authors aim to find placenta immune patterns that could in time help doctors spot or predict fetal distress earlier.
pmc-13479867:
Lei Chang and coauthors published a 2026 review of CRISPR-based diagnostics, from the underlying enzyme trick to cancer detection. Nucleic acid testing stagnated for decades after the polymerase chain reaction, until 2016, when researchers found that CRISPR systems, once they find their target, begin shredding nearby DNA indiscriminately. Engineered reporter strands turn that shredding into a measurable signal.

A typical test runs in three phases: guided target recognition, signal conversion through reporter cutting, and readout by fluorescence, electricity, or color change. The approach proved itself during COVID-19 as a fast, low-equipment alternative to laboratory PCR. The review then turns to cancer, where detecting faint mutation signals in blood could enable earlier diagnosis, and weighs sensitivity limits that still separate promise from practice.
pmc-13480267:
Zhongjie Shi and co-authors describe a 2026 test of a mixed reality headset that guides brain stimulation to the right spot. Magnetic stimulation works only when the coil lands on the correct scalp target, and cap-based guessing can miss by a wide margin. Their system runs on a HoloLens 2 headset with three hand tools, and three researchers aimed at ten points on each of five model heads, standing and lying.

Errors sat near two to two and a half millimetres in both postures, far tighter than manual guessing. Scores differed between researchers but stayed steady within each person across repeats. The team frames the rig as a portable, low-cost guide for stimulation clinics. Tests on real patients, with moving heads and varied hair and skull shapes, remain the next hurdle.
pmc-13481567:
Jr-Wei Wu and co-authors report a 2026 study of narrowed brain arteries in people with lasting headache or brain fog after COVID. The team gathered 108 patients whose symptoms ran past three months, plus controls free of nerve symptoms after recovery. A scoring system graded artery narrowing in front and rear brain circuits, adjusted for both sides.

Narrowing scores rose step by step with the load of symptom types, peaking in patients who carried both headache and fog. Pure fog cases leaned toward front-circuit narrowing, while fog severity itself tracked rear-circuit scores. Headache severity showed no tidy vessel link. The pattern hints that poor front-brain flow may feed fog, while headache draws on wider causes. Vessel checks may deserve a place in long-COVID brain work-ups.
pmc-13481967:
Luis Mario Castellanos-Alvarenga and co-authors describe a 2026 check of a money wellness scale among young adults in Chile. The scale gauges whether people can meet bills, feel secure about the future, and enjoy choices that money allows. The adapted form went to 624 university and technical students aged eighteen to twenty-nine, most of them women.

Scores split cleanly into two parts, money distress and money well-being, with sound consistency. The scale read the same way for men and women in full. Across ethnic and job groups it held with minor item tweaks, which the team freed one by one. In a country where many households lean on store credit, a trusted early-warning tool can steer campus support toward students sliding into money distress.
pmc-13482867:
Jingwen Liang and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how helper cells around pancreatic tumours push cancer cells toward a nerve-like identity that resists drugs. Tumour samples with strong nerve-like markers fared worse, and single-cell maps fingered a factor made by the helper fibroblasts, called PTGDS. Lab tests then fed that factor to cancer cells.

Treated cells grew, moved, and invaded faster and shook off the standard drug gemcitabine more easily. The factor works through a surface receiver that fires a growth pathway inside the cell. Blocking that pathway or removing the receiver undid the nasty shift. The chain gives drug hunters a stromal target, since starving the tumour of helper signals may restore drug sensitivity.
pmc-13483467:
Spancerski and colleagues ran a large contest among vision models to name tree species from photos of cut wood, a skill that helps police illegal logging. Their 2026 benchmark tested 15 versions of the YOLO detector family across three generations and five sizes. The dataset held nearly 78,000 image patches covering 73 forest species, drawn from three different photo collections.

Four models tied at the top, each classifying about 99.9 percent of test patches correctly in the benchmark results. Every model placed the right species in its top three guesses for all test patches. A medium model from the newest generation offered the best speed trade-off, processing over 200 frames per second. Voting across patches from one wood sample pushed that model to perfect image-level accuracy. Spancerski also verified the models looked at real wood anatomy, like pore patterns.
pmc-13483667:
Iwelunmor and colleagues laid out the plan for a trial testing whether a youth-led HIV prevention program in Nigeria can keep running after its first funding ends. The 2026 protocol describes the 4 Youth by Youth program, where young people design and spread HIV services, now moving into a sustainment phase. Earlier work showed the youth approach raised uptake of HIV prevention services among Nigerian teenagers and young adults. Outcomes will include how faithfully sites keep delivering the package over time. Iwelunmor expects the results to teach funders how community-grown programs can outlast their launch grants.
pmc-13485667:
Rhodora Therese Gumabao Torres checks whether camera-based motion tracking without body markers can replace the marker gold standard in knee arthritis. Published in 2026, the comparison records 22 participants with mild to moderate disability walking at chosen and fast speeds plus standing up from a chair. Both systems run simultaneously alongside force plates.

Differences between systems stayed small, with angle errors under six degrees and joint center offsets under five centimeters. Agreement was excellent for knee loading impulse at both walking speeds and for the second loading peak at fast walking. Several angle and moment peaks scored good rather than excellent agreement. Markerless tracking promises cheaper, clinic-friendly gait assessment, and these results show which knee measures can already be trusted from video alone.
pmc-13488267:
Winchana Srivilaithon and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of carbon dioxide targets during resuscitation in Thailand. End-tidal carbon dioxide, measured in exhaled breath during chest compressions, mirrors blood flow and predicts whether the heart restarts. Whether pushing compressions to hit a higher target improves outcomes is untested. They will be assigned at random to one of three targets, a standard level, a higher fixed level, or a level tied to a blood gas measure. All care otherwise follows international resuscitation guidance. The main outcome is sustained return of circulation. Results are not yet available, since recruitment defines the planned work.
pmc-13488567:
Nurten Arslan, Aysel Topan, and Meltem Kurtuncu study problem solving and kind, helpful behavior in Turkish adolescents in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. One thousand students aged ten to fourteen from secondary schools in one province capital took part through face-to-face interviews. Validated scales measured problem-solving skill, with subscales for confidence, self-control, and avoidance, alongside a prosociality scale covering sharing, helping, and empathy-driven action.

Stronger overall problem-solving scores went with higher prosocial scores in the reported correlations. Confidence showed the tightest positive link of the subscales. Higher self-control and avoidance scores instead went with lower prosocial scores, a pattern the authors call negative influence. They propose school programs that build problem-solving confidence to support social and emotional growth.
pmc-13489567:
Ebrahimi and colleagues examined what influences screening among newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients in Iran's Isfahan Province, in 2026 public health research drawn from a larger cohort study. The parent study follows new breast and colorectal cancer cases across several centers. This analysis covered patients diagnosed between January 2020 and January 2022, gathering background, lifestyle, and psychological information through questionnaires about each participant.

The study included 78 patients with colon cancer and 69 with rectal cancer in its final sample. Most patients were aged 45 to 75, married, educated, urban residents, and covered by insurance, and most reported normal stress levels. Screening behavior, especially colonoscopy, rose with higher age, which reached statistical significance in the analysis reported. Higher anxiety scores and a past history of colorectal surgery were also linked to more screening. Ebrahimi argues that awareness efforts should target younger and less anxious patients.
pmc-13490467:
Demsie and a large team surveyed 420 adults with type 2 diabetes in northwest Ethiopia about herbal medicine use and compared their long-term blood sugar control. Herbal cures are common in the region, yet their effect on glycated hemoglobin, the three-month sugar average, is rarely measured. Their 2026 study combined structured talks with medical record reviews across clinic patients sampled systematically during the first half of 2025.

Herbal use proved highly common among the patients surveyed, forming part of routine self-care for many. Users showed clearly poorer sugar control than non-users in the adjusted analyses reported. Urban residence, shorter disease duration, and having no other chronic conditions instead predicted favorable control. Talks suggested many patients never disclose herbal use to their doctors. Demsie recommends doctors ask about herbs directly and study which cures help or harm, rather than ignoring a practice patients will continue anyway.
pmc-13490567:
Xu and team taught a reinforcement-learning agent to schedule three kinds of 5G resources at once for mobile broadband users: subcarriers, transmit power levels, and computing capacity. Schedulers must balance speed, energy, and fairness while channels change constantly, and deciding everything jointly explodes the choice space. Their 2026 design splits the decision into synchronized branches, one per resource, and replays the agent's most instructive past experiences first during training.

In massive MIMO simulations the scheduler reached aggregate throughput of about eleven gigabits per second across the system modeled. Energy efficiency hit about fifty-four bits per joule while learning stayed stable across runs. Branching turned an exponentially growing action space into a linearly scaling one, speeding convergence in the reported experiments. Xu presents the framework as a practical scheduler for dense broadband cells.
pmc-13491067:
Julius W. Jaeger and Robert F. Schwabe comment on how support cells direct liver cell behavior in fatty liver disease in a 2026 article. Fatty liver conditions, driven by metabolism, alcohol, or both, affect a large share of the world, and treatments remain few. Liver cells do the metabolic work, yet two neighbor types, vessel-lining endothelial cells and star-shaped stellate cells, constantly instruct them through released factors, organizing the liver into zones along its blood flow.

The commentary centers on new work naming an endothelial receptor, HEG1, as a gatekeeper of fat balance and zonation, tested in gene-deleted mice across three disease diets. A famous growth signal pathway sits at the network's core, fed by both neighbor types. The authors frame support cells as conductors worth targeting.
pmc-13492167:
Julianna R Cresti and Lyle A Simmons review in 2026 the most common copying error in DNA: the wrong sugar. When cells duplicate their genomes, the copying enzymes grab RNA building blocks roughly once every few thousand letters, because those blocks vastly outnumber the DNA versions. Each stray ribonucleotide twists the DNA and, if left in place, invites mutations and instability.

An enzyme family called RNase H spots these errors and starts a repair pathway that cuts the mistake out and patches the strand with proper DNA letters. Repair failures bring mutation buildups, neurological disease, and death before birth in severe cases. The review compares how bacteria, archaea, and complex cells each run this cleanup, highlighting Bacillus subtilis as a window into the bacterial version.
pmc-13492367:
Sevón and colleagues in Finland tested in 2026 thin fat based films that could slow water loss from open reservoirs. Drought is set to worsen with climate change, and stored water leaks away as vapor each day. A film just one molecule thick can curb that loss if it spreads well and holds tight. The team checked four types of fat like compounds, from fatty alcohols to wax esters, alone and in blends.

They used a Langmuir trough, a shallow bath that lets a film be spread and squeezed while gauges track its strength. Some blends beat the best films now in use at blocking vapor. The mix could be tuned: a dash of one fat type fixed spread, while another firmed the layer. The authors say the lab results give a firm base for field grade covers that waste less water.
pmc-13493767:
Geeta S Boora and five colleagues build in 2026 a blood test workflow that sorts the tumor cells shed by oral cancers into their disguises. Circulating tumor cells drive spread, and they travel as plain epithelial cells, shape-shifted mesenchymal cells, or clusters armored with platelets. Sorting blood from thirty-three mouth cancer patients by surface markers, after stripping away ordinary blood cells, resolved all three states.

Spike-in tests proved the method could find a single cancer cell in a milliliter of blood. Seven in ten patients carried detectable circulating cells, sometimes hundreds per milliliter. Platelet-cloaked clusters dominated the catch at roughly five sixths, a population that epithelial-only tests would largely miss. Pure mesenchymal cells were rare. The authors set a positivity threshold and argue that future liquid biopsies must count the cloaked majority.
pmc-13495167:
Chuntao Wu and co-authors examine, in a 2026 analysis, how often two ways of judging migraine treatment success disagree in the same patient. Success is often counted as a set cut in monthly migraine days, yet patients also judge gain by disability and by how hard attacks hit daily life.

The team reworked public patient-level data from 417 people on their first such drug. Just under a third met all three success marks, while about half were split: classed as responders by one measure and not by another. Feeling-based gains without a frequency gain were far more common than the reverse. Gains on the scales moved together only moderately. The authors do not crown a winner; they argue that judging response by diary counts alone misses real relief some patients report.
pmc-13495667:
Avni S Patel and colleagues measure, in a 2026 geochemistry study, how amorphous carbonate minerals change inside water films only nanometers thick. Shells and other natural carbonates often start as shapeless precursors that later crystallize, and damp air alone can drive the shift. The team tracked how much water vapor these calcium and magnesium carbonates soak up across humidity levels, then watched them age for months in humid air.

Water uptake soared once humidity passed roughly four fifths saturation, and the films settled just a few nanometers thick. Over seven months at near-full humidity the minerals kept recrystallizing, growing varied crystal shapes that hint at pockets of different chemistry. Mixed minerals also split into separate calcium and magnesium crystals, proof that ions travel through the films. The authors discuss ripening and diffusion as the engines of the change.
pmc-13499067:
Efrain M Castillo and colleagues ask in 2026 whether receiving a donor heart that already has coronary artery disease harms transplant outcomes, and whether donor age or treatment era changes the answer. Donor hearts are scarce, so centres increasingly accept organs with existing artery disease. Using a national transplant registry, they followed adults who received heart transplants between 2000 and 2025 and compared survival by donor artery status.

Of 21,805 recipients, about one in eleven received a heart with artery disease, and overall that group showed no clear survival disadvantage. Risk did rise with older donors, however, reaching a clear increase by donor age 60 in their model. Era mattered too, since the same donor feature linked to higher death rates only after 2018, when recipients tended to be sicker. The authors urge a fresh review of donor selection rules.
pmc-13499667:
Riya Mukherjee, Ramendra Pati Pandey, and Chung Ming Chang synthesise in 2026 animal evidence on tiny parcels released by stem cells as a cell-free treatment for osteoarthritis, the wear-related joint disease. These extracellular vesicles carry molecular cargo that may protect cartilage without transplanting living cells. Their meta-analysis pooled preclinical studies in living osteoarthritis models and graded reporting quality against current field standards and a bias tool for animal work.

Cartilage damage scores improved after vesicle treatment in studies using human-derived vesicles. The benefit looked larger still in the smaller set using animal-derived vesicles, with statistical checks suggesting missing studies were unlikely to explain the gains. Results varied widely between studies, however, and dose reported by particle count or protein weight failed to predict benefit, exposing weak standardisation. The authors argue that standard dosing, tracking in the body, and cargo checks must come before regulatory approval.
pmc-13499967:
Durga A Jagdale and Sandeep Shinde review in 2026 newer rehabilitation technologies and training methods for sports-related knee injuries, which sideline athletes with pain, weakness, and slow return to play. Their search kept randomised trials published between 2021 and 2026, and twelve studies qualified. The set covered ligament reconstruction, kneecap tendon pain, and other athletic knee problems, with study quality checked against a standard bias tool.

Interventions ranged from nerve-muscle training with external focus cues and heavy slow tendon loading to Nordic hamstring work, balance and jumping drills, and accelerated schedules. Criteria-based progression also featured, where athletes advance by meeting test targets rather than by calendar. Most approaches improved function, strength, balance, pain, and readiness to return compared with usual care alone. Tendon-focused eccentric loading shone for kneecap tendon pain, while criteria-based programmes stood out after ligament surgery.
pmc-13500467:
Zheng Chen and colleagues run in 2026 a prospective nested case-control study of deep vein thrombosis, dangerous leg vein clots, after hip fracture surgery during the hospital stay. Patients admitted with hip fractures between January 2023 and December 2024 were followed. Those who developed clots were matched two-to-one with clot-free patients of the same department, fracture type, and similar surgery timing. The matched set held 72 cases and 144 controls, compared across background, clinical, and laboratory measures.

Three factors stood as independent predictors in adjusted analysis, namely older age, longer delay from injury to surgery, and higher D-dimer, a blood marker of clot breakdown. Each carried a calculated risk threshold. A curious ward observation, sweating heavily enough after fever medicine to soak a gown, linked to clots in simple comparisons yet faded after adjustment, which the authors flag for further study. The thresholds aim to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13502167:
Monika B Dolinska leads a large multi-author team reporting a 2026 drug screen that found an activator of tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin production. Pigment loss disorders, from albinism to acquired pigment loss, carry skin cancer risk, poor vision, and heavy social stigma, yet medicine has tyrosinase blockers in clinics and almost no activators. The team built high-throughput assays around a human tyrosinase construct, confirmed hits in cells using carbon-13 labelled tyrosine tracing, and modelled the chemistry by computer.

The winner was ampyrone, also called 4-aminoantipyrine. It raised the catalytic activity of normal tyrosinase and of a weakened variant, Pro406Leu, that causes a form of albinism. Melanin rose in healthy and albinism-model pigment cells, in mouse pigment cells of another albinism type, and in 3D human skin cultures. The authors nominate ampyrone as a lead compound for therapies that switch pigment production back on.
pmc-13502667:
Miguel A. Medel leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 synthesis of graphene nanoribbons with a fresh edge shape and record length for their class. Nanoribbons are graphene strips whose electronics hinge on width, length, and edge topology, yet undoped versions had no iterative synthesis, so lengths stayed short and many edges unrealized. The team's route repeats a two-step cycle, borylation then a merged Suzuki coupling and cyclodehydrogenation, adding one pyrene-coronene unit per pass.

Iteration delivered a family of ribbons with a new edge topology at unprecedented length for undoped molecular ribbons. The products absorb light and fluoresce efficiently, with absorptivity and brightness on the order of one hundred thousand on the reported molar scale. Charge carriers move through them at a mobility measured at 475, give or take 32, square centimetres per volt-second. Precision at this length lets physicists test predictions about how ribbon properties scale.
pmc-13502867:
Li and colleagues reported a fifteen-year-old girl whose lupus flare was complicated by a virus-triggered disorder, in a 2026 case report. She arrived with ten days of abdominal pain and four days of fever, a facial rash, and swollen neck glands, after years of sun-worsened facial redness. Testing pointed to systemic lupus erythematosus with macrophage activation syndrome, a state in which immune cells attack tissues.

Li's workup found Epstein-Barr virus triggering Evans syndrome. In Evans syndrome the immune system destroys red blood cells and platelets. The combination is rare and is often mistaken for an immune storm called hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Treatment combined antibiotics, an antiviral, steroids, an immune suppressant, acid protection, and immunoglobulin, and after twenty days she had improved and was discharged for follow-up. The authors stress that history, testing, and diagnosis separate this entity from its look-alikes.
pmc-13503867:
Yuta Nakaniida leads a team comparing how the cornea bends in two forms of glaucoma, in a 2026 study. A device called Corvis ST puffs air at the eye and films how the clear front window dents and rebounds. Earlier work found gaps between the two glaucoma types, but the groups also differed in eye length and sex.

The team matched 48 eyes of each type on key traits, then compared twelve measures from the device. Three measures looked higher in the closed-angle group before full statistical checks. After those checks, none of the gaps held up as firm. The authors call the early trends exploratory and say matched designs are key for such work.
pmc-13504567:
Yufei Chen, Yan Zhang, and Wei Wang review a study of harmful byproducts in disinfected desalinated water, in a 2026 commentary. Desalination now supplies drinking water to more than 300 million people. Plant processes strip out most natural matter but leave traces of bromide and iodide, which cleaners can turn into toxic byproducts.

The study under review sampled three large plants in the United Arab Emirates and ran lab disinfection trials. Fine chemical screening found 55 byproducts, some never before reported in desalinated water. Bromine and iodine forms are known to harm cells and DNA more than chlorine forms. The authors stress that spotting which compounds drive the toxicity is key to safer treatment choices.
pmc-13507667:
Shainur Premji leads a ten-author team weighing whether a nurse-led violence support team in Welsh emergency departments is worth its cost, in 2026 work. Such teams meet victims and others hurt by assault and help them tackle risks that could lead to repeat harm. Violence injuries cost the British health service billions each year. The analysis compared the Welsh Violence Prevention Team with standard care for patients aged 11 and older hurt in assaults.

The team built a model that followed patients for ten years after a first assault visit, tracking later emergency visits. Routine Welsh health data supplied the rates and costs behind the model. Outcomes were counted in years of healthy life, and costs were judged from both health service and wider social views. Readers get a framework for deciding whether early support in the emergency room pays off over time.
pmc-13508267:
Yangjia Cao and six co-authors sort stem cells from umbilical cords to find the subgroup best at supporting blood cell growth, in 2026 work. These mesenchymal stem cells are prized for therapy, yet growth in the lab makes batches uneven, which complicates quality control. The team read gene activity cell by cell in more than 78,000 cells and found 14 subgroups. Cells at a middle stage of lab growth performed best overall. One subgroup, labeled C8, stood out for stem-like qualities, blood support, and calming immune effects.

Signal analysis tied that subgroup's strengths to a pathway called NOTCH, with one receptor doing most of the work. Two marker proteins marked the subgroup clearly. Cells rich in both markers supported blood growth and curbed immune activity better than cells low in them. The markers give makers a handle for picking premium cells for treatment batches.
pmc-13508367:
Congai Chen leads a thirteen-author review of how helper T cells cross the blood-brain barrier after a stroke, and how that traffic might be controlled, in 2026 work. The barrier normally shields the brain, letting nutrients in while keeping toxins and most immune cells out. A stroke tears that shield, and helper T cells flood in. Depending on their subtype, these cells can protect tissue or deepen the injury, and they can loosen the barrier further.

The review walks through the entry steps in detail: capture, sticking, and squeezing through the vessel wall. Named adhesion molecules handle each stage, and the authors explain their roles. They also survey immune-suppressing drugs already used in clinics that limit immune cell entry into the brain. The aim is finer control, blocking harmful traffic while sparing helpful cells, as a companion to standard stroke care.
pmc-13508467:
Ozoemena Eje and five co-authors extract an enzyme from papaya fruit peel and test it as a cleaner for dye-polluted water, in 2026 work. Industrial dyes in wastewater threaten health, and enzymes offer a greener cleanup than harsh chemical methods. The team partly purified the enzyme, a peroxidase, from peel waste in two steps. Tests pinned down its size, its best acidity and heat, and how strongly it grabs two test chemicals.

The process concentrated the enzyme twenty-four-fold while keeping about a fifth of the starting activity. Copper and zinc salts switched it on, while several other metals slowed it. The enzyme held nearly all activity after half an hour at mild heat and kept about half after ninety minutes. It stripped color from several dyes, clearing one green dye by up to about nine tenths.
pmc-13509367:
Abugharsa and colleagues compared gene activity in 2026 in leg veins from people with chronic venous insufficiency, a fault where weak vein valves let blood pool in the legs. They focused on three genes in the Wnt pathway, a signaling route that helps control how blood vessel walls grow and repair. No earlier study had checked how these genes work together in diseased vein tissue.

The team tested vein samples from 32 patients and 28 healthy donors with a precise gene-copying method. Each gene alone showed the same activity in sick and healthy veins. What changed was the pairing: two of the genes rose and fell together far more tightly in diseased veins than in healthy ones. That shift hints that faulty teamwork among genes, not single-gene change, may help drive vein wall damage.
pmc-13509567:
Yang Ren and co-authors probe in 2026 how tuberculous meningitis injures the brain's ventricle lining, using a mouse model driven by the BCG vaccine strain. The lining cells, called ependymal cells, keep spinal fluid moving with tiny beating hairs, and their failure adds to this disease's heavy toll.

Gene profiling showed fluid from activated microglia, the brain's immune cells, disturbed far more genes in lining cells than the bacteria alone did, proving microglia amplify the injury. A gene named Hmgcs2 emerged as a core casualty: its loss shortened the cells' hairs and raised cell death. Sodium butyrate, a gut-derived compound, restored that gene, preserved the hairs, and cut cell death, pointing to a possible protective treatment.
pmc-13510667:
Ronja Marquardt, Simon Hundeshagen, Felix Tilsen, Frank Tavassol, and Waldemar Reich report a 2026 case of neuroblastoma spreading to the jaw in an infant, paired with a review of past cases. Neuroblastoma is a common solid cancer of early childhood, yet jaw spread is rare and can mimic tooth or gland infection. The case concerns an eight-month-old girl with swelling beside the left jaw first taken for gland inflammation.

Imaging showed a destructive jaw lesion, and tissue tests confirmed the cancer. Staging found a left adrenal primary tumor, wide bone marrow spread, and a high-risk gene change. She received a high-risk treatment program and reached remission on scans. She then developed severe lung problems and died shortly before a planned next step. Past cases shared jaw swelling, mouth masses, pain, and loose teeth. The authors urge imaging and biopsy for fast-growing jaw swelling in children.
pmc-13510767:
Bronson and colleagues showed in 2026 that a family of helper proteins is required for Musashi proteins to switch on protein production in cells. Musashi proteins bind RNA, the working copies of genes, and guide stem cell growth. They were long seen as switches that turn protein making off, yet at times they turn it on, and no one knew how.

Working with frog eggs, the team removed a helper called ELAVL4 and found that egg ripening stalled and key Musashi target RNAs stayed unused. Adding the helper back fixed the fault. The helpers grip Musashi directly, without RNA in between. The same pairing showed up in mouse and human cells, and removing the human helper in a cell line shut down Musashi-driven activation. The mechanism seems shared across species.
pmc-13511167:
Xue Yan and six co-authors review a helpful bacterium as a probiotic that raises disease resistance in farmed aquatic animals, in 2026 work. Intensive fish and shellfish farming faces frequent outbreaks and heavy antibiotic use. The bacterium reviewed forms hardy spores, fights a wide range of germs, and steadies host immunity, which makes it a candidate green alternative.

The review groups its actions into four routes. Its actions fall into four routes. It releases fatty compounds that attack pathogens directly. It jams the chemical chatter germs use to coordinate attacks. It reshapes gut communities toward helpful kinds, and it switches on the host's built-in defenses and related markers. Trials also link it to cleaner water and better growth. The authors flag open questions on how strains differ, on safety for wild microbe communities, and on thin long-term evidence in farm settings.
pmc-13511467:
Wong, Kendzerska, and Mak reviewed in 2026 a nightly pill for obstructive sleep apnea, a disorder where the throat closes repeatedly during sleep. Air pressure masks are the standard cure but many patients cannot tolerate them. The pill, called AD109, pairs atomoxetine with aroxybutynin. During sleep, nerve drive to the tongue muscle fades and a braking signal rises, so the targeted pair aims to restore throat muscle tone at its root in the brainstem.

Wong reports two large phase 3 trials in adults who refused or could not use air pressure therapy. After 26 weeks, the pill cut the hourly count of breathing pauses and shallow breaths by roughly 44 to 47 percent more than placebo, and night oxygen levels improved. Side effects were mostly dry mouth, poor sleep, nausea, and hesitant urination, with no serious treatment-linked events. Longer data and direct comparison with masks are still needed.
pmc-13511767:
Mirella Vinci and ten co-authors report a gene finding in a boy with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and oppositional defiant disorder, in 2026 work. Both parents were healthy and unrelated. The team read the protein-coding genes of the child and both parents, sorting the found change by standard medical genetics rules and checking it with prediction tools and protein structure models.

The child carried two copies of a rare change in a gene called LNX2, which is active during brain development and helps guide nerve cell growth and connection. The change sits in a region that handles protein partnerships. It was classed as a variant of uncertain significance, since population records list it without any tied condition and the doubled state has been seen only once before. Structure models predicted a local reshaping of chemical bonds. The authors offer the gene as a candidate needing far more proof.
pmc-13514367:
Shun-Xin Deng and six co-authors set out in 2026 to build a quality-checking framework for Wolfiporia extensa, a fungus long used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its underground mass yields four drug parts, each prescribed for different purposes, yet makers have lacked clear markers to tell them apart. The team measured seven triterpenoid compounds, mapped sugar profiles, and recorded colour values for each part.

Distinct chemical fingerprints emerged: one acid peaked in the outer skin part, another in the red part, and a third in the inner white part, which also carried the most sugars. Simple ratios between two compounds, paired with lightness readings, separated the parts reliably. Extracts behaved differently in cell tests, with the white part shielding nerve-like cells from peroxide damage and the skin part protecting a second cell line. Readers gain a practical grading scheme for a classic remedy.
pmc-13514767:
Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 survey of Microbispora, a little studied genus of rare actinomycetes, bacteria famed for making useful natural products. These microbes live in soils, seas, plants, and insects, yet drug hunters have largely passed them by. The survey lists every compound reported from the genus so far.

Eighty-one compounds are now known, spanning quinones, chromones, macrolides, alkaloids, peptides, and other groups of molecules. Chen notes effects ranging from killing microbes and cancer cells to guarding nerves and boosting plant growth. Gene studies predict many more chemical factories in Microbispora genomes that remain untested. The authors argue the genus is a rich, little explored source for new drug hunting.
pmc-13515067:
Nina Dimitrijevic Jovanovic leads a twelve-author team documenting oral health among hospitalised patients treated for heroin-related opioid use disorder in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Ninety-seven inpatients received structured interviews and dental examinations, including standard counts of decayed, missing, and filled teeth plus a hygiene index. They also rated how mouth problems affected daily life on a fourteen-item questionnaire.

The average tooth index showed extensive lifetime decay experience, hygiene scores pointed to poor cleanliness, and quality-of-life scores were markedly impaired, worst in psychological and social domains. Worse mouths meant worse lives in the data: quality-of-life scores climbed steeply alongside tooth damage and with poorer hygiene. Longer heroin use tracked more damage on all fronts. Regression pinned poorer quality of life on accumulated tooth damage, hygiene, and unstable housing.
pmc-13515567:
Ionel-Daniel Nati leads a twelve-author team exploring why HPV vaccination lags in Romania in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Cervical cancer is largely preventable, yet Romania records the European Union's highest death rates from it, and vaccination runs on a passive opt-in basis. The team surveyed adult women at four clinics between December 2025 and March 2026, asking about HPV knowledge, trust in health authorities, vaccine views, and exposure to online falsehoods.

Only about twenty-nine percent of the women were vaccinated. Knowledge about HPV and trust in health authorities each tracked a stronger intention to vaccinate. Leaning on official sources went with seeing the vaccine as safer. Negative online content linked weakly to lower knowledge but did not directly move vaccination intent. Nati's team argues that health literacy and institutional trust are the pillars of acceptance.
pmc-13515767:
Yaqian Liang and seven colleagues characterise three bacteria-eating viruses, called phages, that attack Staphylococcus aureus, in a 2026 study. This germ threatens people, food safety, and livestock, and phages are candidate weapons against drug-resistant strains. The team isolated three phages from sewage and profiled them with electron microscopy, killing assays, and full genome sequencing.

Two phages showed the long-tailed siphovirus shape and one the contractile myovirus shape. The myovirus-like phage killed the widest range of strains and kept killing longest, and it also weathered heat and ultraviolet light best. All three stayed infectious across a broad span of acidity and cool-to-room temperatures. Their genomes ran to roughly forty-four thousand letters, with no antibiotic resistance genes found. Some genes hinted at a dormant lifestyle, though, so the authors say safety checks must go further before any farm or clinic use.
pmc-13516367:
Petar Vasilev and co-authors present two case reports, published in 2026. Both infants came from the same family. Each developed severe hepatitis. The cause was linked to hepatitis B virus. Liver infection from this virus is rare in infancy. It is usually mild there. The siblings fell ill two years apart. Their outcomes differed sharply.

The first infant was a five-month-old girl. She suffered fulminant liver failure. She died before full testing could confirm the cause. Her brother fell ill at four months old. His acute infection was confirmed. Other possible infections were present too. He needed prolonged hospital care. He recovered, and the virus later cleared. Testing relatives found chronic hepatitis B in the mother and grandmother. Hepatitis D virus was also present.
pmc-13517167:
Monica-Daniela Padurariu-Covit and five colleagues track blood counts and survival in people newly diagnosed with HIV in a 2026 cohort study. Low blood counts are common at diagnosis, but their warning value is fuzzy. The team reviewed patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2024 at one centre, comparing blood, immune, viral, and inflammation measures at entry and after twelve months of therapy.

Most arrived with advanced disease and deep immune suppression. Anaemia was the commonest problem and travelled with lower defender-cell counts, higher virus levels, and worse survival. High inflammation readings and shortages across several blood lines also spelled trouble. Patients short in two or more lines died significantly more often, a pattern the authors read as a marker of body-wide decline. Counts and immunity recovered markedly after a year of treatment. The team proposes multi-line shortages as a cheap early risk flag.
pmc-13518867:
Shuyi Sun and a large team report in 2026 an optical sensor method that adds up wireless data without demanding tight timing between senders. Internet of Things networks drown in data, and over-the-air computation normally requires signals to arrive in lockstep, which costs overhead. Their sensors trap light-generated charges in defects, holding a fading memory of incoming pulses.

Within one communication window, the system merged signals offset by up to 120 percent of the pulse length, with errors below 1.5 percent on a normalized measure. Pulsed low-frequency readout kept energy use low. A distributed temperature prediction test converged faster with a simpler setup, hinting at practical edge sensing networks.
pmc-13518967:
Burke J Minsley leads a nine-author team mapping salty groundwater hidden beneath coastal Louisiana in 2026 with airborne electromagnetic surveys. Managers usually blame modern seawater creeping inland, yet geology can strand ancient salt underground. Their surveys reveal a buried pattern spanning more than 10,000 square kilometers.

The three-dimensional salinity pattern mirrors aquifers around modern Delaware Bay, fingerprinting a drowned river valley from the last ice age. As post-glacial seas rose, the Mississippi's incised valley flooded into a paleo-estuary, trapping seawater that still lingers under the delta plain. Minsley and colleagues offer the finding as a framework for spotting legacy salt along other coastlines, where it can threaten wells.
pmc-13519867:
Pavithra R and co-authors recount in this 2026 case a painless tearing of the aorta in a thirty-four year old man, a presentation that hides a deadly emergency. Aortic dissection usually announces itself with severe tearing chest pain, but about one case in ten has none.

The man arrived with sudden weakness on his left side, slurred speech, and fading consciousness, looking like a stroke. Scans revealed a dissection running from the top of the aorta down into the abdomen and into a neck artery, which had caused his stroke. Clot-busting treatment was withheld because it is forbidden in dissection. The authors urge doctors to consider this diagnosis in young stroke patients, since fast imaging decides the outcome.
pmc-13520167:
Zhu and colleagues listen to dialysis patients themselves describe the ethical knots of life on a blood-filtering machine, a perspective research usually takes from clinicians instead. Their 2026 study interviewed 35 haemodialysis patients at four hospitals of traditional Chinese medicine in Shandong Province. It organised the dilemmas using ecological systems theory, which sorts influences from the personal up to the societal.

Three levels of dilemma emerged, broken into twelve subthemes. Personal struggles sat at the centre. Clashes and obligations among family, fellow patients, and care providers formed the middle ring. Policy, cultural, and community pressures formed the outer ring. Crucially, the levels feed each other, so a funding policy can become a family argument that becomes a patient's private guilt. The resulting layered model is the paper's contribution: a map showing ethics committees and managers where an intervention at one level might relieve pressure at another.
pmc-13520367:
Juanjuan Guo and colleagues study in 2026 how heat harms flower bud formation in red raspberry and whether spraying salicylic acid can ease the damage. The double-season variety Polka was tracked through eight bud stages lasting about 28 days.

Heat at the pollen mother cell stage disrupted the nourishing tapetum layer, leading to faulty pollen and malformed male flower parts. Growth hormones fell while a stress hormone rose, upsetting balance. Salicylic acid at the tested dose eased anther damage and steadied hormone levels, according to the opening summary. Growers facing hotter summers gain a candidate spray treatment with a stated dose and timing logic.
pmc-13521467:
Ana G. Del Hierro and colleagues build in 2026 software sensors that infer yeast biomass in real time during dense fermentations, where lab weighing and diluted optical checks are too slow for control. Online near-infrared probes give continuous signals, yet scattering bends those signals at high density.

Nineteen fed-batch runs across three industrial yeast species trained fourteen candidate conversion models. Careful leave-one-batch-out checking prevented leakage between related runs. Chosen simple models predicted dry weight well across species, with noisier results for the diluted optical target. Paired full and pocket-calculator versions suit both automated plants and manual operations.
pmc-13522567:
Giorgia Del Missier, Kiyan Shabestary, and Rodrigo Ledesma-Amaro present a tool paper, published in 2026. It introduces WASP, a pipeline for working out protein functions. WASP uses computed three-dimensional shapes. It does not rely on gene sequences alone. AlphaFold now supplies shapes for most proteins. Comparing shapes can fill label gaps. Matching sequences leaves those gaps even in well-studied species.

In tests, known labels were hidden on purpose. WASP recovered them better than leading sequence-based tools. It labelled a fifth to a third of proteins with no known function. This held across twenty species of practical interest. The authors show its use in curating genome-scale metabolic models for biotechnology.
pmc-13522867:
Ameena M Khan Sullivan and colleagues test how simulated night shifts alter responses to meals in a 2026 laboratory study. Nine healthy young adults who did not normally work shifts completed one day shift and then two night shifts, with sleep and meals delayed by ten hours. Four identical meals were eaten per shift, and blood glucose, insulin, and fats were measured hourly alongside hunger ratings.

Lipid rhythms shifted with the new schedule and flattened noticeably. Night shifts raised glucose and insulin responses after meals, while insulin failed to fully compensate, signaling lower glucose tolerance. Time of day mattered in both schedules, with early evening meals producing the highest glucose responses. The authors propose mistimed eating as one route by which shift work raises metabolic disease risk.
pmc-13523267:
Yujie Shi, Ye Jin, and Hui Yu investigate a small RNA as a marker for newborn breathing disease in a 2026 study. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a major cause of illness and death, especially in preterm infants. Blood and amniotic fluid from thirty-five affected newborns and thirty-five healthy controls were compared for levels of one microRNA, and cell experiments tested its effect on lung surface cells.

The microRNA was elevated in both blood and amniotic fluid of affected newborns, and each fluid distinguished cases from controls with good accuracy. Blocking the microRNA in lung cells improved cell survival and raised output of a key surfactant protein, whose gene it directly regulates. The authors suggest the molecule participates in fetal lung development and could serve as a biomarker for the syndrome.
pmc-13523367:
Patricia González-Berdullas leads a team validating a drug measurement method using saliva and finger-prick blood in a 2026 study. Monitoring the antibiotic linezolid helps balance benefit against toxicity, yet standard monitoring needs venous blood. The new laboratory method measured the drug and its two main breakdown products in oral fluid and in capillary blood collected by a volumetric microsampling device, following international validation guidelines.

The assay performed within accepted accuracy and precision limits across all sample types. In paired specimens from thirty-five treated patients, drug levels in both new sample types tracked plasma levels strongly. Breakdown products behaved less cleanly: they were biased in capillary blood, needing correction factors, and rarely detectable in oral fluid. The authors support the new sampling routes for the parent drug.
pmc-13523467:
Muhammed M. Faiz and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two drugs added to a scalp nerve block for awake brain surgery. Blocking scalp nerves eases pain during awake craniotomy, a procedure where the patient stays conscious, yet a local anesthetic alone wears off quickly. Dexmedetomidine and ketamine were tested as additives to ropivacaine.

Forty-six adults were randomized evenly between the two mixtures. Patients given ketamine waited longer before asking for rescue pain relief, roughly 18.7 hours against 14.7 hours, and reported lower pain scores at several later time points. They also used less rescue medicine. Breathing depression was more common with dexmedetomidine, while that drug better blunted heart rate and blood pressure responses during surgery. The authors call for larger multicenter trials to settle the best choice.
pmc-13525167:
Ong and colleagues tested in 2026 whether swinging reduces academic stress in nursing students. Swinging stimulates the vestibular system, the inner-ear balance sense, and is linked to relaxation. The quasi-experimental study enrolled seventy-eight student nurses in Baguio City, split into swinging and control groups. Stress was measured with a standard academic stress scale, and the team varied swinging duration and body position.

The swinging group showed a significant drop in academic stress compared with controls. How long students swung, and in what position, changed how much stress fell. They recommend building vestibular stimulation into nursing education. That includes campus spaces designed for swinging breaks. The study adds a low-cost, non-drug option to the student stress toolkit, tested across year levels of the nursing programme.
pmc-13525667:
Shiqiong Huang and colleagues run a 2026 retrospective study of adverse drug reactions among hospitalized patients with HIV and AIDS in China, using a variable-selection regression method to hunt for risk factors. Such reactions add heavily to hospital burden in this population. Suspected reactions were judged for causality with an international monitoring system.

Among 918 patients, 210 experienced a reaction, an incidence of 22.88 percent. Blood and lymphatic disorders were the commonest manifestation class. Antibacterial drugs caused the largest share, followed closely by antivirals. The selection model singled out one clear factor, the number of medications given during hospitalization, which raised the odds of a reaction substantially. The authors propose the count as a simple flag for closer monitoring and regimen review.
pmc-13525967:
Salvatore Alessio Angileri leads a large team in a 2026 review of interventional radiology for slipped discs, a common cause of spinal pain and nerve pain. Most patients recover with rest and basic care, yet lasting cases need options between drugs and open surgery. Needle techniques guided by imaging fill that middle step.

A structured search of PubMed and Scopus covered mechanical, thermal, chemical, and healing methods for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar slipped discs. Noted results included pain relief, recovery, complications, and repeat procedures. Findings suggest needle procedures can give real short- and medium-term gains in chosen patients whose symptoms match imaging, with less cutting and faster recovery in skilled hands. The authors note the findings are mostly observational and call for trials across many centers with uniform reporting.
pmc-13528067:
Yongyi Pan and eleven colleagues test a plant compound against obesity-linked male infertility in a 2026 mouse study. Puerarin comes from the kudzu plant root. Mice on a high-fat diet gained weight and made less testosterone. Their sperm counts and movement fell. The team combined gene scans with protein hunting to find the compound's target.

Puerarin trimmed weight gain and fat, and it cleaned up blood lipids. Testes kept a healthier shape, and testosterone, count, and motility rose. The compound latched onto a helper protein called GRP78. That grip steadied StAR, a protein that starts testosterone making. Blocking GRP78 in cells undid the benefit. The authors name the GRP78 to StAR route as the mechanism. Human testing would be a distant next step.
pmc-13528167:
Csilla Kurdi and nine colleagues compare amino acid patterns in egg follicle fluid across three infertility-linked conditions in a 2026 study. The fluid bathes the egg and mirrors body metabolism. Samples totaled 171 from IVF patients. Groups covered insulin resistance, endometriosis, and thyroid trouble. Twenty amino acids were measured with precise lab methods.

Overall patterns looked alike across groups. Disease still left a modest but real fingerprint. Insulin resistance came with lower glycine and arginine. Thyroid trouble came with lower histidine, tryptophan, and lysine. Endometriosis stood out for higher histidine. The shifts held after accounting for body weight. Single amino acids sorted the groups poorly. The authors favor whole-pattern readouts. They say the follicle senses whole-body metabolic health in a quiet, spread-out way.
pmc-13529867:
Shimosato and Goyama review a rare but instructive form of acute myeloid leukaemia driven by rearrangements of the NPM1 gene. The common NPM1 story is a small mutation found in up to two fifths of adult cases, with well-mapped behaviour. Rearrangements, where NPM1 fuses with partners such as MLF1 or RARA, are far rarer and were long neglected. Their 2026 synthesis gathers the emerging evidence on how these fusions look clinically and how they cause disease.

Reassuringly for drug developers, the fusions work through the same machinery as the common mutation. The NPM1 protein ends up stranded in the cytoplasm, partners with the export protein XPO1, and holds developmental HOX genes switched on, driving the leukaemia. Clinically, rearranged cases skew younger and may carry a worse outlook, though the authors flag the small numbers behind that claim.
pmc-13530267:
Mohammad Khorsandi and colleagues test in 2026 green solvents that could dissolve a poorly soluble drug ingredient called 4-hydroxycoumarin. Three acidic deep eutectic solvents, each built from choline chloride plus a simple acid, competed against plain water. Standard shaking-flask measurements spanned a small temperature range.

The propionic acid version lifted solubility more than five hundredfold over water, beating the acetic and lactic versions. Math models fit the data closely, and heating analysis showed dissolving absorbs heat. Cell tests on colon cancer cells found moderate killing power that varied with solvent mix, supporting early drug formulation work.
pmc-13531667:
Silva-Ramos and co-authors combed fleas from rural dogs across 24 municipalities of Cundinamarca, Colombia. They checked them for two bacterial genera that fleas carry to people: Rickettsia, which causes spotted fevers, and Bartonella, behind cat-scratch disease and other illnesses. Colombian data on dog fleas were thin. Their 2026 field study examined 116 dogs in 2019 and 2020, identified the fleas, pooled them, and screened the pools with sensitive DNA tests, following up positives for species identification.

About two fifths of dogs carried fleas, and nearly all the fleas were the cat flea species that happily bites dogs and humans alike. Rickettsia turned up in the large majority of pools, mostly Rickettsia asembonensis with some Rickettsia felis. Bartonella appeared in over a quarter of pools, though sequencing could not pin its species down.
pmc-13531867:
Hongchun Li and colleagues show in 2026 that silencing the Tau protein protects young mice from lasting thinking damage after newborn sepsis. Infection in the first month of life often leaves survivors with cognitive harm into adolescence. Tau, a nerve fiber protein, was the suspect mediator in this mouse work.

Turning Tau down softened memory loss after early inflammation. Brain checks showed reshaped branching in a memory region and renewed birth of nerve cells there in adulthood. The authors nominate Tau as a treatment target for sepsis-related brain injury, with structure and cell renewal as the routes.
pmc-13531967:
Jiangyuan Liu, Johan H Gibcus, and Job Dekker present in 2026 a workflow that calls DNA loops jointly across related chromosome-folding datasets. Loop calls from Hi-C maps vary wildly between similar samples, muddying comparisons. Their tool, UnionLoops, first builds one shared candidate set, then applies uniform filtering and scores support sample by sample.

Joint calling found more shared loops, trimmed spurious one-off calls, and matched independent protein occupancy evidence better than single-sample routes. Cleaner loop maps sharpen reading of how genome folding shifts across conditions, a basic need for studies of development and disease across sample groups.
pmc-13532867:
Yanqiu Wang and colleagues tested what happens while focused ultrasound is beamed at the brain's movement area, rather than after it ends. They measured how strongly one side of the brain reins in the other, a balance key to smooth movement.

Fifteen healthy volunteers received ultrasound to one movement area while magnetic pulses measured the cross-brain braking at two time gaps. Ultrasound weakened the long-gap braking from the treated side to the opposite side during the beaming. The short-gap braking stayed unchanged, and the opposite side's own excitability did not shift either. Wang reads this as ultrasound tuning a complex circuit, and offers it as a probe of how the two brain halves interact.
pmc-13534667:
Mengyue Wei and colleagues optimise in 2026 an ethanol extract of Litsea cubeba fruit and probe how it kills Staphylococcus aureus. The plant has a long history as a spice and folk remedy, and natural germ killers are sought for food and drug use. Response surface methods tuned heat, time, and liquid ratio for the best yield.

Best settings gave a high antibacterial rate, and chemical scans found 20 compounds led by fatty acids. The extract killed germs at low doses and broke their walls and membranes, leaking cell contents. The work supports the fruit as a natural antibacterial source.
pmc-13534767:
Mónika Koós and a large global team develop in 2026 the Paraphilic Disorders Short Screen, a brief tool aligned with current ICD-11 rules. No reliable screen existed for these disorders under the new guidance. Data came from 82,243 adults across 42 countries in 26 languages, with expert-led item design.

The screen covers seven paraphilias in 21 items, with cut scores set per guidance. Voyeuristic interest was most common, and groups meeting disorder cut-offs showed worse depression and anxiety than others. Clinicians and researchers gain a validated way to flag at-risk people across cultures.
pmc-13536267:
Michael Rouse, Yumna Kaleem, and Justin M Yeung discuss in 2026 how artificial intelligence can lower barriers to research for surgical trainees. Research is now core to training, yet cost, time, thin mentoring, and ethics delays block many juniors. Their view maps AI help across each research stage.

Tools can aid idea shaping, literature search, protocol drafting, ethics forms in plain language, data extraction, and analysis code. The authors stress that AI should support, not replace, core skills like design judgement and critical reading. Risks and limits must stay in view for safe trainee use.
pmc-13536767:
Laura Barberán-Bernardos, Miguel Ángel Ariza-Gracia, and David P Piñero compare two eye imaging devices in a 2026 agreement study. Both devices measure front eye shape, corneal thickness, and chamber size used in diagnosis and surgical planning. Fifty-five healthy eyes were measured with each device by the same examiner. Paired tests and agreement plots assessed whether readings could be swapped in practice.

Front corneal curvature agreed well enough for shared use, with no clear average gap. Other measures differed clearly, including back curvature, chamber depth, thickness, and chamber angle, with one device tending toward deeper chambers and narrower angles. Thickness agreement ranges were wide. The authors warn against swapping devices freely for thickness checks before lens surgery or for chamber measures guiding implant choices.
pmc-13536867:
Zichun Wang and colleagues track care delays for migrant tuberculosis patients in suburban Shanghai in a 2026 review of cases from 2015 to 2024. Two delays matter, the wait before a patient first seeks care and the wait before the system confirms diagnosis. Records held 3,178 lung tuberculosis cases, split almost evenly between locals and migrants in Fengxian District. Trends and risk factors for each delay were compared.

Migrants waited fewer days before seeking care than locals, yet waited longer for confirmed diagnosis. The first wait among migrants rose steadily from 2017 onward. Female sex, middle age, and first seeking care outside the district raised the first wait, while test results and care location shaped the second wait. The authors urge better cross-district coordination and stronger local lab testing.
pmc-13538567:
Abdalla Elbialy presents a framework that sharpens spot-based tissue gene maps to single-cell detail without outside references in a 2026 study. Spot platforms average several cells per reading, while rival sharpening tools need reference data or fresh training per dataset. The morphology-guided system works training-free, validated on one colon cancer sample measured across four platforms, including a true single-cell reference.

On the finest spot input, the system matched the single-cell reference more closely than any rival tested. Across six distribution checks on a shared gene panel, its variants led most metrics with no rival winning any. Trained rivals merely tracked raw readings on matched regions. The authors highlight per-cell records with coordinates as output no raw spot reading can supply.
pmc-13540867:
Weishan Lin leads a 2026 study explaining part of the bone fragility seen in spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that wastes muscle and leaves many patients with osteoporosis. Muscle talks to bone partly through tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, and patient muscle samples hinted that this traffic was disturbed.

Patients and model mice both showed muscle releasing far fewer vesicles. Those vesicles, when supplied in adequate doses, encouraged bone-forming cells and restrained bone-eating cells just as well as vesicles from healthy muscle, and replenishing them rescued bone in the mice. The chain ran from the missing SMN protein down to a release protein, SNAP23, whose fall throttled vesicle secretion.
pmc-13540967:
Laura L Jelliffe-Pawlowski leads a 2026 California study building an index of preterm birth risk that only counts risk factors medicine can actually act on. Preterm birth is the leading killer of young children, and proven interventions for many maternal conditions reach fewer than half of eligible women.

Linked records for 1.9 million singleton births between 2016 and 2020 were split into training and testing sets. Eighteen candidate risks with evidence-based responses, spanning clinical, behavioural, and social domains, fed the index. Conditions such as chronic hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, asthma, and mental illness anchor the list. The study examines how well the index flags risk through pregnancy and which factors combine most dangerously.
pmc-13542067:
Hilal Kalkan and seven colleagues monitor, in a 2026 field study, whether pole vaulters keep their run-up speed across repeated attempts as effort builds inside the body. Approach speed in the final metres is the main mechanical driver of jump height, so any fade matters to coaches.

Eleven competitive vaulters, four women and seven men, made four jumps twenty centimetres below their personal bests with short rests. Blood lactate and heart rate stayed statistically flat between attempts, while felt exertion rose only late in the set. Run-up speed and every step measure held steady throughout. The authors conclude that this submaximal protocol preserves speed even as internal signals climb unevenly.
pmc-13543467:
Xueqin Shi and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective study building a metabolic risk profile for children and adolescents with obesity, combining hormone measures with common gene variants. Records from 2021 to 2025 supplied 429 young patients, whose clinical, blood, and endocrine data were reviewed alongside genotyping at three obesity-linked sites in the FTO, MC4R, and LEPR genes. Metabolic syndrome was judged by paediatric criteria, and models tested which factors predicted it.

Nearly forty-four percent met the syndrome definition. Insulin resistance was widespread even before puberty and was strongly tied to the syndrome. Higher leptin, a fat-derived hormone, raised risk, while higher adiponectin lowered it. Carrying risk versions of FTO or MC4R each independently predicted the syndrome as well. A combined hormone-and-gene model separated cases reasonably well, suggesting clinics could flag high-risk children with obesity earlier than symptoms alone allow.
pmc-13544967:
Murad-Kassam and colleagues review hospital experiences of older adults with dementia from ethno-racial communities in this 2026 scoping review. Dementia care in hospital is often complicated by racism, stigma, staff bias, and a lack of culturally and linguistically suitable services. Searching six databases, the team gathered studies about patients aged 60 and over and their caregivers, with no limits on year or country.

Only eleven studies qualified from an initial 3,395 records, itself a sign of how thin the evidence is. The findings grouped into five areas. They covered factors before admission and care during the stay. Discharge and readmission formed another area. So did gaps in culturally tailored practices and challenges faced by caregivers. The authors describe a persistent failure to provide culturally focused dementia care across the whole hospital journey and call for research following families through it.
pmc-13545067:
Manfredi and co-authors review how speech and language break down across childhood psychiatric disorders, in this 2026 article. They also review what brain imaging reveals about why. Language supports social ties. So its breakdown in autism, schizophrenia, ADHD, and depression carries consequences far beyond vocabulary. Yet the neurobiology in young people remains patchily mapped.

The authors survey systematic reviews and first studies. The studies used EEG, MRI, and near-infrared spectroscopy. Every condition looked at shows both altered speech function and matching brain changes. The evidence base is lopsided, though. Autism leads the child literature. Schizophrenia and depression research mostly recruited adults. Those fields simply assumed developmental continuity. The central message is a gap statement. The neural causes of the alteration in developing psychiatric populations are largely not studied. They deserve dedicated child and adolescent imaging work.
pmc-13545567:
Tingting Jiang and colleagues described in 2026 a difficult case of chyle fluid collecting around the lung after a double lung transplant. The patient, a 31-year-old woman with a rare lung disease, developed the collection 39 days after surgery. An earlier attempt to seal the space instead left a honeycomb of separate pockets that ordinary drains could not reach.

Dissolving the pocket walls with a clot-breaking drug is risky so soon after transplant, since bleeding could damage delicate surgical joins. The team used contrast-enhanced ultrasound to tell bloodless fibers from living tissue, then injected a low dose of urokinase only where it was safe. Drainage and repeat sealing followed, the lung re-expanded fully, and the problem did not return.
pmc-13546267:
Yang Zhi and co-authors reviewed in 2026 what is known about the Notch1 signaling pathway in diabetic foot. In this serious complication, nerve damage, poor circulation, and slow healing can lead to amputation. Notch1 passes messages between neighboring cells and helps govern blood vessel growth, inflammation, and cell fate. Evidence gathered in the review links faulty Notch1 activity to several of the processes that keep diabetic foot wounds open.

The authors walk through the pathway's roles in vessel formation, immune response, nerve injury, and tissue repair, then survey treatments that try to adjust its activity. Their aim is to give researchers a clearer map of the mechanism and to point toward targeted therapies for ulcers that resist standard care.
pmc-13547367:
Hui Li and colleagues traced in 2026 a chain of molecular switches that slows prostate cancer when one long non-coding RNA is present. Both that RNA, LINC00222, and a protective gene it controls, FOXO3, run low in prostate tumors. Raising FOXO3 in cancer cells shifted them toward a less mobile state and made them more sensitive to the chemotherapy drug docetaxel.

The RNA works by soaking up a small regulatory molecule that would otherwise silence FOXO3. Freed FOXO3 then raises a partner protein that reins in the beta-catenin growth pathway. Raising LINC00222 in cells slowed growth and spread while raising cell death, and animal experiments confirmed the braking effect. The authors present the chain as a candidate route for new treatments.
pmc-13548067:
Marco Tozzi and colleagues showed that brown fat cells release the energy molecule ATP when adrenaline-like signals switch them into heat-making mode. The released ATP then amplifies the very signals that freed it. Brown fat burns fuel to produce heat in the cold. Working with cultured brown fat cells and mouse tissue, the team tracked ATP release in real time and measured oxygen use, sugar breakdown, and fat splitting.

Release ran through a channel protein called pannexin-1 under control of the cell's main adrenaline relay. Glucose raised release while insulin trimmed it. Blocking the channel or mopping up outside ATP weakened the fat-burning responses, and both ATP and adrenaline raised calcium signals on different schedules. Cold exposure reshaped the tissue's ATP receptor mix.
pmc-13548467:
Alexandre Bourdiol and a French study group laid out in 2026 the DEXA-BURN trial protocol, testing whether an early course of the steroid dexamethasone can cut major complications after severe burns. Badly burned patients suffer intense, lasting inflammation with frequent lung and kidney failure, yet no large trial has tested steroids in this group. The double-blind trial runs in ten French intensive care units.

Adults with burns over at least a fifth of the body who arrive within a day and need a ventilator will be randomized to five days of intravenous dexamethasone or a placebo. The main measure combines serious lung injury and kidney injury within 28 days, with deaths at 90 days tested next in a fixed sequence. Enrollment targets 478 patients, and side effects of steroids are tracked closely.
pmc-13548567:
Wenfan Gao and colleagues examine what drives blood levels of olanzapine, a widely used schizophrenia medicine, in a 2026 retrospective study of 104 Chinese patients. The drug's levels vary greatly between people, and it often disturbs metabolism. After four weeks of treatment, the team compared drug concentrations and dose-adjusted levels across sex, age, and body mass groups, then checked links with metabolic measures and inflammatory proteins.

Women carried higher drug levels and higher dose-adjusted levels than men. Heavier body mass went with lower raw levels, while age showed no clear effect. Metabolic measures did not track with drug levels during this short window. Higher drug levels instead went with lower levels of three inflammatory signals, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. The authors suggest sex and body size deserve attention when dosing, and that inflammation links merit longer study.
pmc-13550467:
Li and colleagues re-sequenced in 2026 the genomes of 984 soybean lines to map structural variations, large DNA changes such as insertions and deletions, and link them to crop traits. Such variants shape many traits but were poorly charted in soybean. Combining their 940 new sequences with public data, the team built a graph-based genome, a reference that holds many variant paths at once, to catch changes a single reference misses.

Li catalogued over 600,000 structural variants plus tens of thousands of presence-absence changes that affect gene activity widely. The variants proved a core force in soybean domestication and later breeding gains. Trait mapping pinned down concrete cases: inserted jumping genes that alter seed coat colour, insertions in a pigment gene that change flower colour, and a deletion that enlarges seeds. The map gives breeders a resource for faster, targeted crop improvement.
pmc-13551767:
Betül Esra Çevik and Hümeyra Hançer Tok published a 2026 randomized trial of fall-prevention education for older adults in Türkiye. Sixty-six adults attending a family health center in Central Anatolia, all classed high risk on a standard fall scale, joined the pretest-posttest study. The intervention group received two interactive sessions with presentations and discussion, while controls received only an information brochure.

Safe fall behavior scores rose significantly in the taught group and did not move in the brochure group in the reported comparisons. Post-test scores also separated the groups in favor of teaching. The authors conclude that passive leaflets do not change behavior, while nurse-led interactive education does, a practical point for clinics serving high-risk older adults.
pmc-13551967:
Ana R. Silverstein and thirteen colleagues reported in 2026 on a mitochondrial DNA variant tied to immune differences between the sexes. Scanning mitochondrial variants against traits in a large United States aging study flagged one variant linked to sex-specific immune composition. Because the mitochondrial genome was recently re-annotated to include tiny protein-coding segments, the team could map that variant to a small gene encoding a previously unknown microprotein.

They named the microprotein MASL and confirmed the variant's immune links in two large cohorts using phenome-wide scans. A targeted sequencing method showed sex differences in gene expression near the variant, and blood levels of MASL itself differed by sex in the reported measurements. Synthesized MASL also acted differently in male and female mice, opening a new corner of mitochondrial biology.
pmc-13553667:
Amanda Liesegang, Andy Wu, Alexander Heriot, and Glen Guerra review the rarer inherited conditions that fill the colon with polyps.
